pKa.desc: The negative common logarithm of the acid dissociation constant Ka. The smaller it is, the stronger the acid. Typical values: carboxylic acids about 4–5, phenol about 10, water 15.7, alcohols about 16.

about.h: What pKa means and how to read it
about.p: pKa is the negative common logarithm of the acid dissociation constant Ka (pKa = −log Ka), and it expresses how strongly an acid HA tends to release H⁺ in water and become A⁻. The larger Ka, the stronger the acid and the smaller the pKa. A difference of 1 in pKa means a tenfold difference in Ka, so acetic acid at pKa 4.8 is about 10¹¹ times stronger than ethanol at pKa 16. Values change with temperature and solvent, so comparisons normally use values in water at 25 °C. For acids too weak or too strong to measure in water, values in other solvents such as DMSO or extrapolated values are used.

Typical values used in organic chemistry are about 4–5 for carboxylic acids (acetic acid 4.76, benzoic acid 4.2), about 10 for phenol, about 16 for alcohols, 15.7 for water, about 9–11 for ammonium ions (9.25 for NH4⁺) and about 25 for terminal alkynes. Among strong acids, hydrogen chloride is about −7 and the first dissociation of sulfuric acid about −3, and protonated carbonyl compounds also have negative values. Alkane C−H bonds, by contrast, are about 50 and show almost no acidity. With these values you can quickly judge whether the base used in a reaction can deprotonate the substrate.

The equilibrium constant of the acid–base reaction HA + B⁻ ⇌ A⁻ + HB is K = 10^(pKa(HB) − pKa(HA)), and the equilibrium lies toward forming the weaker acid, the one with the larger pKa. For example, for acetic acid (4.76) and ammonia (NH4⁺ 9.25), K is about 3×10⁴ and the equilibrium lies far to the right, while for phenol (10.0) and bicarbonate ion (H2CO3 6.4), K is small, about 2.5×10⁻⁴, and they hardly react. This reasoning applies directly to separating acidic, neutral and basic substances by extraction and to choosing bases for synthesis.

The proportions of the neutral and ionized forms of a weak acid or weak base are set by the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]). When the pH equals the pKa, the two are half and half; for a weak acid, at a pH one unit above the pKa the ionized form is about 91%, and two units above, about 99%. The neutral form is thought to cross lipid membranes more readily and the ionized form to dissolve in water more readily, so the absorption, distribution and solubility of drugs, and even how strongly they are retained in liquid chromatography, are considered in terms of the relationship between pKa and the surrounding pH.

faq.q: Is a smaller pKa a stronger acid?
faq.a: Yes. Because pKa = −log Ka, the larger Ka (the more readily the acid dissociates), the smaller the pKa. A pKa one unit smaller means the acid is ten times stronger in terms of Ka.

faq.q: Can base strength also be expressed with pKa?
faq.a: Base strength is generally expressed by the pKa of the conjugate acid. The larger the conjugate acid's pKa, the stronger the base; for example, ammonia (pKa of NH4⁺ 9.25) is a stronger base than aniline (pKa of the anilinium ion about 4.6).

faq.q: What is the difference between pKa and pH?
faq.a: pKa is a constant characteristic of a particular acid, while pH expresses the hydrogen-ion activity of a solution. When the pH of a solution equals the pKa of the acid, the acid is exactly half in its neutral form and half as the ionized conjugate base.

混成軌道.desc: Equivalent orbitals formed by mixing an atom's s and p orbitals. sp³ gives a tetrahedral shape (about 109.5°), sp² trigonal planar (120°) and sp linear (180°).

about.p: Carbon's valence electrons are in the 2s orbital and three 2p orbitals, but using these as they are cannot explain why the four C−H bonds of methane are equivalent and point toward the corners of a tetrahedron. The idea of mixing s and p orbitals to make new orbitals of matching shape and energy (hybrid orbitals) was put forward by Pauling in 1931. Hybrid orbitals point in the directions of bonds, so they help in understanding molecular shapes and bond angles intuitively. To treat the energies and electron distribution of molecules quantitatively, on the other hand, molecular orbital theory is used.

about.h: Identifying the type and bond angles
about.p: The hybridization type can be judged from the sum of the number of atoms bonded to the atom and the number of lone pairs. Four means sp³ (tetrahedral, about 109.5°), three sp² (trigonal planar, 120°) and two sp (linear, 180°). The nitrogen of ammonia and the oxygen of water are also close to sp³, and because lone pairs push on the bonds, their bond angles are smaller than the tetrahedral angle, about 107° and about 104.5° respectively. In sp² and sp atoms, the p orbitals not used in hybridization form π bonds.

The fraction of s orbital in a hybrid orbital (s character) is 25% for sp³, 33% for sp² and 50% for sp. The higher the s character, the closer the electrons are held to the nucleus, so bonds are shorter and the carbon is more electronegative. C−C bond lengths are about 0.154 nm for a single bond, about 0.134 nm for a double bond and about 0.120 nm for a triple bond. The acidity of C−H bonds also changes greatly with s character: the pKa is about 50 for ethane, about 44 for ethylene and about 25 for acetylene, and terminal alkynes can be deprotonated with strong bases.

Hybrid orbitals are a model for explaining molecular shape and do not directly represent real orbitals. In the photoelectron spectrum of methane, the ionization energies of the valence electrons split into two values rather than four equal ones, in line with molecular orbital predictions. Atoms involved in resonance also change hybridization. The nitrogens of amides, aniline and pyrrole use their lone pair in the π system and adopt a planar shape close to sp². The idea of explaining hypervalent compounds with hybrids involving d orbitals is now rarely used.

faq.q: How do you identify the type of hybridization?
faq.a: Add the number of bonded atoms and the number of lone pairs. Four means sp³, three sp² and two sp. A double or triple bond counts as one partner atom.

faq.q: Do nitrogen and oxygen also form hybrid orbitals?
faq.a: Yes. The nitrogen of ammonia and the oxygen of water are close to sp³, and their lone pairs also occupy hybrid orbitals. The nitrogen of pyridine is sp², with its lone pair in the plane of the ring.

faq.q: What is the difference between hybrid orbitals and molecular orbitals?
faq.a: Hybrid orbitals are an idea that mixes the orbitals of one atom to express the directions of bonds. Molecular orbitals spread over the whole molecule and explain electron energies and spectroscopic results more accurately.

共鳴.desc: The idea of representing a real molecule as a superposition of several structures (resonance structures) that differ only in the arrangement of electrons. Molecules and ions with delocalized charge or π electrons are stabilized.

about.p: Resonance represents a molecule or ion whose electron distribution cannot be described well by a single structural formula as a superposition of several formulas (resonance structures) that differ only in the arrangement of electrons. The real molecule is none of the resonance structures but a single structure intermediate between them (the resonance hybrid). Resonance structures are joined by a double-headed arrow ↔, distinct from the equilibrium arrow ⇌. The resonance structures do not interconvert, so, for example, the two C−O bonds of the acetate ion are always equivalent. Resonance structures are a way of approximately expressing an electron distribution that one formula cannot capture.

about.h: Evidence in bond lengths and energies
about.p: Both C−O bonds of the acetate ion are about 0.126 nm, between C=O (about 0.121 nm) and C−O (about 0.134 nm). All six C−C bonds of benzene are likewise about 0.139 nm, between a single bond (about 0.154 nm) and a double bond (about 0.134 nm). In energy terms too, the heat of hydrogenation of benzene is about 150 kJ/mol smaller than expected from three cyclohexenes, and benzene is stabilized by that amount. In this way, molecules with delocalized electrons are more stable than a single structural formula would predict.

about.h: Drawing resonance structures and their weights
about.p: In resonance structures the positions of the atoms stay fixed and only π electrons and lone pairs are moved. The total number of electrons and the number of unpaired electrons are not changed either. Not every structure contributes equally: structures in which all atoms satisfy the octet, with less charge separation, and with negative charge on the more electronegative atoms contribute more. When several equivalent structures can be drawn, the stabilization is especially large. Tautomerism, in which atom positions change, is not resonance but an equilibrium between different compounds.

about.h: A tool for explaining properties and reactivity
about.p: Resonance is often used to explain the strengths of acids and bases. Acetic acid (pKa about 4.8) is a far stronger acid than ethanol (about 16) because the negative charge of its conjugate base is spread over two oxygens. Aniline is a weak base because the nitrogen's lone pair is delocalized into the ring. Drawing the resonance structures of intermediates also explains why the C−N bond of an amide has partial double-bond character and rotates with difficulty, and where substituents enter in electrophilic aromatic substitution. In this way a single idea explains many properties consistently.

faq.q: What is the difference between resonance and tautomerism?
faq.a: Resonance is a way of representing one molecule with several structural formulas, and the atoms do not move. Tautomerism is an equilibrium between different compounds in which an atom such as hydrogen moves, and the tautomers can sometimes be isolated.

faq.q: Do resonance structures actually exist?
faq.a: The individual resonance structures do not exist. The real molecule is a single resonance hybrid that superimposes them, and it is not flipping rapidly between two structures either.

faq.q: What is the difference between the resonance effect and the inductive effect?
faq.a: The resonance effect is the shift of electrons by delocalization of π electrons and lone pairs, and it reaches distant positions. The inductive effect is polarization through σ bonds and weakens rapidly with distance.

誘起効果.desc: The polarization of electrons through σ bonds caused by differences in electronegativity. Electron-withdrawing groups such as chlorine stabilize the conjugate base of a carboxylic acid and strengthen its acidity. It falls off sharply with distance.

about.p: The inductive effect is the polarization of σ-bond electrons by differences in electronegativity, transmitted in turn to neighbouring bonds. Electronegative atoms and groups such as F, Cl, O, nitro and trifluoromethyl attract electrons (−I effect) and polarize nearby carbons positive. Alkyl groups are often treated as weak electron donors. The inductive effect weakens greatly with each intervening bond and is usually almost gone three or four bonds away. The more electronegative the atom, the more strongly it attracts electrons. The CF3 group, for example, is a strong electron-withdrawing group in which the effects of three fluorines add up.

about.h: Its size seen in acid strength
about.p: The inductive effect shows up clearly in changes in the pKa of carboxylic acids. In water at 25 °C, acetic acid has a pKa of 4.76, but chloroacetic acid with one chlorine is about 2.9, with two about 1.3 and with three about 0.7, becoming stronger. Electron-withdrawing groups spread out and stabilize the negative charge of the conjugate base. Distance matters greatly: adding chlorine to butanoic acid (about 4.8) gives about 2.9 at the 2-position, about 4.1 at the 3-position and about 4.5 at the 4-position, the effect shrinking with distance from the carboxy group. This shows that the effect decays through σ bonds.

about.h: How it differs from the resonance effect
about.p: The resonance effect is the shift of electrons by delocalization of π electrons and lone pairs, and in a conjugated system it reaches distant positions. One substituent can have the two effects in opposite directions: a methoxy group withdraws electrons inductively but donates strongly by resonance, so it activates an aromatic ring. Halogens deactivate the ring by the inductive effect while being ortho/para-directing by resonance. A nitro group is a strong electron-withdrawing group by both inductive and resonance effects. It is important to consider the direction and size of the two effects separately.

The inductive effect also appears in basicity. The conjugate acid of ethylamine has a pKa of about 10.7, but for 2,2,2-trifluoroethylamine it falls to about 5.7, greatly weakening the basicity. In drug design, fluorine is sometimes introduced near an amine to adjust its pKa and change membrane permeability and metabolism. That carbocations are more stable the more alkyl groups they bear, being most stable when tertiary, is also explained by electron donation from alkyl groups (inductive effect and hyperconjugation). The substituent constants of the Hammett equation also include an inductive contribution.

faq.q: What is the difference between the inductive and resonance effects?
faq.a: The inductive effect is polarization through σ bonds and weakens rapidly with distance. The resonance effect is delocalization of π electrons and lone pairs and, in a conjugated system, reaches distant positions.

faq.q: What are some electron-withdrawing groups?
faq.a: Groups that withdraw electrons inductively include halogens such as F, Cl and Br, OH, OR, nitro, cyano, trifluoromethyl and ammonio groups.

faq.q: How far does the inductive effect reach?
faq.a: It weakens greatly with each intervening bond. In chlorobutanoic acids, the pKa is about 2.9 with chlorine at the 2-position but about 4.5 at the 4-position, close to butanoic acid (about 4.8).

ヘンダーソン・ハッセルバルヒの式.desc: The equation pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), used to find the pH of a buffer and the proportions of the neutral and ionized forms of a weak acid. At pH = pKa the two are equal.

about.h: Origin and meaning of the equation
about.p: This equation is simply the acid dissociation expression Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA] with the logarithm taken on both sides and rearranged; it is not a new law. In 1908 Henderson gave an equation for the hydrogen ion concentration of a buffer, and in 1916 Hasselbalch rewrote it in logarithmic form using pH. Both were studying acid–base balance in blood, so the equation was born in physiology. It shows at a glance that pH is set by just two things: the strength of the acid (pKa) and the ratio of the acid to its conjugate base.

about.h: Blood pH and the carbonic acid buffer
about.p: Blood pH is maintained mainly by the carbonic acid–bicarbonate buffer system. In clinical practice the concentration of dissolved carbon dioxide is expressed as the partial pressure PCO2 (mmHg) multiplied by 0.03 mmol/(L·mmHg), giving pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3⁻]/(0.03 × PCO2)). With [HCO3⁻] = 24 mmol/L and PCO2 = 40 mmHg, the ratio is 24/1.2 = 20, so pH = 6.1 + 1.30 = 7.40. Because PCO2 is regulated by breathing and [HCO3⁻] by the kidneys, the cause of an acid–base disorder can be read from the two values.

about.h: Mix-ups when applying it to bases
about.p: For a base such as an amine, the pKa to use is that of the conjugate acid BH⁺: pH = pKa(BH⁺) + log([B]/[BH⁺]). Plugging in the base's pKb directly, or inverting the ratio, are common mistakes. For example, pyridine (conjugate acid pKa about 5.2) at pH 7.2 has [B]/[BH⁺] = 10² = 100, so it is almost entirely in the uncharged form. If you identify the “base form” not by its charge but as the form with one fewer proton, the same equation handles both acids and bases.

about.h: Use with acids that dissociate in several steps
about.p: For an acid such as citric acid (pKa 3.13, 4.76, 6.40), whose stepwise pKa values are only about 2 apart, dissociation in the neighboring steps cannot be ignored when calculating the ratio for one step, and a single equation does not give an accurate pH. When the pKa values are well separated, as for phosphoric acid (pKa about 2.1, 7.2, 12.3), it is enough to consider the pair for the step nearest the target pH, for example only H2PO4⁻ and HPO4²⁻ near pH 7. First check which pair dominates from where the pH lies relative to the pKa values.

faq.q: Can amounts in moles be used instead of concentrations?
faq.a: Since it is a ratio of two components in the same solution, the volume cancels, and the mole ratio gives the same pH. When making a buffer, the pH can be calculated directly from the amounts of acid and salt added.

faq.q: Which pKa value should I use?
faq.a: Ideally the value at the temperature and ionic strength of use. Tabulated values are often thermodynamic values at 25℃ and zero ionic strength, and in solutions with a lot of salt the pH can differ from the calculation by about 0.1–0.2.

faq.q: Over what pH range does the equation work?
faq.a: It works well when the ratio of acid to conjugate base is about 0.1–10, that is, pH within pKa ± 1, and the concentrations are reasonably high. Outside that range the ionization of water and of the acid itself must be included in the calculation.

キラリティ.desc: The property of not being superimposable on one's mirror image. A chiral molecule exists as a pair of enantiomers. It is usually caused by an asymmetric carbon, but axial chirality and other types also exist.

about.p: The property of not being superimposable on one's mirror image is called chirality, and such molecules are called chiral molecules. It is likened to the relationship between right and left hands, and the word comes from the Greek for "hand". A molecule that is superimposable on its mirror image is achiral. A chiral molecule exists as a pair of enantiomers that are mirror images of each other. Whether a molecule is chiral depends on whether it has a mirror plane or a center of symmetry (more generally, an improper rotation axis); a molecule with none of these is chiral.

The most common source of chirality is an sp³ carbon bonded to four different groups (an asymmetric carbon, or chiral center). A molecule with exactly one asymmetric carbon is always chiral, but with two or more, meso compounds that are achiral because of an internal mirror plane can appear. Conversely, some molecules are chiral without any asymmetric carbon: examples are biaryls with hindered rotation about a single bond (axial chirality), substituted allenes and helical helicenes. It is important to judge chirality by the symmetry of the whole molecule.

Enzymes and receptors in the body are made of chiral proteins, so enantiomers can act differently in the body. There are known examples in which one enantiomer has the therapeutic effect while the other is inactive or has a different action. In drug development, therefore, the enantiomers are separated and each is evaluated, and where necessary the drug is manufactured as a single enantiomer. Enantiomeric excess (ee) is used as the measure of purity and is determined by methods such as HPLC on a chiral stationary phase.

faq.q: Does a chiral molecule always have an asymmetric carbon?
faq.a: No. Some molecules, such as biaryls with axial chirality and allenes, are chiral without an asymmetric carbon. Conversely, some molecules, such as meso compounds, are achiral even though they have asymmetric carbons.

faq.q: How do you decide whether a molecule is chiral?
faq.a: Check whether the molecule has a mirror plane or a center of symmetry. If it has neither, it very likely cannot be superimposed on its mirror image and is chiral; strictly, the condition is that it has no improper rotation axis.

faq.q: How are enantiomers told apart?
faq.a: By measuring the direction in which they rotate polarized light with a polarimeter, or by using interactions with something chiral, such as chromatography on a chiral stationary phase or NMR with a chiral shift reagent added.

不斉炭素.desc: An sp³ carbon bonded to four different atoms or groups, also called a chiral center. A molecule with exactly one such carbon is always chiral.

about.h: How to find an asymmetric carbon
about.p: An asymmetric carbon is an sp³ carbon bonded to four mutually different atoms or groups. To find one, check for each carbon whether its four bonding partners are all different. CH2 and CH3 carbons and doubly bonded carbons cannot be asymmetric carbons. A ring carbon is an asymmetric carbon if the structures reached by following the ring in the two directions differ. For example, C3 of 3-methylcyclohexanone is an asymmetric carbon, but C1 of methylcyclohexane is not, because both sides of the ring are the same.

A molecule with n asymmetric carbons has at most 2ⁿ stereoisomers. Aldohexoses, with four asymmetric carbons, have 16, and cholesterol, with eight, could have 256, yet only one of them occurs in nature. Symmetry in the molecule produces meso compounds and reduces the number: tartaric acid has two asymmetric carbons but only three stereoisomers. Any two stereoisomers are related either as enantiomers or as diastereomers. In synthesizing natural products with many stereocenters, only the one target among these must be made selectively.

A molecule with exactly one asymmetric carbon is always chiral. But the presence of asymmetric carbons and chirality do not coincide. A meso compound with two or more asymmetric carbons and an internal mirror plane is achiral. Conversely, some molecules are chiral without any asymmetric carbon, such as biaryls with hindered rotation (axial chirality) and substituted allenes. Atoms other than carbon can also be stereocenters, such as the sulfur of a sulfoxide or the phosphorus of a phosphine with different substituents. The nitrogen of an amine inverts quickly, so its enantiomers usually cannot be separated.

The spatial arrangement at an asymmetric carbon is described as R or S using the CIP priority rules. Rank the four substituents by atomic number, view the molecule with the lowest-priority group pointing away, and if the remaining groups run 1→2→3 clockwise it is R; counterclockwise, S. In a wedge drawing with the lowest-priority group pointing toward the viewer, the result is the reverse of what you see. R/S has no connection with the direction of optical rotation (+/−), and even when a reaction preserves the configuration, the descriptor can change if the substituent priorities change. Changes in configuration should therefore be checked from the spatial arrangement, not the descriptor.

faq.q: Do asymmetric carbon and chiral center mean the same thing?
faq.a: For carbon they are used almost interchangeably. Chiral center and stereocenter are broader terms that are also applied to atoms other than carbon, such as sulfur and phosphorus. "Asymmetric carbon" refers only to carbon.

faq.q: How many stereoisomers are there with n asymmetric carbons?
faq.a: At most 2ⁿ. When the molecule has a mirror plane and forms a meso compound, there are fewer. Tartaric acid, for example, has three rather than 2² = 4.

faq.q: Are there chiral molecules without an asymmetric carbon?
faq.a: Yes. Biaryls with axial chirality due to hindered rotation, substituted allenes and helical helicenes are chiral molecules that cannot be superimposed on their mirror images even though they have no asymmetric carbon.

エナンチオマー.desc: Stereoisomers that are mirror images of each other and cannot be superimposed. Their physical properties in an achiral environment are identical, and they rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions.

about.p: Enantiomers are a pair of stereoisomers that are mirror images of each other, like right and left hands, and cannot be superimposed. A molecule that is chiral always has a pair of enantiomers. For molecules with stereocenters, the enantiomer is the one with the configuration at every stereocenter inverted; the enantiomer of the (2R,3R) isomer is (2S,3S). One with only some stereocenters inverted is not a mirror image and is therefore a diastereomer. Whether two structures are mirror images is judged from the shape of the whole molecule, not from the stereocenter descriptors.

about.h: Properties that are the same and that differ
about.p: Enantiomers have identical interatomic distances and angles, so their melting points, boiling points, densities, solubilities in achiral solvents, and IR and NMR spectra are equal. Differences appear only when they interact with something chiral, such as plane-polarized light or chiral molecules. Their specific rotations are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign, and their retention times differ in chromatography on a chiral stationary phase. A 1 : 1 mixture of the two is called a racemate, and its optical rotation is zero. In a chiral environment such as the body, they can even differ in smell or taste.

How much one enantiomer predominates is expressed by the enantiomeric excess (ee). ee = |R − S|/(R + S) × 100, so a sample of 90% R and 10% S has an ee of 80%. A racemate has an ee of 0%, and a single pure enantiomer 100%. The optical purity, the specific rotation divided by that of the pure enantiomer, equals the ee if rotation is proportional to the ee. In current practice, ee is usually determined from the ratio of the two peak areas by HPLC or GC on a chiral stationary phase.

Receptors and enzymes in the body are chiral proteins, so the enantiomers of a drug can differ in action and metabolism. The more active one is called the eutomer. For this reason the two enantiomers of a chiral drug are evaluated separately, and if necessary only one is manufactured. To obtain a single enantiomer, asymmetric synthesis is used, as well as optical resolution, in which the enantiomers are converted into diastereomeric salts and separated by crystallization, and preparative separation on a chiral column. For a compound that racemizes easily in the body, giving only one enantiomer loses that advantage, because both form in the body.

faq.q: What is the difference between enantiomers and diastereomers?
faq.a: Enantiomers are a pair that are mirror images of each other, with the configuration at every stereocenter inverted. Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images, and they differ in properties such as melting point and solubility.

faq.q: Is the R isomer always dextrorotatory?
faq.a: No. R/S describes the spatial arrangement determined by substituent priorities and has no general relationship to the direction of optical rotation (+/−). The sign is determined by measurement.

faq.q: What is a racemate?
faq.a: A mixture containing equal amounts of the two enantiomers. The rotations cancel, so its optical rotation is zero; it is indicated by (±) or the prefix rac-.

ジアステレオマー.desc: Stereoisomers that are not mirror images. They include isomers differing in configuration at only some stereocenters and cis–trans isomers, and their properties, such as melting point and solubility, differ.

about.h: Stereoisomers that are not mirror images
about.p: Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other. They include molecules with two or more stereocenters that differ in the configuration at only some of them (for example (2R,3R) and (2R,3S)) and cis/trans isomers of double bonds and rings (E/Z isomers). Diastereomers that differ at only one stereocenter are called epimers; glucose and mannose are C2 epimers. The α and β forms of a cyclic sugar that differ only at the anomeric carbon (anomers) are also diastereomers.

Diastereomers differ in interatomic distances and shape, so their melting points, boiling points, solubilities, NMR spectra and chromatographic retention differ. For example, cis maleic acid melts at about 135 °C, while trans fumaric acid does not melt until a much higher temperature, and their solubilities in water also differ greatly. Unlike enantiomers, they can therefore be separated by ordinary recrystallization, distillation and silica gel column chromatography. Their reactivity often differs too, making them targets of selective synthesis. In NMR, the diastereomer ratio can be read directly from the ratio of signal integrals.

Enantiomers, with identical properties, are hard to separate directly, so they are converted into diastereomers by reaction with a chiral reagent and then separated. When a racemic carboxylic acid is made into a salt with an optically active amine, the two diastereomeric salts differ in solubility and can be separated by recrystallization, and acid treatment releases one enantiomer (optical resolution). Converting to diastereomers with a chiral derivatizing agent such as Mosher's acid also lets the enantiomer ratio be determined by NMR.

A molecule with n stereocenters has at most 2ⁿ stereoisomers, and from the standpoint of any one of them, only one is its enantiomer and all the rest are diastereomers. Among the 16 aldohexoses, the enantiomer of D-glucose is L-glucose alone, and the other 14 are its diastereomers. A reaction that favors one diastereomer is called diastereoselective, and the ratio is expressed as d.r. (diastereomeric ratio). When meso compounds arise, the number of stereoisomers is fewer than 2ⁿ. For example, a compound with three stereocenters has up to eight stereoisomers, six of which are diastereomers of any given one.

faq.q: What is the difference between diastereomers and enantiomers?
faq.a: Enantiomers are mirror images of each other and have the same properties in an achiral environment. Diastereomers are not mirror images and differ in properties such as melting point and solubility, so they can be separated by ordinary methods.

faq.q: Are cis/trans isomers diastereomers?
faq.a: Yes. Cis/trans (E/Z) isomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other, so they are included among diastereomers. Their properties, such as melting and boiling points, also differ.

faq.q: What is an epimer?
faq.a: A diastereomer that differs in configuration at only one of several stereocenters. D-glucose and D-mannose are C2 epimers, and D-glucose and D-galactose are C4 epimers.

メソ体.desc: A compound with two or more asymmetric carbons that is nonetheless achiral, because an internal mirror plane or similar makes it superimposable on its mirror image. It is not optically active. Example: (2R,3S)-tartaric acid.

about.p: A meso compound has two or more asymmetric carbons (stereocenters) but is superimposable on its mirror image, and therefore achiral, because it has an internal mirror plane or center of symmetry. In the typical example, (2R,3S)-tartaric acid, C2 and C3 carry the same set of substituents with opposite configurations, so a mirror plane can be drawn through the middle of the molecule. One half of the molecule is the mirror image of the other, so the rotations cancel within the molecule and it shows no optical activity. A meso compound has no mirror-image partner (enantiomer).

With n stereocenters there are at most 2ⁿ stereoisomers, but meso compounds reduce that number. For molecules whose two ends are the same, such as tartaric acid and 2,3-dibromobutane, there are three in total: the (R,R) and (S,S) enantiomeric pair and one (R,S) meso compound. (R,S) and (S,R), though named differently, are the same molecule and coincide on rotation. Among cyclic compounds, too, cis-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane and cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane are meso compounds that are achiral overall. 2,3-Butanediol likewise exists in three forms: (R,R), (S,S) and meso.

about.h: How it differs from a racemate
about.p: Both a meso compound and a racemate have zero optical rotation, but they are entirely different. A racemate is a mixture containing equal amounts of two enantiomers, and the rotations cancel between molecules. Using a chiral reagent or chiral column, it can be separated into its two components (optical resolution). A meso compound is a single compound whose molecules are themselves achiral, so it cannot be resolved by any method. Its melting point and solubility also differ from those of the racemate, and the meso compound is a diastereomer of the chiral isomers.

In stereospecific reactions, the configuration of the starting material decides whether a meso compound or a racemate forms. Anti addition of bromine to trans-2-butene gives meso-2,3-dibromobutane, while cis-2-butene gives the racemate. In syn dihydroxylation with OsO4 it is the other way round: cis-2-butene gives the meso diol. Reacting only one of the two equivalent functional groups of a meso compound with an enzyme or chiral catalyst gives an optically active compound in one step (desymmetrization), a technique used in asymmetric synthesis.

faq.q: What is the difference between a meso compound and a racemate?
faq.a: A meso compound is a single compound whose molecules are themselves achiral. A racemate is an equal mixture of two enantiomers and can be separated by optical resolution. Both have zero optical rotation.

faq.q: How do you recognize a meso compound?
faq.a: Check whether the molecule has two or more stereocenters and an internal mirror plane or center of symmetry. If the two ends are structurally the same and the stereocenter descriptors form an (R,S) pair, it is likely to be meso.

faq.q: Why does a meso compound show no optical activity?
faq.a: Because one half of the molecule is the mirror image of the other and the molecule as a whole is achiral. It is explained as the rotation due to one half being cancelled by the other half.

CIP順位則.desc: Rules for ranking the substituents on a stereocenter. The higher the atomic number of the directly attached atom, the higher the priority; if tied, the next atoms are compared. Used for R/S and E/Z descriptors.

about.p: The CIP priority rules, named from the initials of Cahn, Ingold and Prelog, assign priorities to the substituents on a stereocenter or double bond. First compare the atomic numbers of the atoms directly attached to the stereocenter; the larger ranks higher. If they are the same, list the three atoms attached to each of those atoms in order of decreasing atomic number and compare the sets from the front. If that still does not decide it, move outward along the higher-ranked branches first and decide at the first point of difference. Among isotopes of the same element, the one with the larger mass number ranks higher.

about.h: The first difference, not number or size
about.p: A common mistake is to compare substituents by size or number of atoms. −CH2OH has (O, H, H) and −C(CH3)3 has (C, C, C); at the first atoms compared, O is larger than C, so −CH2OH outranks the carbon-rich tert-butyl group. Also, double and triple bonds are counted by duplicating the partner atom. The vinyl group −CH=CH2 gives (C, C, H), the same as isopropyl, but at the next level the =CH2 carbon has (C, H, H), so vinyl ranks higher.

about.h: Using them for R/S and E/Z
about.p: To assign R/S, view the molecule with the lowest-priority substituent pointing away from you; if the remaining 1→2→3 run clockwise it is R, and counterclockwise S. For double bonds, determine the higher-priority substituent on each carbon; if the higher-priority groups are on the same side it is Z, and on opposite sides E. This does not always match cis/trans. Because the descriptors are conventions for naming configurations, R and S can switch even when a reaction does not change the configuration, if the priorities of the substituents change. They also do not correspond to the direction of optical rotation.

about.h: Complex cases and the current rules
about.p: For substituents containing rings or other stereocenters, the connectivity is expanded into a tree (a hierarchical digraph) for comparison. For cases that atoms alone cannot settle, there are additional rules, such as ranking Z above E and like pairs of descriptors (such as R,R) above unlike pairs. The rules have been revised repeatedly since they were proposed in 1956 and are now set out in the current IUPAC nomenclature recommendations (2013). For complex molecules, it is safer to check by hand the assignments made automatically by structure-drawing software.

faq.q: How are double bonds counted in the CIP rules?
faq.a: The partner atom of a double bond is counted twice, as if another copy were attached. The carbon of −CH=O is treated as (O, O, H), and for a triple bond the partner is duplicated twice. Beyond a duplicated atom, phantom atoms of atomic number zero are assumed.

faq.q: Which ranks higher, deuterium or hydrogen?
faq.a: They have the same atomic number, so deuterium, with the larger mass number, ranks higher. This makes it possible to assign R/S even to molecules that are stereocenters only because of an isotopic difference, such as CHD.

faq.q: When SN2 inverts a stereocenter, does R always become S?
faq.a: Not necessarily. R/S is determined by the priorities of the substituents, so if the leaving group and the incoming group rank differently relative to the other groups, the descriptor may stay the same even though the configuration is inverted. Think in terms of the spatial arrangement itself, not the label.

鏡像体過剰率.desc: A measure of the purity of a mixture of enantiomers, abbreviated ee: the proportion of the major enantiomer minus that of the minor one. 90% R and 10% S gives an ee of 80%.

about.p: Enantiomeric excess (ee) is the difference between the proportions of the major and minor enantiomers in a mixture, expressed as a percentage: ee = (R − S)/(R + S) × 100%. A racemate is 0% and a single enantiomer 100%. Working backward, the major enantiomer is (100 + ee)/2 %, so 90% ee corresponds to 95:5 and 99% ee to 99.5:0.5. Recently, reporting the enantiomeric ratio (er), which gives the proportions directly, has also been recommended. For ratios of diastereomers, diastereomeric excess (de) is used.

It is tempting to assume that lowering the ee of the ligand of an asymmetric catalyst lowers the product ee in proportion, but cases where they are not proportional are known. When the catalyst works as an associated pair of molecules, for example, the product ee can be higher than expected from the ligand ee; this is called a positive nonlinear effect. Negative nonlinear effects, giving lower ee, also occur. Even chromatography on an achiral column or sublimation can change the ee from fraction to fraction, so it is important to note which fraction was measured during purification.

The higher the ee, the smaller the minor peak. At 99% ee the minor enantiomer is only 0.5% of the total, and the value changes considerably with how the baseline is drawn and with overlap from the tail of the large peak. Before comparing, run a racemic sample under the same conditions and confirm that the two peaks are separated and give equal areas. In NMR, the sample is converted to diastereomers with a chiral derivatizing agent such as Mosher's acid, or a chiral shift reagent is added, so that the signals separate and can be integrated.

about.h: Use in asymmetric synthesis and pharmaceuticals
about.p: The performance of asymmetric syntheses and catalysts is compared by ee along with yield. In kinetic resolution, only one enantiomer reacts, so the ee of the remaining starting material rises as the reaction proceeds, but the yield is at most 50%. Repeated crystallization often raises ee, although the behavior differs depending on whether the compound forms a racemic compound or a conglomerate. In pharmaceuticals, the unwanted enantiomer is controlled as an impurity, so analytical methods that can show a high ee accurately are required.

faq.q: At 80% ee, what are the proportions of each enantiomer?
faq.a: The major enantiomer is (100 + 80)/2 = 90% and the minor one 10%. You can also view it as 80% of the total being a single enantiomer and the remaining 20% being racemate.

faq.q: Are ee and optical purity the same?
faq.a: They agree when specific rotation is proportional to ee, but strictly they are different quantities. Optical purity comes from a ratio of specific rotations and ee from a ratio of amounts. When proportionality fails, for example because of association, the values disagree.

faq.q: How is ee measured?
faq.a: Usually by separating the two enantiomers by HPLC or GC with a chiral column and calculating from the peak areas. It can also be determined by NMR with chiral derivatizing agents or shift reagents.

比旋光度.desc: The observed rotation divided by the path length (dm) and the concentration (g/mL): [α] = α/(l·c). It is characteristic of a substance but changes with temperature, wavelength and solvent.

about.p: The optical rotation α measured with a polarimeter changes in proportion to concentration and path length even for the same substance. Dividing by the path length l (dm) and concentration c (g/mL) to give [α] = α/(l·c) yields a value characteristic of the substance, the specific rotation. The path length is in dm because polarimeter cells are standardized on a length of 1 dm (10 cm). For a pure liquid, the density (g/mL) is used instead of concentration. Only chiral substances give non-zero values, and enantiomers give values equal in magnitude and opposite in sign.

about.h: Stating conditions and a worked example
about.p: Specific rotation changes with temperature and wavelength, so it is written as [α]D²⁰, with the wavelength as a subscript (D is the sodium D line, 589 nm) and the temperature (°C) as a superscript, along with the solvent and concentration. By convention the stated concentration is in g/100 mL: (c 1.0, H2O) means 1.0 g/100 mL, which differs by a factor of 100 from the g/mL used in the formula, so take care. For example, sucrose, with a specific rotation of +66.5°, made up as a 10.0 g/100 mL aqueous solution and measured in a 1.00 dm cell gives α = 66.5 × 1.00 × 0.100 = +6.65°.

The specific rotation of a mixture is the average of the components' specific rotations weighted by their proportions. In aqueous glucose, the α form (+112°) and β form (+18.7°) interconvert via the open-chain structure, and the specific rotation approaches an equilibrium value of about +52.7° (mutarotation). The specific rotation of a sample divided by that of the pure enantiomer is called the optical purity; if rotation is proportional to composition, it equals the enantiomeric excess. Some cases are not proportional, for example because of association between molecules, so today the ee is often checked by chiral HPLC.

about.h: The sign is not directly tied to structure
about.p: The sign of the specific rotation (+ for dextrorotatory, − for levorotatory) is a measured quantity and has no general correspondence with R/S or D/L descriptors. D-Glucose is dextrorotatory, but D-fructose is levorotatory. Even for the same compound, the value changes greatly with solvent, pH, concentration and temperature, and some amino acids have opposite signs in water and in hydrochloric acid. When comparing with literature values, matching the measurement conditions is essential. The variation with wavelength (optical rotatory dispersion) is also used to infer absolute configuration.

faq.q: What are the units of specific rotation?
faq.a: Formally deg·mL·g⁻¹·dm⁻¹, but by convention it is often written with just "°". In the calculation, express concentration and path length in the units the formula assumes (g/mL and dm).

faq.q: What is the difference between optical rotation and specific rotation?
faq.a: Optical rotation is the measured angle itself and changes with concentration and path length. Specific rotation is that angle divided by concentration and path length, a value characteristic of the substance. Compare values with matching units.

faq.q: What is the sodium D line?
faq.a: The yellow light of wavelength about 589 nm emitted by a sodium lamp. It is the standard light for specific rotation measurements, and the D in [α]D indicates a measurement made with it.

いす形配座.desc: The most stable conformation of cyclohexane. Its bond angles are nearly tetrahedral and all its bonds are staggered. Each carbon has an axial and an equatorial bond.

about.p: In a planar regular hexagon the C−C−C bond angle would be 120°, far from the tetrahedral angle (109.5°). By puckering into the chair, cyclohexane keeps its bond angles at about 111° and arranges all bonds on adjacent carbons in staggered conformations. As a result there is almost no angle strain or torsional strain, and the ring strain estimated from heats of combustion is nearly zero. Conformations higher in energy than the chair include the twist-boat (about 23 kJ/mol higher) and the boat (about 29 kJ/mol higher).

In the chair, each carbon has one axial bond, roughly perpendicular to the mean plane of the ring, and one equatorial bond, extending outward from the ring. The axial bonds alternate up and down from carbon to carbon. A substituent in an axial position comes close to the axial hydrogens at positions 3 and 5 on the same side, causing steric repulsion (1,3-diaxial interactions), so equatorial is usually more stable. For a methyl group the difference is about 7.3 kJ/mol in Gibbs energy, and at 25 °C about 95% is in the equatorial conformation.

A chair flips to the other chair through a half-chair transition state. Axial and equatorial positions are exchanged, but bonds pointing up stay pointing up. The barrier to ring flipping is small, about 45 kJ/mol, and flipping is very fast at room temperature, so the two conformations cannot be separated. In ¹H NMR the axial and equatorial hydrogens are averaged into a single signal, and they are observed separately only on cooling to around −100 °C. A large tert-butyl group locks the ring almost entirely into one chair.

Positional relationships in the chair govern how readily reactions occur. In E2 reactions of cyclohexane rings, the leaving group and the β hydrogen must be trans-diaxial, so the product changes with the orientation of the substituents. β-D-Glucopyranose can place all ring substituents equatorial, so the β form predominates at equilibrium. Trans-fused rings, as in steroids, cannot flip and are locked in shape. For a substituted cyclohexane, the basic approach is to draw both chairs first and judge the more stable conformation from the orientation of the large substituents.

faq.q: Which is more stable, the chair or the boat?
faq.a: The chair. In the boat the bow and stern hydrogens clash and bonds on adjacent carbons are eclipsed, so it lies about 29 kJ/mol higher in energy than the chair.

faq.q: How do I tell axial from equatorial?
faq.a: Axial bonds point up or down, roughly perpendicular to the mean plane of the ring, while equatorial bonds extend sideways outward from the ring. Each carbon has one of each, and the axial bonds alternate up and down from carbon to carbon.

faq.q: Does ring flipping interchange cis and trans?
faq.a: No. Flipping changes only the axial/equatorial relationship; bonds pointing up stay up, so the cis/trans relationship of substituents is preserved.

SN2反応.desc: A nucleophilic substitution in which the nucleophile attacks carbon from the side opposite the leaving group, with bond formation and bond breaking in a single step. The rate is proportional to the concentrations of both substrate and nucleophile, and it goes with inversion of configuration.

about.p: The SN2 reaction (bimolecular nucleophilic substitution) is a reaction in which the nucleophile attacks carbon from exactly the opposite side of the leaving group, and the formation of the new bond and the breaking of the old one proceed simultaneously in a single step. In the transition state, the three substituents on the central carbon lie nearly in a plane, and the nucleophile and leaving group are partially bonded from either side in a five-coordinate arrangement. There is no intermediate and only one energy barrier. The rate law is v = k[substrate][nucleophile], first order in each and second order overall.

Because the nucleophile attacks from the back, the configuration of the reacting carbon turns inside out like an umbrella in the wind (Walden inversion). From an optically active secondary alkyl halide, a product with inverted configuration is obtained almost exclusively. However, because R/S labels are determined by substituent priorities, if the leaving group and the nucleophile occupy different places in the priority order, the label may not change despite inversion. Whether inversion occurred must be checked from the spatial arrangement, not from the label.

SN2 slows down when the back of the carbon is crowded, so substrate reactivity runs methyl > primary > secondary ≫ tertiary, and tertiary substrates hardly react. Neopentyl-type substrates, branched at the β position, are also very slow. Stronger nucleophiles are favorable, as are leaving groups that are weak bases, such as I⁻, Br⁻ and TsO⁻. Polar aprotic solvents such as DMSO, DMF and acetone, which do not wrap anionic nucleophiles in hydrogen bonds, are particularly suitable.

faq.q: What do the S, N and 2 in SN2 stand for?
faq.a: S stands for substitution and N for nucleophilic, and 2 indicates that it is a bimolecular reaction in which two molecules, the substrate and the nucleophile, take part in the rate-determining step.

faq.q: How do you tell SN2 from SN1?
faq.a: Judge by the substrate class, the strength of the nucleophile and the solvent. A primary substrate, a strong nucleophile and an aprotic solvent favor SN2; a tertiary substrate, a weak nucleophile and a protic solvent favor SN1. In stereochemistry, inversion is the sign of SN2 and racemization the sign of SN1.

faq.q: Why don't tertiary alkyl halides undergo SN2?
faq.a: Because the central carbon carries three alkyl groups and there is no room for the nucleophile to approach from the back. Instead, SN1 or E1 through a carbocation, or E2 if a strong base is present, takes place.

E2反応.desc: A single-step elimination in which a base removes a β-hydrogen as the leaving group departs, forming a double bond. The rate is proportional to the concentrations of substrate and base, and it is fastest in the antiperiplanar arrangement.

about.p: The E2 reaction (bimolecular elimination) is a single-step reaction in which a base removes a hydrogen from the β carbon as a proton while the leaving group departs from the α carbon at the same time, forming a C=C double bond. The rate law is v = k[substrate][base], first order in both the substrate and the base. It does not go through a carbocation, so no rearrangement occurs. Because it proceeds rapidly even with tertiary halides when a strong base is present, alkenes can be obtained efficiently even from crowded substrates that do not undergo SN2.

E2 is fastest in the antiperiplanar arrangement, in which the C−H bond being broken and the C−X bond being cleaved lie in the same plane pointing in opposite directions (a 180° dihedral angle). Because of this stereochemical requirement, diastereomers can give alkenes of different E/Z geometry. On a cyclohexane ring, E2 occurs poorly unless the leaving group and the β-hydrogen are both axial (trans-diaxial), and the reaction is very slow for substrates whose leaving group is locked equatorial.

When there are β-hydrogens at several positions, a small base such as ethoxide gives the more substituted, more stable alkene as the major product (Zaitsev's rule). With a bulky base such as tert-butoxide, the sterically accessible outer hydrogens are removed and the less substituted alkene becomes the major product (the Hofmann product). Elimination from quaternary ammonium salts (Hofmann elimination) also gives mainly the less substituted alkene. The choice of base and leaving group lets you change the product ratio.

faq.q: What is the difference between E2 and E1?
faq.a: E2 is a single-step reaction with a base, and its rate also depends on the base concentration. E1 is a two-step reaction in which the leaving group first departs to form a carbocation and a proton is then lost; its rate depends only on the substrate concentration, and it can involve rearrangements.

faq.q: Which happens, E2 or SN2?
faq.a: Strong, bulky bases, crowded substrates and high temperatures favor E2. With a primary substrate and a good nucleophile of low basicity (I⁻, CN⁻, N3⁻ and the like), SN2 dominates.

faq.q: Does Zaitsev's rule always hold?
faq.a: No. With bulky bases, poor leaving groups such as fluoride, or cyclic substrates that cannot adopt an antiperiplanar arrangement, the less substituted alkene may be formed predominantly.

カルボカチオン.desc: A cation containing a positively charged three-coordinate carbon. It is trigonal planar with an empty p orbital. Stability runs tertiary > secondary > primary, and it is the intermediate in SN1, E1 and addition reactions.

about.p: A carbocation is a cation containing a positively charged three-coordinate carbon; the positive carbon is sp² hybridized and trigonal planar, with one empty p orbital. Stability runs tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl, which is explained by hyperconjugation, the flow of electrons from neighboring C−H and C−C bonds into the empty p orbital, and by the inductive effect of alkyl groups. Allylic and benzylic cations are especially stable because the positive charge is delocalized by resonance, and they undergo SN1 readily even when primary.

SN1, E1, the addition of hydrogen halides to alkenes, and the acid-catalyzed hydration of alkenes and dehydration of alcohols proceed through carbocation intermediates. The step that forms the carbocation is often rate-determining, and the pathway that gives the more stable carbocation is preferred. Markovnikov's rule can also be explained by addition through the more stable carbocation being dominant. Because the intermediate is planar, the nucleophile can attack from either face, and stereocenters tend to racemize.

If the carbon next to a carbocation carries a hydrogen or alkyl group whose migration would give a more stable carbocation, a 1,2-hydride shift or 1,2-alkyl shift occurs rapidly. For example, treating 3-methyl-2-butanol with HBr rearranges the secondary carbocation to a tertiary one, giving mainly 2-bromo-2-methylbutane. In reactions through carbocations, keep in mind that the carbon skeleton and the position of functional groups in the product can differ from those of the starting material.

faq.q: What is the difference between a carbocation and a carbanion?
faq.a: A carbocation is a carbon with a positive charge and an empty p orbital, an electrophilic species that accepts electrons. A carbanion is a carbon with a negative charge and a lone pair, which acts as a nucleophile or base.

faq.q: Why are tertiary carbocations stable?
faq.a: Because hyperconjugation, in which electrons of the alkyl groups' C−H and C−C bonds partly flow into the empty p orbital of the positive carbon, and the inductive effect spread out the positive charge. The more alkyl groups, the greater the stabilization.

faq.q: When do rearrangements occur?
faq.a: They tend to occur when the migration of a hydrogen or alkyl group can give a more stable carbocation, such as secondary to tertiary. Watch for them in reactions through carbocations, such as SN1, E1 and reactions of alcohols under acidic conditions.

SN1反応.desc: A two-step nucleophilic substitution whose rate-determining step is the departure of the leaving group to form a carbocation. The rate is proportional only to the substrate concentration; it occurs readily with tertiary substrates and is accompanied by racemization.

about.h: A substitution that proceeds in two steps
about.p: The SN1 reaction (unimolecular nucleophilic substitution) is a two-step reaction in which the leaving group first departs with its electron pair to give a carbocation, and a nucleophile then bonds to that carbocation. The first step, which only breaks a bond, is slow and rate-determining, so the rate law is v = k[RX], first order in substrate. The nucleophile reacts after the rate-determining step, so its concentration and strength have little effect on the rate. Solvolysis, in which the solvent acts as the nucleophile, is a typical SN1 example.

The more stable the carbocation, the faster the first step, so reactivity follows tertiary > secondary ≫ primary, and benzylic and allylic substrates, whose positive charge is spread by resonance, also react readily. Leaving groups that depart well are favorable. Suitable solvents are highly polar protic ones such as water and alcohols, which can stabilize both the cation and the anion formed. For the same substrate, solvolysis is much faster in a mixed solvent rich in water than in ethanol.

A carbocation is a trigonal planar sp² carbon, so nucleophiles can attack from either side, and an optically active substrate gives a product close to racemic. In practice, the departed anion blocks one face for a while, so the inverted product can be slightly favored. Carbocations can also rearrange to more stable carbocations. When 3-methyl-2-butanol is treated with hydrogen bromide, a hydride shifts from the secondary cation to give a tertiary cation, and 2-bromo-2-methylbutane forms as the main product. With neopentyl-type substrates, a methyl group migrates instead (a methyl shift).

The carbocation formed in SN1 can also lose a β hydrogen to become an alkene instead of bonding to a nucleophile (the E1 reaction). SN1 and E1 share the rate-determining step, so the two products are usually mixed, and raising the temperature increases the proportion of elimination. Even with tertiary substrates, a high concentration of strong base makes E2, in which the base removes a β hydrogen before a carbocation forms, the main reaction. With a weak nucleophile in a protic solvent the path is SN1/E1, and with a strong base E2: the route changes with conditions.

faq.q: What do the S, N and 1 in SN1 stand for?
faq.a: S stands for substitution, N for nucleophilic, and 1 indicates a unimolecular reaction in which only one molecule, the substrate, is involved in the rate-determining step.

faq.q: Why does racemization occur in the SN1 reaction?
faq.a: Because the carbocation intermediate is planar, and the nucleophile can attack from either side with nearly equal probability. If the leaving group shields one face for a while, the inverted product can be slightly favored.

faq.q: How do you tell SN1 from SN2?
faq.a: By the rate law: SN1 is first order in substrate only, SN2 first order in both substrate and nucleophile. In stereochemistry, SN1 shows racemization and SN2 inversion.

E1反応.desc: A two-step elimination that proceeds through a carbocation. It shares its intermediate with SN1, so the two compete. It is favored by heating and can involve carbocation rearrangements.

about.h: An elimination that shares its first step with SN1
about.p: An E1 reaction (unimolecular elimination) takes place in two steps. First the leaving group departs to give a carbocation, and then a weak base such as the solvent removes a proton from the carbon next to the cationic center, forming a C=C double bond. The rate-determining step is the first one, formation of the carbocation, so the rate law is v = k[RX] and does not depend on the concentration of base. In the second step, the electrons of a C−H bond lined up parallel to the empty p orbital are used to make the double bond, so the β hydrogen must be oriented where it can overlap with that p orbital.

In E1, the proton is lost from a carbocation that has already become planar, so there is no requirement for an antiperiplanar arrangement as in E2. As a result, the more substituted and more stable alkene (the Zaitsev product) and the sterically favored E isomer are formed mainly. For example, in the solvolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, more 2-methyl-2-butene forms than 2-methyl-1-butene. E1 is stereoselective, with the product ratio set by product stability, but it is not stereospecific in the way E2 is.

Dehydration of secondary and tertiary alcohols with concentrated sulfuric acid or phosphoric acid is a common laboratory E1 reaction. The OH group is protonated to become water, a good leaving group, and the alkene forms by way of a carbocation. The temperatures needed are roughly 25–80 ℃ for tertiary alcohols and 100–140 ℃ for secondary ones; the more stable the carbocation, the lower the temperature. Because the reaction is an equilibrium, removing the low-boiling alkene by distillation drives it toward products. 2-Methylcyclohexanol gives mainly 1-methylcyclohexene.

about.h: How E1, E2, and E1cB are related
about.p: Elimination reactions are divided into three types according to the order in which the C−X and C−H bonds break. In E1 the C−X bond breaks first; in E2 both break at the same time; and in E1cB the C−H bond breaks first to give a carbanion. E1cB occurs when an anion next to a carbonyl group is stabilized and the leaving group, such as OH, departs reluctantly, as in the dehydration of aldol adducts. Real reactions can fall anywhere along a continuum between these types, and the mechanism shifts with the combination of substrate, base, and solvent.

faq.q: Why does raising the temperature favor elimination over substitution?
faq.a: Elimination turns one molecule into two or more, so its entropy increase is larger than that of substitution. In ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, the entropy term matters more at higher temperature, which favors elimination.

faq.q: Is the E1 reaction stereospecific?
faq.a: No. It goes through a planar carbocation, so information about the starting material's configuration is lost. The E/Z ratio of the alkene is set by stereoselectivity based on product stability, and the E isomer usually predominates.

faq.q: What is the difference between E1 and E1cB?
faq.a: In E1 the leaving group departs first and the reaction passes through a carbocation, whereas in E1cB a base first removes a proton and the reaction passes through a carbanion (the conjugate base). E1cB occurs with substrates that have an acidic C−H and a poor leaving group.

脱離基.desc: An atom or group that departs from the substrate with an electron pair in substitution and elimination reactions. The weaker the base, the better the leaving group; examples are I⁻, Br⁻ and TsO⁻. OH⁻ leaves poorly.

about.h: The role of a leaving group
about.p: A leaving group is an atom or group that departs from the substrate taking the bonding electron pair with it in substitution and elimination reactions. SN1, SN2, E1 and E2 reactions all include a step in which the bond between carbon and the leaving group breaks, so how readily the leaving group departs greatly affects the rate. Typical examples are the halogen of an alkyl halide, the sulfonate of a sulfonate ester and water from a protonated alcohol. In nucleophilic acyl substitution of carboxylic acid derivatives, chloride ions and alkoxides also act as leaving groups.

about.h: What makes a good leaving group
about.p: A good leaving group is a weak base that can exist stably after departing. The guide is the pKa of its conjugate acid: the stronger the conjugate acid, the more easily it leaves. HI, HBr and HCl are strong acids, so I⁻, Br⁻ and Cl⁻ are good leaving groups, and in SN2 their ease of departure is I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ ≫ F⁻. TsO⁻, the anion of p-toluenesulfonic acid (pKa about −2.8), is also an excellent leaving group with its negative charge spread over three oxygens. In contrast, OH⁻, the conjugate base of water (pKa 15.7), alkoxides and amide ions hardly leave at all.

about.h: Turning a poor leaving group into a good one
about.p: The OH of an alcohol does not leave as it is, so it is converted into a good leaving group before reaction. Protonating the OH with a strong acid lets it leave as neutral water. Converting it to a tosylate with p-toluenesulfonyl chloride sulfonylates the O without breaking the C−O bond, giving an excellent leaving group while keeping the carbon's configuration. The subsequent SN2 inverts the configuration, so overall an inverted product is obtained. Conversion to the halide with thionyl chloride or phosphorus tribromide is also used.

about.h: When the leaving group changes the product
about.p: The leaving group affects not only the rate but also which product forms. In E2 reactions of substrates with a poor, bulky leaving group such as the trimethylammonio group, the less substituted alkene predominates (the Hofmann rule). Halides usually follow the Zaitsev rule, giving mainly the more substituted alkene, a contrast. The reactivity order of carboxylic acid derivatives, acid chloride > anhydride > ester > amide, can also be broadly explained by differences in the basicity of the departing group.

faq.q: How do you recognize a good leaving group?
faq.a: The weaker the base that the departing anion or molecule is, the better the leaving group. It is easy to judge by choosing those whose conjugate acid has a small pKa (is a strong acid).

faq.q: Why does OH leave with difficulty?
faq.a: Because the departing OH⁻ is a strong, unstable base. Protonate it with acid so it leaves as water, or convert it to a tosylate or halide before the reaction.

faq.q: What is the difference between a leaving group and a nucleophile?
faq.a: A nucleophile donates an electron pair to form a new bond; a leaving group departs taking an electron pair with it. Some species, such as I⁻, play both roles well.

ザイツェフ則.desc: The empirical rule that elimination gives as the major product the more stable alkene, with more alkyl groups on the double-bond carbons. It may not hold when a bulky base is used.

about.h: Which alkene becomes the major product
about.p: Zaitsev's rule is the empirical rule that when an elimination from an alkyl halide or similar compound can form a double bond in more than one position, the alkene with more alkyl groups on the double-bond carbons is the major product. It was reported in 1875 by the Russian chemist Zaitsev. For example, when 2-bromobutane reacts with sodium ethoxide, more 2-butene than 1-butene forms, and among the 2-butenes the sterically favored trans isomer predominates. The name is also spelled Saytzeff.

about.h: Why more substituted alkenes are favored
about.p: Alkenes become more stable as more alkyl groups are attached to the double bond. Comparing heats of hydrogenation shows this: disubstituted alkenes release less heat than monosubstituted ones, and trisubstituted less than disubstituted. The main reason is thought to be hyperconjugation, in which electrons of the C−H bonds of the alkyl groups flow into the π bond. In the E2 transition state the double bond has already partly formed, so the stability of the product is reflected in the energy of the transition state, and the pathway to the more stable alkene is faster.

Zaitsev's rule is only a tendency reflecting thermodynamic stability and does not always hold. In E2 reactions on cyclohexane rings, only hydrogens trans-diaxial to the leaving group can be removed. As a result, elimination of menthyl chloride with sodium ethoxide gives only the less substituted alkene, whereas its stereoisomer neomenthyl chloride gives mainly the more substituted alkene. With a poor leaving group such as fluoride, the more acidic hydrogens at the chain end are removed more readily, and more of the less substituted alkene forms.

To predict the product of an elimination, first list all removable β hydrogens and compare the degree of substitution of the alkene each would give. Then adjust the Zaitsev prediction for the size of the base, the type of leaving group, the ring conformation and so on. When an alkene that can conjugate, such as a conjugated diene or a styrene-type alkene, can form, stabilization by conjugation often takes priority over the degree of substitution. E1 reactions proceed through carbocations under conditions closer to equilibrium, and the Zaitsev product often predominates.

faq.q: What is the difference between Zaitsev's rule and Hofmann's rule?
faq.a: Zaitsev's rule describes the tendency for the more substituted, more stable alkene to predominate, and Hofmann's rule the tendency for the less substituted alkene to predominate. Bulky bases and eliminations of quaternary ammonium salts tend to follow Hofmann's rule.

faq.q: Does Zaitsev's rule hold in E1 reactions?
faq.a: In many cases, yes, because when a hydrogen leaves the carbocation, the direction that forms the more stable alkene is favored. However, if the carbocation rearranges, an alkene with an unexpected skeleton may form.

faq.q: Is Zaitsev's rule related to Markovnikov's rule?
faq.a: They are different rules. Zaitsev's rule predicts where the double bond forms in elimination, and Markovnikov's rule predicts which carbon receives the H when HX or a similar reagent adds to an alkene. They are similar in that both are explained by the pathway that forms a more stable product or intermediate being favored.

マルコフニコフ則.desc: The rule that when HX or a similar reagent adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the hydrogen atom goes to the carbon that already has more hydrogens. It is explained by the reaction passing through the more stable carbocation.

about.h: From empirical rule to mechanistic rule
about.p: Markovnikov's rule is an empirical rule formulated in 1870 by the Russian chemist Markovnikov to describe the direction in which hydrogen halides add to unsymmetrical alkenes. Its original form was “the halogen goes to the carbon with fewer hydrogens.” Today it is restated on a mechanistic basis: the electrophile adds to the π bond in the direction that gives the more stable carbocation. Stated this way, the same idea applies to substrates where counting hydrogens does not decide the outcome and to electrophiles other than H⁺.

Additions in the same direction are seen beyond hydrogen halides. In acid-catalyzed hydration, 2-methylpropene gives the tertiary alcohol 2-methyl-2-propanol. Oxymercuration–demercuration, in which mercury(II) acetate is added and the mercury is then removed with sodium borohydride, does not pass through a free carbocation, so it gives the Markovnikov alcohol without rearrangement. In the bromohydrins formed with bromine water, the OH group also ends up on the more substituted carbon.

about.h: When the rule does not apply
about.p: The radical addition of HBr in the presence of peroxides and hydroboration give anti-Markovnikov products. And when an electron-withdrawing group is next to the double bond, counting hydrogens predicts the opposite of the product actually formed. When HX adds to 3,3,3-trifluoropropene, a carbocation on the carbon right next to the CF3 group would be strongly destabilized, so the halogen goes to the terminal carbon. If you understand that the essence of the rule lies in the stability of the intermediate rather than in the number of hydrogens, such cases can also be predicted.

When the carbocation formed can become a more stable cation by a hydride or alkyl group moving from the neighboring carbon, the skeleton reorganizes during the addition. When hydrogen chloride adds to 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene, a secondary cation forms first, a neighboring methyl group shifts to give a tertiary cation, and the rearranged 2-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane forms in substantial amounts alongside the unrearranged 3-chloro-2,2-dimethylbutane. Both the product predicted by Markovnikov's rule and the rearranged product can be obtained, so it is important to check the carbon skeleton as well.

faq.q: What is anti-Markovnikov addition?
faq.a: Addition in the direction opposite to that predicted by Markovnikov's rule, with the hydrogen going to the more substituted carbon. Typical examples are the radical addition of HBr in the presence of peroxides and the synthesis of alcohols by hydroboration followed by oxidation.

faq.q: Does Markovnikov's rule apply to alkynes too?
faq.a: Yes. Adding two molecules of HX to a terminal alkyne gives a compound with both halogens on the same internal carbon. Hydration catalyzed by mercury(II) salts gives a methyl ketone.

faq.q: What happens when both carbons of the double bond carry the same number of substituents?
faq.a: Carbocations of almost the same stability form in either direction, so there is little regioselectivity. Adding HBr to 2-pentene gives a mixture of 2-bromopentane and 3-bromopentane.

ヒドロホウ素化.desc: A reaction in which the B−H bond of borane adds syn to an alkene. Subsequent oxidation with basic hydrogen peroxide gives the anti-Markovnikov alcohol with retention of configuration.

about.h: The boron chemistry that Brown opened up
about.p: Hydroboration is the addition of the B−H bond of a borane to an alkene or alkyne to give an organoboron compound. Brown developed it systematically in the 1950s and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1979. Borane BH3 exists on its own as the dimer diborane, so it is used as a complex with THF or dimethyl sulfide. All three B−H bonds of BH3 can add, so unless the alkene is crowded, one molecule of BH3 reacts with three molecules of alkene to give a trialkylborane.

The addition passes through a cyclic transition state in which four atoms rearrange their bonds at once, and boron goes to the less hindered, less substituted carbon. Because boron accepts electrons, the more substituted carbon carries a slight positive charge in the transition state, which also favors the same direction. With terminal alkenes, even BH3 places most of the boron on the terminal carbon, but bulky boranes such as 9-BBN and disiamylborane raise the selectivity further. Bulky boranes also help to distinguish conjugated dienes and multiple double bonds.

about.h: Transformations of the C−B bond beyond oxidation
about.p: In oxidation with basic hydrogen peroxide, a peroxide ion bonds to boron, an alkyl group then migrates from boron to oxygen with retention of configuration, and hydrolysis gives the alcohol. The C−B bond can be converted into many other functional groups as well. Treatment with a carboxylic acid gives a C−H bond, achieving a syn reduction of the alkene, and alkylboranes obtained with 9-BBN can be used in palladium-catalyzed Suzuki–Miyaura coupling. Hydroboration and oxidation of a terminal alkyne give an aldehyde via the enol.

Adding BH3 to α-pinene, which occurs in nature largely as one enantiomer, gives the chiral diisopinocampheylborane (Ipc2BH). Using it to hydroborate a prochiral alkene favors addition from one face, and an optically active alcohol is obtained after oxidation. Reported by Brown in 1961, it is an early landmark example of asymmetric synthesis without a catalyst. Today, methods in which catecholborane or pinacolborane is added catalytically with rhodium or other metal complexes are also used.

faq.q: Why does hydroboration not involve rearrangement?
faq.a: Because the B−H bond adds in a single concerted step without forming a carbocation. Unlike acid-catalyzed hydration, the carbon skeleton is not reorganized, and the OH group can be placed on the less substituted carbon.

faq.q: How many molecules of alkene does one molecule of BH3 react with?
faq.a: Three, as long as they are not crowded. With crowded alkenes it tends to stop at two (trisubstituted) or one (tetrasubstituted), and this property is used to make highly selective boranes such as disiamylborane and thexylborane.

faq.q: Why is the configuration retained in the oxidation?
faq.a: Because the oxidation proceeds by a rearrangement in which the carbon moves from boron to the neighboring oxygen together with the electron pair of the C−B bond. The carbon never becomes a planar intermediate with its bond broken, so the stereochemistry set in the addition is preserved.

芳香族求電子置換反応.desc: A reaction in which a hydrogen on a benzene ring is replaced by an electrophile, such as nitration, halogenation, sulfonation and the Friedel–Crafts reactions. It proceeds through a σ complex.

about.p: Alkenes add bromine rapidly, but benzene hardly reacts with bromine alone, and when a Lewis acid is added it undergoes substitution rather than addition. The intermediate formed when the electrophile takes up π electrons (the σ complex, or arenium ion) is an unstable cation that has lost its aromaticity, and the first step that forms it is slow and rate-determining. After that, releasing H⁺ to regain the aromatic ring is far more favorable than remaining as a nonaromatic adduct, so the overall product is one in which a hydrogen has been replaced.

Although the benzene ring is rich in electrons, it is stable, so a strong electrophile is needed. In halogenation, FeBr3 or AlCl3 polarizes the halogen molecule and delivers a positively polarized halogen to the ring. Iodine is unreactive, so an oxidant such as nitric acid is added, while fluorine reacts too violently to be used directly with ease. In sulfonation the electrophile is SO3 in fuming sulfuric acid, and in Friedel–Crafts reactions it is the carbocation or acylium ion formed from an alkyl halide or acyl halide and a Lewis acid.

Sulfonation is reversible: heating with dilute acid removes the sulfo group. Using this, the para position can be temporarily blocked with a sulfo group so that a substituent enters the ortho position, after which the sulfo group is removed (a blocking group). Friedel–Crafts reactions have many limitations: they do not proceed with strongly deactivated rings such as nitrobenzene, and with rings bearing an amino group the amine binds the Lewis acid and stops the reaction. In alkylation the product is more activated than the starting material, so multiple substitution occurs readily.

Substituents greatly change not only the position of substitution but also its rate. In competition experiments with nitric acid in acetic anhydride, nitration of toluene is about 25 times faster than that of benzene, and strong activating groups such as methoxy and hydroxy groups make it orders of magnitude faster still. Phenol reacts with bromine water without a catalyst to give a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol, which is used as a test for phenol. Conversely, a strong deactivating group such as a nitro group makes the reaction far slower than for benzene, and harsher conditions are needed.

faq.q: Why does benzene undergo substitution rather than addition?
faq.a: An addition product would lose the large stabilization of aromaticity, whereas loss of H⁺ from the σ complex restores the aromatic ring. The difference in product stability is what selects the substitution pathway.

faq.q: What is the Lewis acid catalyst added for?
faq.a: It coordinates to Br2, Cl2, alkyl halides and the like, polarizing the bond to create a strong electrophile that the benzene ring can attack. It acts as a catalyst when it is regenerated after the reaction.

faq.q: How does it differ from nucleophilic aromatic substitution?
faq.a: Nucleophilic substitution takes place on rings bearing a strong electron-withdrawing group such as a nitro group and a leaving group such as a halogen, through addition of a nucleophile to give a negatively charged intermediate. The partner the ring accepts and the charge of the intermediate are the reverse of electrophilic substitution.

配向性.desc: The property that decides where a new substituent enters in electrophilic substitution of a substituted benzene. Methyl and OH groups are ortho/para-directing, and nitro and carbonyl groups are meta-directing.

about.h: Substituents decide where the new group enters
about.p: When a substituted benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution, the position the new substituent enters is largely determined by the substituent already present.
