This property is the directing effect. −OH, −OCH3, −NH2 and alkyl groups are activating and ortho/para-directing; halogens slow the reaction yet are ortho/para-directing; and −NO2, −CN, −SO3H, −CHO, −COR, −COOR and −CF3 slow the reaction and are meta-directing. The directing effect and the rate (activation or deactivation) should be considered separately. Almost all activating groups are ortho/para-directing, and all meta-directing groups are deactivating.

about.h: Thinking with the resonance structures of the intermediate
about.p: The directing effect is explained by the stability of the intermediate (σ complex) formed when the electrophile adds. Attack at the ortho or para position gives a resonance structure with the positive charge on the carbon bearing the substituent. If the substituent is O or N with a lone pair, those electrons directly stabilize the positive charge, so ortho/para products are favored. Conversely, when a positively polarized atom is attached, as in a nitro group, that structure is strongly destabilized, so meta attack, in which that structure does not appear, is relatively favored.

There are two ortho positions and one para position, so statistically the ortho product should predominate, but the actual ratio changes with the size of the substituent. In the nitration of toluene, depending on conditions, the ortho product is around 60%, the para product 30–40% and the meta product a few per cent. The bulkier the substituent, the more crowded the ortho positions and the larger the share of para product. In the nitration of nitrobenzene, more than 90% is the meta product. When separation is needed, differences in the properties of the ortho and para products are exploited.

When making disubstituted benzenes, the order of introducing substituents is important. m-Bromonitrobenzene is made by nitration first, then bromination. p-Bromonitrobenzene is made by bromination first, then nitration, separating it from the ortho product. With two substituents, the directing effect of the stronger activator usually wins. Aniline becomes the anilinium ion in strong acid and is meta-directing, so it is sometimes acetylated to the amide before reaction. The amide nitrogen activates more mildly than the amino group, and the para product is obtained mainly.

faq.q: Why are halogens ortho/para-directing even though they are deactivating?
faq.a: The rate is lowered by their strong inductive effect (electron withdrawal), but the position of entry is decided by the lone pairs stabilizing the positive charge of the σ complex by resonance.

faq.q: How do you tell ortho/para directors from meta directors?
faq.a: If the atom attached to the ring has a lone pair, or the group is alkyl, it is ortho/para-directing. If the attached atom is positively polarized and multiply bonded to an electronegative atom, it is meta-directing.

faq.q: What happens with two substituents?
faq.a: Usually the directing effect of the stronger activator wins. Where both direct to the same position, substitution goes there, and crowded positions are entered less readily.

グリニャール試薬.desc: An organomagnesium compound, RMgX, made from an alkyl halide and magnesium in dry ether. It is a strong nucleophile and base, and it reacts with carbonyl compounds to give alcohols.

about.p: A Grignard reagent is an organomagnesium compound RMgX made by reacting an alkyl or aryl halide with magnesium in dry diethyl ether or THF. Grignard discovered it around 1900, and it was recognized by the 1912 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The C−Mg bond is strongly polarized with the carbon negative, so the normally electrophilic carbon of an alkyl halide is turned into a nucleophilic carbon. In solution, the ether coordinates to the magnesium and stabilizes the reagent. In solution, RMgX is in equilibrium with R2Mg and MgX2 (the Schlenk equilibrium).

The magnesium surface is covered with an oxide film, so the reaction is started by adding a little iodine or 1,2-dibromoethane, or by scratching to expose fresh metal. Once started, it is exothermic, so the halide is added gradually. Halide reactivity is I > Br > Cl, and aryl chlorides often need THF. Moisture destroys the reagent, so glassware is dried and the work is done under an inert gas such as nitrogen. Watch also for the Wurtz-type side reaction in which the reagent couples with the halide.

about.h: What it reacts with and what forms
about.p: Grignard reagents add to carbonyl carbons, and acid workup gives alcohols. Formaldehyde gives primary alcohols, other aldehydes secondary and ketones tertiary alcohols. Esters react with two equivalents to give tertiary alcohols bearing two identical groups. Reaction with carbon dioxide gives a carboxylic acid with one more carbon; with an epoxide, attack at the less hindered carbon gives an alcohol two carbons longer; and with a nitrile, a ketone is obtained after hydrolysis. For any of these, working backwards from the new C−C bond tells you which reagent and substrate are needed.

about.h: Its nature as a strong base
about.p: The carbon of a Grignard reagent is also a very strong base and reacts at once with any acid stronger than its conjugate acid, the alkane (pKa about 50). If water, alcohols, carboxylic acids, terminal alkynes or amines with N−H are present in the same molecule or solvent, the reagent is turned into alkane and lost. For this reason, OH groups and the like are protected, for example as silyl ethers, before the reagent is made. With sterically crowded ketones, the reagent may remove an α-hydrogen instead of adding, giving an enolate and returning the starting ketone.

faq.q: Why must water be avoided in Grignard reactions?
faq.a: Water protonates the Grignard reagent and turns it into an alkane. This is an acid–base reaction, not oxidation, and the O−H of alcohols and carboxylic acids destroys the reagent in the same way.

faq.q: What does a Grignard reagent form with an ester?
faq.a: The first equivalent adds to give a ketone, which is more reactive, so a second equivalent adds at once. Acid workup gives a tertiary alcohol with two identical alkyl groups.

faq.q: Why is ether used as the solvent?
faq.a: The ether oxygen coordinates to magnesium, dissolving and stabilizing the reagent, and ether has no acidic hydrogens. Diethyl ether and THF are commonly used.

アルドール反応.desc: A reaction in which an enolate adds as a nucleophile to another carbonyl compound, giving a β-hydroxy carbonyl compound. On heating it dehydrates to an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compound.

about.h: Reversible addition and condensation by dehydration
about.p: Aldol addition is reversible, and the product is not always much more stable than the starting materials. Between two aldehydes the adduct is often favored, but between two ketones the equilibrium lies toward the starting materials; diacetone alcohol from acetone amounts to only a few percent at equilibrium. When heat, acid, or base dehydrates the adduct to a conjugated α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compound, the reaction practically stops running backward (aldol condensation). In glycolysis, the enzyme aldolase uses a retro-aldol reaction to split a six-carbon sugar into two three-carbon sugars.

If two different carbonyl compounds are mixed and base is added, each can act as both the enolate and the acceptor, giving a mixture of four products. To avoid this, one partner is chosen to have no α hydrogens, such as benzaldehyde or formaldehyde. The Claisen–Schmidt condensation of benzaldehyde with acetone to give benzalacetone is an example. Other approaches include forming one enolate completely with a strong base before adding the partner, and the Mukaiyama aldol reaction (1973), which uses a silyl enol ether and a Lewis acid.

An aldol reaction creates two stereocenters at once, giving syn and anti diastereomers. Zimmerman and Traxler proposed that a metal-bound enolate and the aldehyde pass through a chair-like six-membered transition state, which explains why Z enolates give syn products and E enolates give anti products. With boron enolates, whose bonds are short, this selectivity is especially high. Enantiomers can also be made selectively, by Evans's method with a chiral oxazolidinone auxiliary or by organocatalytic reactions using proline as the catalyst.

about.h: Roles in synthesis and in living things
about.p: Because the aldol reaction forms a C−C bond while keeping an oxygen functional group, it is central to the synthesis of polyketide natural products, which carry many hydroxy groups. The Robinson annulation, a Michael addition to a ketone followed by an intramolecular aldol condensation to form a six-membered ring, has long been used to build frameworks such as steroids. Aldolases in living cells come in two classes: class I, in which a lysine residue forms an imine with the carbonyl group and the reaction goes through an enamine, and class II, which uses a zinc ion to stabilize the enolate.

faq.q: What is the difference between aldol addition and aldol condensation?
faq.a: Aldol addition is the reversible reaction that stops at the β-hydroxy carbonyl compound. Aldol condensation goes further, losing water to give an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compound, and proceeds with heating or under harsher conditions.

faq.q: Why do aldol reactions between two ketones proceed poorly?
faq.a: A ketone carbonyl is more crowded than an aldehyde's and electronically less electrophilic, so the adduct gains less stabilization and the equilibrium lies toward the starting materials. The reaction is driven by dehydration or by removing the product from the system.

faq.q: Do aldol reactions also occur under acidic conditions?
faq.a: Yes. Under acidic conditions the enol, instead of the enolate, acts as the nucleophile and adds to the protonated carbonyl group. Dehydration is also fast in acid, so the reaction tends to go on to the α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compound.

けん化.desc: Hydrolysis of an ester with a base such as sodium hydroxide to give a carboxylate salt and an alcohol. The carboxylate formed does not undergo the reverse reaction, so it goes almost to completion.

about.p: Saponification is the hydrolysis of an ester with a base such as sodium or potassium hydroxide to give a salt of the carboxylic acid and an alcohol. The name comes from boiling fats (glycerol esters of fatty acids) with base to make soap (sodium salts of fatty acids) and glycerol. As in RCOOR' + NaOH → RCOONa + R'OH, hydroxide is a reagent consumed in one equivalent, not a catalyst. When the carboxylic acid itself is wanted, a strong acid is added after the reaction to acidify the mixture.

Hydroxide attacks the ester's carbonyl carbon to give a negatively charged tetrahedral intermediate, from which an alkoxide departs to give a carboxylic acid. The carboxylic acid (pKa about 4–5) reacts at once with base to become a carboxylate ion, which has lost its electrophilicity and does not react with the alcohol to return. Unlike acid-catalyzed hydrolysis, which stops at equilibrium, saponification therefore goes almost to completion. Experiments with ¹⁸O labeling showed that the bond broken is the one between the acyl group and oxygen.

about.h: Using the saponification value to examine fats
about.p: The mass (mg) of potassium hydroxide needed to saponify 1 g of fat is called the saponification value. One triglyceride molecule has three ester bonds, so three molecules of KOH are needed. For triolein (molar mass 885.4 g/mol), for example, it is 3 × 56.11 × 1000 ÷ 885.4 ≈ 190. The shorter the fatty-acid chains and the lower their average molar mass, the larger the saponification value. In measurement, the fat is saponified with excess KOH, the remaining KOH is back-titrated with hydrochloric acid, and the value is found from the difference from a blank.

The rate of saponification is first order in both ester and hydroxide, second order overall. Esters with a more hindered carbonyl carbon react more slowly, and electron-withdrawing groups on an aromatic ring stabilize the tetrahedral intermediate and speed the reaction. Amides are saponified far less readily than esters and need strong heating. In synthesis, carboxylic acids protected as methyl or ethyl esters are often released by gentle saponification with lithium hydroxide or the like. When groups that hydrolyze easily are present, temperature and the amount of base are kept low.

faq.q: What is the difference between saponification and hydrolysis?
faq.a: Saponification is the hydrolysis of an ester using a base, and the product is a salt of the carboxylic acid. Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis stops at equilibrium, but saponification goes almost to completion.

faq.q: What is the saponification value?
faq.a: The number of mg of potassium hydroxide needed to saponify 1 g of fat. It is larger for fats with shorter fatty-acid chains and serves as an indicator for distinguishing types of fat.

faq.q: How do you obtain the carboxylic acid after saponification?
faq.a: Add a strong acid such as hydrochloric acid to the aqueous solution of the carboxylate salt to make it acidic. The free carboxylic acid is recovered by extraction or filtration; acids poorly soluble in water are obtained as a precipitate.

ランベルト・ベールの法則.desc: The law that the absorbance A is proportional to the concentration c of the absorbing substance and the path length l: A = εcl, where ε is the molar absorptivity. It is the basis of quantitation by UV-Vis absorption spectrophotometry.

about.p: The Beer–Lambert law states that the absorbance A is proportional to the molar concentration c of the absorbing substance and the path length l, written A = εcl. The proportionality constant ε is the molar absorptivity, set by the substance, the wavelength and the solvent. Absorbance is defined as A = −log T = log(I₀/I) and is found from the incident intensity I₀ and the transmitted intensity I. Transmittance T falls exponentially with concentration, so absorbance, which is proportional to concentration, is used for quantitation. A transmittance of 10% corresponds to an absorbance of 1.0, and 1% to 2.0.

The basic approach is to measure the absorbance of standards of known concentration to make a calibration curve and then find the concentration from the sample's absorbance. If ε is known, you can also calculate directly with c = A/(εl). For example, for a compound with ε = 1.5×10⁴ L/(mol·cm), A = 0.45 in a cell with a 1.00 cm path length gives c = 3.0×10⁻⁵ mol/L. If the absorbance is too high, the transmitted light becomes weak and errors grow, so you bring it into a convenient range by diluting or using a cell with a shorter path, then multiply by the factor to recover the original value.

At high concentrations, interactions and aggregation between molecules and changes in refractive index make absorbance no longer proportional to concentration. Other causes of deviation from linearity are light from the monochromator that is not perfectly monochromatic, stray light, scattering from turbid samples, fluorescence of the sample, and chemical equilibria such as dissociation and complexation that change the concentration of the absorbing species. When several components absorb at the same wavelength, the additivity of absorbance (the total is the sum of the components) is used: measuring at several wavelengths and solving simultaneous equations gives each component's concentration.

faq.q: What are the units of molar absorptivity?
faq.a: With concentration in mol/L and path length in cm, ε has units of L/(mol·cm). Absorbance A is dimensionless.

faq.q: How do you convert between transmittance and absorbance?
faq.a: A = −log T. A transmittance of 10% gives A = 1.0, 1% gives A = 2.0, and 50% gives A ≈ 0.30.

faq.q: Why use absorbance rather than transmittance?
faq.a: Because absorbance is proportional to concentration and path length, the calibration curve is a straight line and calculations are easy. Transmittance changes exponentially with concentration.

波数.desc: The number of waves per centimeter, the reciprocal of the wavelength (unit cm⁻¹). It is proportional to energy. IR mainly covers 4000–400 cm⁻¹. λ (µm) = 10000/wavenumber.

about.p: The wavenumber ν̃ is the number of waves contained in a length of 1 cm, the reciprocal of the wavelength λ (ν̃ = 1/λ). Its unit is cm⁻¹, sometimes read as the kayser. A photon's energy is proportional to the wavenumber, E = hcν̃, so wavenumber can be used as a measure of energy. 1 eV corresponds to about 8066 cm⁻¹, and the thermal energy kBT at 25 °C is about 207 cm⁻¹. Infrared spectroscopy uses wavenumber more than wavelength because it is proportional to energy and gives convenient numbers in the hundreds to thousands.

The conversion to wavelength is λ(µm) = 10000/ν̃(cm⁻¹); the mid-infrared 4000–400 cm⁻¹ corresponds to 2.5–25 µm. For example, 1700 cm⁻¹ is about 5.88 µm. The frequency ν is ν = cν̃; with the speed of light c in cm/s, 3000 cm⁻¹ is about 9.0×10¹³ Hz. Frequency is the number of oscillations per second and wavenumber the number of waves per length: despite similar names they are different quantities. In Raman spectroscopy, the difference in wavenumber between incident and scattered light (the Raman shift) is expressed in cm⁻¹.

Treating a molecular vibration as a harmonic oscillator gives ν̃ = (1/2πc)√(k/μ): the larger the bond force constant k, the higher the wavenumber, and the larger the reduced mass μ, the lower. So stronger bonds appear at higher wavenumbers, as in C≡N (about 2250 cm⁻¹) > C=O (about 1715 cm⁻¹) > C−O (about 1100 cm⁻¹), and O−H and C−H, containing light hydrogen, appear at high wavenumbers around 3000 cm⁻¹. Replacing hydrogen with deuterium lowers the C−H stretch at about 3000 cm⁻¹ to about 2200 cm⁻¹.

IR spectra are usually drawn with high wavenumber (4000 cm⁻¹) on the left and low wavenumber on the right. Above about 1500 cm⁻¹, characteristic absorptions of individual functional groups appear and are used for assignment. Below about 1500 cm⁻¹, many vibrations overlap to give a pattern unique to each compound, so this is called the fingerprint region and is used for matching against spectra of known substances. Absorption positions shift with hydrogen bonding, conjugation, ring strain and so on, so read the typical values on the understanding that they have ranges.

faq.q: What is the difference between wavenumber and frequency?
faq.a: Wavenumber is the number of waves per 1 cm (cm⁻¹); frequency is the number of oscillations per second (Hz). They are converted with the speed of light c as ν = cν̃, and both are proportional to energy.

faq.q: How do you convert wavenumber to wavelength?
faq.a: λ(µm) = 10000/ν̃(cm⁻¹). 2000 cm⁻¹ is 5.0 µm, and 1000 cm⁻¹ is 10 µm. In nm, it is 10⁷/ν̃.

faq.q: Does a larger wavenumber mean higher energy?
faq.a: Yes. Since E = hcν̃, energy increases in proportion to wavenumber. The relationship to wavelength is the reverse: the shorter the wavelength, the larger the wavenumber.

吸光度.desc: A quantity expressing how strongly a sample absorbs light: A = −log T = log(I₀/I). A transmittance of 10% gives A = 1.0. It is proportional to concentration and path length, so it is used for quantitation.

about.p: Absorbance A is defined from the intensity of light entering the sample, I₀, and of the transmitted light, I, as A = log(I₀/I) = −log T, and it has no units. A transmittance T of 10% gives A = 1.0, 1% gives 2.0 and 50% gives about 0.30. Each increase of 1 in absorbance cuts the transmitted light to one tenth. It is a different quantity from the fraction of light absorbed (1 − T); for example, A = 0.30 means about half the light is absorbed. A spectrophotometer uses a cell containing only the solvent as the reference and displays the sample's absorbance as the difference.

According to the Beer–Lambert law A = εcl, absorbance is proportional to the concentration c of the absorbing substance and the path length l. This is why quantitation uses absorbance rather than transmittance. For example, the molar absorption coefficient of NADH at 340 nm is about 6.22×10³ L/(mol·cm), so A = 0.311 in a 1 cm cell corresponds to a concentration of about 5.0×10⁻⁵ mol/L. When several components absorb at the same wavelength, the absorbance is the sum of their absorbances (additivity). Using this, the components of a mixture can be quantified by solving simultaneous equations.

about.h: The range of absorbance suited to measurement
about.p: If the absorbance is too small, the difference between I₀ and I is slight and errors are large; if it is too large, the transmitted light is too weak and strongly affected by stray light. Assuming a constant error in reading transmittance, the relative error in concentration is smallest at A ≈ 0.43, and in practice a range of about 0.2–0.8 is often used as a guide. At high absorbance, stray light makes the measured value level off below the true value. When outside the range, dilute the sample or change to a cell with a different path length.

The value a spectrophotometer shows includes not only light that was absorbed but also light scattered by particles that did not reach the detector. The "OD600" used to measure the turbidity of bacterial cultures at 600 nm is mostly an apparent absorbance due to scattering, and its value depends on the instrument's optics. When quantifying a turbid sample by absorbance, remove the particles by filtration or centrifugation, or subtract the value at a wavelength where the analyte does not absorb. An absorbance defined with the natural logarithm is about 2.303 times the common-log value, so check the definition used in the literature.

faq.q: Does absorbance have units?
faq.a: No. It is the logarithm of a ratio of light intensities, so it is dimensionless. It is sometimes labeled "Abs", but that indicates absorbance rather than a unit.

faq.q: How do you convert between absorbance and transmittance?
faq.a: Use A = −log T. A transmittance of 10% gives A = 1.0, 1% gives 2.0 and 50% about 0.30. Conversely T = 10 to the power −A, so A = 0.5 corresponds to a transmittance of about 32%.

faq.q: Can absorbance above 2 not be measured?
faq.a: It can be measured, but the transmitted light is weak, under 1%, and linearity tends to suffer from stray light. For quantitation, dilute the sample or use a shorter path-length cell to bring it into range.

モル吸光係数.desc: The proportionality constant ε in the Beer–Lambert law, A = εcl, in L/(mol·cm). It depends on the substance, wavelength and solvent; the larger it is, the more strongly even a small amount absorbs.

about.h: A number expressing the probability of absorption
about.p: The molar absorptivity ε expresses how readily light of a given wavelength is absorbed by a molecule, as the absorbance of a 1 mol/L solution measured with a 1 cm path length. Converted to the absorption cross section σ (cm²) per molecule, σ = 2303ε/NA ≈ 3.82×10⁻²¹ × ε, so ε = 1×10⁴ L/(mol·cm) corresponds to about 3.8×10⁻¹⁷ cm². In SI units it may be expressed in m²/mol, with 1 L/(mol·cm) = 0.1 m²/mol. IUPAC recommends the name molar absorption coefficient, and older literature sometimes calls it the molar extinction coefficient.

about.h: The size of the value reveals the kind of transition
about.p: The size of ε reflects the kind of electronic transition responsible for an absorption. Allowed transitions, such as the π→π* transitions of conjugated polyenes, give large values; β-carotene exceeds 10⁵ at about 450 nm in the visible region. By contrast, the d−d transitions seen in aqueous solutions of transition-metal ions are forbidden by the Laporte rule, and most have small values of 100 or less. The intensity of a whole band is sometimes compared using the oscillator strength f, which is proportional to ε integrated over wavenumber: f ≈ 4.32×10⁻⁹ × ∫ε dν̃, and for allowed transitions f approaches 1.

The reliable way to find ε is to measure solutions of different concentrations made from a sample of known purity and take the slope of the absorbance–concentration line. Finding it from a single point carries weighing and dilution errors straight into the result. ε also changes with solvent, pH and temperature, and for substances involved in acid–base or association equilibria it must be stated which form the value refers to. In addition, if the spectral bandwidth of the instrument is wide compared with the width of the band, the peak value of a sharp band is measured too low. When using literature values, check that the measurement conditions match.

Protein concentrations are often found from the absorbance at 280 nm. Here ε is widely estimated from the amino acid sequence by summing 5500 L/(mol·cm) per tryptophan, 1490 per tyrosine and 125 per cystine (the method of Pace and coworkers). For nucleic acids, a mass-based coefficient is used instead of the molar absorptivity, with the rule of thumb that an absorbance of 1.0 at 260 nm corresponds to about 50 µg/mL of double-stranded DNA. In both cases, watch out for turbidity and absorption by contaminants.

faq.q: Are molar absorptivity and molar absorption coefficient the same thing?
faq.a: They refer to the same quantity. IUPAC recommends “molar absorption coefficient,” but “molar absorptivity” is also widely used, and older literature calls it the “molar extinction coefficient.”

faq.q: Why can substances with large ε be measured down to lower concentrations?
faq.a: Because the same concentration gives a larger absorbance. With ε = 1×10⁵, even 1×10⁻⁶ mol/L gives an absorbance of 0.1 in a 1 cm cell, which lies in the range that can be measured accurately.

faq.q: How is ε for a protein determined?
faq.a: Measuring it on the purified protein is most reliable, but it is usually calculated from the numbers of tryptophan, tyrosine and cystine residues in the sequence. The environment within the folded structure shifts the value by a few percent, so for exact quantitation it is compared with a measured value.

蛍光量子収率.desc: The ratio of the number of photons emitted as fluorescence to the number of photons a molecule absorbs, a value between 0 and 1. It is often determined by the relative method, comparing with a reference of known quantum yield.

about.h: The fraction of absorbed light that becomes fluorescence
about.p: The fluorescence quantum yield Φ is the ratio of the number of photons emitted as fluorescence to the number of photons absorbed by a molecule, taking values from 0 to 1. Excited molecules return to the ground state not only by emitting fluorescence but also by internal conversion, losing energy as heat, by intersystem crossing to a triplet state, and by quenching by other molecules. With kr the rate constant for fluorescence and knr the sum of the rate constants for all other deactivation, Φ = kr/(kr + knr). Which pathway is fastest makes fluorescence intensity vary greatly even among molecules that absorb light similarly.

The excited-state lifetime τ is 1/(kr + knr), so Φ = kr·τ. Measuring both the quantum yield and the lifetime lets you separate the rate constant for fluorescence from that for other deactivation. For example, if Φ = 0.80 and τ = 4.0 ns, then kr = 0.80/4.0 ns = 2.0×10⁸ s⁻¹ and knr = 5.0×10⁷ s⁻¹. When adding a quencher lowers Φ, a lifetime shortened by the same proportion indicates dynamic quenching by collisions, while an unchanged lifetime indicates static quenching by complex formation in the ground state.

In the commonly used relative method, a reference with known quantum yield (such as quinine sulfate or fluorescein) and the sample are measured under the same conditions, and Φ = Φref × (F/Fref) × (Aref/A) × (n²/nref²). F is the integrated fluorescence intensity, A the absorbance at the excitation wavelength and n the refractive index of the solvent. To avoid inner-filter effects, measurements are made on dilute solutions with absorbance of about 0.1 or less. With an integrating sphere, the quantum yield can also be obtained by an absolute method that directly counts absorbed and emitted photons without a reference.

about.h: Structure and environment that govern quantum yield
about.p: The more rigid the molecular framework, the more thermal deactivation by vibration and rotation is suppressed, and quantum yields tend to be higher. Fluorescein, whose framework is locked by an oxygen bridge, shows strong fluorescence as an example. In molecules containing heavy atoms, intersystem crossing becomes faster and fluorescence weakens, and dissolved oxygen also causes quenching. Values also change with temperature, solvent and pH. In designing fluorescent probes and OLED materials, brightness, the product of quantum yield and molar absorption coefficient, is used as a measure of performance.

faq.q: Can the fluorescence quantum yield exceed 1?
faq.a: At most one fluorescence photon is emitted per photon absorbed, so ordinary fluorescence does not exceed 1. If a value above 1 is obtained, suspect errors in the reference, absorbance or refractive index correction.

faq.q: Why keep the absorbance low when measuring quantum yield?
faq.a: At high absorbance, inner-filter effects, in which excitation light is absorbed near the entrance of the cell or fluorescence is reabsorbed, make the fluorescence intensity no longer proportional to the amount of light absorbed.

faq.q: Are quantum yield and fluorescence brightness the same?
faq.a: No. Brightness is determined by the product of how much light is absorbed (the molar absorption coefficient) and how much of it becomes fluorescence (the quantum yield).

ストークスシフト.desc: The difference between the maximum of the absorption (excitation) spectrum and the maximum of the fluorescence spectrum. Because part of the energy is lost by vibrational relaxation and the like in the excited state, fluorescence appears on the long-wavelength side.

about.h: The gap between absorption and fluorescence
about.p: The Stokes shift is the difference between the maximum of the absorption (excitation) spectrum and the maximum of the fluorescence spectrum. It is named after Stokes, who reported in 1852 that a quinine solution absorbs ultraviolet light and emits blue light whose wavelength is longer than that of the light shone on it. The difference is properly expressed in wavenumbers (cm⁻¹), which are proportional to energy; for example, with an absorption maximum at 490 nm and a fluorescence maximum at 515 nm the difference is 25 nm, or about 990 cm⁻¹. A difference in nm looks larger in the long-wavelength region even for the same energy difference.

about.h: Two relaxations that create the shift
about.p: Just after absorbing light, a molecule is in a high vibrational level of the excited state, with the same nuclear arrangement and solvent orientation as in the ground state (the Franck–Condon principle). Before it fluoresces, the molecule's structure changes to a shape suited to the excited state, and the surrounding solvent molecules also reorient to suit the new charge distribution, losing part of the energy as heat. The more a molecule's dipole moment changes on excitation, the larger its Stokes shift in polar solvents, a relation described by the Lippert–Mataga equation.

It is not true that fluorescence never appears at shorter wavelengths than the excitation light. Emission from molecules that are thermally vibrationally excited, and upconversion in which two photons are absorbed in turn, can give light on the short-wavelength side (anti-Stokes emission). The lines on the long-wavelength side of the incident light in Raman scattering are called Stokes lines, and those on the short-wavelength side anti-Stokes lines, for the same reason. Fluorescence spectra are also often roughly mirror images of absorption spectra, so comparing the shapes, not just the difference between maxima, makes interpretation easier.

about.h: A guide to choosing fluorescent dyes
about.p: With dyes that have a small Stokes shift, scattered excitation light tends to overlap the fluorescence, and the dye can reabsorb the fluorescence it emits. Bright dyes such as fluorescein and rhodamine have rather small shifts of about 20–30 nm. For microscopy imaging and simultaneous multicolor detection, dyes with larger shifts are therefore preferred. Dyes in which a proton moves within the molecule in the excited state, and dyes whose charge becomes strongly polarized on excitation, have been designed with shifts of 100 nm or more.

faq.q: Should the Stokes shift be expressed in nm or in cm⁻¹?
faq.a: To compare energy differences, cm⁻¹ is appropriate. Differences in nm are easy to grasp and widely used, but the same energy difference gives a larger value for longer-wavelength dyes, so take care when comparing dyes at different wavelengths.

faq.q: What is the benefit of a large Stokes shift?
faq.a: Fluorescence is easier to separate from scattered excitation light and stray light, so filters can cut the background. Reabsorption between dye molecules is also less likely, which helps with concentrated samples and multicolor detection.

faq.q: Why does the Stokes shift change with the solvent?
faq.a: For molecules whose dipole moment increases in the excited state, polar solvent molecules align and stabilize the excited state, lowering the energy of the fluorescence. This property is used in probes that report the polarity of their surroundings.

化学シフト.desc: In NMR, the shift in resonance position caused by differences in shielding by the electrons around a nucleus. It is expressed in ppm relative to TMS (δ 0) and is larger near highly electronegative atoms.

about.p: In NMR, the electrons around a nucleus slightly cancel (shield) the external magnetic field, so even nuclei of the same kind have slightly different resonance frequencies depending on their chemical environment. The chemical shift δ expresses this difference as the offset from the reference compound tetramethylsilane (TMS), in Hz, divided by the spectrometer frequency in MHz; its unit is ppm. Expressed in ppm, the value is the same regardless of the field strength of the instrument; for example, an offset of 2920 Hz on a 400 MHz instrument is δ 7.30.

Rough ¹H NMR values are δ 0.9–1.7 for alkane C−H, 2–2.7 for C−H next to a carbonyl or benzene ring, 3.3–4.5 for C−H on carbons bearing oxygen or halogen, 4.5–6.5 for alkene C−H, 6.5–8.5 for aromatic C−H, 9–10 for aldehydes and 10–13 for carboxylic acid O−H. The closer a highly electronegative atom, the weaker the shielding and the larger δ becomes (further downfield). When several electron-withdrawing groups act together, their effects roughly add up.

The π electrons of benzene rings, C=O and C=C set up ring currents and the like in a magnetic field, strengthening or weakening the field depending on location (magnetic anisotropy). This is why aromatic and aldehyde protons appear especially far downfield. ¹³C NMR chemical shifts span a wide range, about 0–220 ppm: sp³ carbons appear at 0–90, aromatic and alkene carbons at 100–160 and carbonyl carbons around 160–220 ppm. Because the range is so wide, signals rarely overlap in ¹³C spectra.

faq.q: What do downfield and upfield mean?
faq.a: The side with larger δ (the left of the spectrum) is called downfield, and the side with smaller δ (the right) upfield. The less shielded a proton, the further downfield it appears.

faq.q: Why is it expressed in ppm?
faq.a: Because the offset in resonance frequency (Hz) is proportional to the field strength of the instrument, dividing by the spectrometer frequency to get ppm gives values that can be compared on any instrument.

faq.q: Why does the position of O−H and N−H signals vary?
faq.a: Because the extent of hydrogen bonding changes with concentration, solvent and temperature, and proton exchange also occurs. Adding D2O exchanges H for D and makes the signal disappear, which is useful for confirming assignments.

スピン結合.desc: The phenomenon in which nearby nonequivalent nuclei split each other's signals through the bonding electrons. With n equivalent protons next door, a signal splits into n+1 lines.

about.p: Spin–spin coupling is the phenomenon in which nearby magnetically nonequivalent nuclei slightly change the field each other feels through the bonding electrons. Depending on whether the spin of a neighboring proton is aligned with or against the field, the resonance frequency of the observed proton shifts slightly, so its signal splits into several lines. The spacing of the splitting is called the coupling constant J and is expressed in Hz. J is determined by molecular structure and is independent of the instrument's field strength, so it provides structural clues.

With n equivalent protons on the neighboring carbon, a signal splits into n + 1 lines, with intensities following Pascal's triangle (doublet 1:1, triplet 1:2:1, quartet 1:3:3:1). In an ethyl group, the CH3 becomes a triplet from the neighboring CH2 and the CH2 a quartet from the neighboring CH3, a combination that marks an ethyl group. In an isopropyl group, the two CH3 groups are a doublet and the CH a septet. Chemically equivalent protons do not split each other.

The size of J reflects the number of bonds between the nuclei and their angles. Coupling between protons on adjacent carbons (³J) is usually about 6–8 Hz, but in alkenes the trans arrangement gives about 12–18 Hz and the cis arrangement about 6–12 Hz, a difference used to assign E/Z geometry. In cyclohexanes, the coupling between two axial protons is large, about 8–13 Hz, which helps assign conformations. Coupling to several kinds of protons with different coupling constants gives patterns such as a doublet of doublets rather than the simple n + 1 form.

faq.q: When can the n+1 rule be used?
faq.a: When all the neighboring protons couple with nearly the same J. Coupling to two kinds of protons (n and m of them) with different coupling constants gives up to (n+1)(m+1) lines.

faq.q: Why is an OH proton often not split?
faq.a: In many solvents the OH proton exchanges rapidly between molecules, so its coupling to neighboring protons is averaged away and it appears as a broad singlet.

faq.q: Does the coupling constant J change with the instrument?
faq.a: No. The difference in chemical shift expressed in Hz, on the other hand, grows in proportion to the spectrometer frequency, so multiplets overlap less on higher-field instruments.

分子イオンピーク.desc: In a mass spectrum, the peak due to the radical cation M⁺· formed when one electron is removed from the molecule. Its m/z gives the molecular weight. It is not necessarily the base peak.

about.p: In electron ionization (EI) mass spectrometry, vaporized molecules are hit with electrons of about 70 eV, knocking one electron out of the molecule to form the radical cation M⁺·. This is called the molecular ion, and its m/z equals the nominal molecular weight calculated with the most abundant isotopes. The molecular-ion peak tells you the compound's molecular weight directly and is the first peak to check in structure determination. It is not necessarily the most intense peak (the base peak), however, and for compounds that fragment easily it may be almost invisible.

Just to the right of the molecular ion appear small peaks from molecules containing heavier isotopes. The natural abundance of ¹³C is about 1.1%, so for a molecule with n carbons the M+1 peak is roughly 1.1n% of M. Chlorine occurs as ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl in about a 3:1 ratio and bromine as ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br in about 1:1, so molecules containing one of these show characteristic pairs of peaks, M:M+2 ≈ 3:1 and 1:1 respectively, which help determine whether halogens are present and how many.

about.h: The nitrogen rule and soft ionization
about.p: For molecules made of C, H, N, O and similar elements, an odd number of nitrogens gives an odd molecular weight, and zero or an even number gives an even one (the nitrogen rule). When the molecular ion is too weak to give the molecular weight, soft ionization such as chemical ionization (CI) or electrospray ionization (ESI) is used, and the molecular weight is found from the protonated molecule [M+H]⁺ or the sodium adduct [M+Na]⁺. Measuring the accurate mass by high-resolution MS can then narrow things down to the molecular formula.

faq.q: Are the molecular-ion peak and the base peak the same?
faq.a: Not necessarily. The base peak is the most intense peak in the spectrum and is often a stable fragment ion. In neopentane, for example, m/z 57 is the base peak, and the molecular ion (m/z 72) is barely visible.

faq.q: How do you recognize the molecular-ion peak?
faq.a: Check that it is on the highest-m/z side of the spectrum, that there are no neighboring peaks at chemically impossible mass differences such as 3–14 below it, and that it is consistent with the nitrogen rule and isotope patterns.

faq.q: Are the peaks in an ESI spectrum also molecular ions?
faq.a: In ESI, mainly [M+H]⁺, [M−H]⁻ and adduct ions are observed, which strictly are not radical-cation molecular ions. Subtract the mass of the added ion from the m/z to find the molecular weight.

窒素ルール.desc: The rule that for molecules made of C, H, N, O and similar elements, an odd number of nitrogen atoms gives an odd molecular weight, and zero or an even number gives an even one. Used in interpreting molecular ions.

about.h: Combinations of mass and valence for each element
about.p: The nitrogen rule follows from the parity of the integer masses and valences of the main isotopes. Hydrogen has mass 1 and valence 1, carbon 12 and 4, oxygen 16 and 2, the halogen ³⁵Cl 35 and 1, sulfur ³²S 32 and 2, silicon 28 and 4, and phosphorus 31 and 3, so in every case mass and valence have the same parity. Only nitrogen has an even mass, 14, but an odd valence, 3, so the molecular mass is odd only when there is an odd number of nitrogen atoms. The rule therefore applies unchanged to molecules containing halogens, sulfur, phosphorus or silicon.

The molecular ion is an odd-electron ion with an unpaired electron, but most fragments formed by simple bond cleavage are even-electron ions, and their parity is reversed. For a compound without nitrogen, the molecular ion appears at an even m/z and even-electron fragments at odd m/z. Primary amines often show CH2=NH2⁺ at m/z 30 from cleavage of the bond next to nitrogen; as an even-electron ion containing one nitrogen, it is even. Odd-electron ions formed when a neutral molecule is lost with rearrangement keep the original parity.

The rule holds for the integer masses of ions made only of the main isotopes. In deuterium-labeled compounds, deuterium, with mass 2 and valence 1, reverses the parity. For example, the molecular ion of chloroform CHCl3 is at m/z 118, but CDCl3 appears at 119, odd even though there is no nitrogen. When the molecular mass goes well beyond a thousand, the fractional parts of hydrogen's mass add up and reading the integer mass becomes ambiguous. Nor can the rule be applied as it stands to metal-containing complexes or multiply charged ions.

If the peak at the highest m/z in an electron ionization spectrum is odd, it is either a molecular ion containing an odd number of nitrogens or a fragment that is not the molecular ion at all. Judge this together with the isotope peak pattern and the absence of impossible mass differences. With soft ionization, [M+H]⁺ and [M+Na]⁺ dominate, so subtract the attached ion to get back to the molecular mass before applying the rule. When narrowing down candidate formulas with high-resolution mass spectrometry, the parity condition also reduces the number of candidates.

faq.q: With two nitrogen atoms, is the molecular mass even or odd?
faq.a: Even. With zero or an even number of nitrogens the molecular mass is even. For example, urea CH4N2O is 60 and pyrazine C4H4N2 is 80; both contain two nitrogens and are even.

faq.q: Can it be used for compounds containing halogens or sulfur?
faq.a: Yes. Chlorine, bromine and iodine have odd mass and odd valence, and sulfur has even mass and even valence, so they do not change the parity relation. The integer mass, however, is calculated with the most abundant isotopes.

faq.q: If the molecular mass is odd, does the compound always contain nitrogen?
faq.a: For molecules made of C, H, O, halogens, S, P and Si, it contains an odd number of nitrogens. This assumes, however, that the observed ion is the molecular ion and that there is no labeling with deuterium or the like.

マクラファティ転位.desc: A rearrangement in mass spectrometry in which a γ-hydrogen moves to the carbonyl oxygen, the α–β bond breaks and a neutral alkene is lost. 2-Hexanone gives an ion at m/z 58.

about.h: A γ hydrogen moves and a neutral molecule leaves
about.p: The McLafferty rearrangement is a representative rearrangement seen in electron ionization mass spectra, reported systematically by McLafferty in 1959. When there is a hydrogen on the γ carbon counted from an unsaturated group such as a carbonyl, the γ hydrogen moves to the carbonyl oxygen through a six-membered transition state, the bond between the α and β carbons breaks, and a neutral alkene leaves. What remains is an enol radical cation. Unlike simple cleavage, in which just one bond breaks, it involves hydrogen transfer and is therefore called a rearrangement.

Characteristic ions appear for each class of compound. Typical values are m/z 44 for straight-chain aldehydes, m/z 58 for methyl ketones, m/z 74 for methyl esters, m/z 60 for carboxylic acids and m/z 59 for primary amides. Alkylbenzenes with chains of propyl or longer undergo the same type of rearrangement with the benzene ring as the unsaturated group, giving an ion at m/z 92. If the α carbon carries a methyl group or similar, m/z increases by 14 for each, which helps locate branching.

about.h: Recognizing it as an odd-electron ion
about.p: Because a neutral molecule is lost in the McLafferty rearrangement, the resulting ion is an odd-electron ion with an unpaired electron, like the molecular ion. For compounds without nitrogen, if the molecular weight is even, the m/z of this ion is also even. Processes such as α cleavage, in which one bond breaks and a radical is lost, give even-electron ions, whose m/z is odd for compounds without nitrogen. A prominent peak at an even m/z in a spectrum is therefore a clue to suspect an ion formed by rearrangement.

about.h: Use in structure determination and limitations
about.p: The McLafferty rearrangement provides clues to the presence of a γ hydrogen and to the length and branching of the chains on either side of the carbonyl. If both sides of the carbonyl have long enough chains, the rearrangement can occur twice in succession. On the other hand, it does not occur in compounds lacking a γ hydrogen or in compounds that cannot adopt the six-membered transition state because of ring strain and the like. Because mass alone sometimes cannot distinguish it from other ions with the same m/z, it may be confirmed by accurate mass measurement or by comparison with deuterium-labeled compounds.

faq.q: What conditions are needed for a McLafferty rearrangement?
faq.a: An unsaturated group such as a carbonyl, and a hydrogen on the γ carbon counted from it. The molecule must also be able to adopt the six-membered transition state.

faq.q: What is the difference between the McLafferty rearrangement and α cleavage?
faq.a: In α cleavage the bond next to the carbonyl breaks and a radical leaves, giving an even-electron ion. In the McLafferty rearrangement a neutral alkene leaves with hydrogen transfer, giving an odd-electron ion.

faq.q: What ion forms from 2-pentanone?
faq.a: A hydrogen on C5, the γ position, moves to the carbonyl oxygen, ethylene (mass 28) leaves, and an ion at m/z 58 forms. For methyl ketones, m/z 58 is a marker regardless of chain length.

同位体ピーク.desc: A peak due to molecules containing heavier isotopes. One chlorine gives M:M+2 ≈ 3:1 and one bromine about 1:1, which is used to judge whether halogens are present and how many.

about.p: The pattern of isotope peaks is determined by the natural isotopic composition of the elements present. Fluorine, phosphorus and iodine have essentially only one isotope in nature and produce no isotope peaks. Carbon (¹³C about 1.1%) and nitrogen (¹⁵N about 0.4%) contribute to M+1, one mass unit heavier. Oxygen (¹⁸O about 0.2%), sulfur (³⁴S about 4.2%), silicon (³⁰Si about 3.1%), chlorine and bromine contribute to M+2, two mass units heavier. Metals such as tin, palladium and platinum have many isotopes and show characteristic series of many peaks.

In carbon-rich molecules, the fraction of molecules containing no ¹³C decreases. In a molecule with 100 carbons, the M+1 peak containing one ¹³C is larger than the all-¹²C M peak, by a ratio of about 1.08. In still larger proteins, the peak for molecules made only of the lightest isotopes becomes almost invisible. So for small molecules the monoisotopic mass, calculated with the lightest isotope of each element, is used, while for large molecules the average mass or the mass of the most intense isotope peak is used instead.

Electrospray ionization often gives multiply charged ions carrying several protons. Isotope peaks differ in mass by about 1, so for an ion of charge z the m/z spacing between neighboring isotope peaks is 1/z. A spacing of 0.5 means a doubly charged ion, 0.33 a triply charged one. With high enough resolution, the difference of about 0.011 within the same M+2, between species containing ³⁴S (+1.9958) and those containing two ¹³C (+2.0067), can be resolved to judge whether sulfur is present. Near m/z 500 this needs a resolution of about 46,000.

Compounds labeled with deuterium, ¹³C or ¹⁸O have nearly the same chemical properties and differ only in mass, so shifts in the positions of isotope peaks let you trace where atoms went in a reaction. When an ester was made from ¹⁸O-labeled methanol and benzoic acid, the ¹⁸O stayed in the ester and did not appear in the water, which showed that acid-catalyzed esterification breaks the C−O bond of the carboxylic acid. In ESI, the number of exchangeable hydrogens, such as OH and NH, can be counted from how much the mass increases when the solvent is replaced with heavy water.

faq.q: What is the difference between monoisotopic mass and average mass?
faq.a: Monoisotopic mass is calculated using only the most abundant isotope of each element and corresponds to the M peak in the mass spectrum of a small molecule. Average mass is weighted by natural isotopic composition and corresponds to the molecular weight used in stoichiometric calculations.

faq.q: Why can the spacing between isotope peaks be 0.5?
faq.a: Because the ion is doubly charged. A mass difference of 1 divided by a charge of 2 gives an m/z spacing of 0.5. The reciprocal of the spacing gives the charge of the ion, from which the mass of the molecule can be found.

faq.q: Can the M+1 peak be larger than M?
faq.a: Yes. For molecules with more than about 90 carbons, molecules containing one ¹³C outnumber those made only of ¹²C. This is often seen in the mass spectra of peptides and proteins.

高分解能質量分析.desc: Mass spectrometry that measures ion masses to about four decimal places. It distinguishes species with the same nominal mass, such as CO, N2 and C2H4, and fixes the molecular formula from the accurate mass.

about.h: Resolution and mass accuracy are different things
about.p: Resolution expresses how well two peaks of similar mass can be separated and is usually given as m/Δm, the peak m/z divided by its width at half height. Mass accuracy is how close the measured value is to the theoretical value, with the error expressed in ppm (parts per million). For example, the theoretical value for [M+H]⁺ of caffeine is m/z 195.0877, and a deviation of 0.001 is an error of about 5 ppm. Even at high resolution, accuracy is poor if the calibration is off; conversely, even at low resolution, accurate measurement is sometimes possible if no other ion overlaps.

High-resolution measurements use time-of-flight (TOF) analyzers, which measure the flight time of ions; Orbitraps, which measure the frequency at which ions circle an electrode; Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance (FT-ICR) instruments, which measure the frequency of circular motion in a strong magnetic field; and double-focusing instruments combining magnetic and electric fields. Resolution is roughly several tens of thousands for TOF and several hundred thousand for Orbitraps, and for FT-ICR it can exceed a million. Combined with liquid chromatography, they allow the formula of each component of a mixture to be estimated.

The larger the mass, the faster the number of candidate formulas within the same error window grows. Around m/z 500 many candidates remain even at an accuracy of a few ppm, so they are narrowed down using isotope peak intensity ratios, the nitrogen rule, the requirement that the degree of unsaturation not be negative, and so on. Also, a cation is lighter by the mass of one electron (0.00055), and forgetting this shifts the value by about 2.7 ppm at m/z 200. Keep in mind too that a high-resolution value only indicates a formula and cannot distinguish isomers with different structures.

As evidence for the composition of newly synthesized compounds, many journals accept high-resolution mass spectrometry data in place of elemental analysis. A difference of within 5 ppm from the calculated value is often used as a guideline, although the criterion varies between journals. In measurement, using a lock mass, a substance of known mass introduced at the same time for calibration, improves accuracy. In identifying impurities and metabolites of drugs, searching for unknown pollutants in the environment, and metabolomics, which surveys metabolites comprehensively, the accurate mass is the first clue. Reports state the type of ion, such as [M+Na]⁺, along with the formula.

faq.q: How is the ppm error calculated?
faq.a: It is (measured value − theoretical value) ÷ theoretical value × 10⁶. If an ion of m/z 195.0877 is measured as 195.0887, the error is 0.0010 ÷ 195.0877 × 10⁶ ≈ 5.1 ppm.

faq.q: Can high-resolution mass spectrometry distinguish isomers?
faq.a: Isomers with the same formula have the same accurate mass, so they cannot be distinguished. They are told apart in combination with differences in chromatographic retention, tandem mass spectrometry that breaks ions apart to examine the fragments, NMR and so on.

faq.q: Do I need to account for the mass of the electron?
faq.a: Yes, if comparing at ppm accuracy. A singly charged cation is lighter than the neutral molecule by one electron (about 0.00055), equivalent to about 2.7 ppm at m/z 200. Most analysis software corrects for this automatically.

理論段数.desc: A number expressing the separation efficiency of a chromatographic column, found as N = 16(tR/W)² or 5.54(tR/W½)². The larger it is, the sharper the peaks. Resolution is proportional to √N.

about.p: The theoretical plate number N is a number expressing the separation efficiency of a chromatographic column, borrowed from the analogy of the plates in a distillation column. It shows how much a component's band spreads as it travels through the column, and for a Gaussian peak it is N = (tR/σ)². In practice it is found from the baseline width W of the peak as N = 16(tR/W)², or from the width at half height W½ as N = 5.54(tR/W½)². For example, a retention time of 10.0 min and a baseline width of 0.40 min give N = 10000 plates. The larger N, the sharper the peak at the same retention time.

The column length L divided by the plate number, H = L/N, is called the plate height (HETP) and represents the length per plate. The smaller H, the more efficient the column, and it allows columns of different lengths to be compared. In HPLC, smaller packing particles give smaller H; for example, a 150 mm column with N = 13850 plates has H ≈ 11 µm. H changes with the mobile-phase flow velocity, a relationship described by the van Deemter equation, and there is an optimum flow velocity at which H is smallest.

The resolution Rs, which expresses how well two peaks are separated, is determined by the square root of the plate number, the separation factor α and the retention factor k, as Rs = (√N/4)·((α − 1)/α)·(k/(1 + k)). Quadrupling N only doubles Rs, so to improve a separation it is often more effective to increase α by changing the mobile or stationary phase. When peak shapes depart from Gaussian (tailing and so on), the plate number depends on how it is calculated, so compare values obtained by the same method.

faq.q: How is the plate number calculated?
faq.a: From the retention time and peak width, with N = 16(tR/W)² (baseline width) or N = 5.54(tR/W½)² (width at half height). Express the retention time and width in the same units.

faq.q: Does the plate number differ between components?
faq.a: Yes. Even on the same column, the value changes with a component's diffusion coefficient and retention factor and with the flow rate. Column performance specifications use values for designated test compounds and conditions.

faq.q: How can the plate number be increased?
faq.a: Use packings with smaller particles, lengthen the column, bring the flow rate close to its optimum, and reduce the volume of extra-column tubing and the detector cell.

保持係数.desc: k = (tR − t0)/t0, the ratio of the time a component spends in the stationary phase to the time it spends in the mobile phase. Also called the capacity factor. It does not depend on column length or flow rate.

about.p: The retention factor k is the ratio of the time a component spends in the stationary phase to the time it spends in the mobile phase in chromatography, found as k = (tR − t0)/t0. t0 is the time for a component that is not retained by the stationary phase to emerge (the hold-up time). k is also the ratio of the amount of a component in the stationary phase to that in the mobile phase inside the column, equal to the product of the distribution constant and the phase volume ratio. Unlike retention time, it stays the same when column length or flow rate changes, so it can be used to compare analyses under different conditions.

For example, with t0 = 2.0 min and tR = 9.0 min, k = (9.0 − 2.0)/2.0 = 3.5. The fraction of time a component spends in the mobile phase is 1/(1 + k), so at k = 3.5 it is moving along the column only about 22% of the time. If k is too small, it is hard to separate from interferences near t0; if too large, peaks become broad and low and analysis takes longer, so in practice k is often adjusted to about 2–10. In reversed-phase HPLC, t0 is measured with a weakly retained substance such as uracil.

In reversed-phase HPLC, increasing the proportion of organic solvent in the mobile phase makes k smaller. A rule of thumb says that adding 10% more organic solvent cuts k to roughly one half to one third. Raising the temperature generally makes k smaller as well. For acidic and basic components, changing the mobile-phase pH alters the proportions of molecular and ionic forms and changes k greatly. In GC, it is adjusted by column temperature and temperature programming. Gradient elution is a way of lowering k during the analysis. Knowing how k responds to changes in conditions makes searching for separation conditions efficient.

In the resolution equation Rs = (√N/4)·((α − 1)/α)·(k/(1 + k)), the k term k/(1 + k) is 0.50 at k = 1, 0.67 at k = 2, 0.83 at k = 5 and 0.91 at k = 10. At small k, stronger retention improves separation, but above 10 there is little further gain. The ratio of the retention factors of two components is the separation factor α. It relates to the Rf value of thin-layer chromatography as k = (1 − Rf)/Rf, so the smaller Rf, the larger k.

faq.q: What is the difference between retention factor and retention time?
faq.a: Retention time is the time from injection to the peak and changes with column length and flow rate. The retention factor is retention time minus t0, divided by t0, and does not depend on those conditions.

faq.q: Are the retention factor and capacity factor the same?
faq.a: They are the same quantity. It used to be called the capacity factor (k'), and current IUPAC terminology calls it the retention factor (k). The symbol k' is still widely seen.

faq.q: How is the hold-up time t0 found?
faq.a: Inject a substance that is not retained by the stationary phase and measure when its peak appears. Uracil or thiourea is used in reversed-phase HPLC, and methane or similar in GC.

分離係数.desc: The ratio of the retention factors of two components, α = k2/k1 (with the later-eluting component in the numerator). It expresses the selectivity of the stationary and mobile phases; at α = 1 no increase in plate number will separate them.

about.p: The separation factor α is the ratio of the retention factors of two adjacent peaks, α = k2/k1, with the later-eluting component in the numerator so that it is 1 or greater. The retention factor is the ratio of the amount of a component in the stationary phase to that in the mobile phase, so α expresses the difference in how readily the two components partition, that is, the selectivity of the stationary and mobile phase combination. Note that it is the ratio of retention factors, from which the hold-up time has been subtracted, not of retention times. At α = 1 the two components move at the same speed and cannot be separated by any column, however efficient.

The retention factor is proportional to the partition equilibrium constant, so ln α corresponds to the difference between the standard Gibbs energies of partitioning of the two components. At 25 °C, α = 1.10 corresponds to a difference of only RT ln 1.10 ≈ 0.24 kJ/mol. Chromatography accumulates such small differences by repeating partitioning thousands of times along the column, turning them into a visible separation. When enantiomers are separated on a chiral stationary phase, α is also often around 1.1, and slight differences in interaction decide the separation.

In a sample with many components, the α of every pair of peaks cannot be increased at once. When setting conditions, focus on the pair whose α is closest to 1 (the critical pair) and choose the mobile and stationary phases so that its resolution reaches the target, usually 1.5 or more. Changing conditions can increase α for one pair while bringing another pair closer or swapping the elution order, so all peaks must be rechecked. Also, at very small retention factors, the actual separation is inadequate even with the same α.

In liquid chromatography, α is adjusted by switching the organic solvent in the mobile phase from methanol to acetonitrile, changing the buffer pH to shift the retention of ionizable components, switching the stationary phase from C18 to one with phenyl groups or similar, or changing the temperature. The basic approach is to choose interactions that can discriminate the structural differences between the components. In solvent extraction, the ratio of the distribution ratios of two components is also called the separation factor and is likewise used as a measure of how easily they can be separated.

faq.q: What is the difference between separation factor and resolution?
faq.a: The separation factor is the ratio of retention of two components and expresses only the selectivity of the stationary and mobile phases. Resolution expresses how well the peaks are actually separated, from their spacing and width, and depends on the plate number and retention factor as well as selectivity.

faq.q: Why not calculate the separation factor from the ratio of retention times?
faq.a: Retention times include the time the mobile phase takes to flow through regardless of the stationary phase (the hold-up time). Selectivity is not represented correctly unless you compare retention factors, from which it has been subtracted.

faq.q: How can the separation factor be increased?
faq.a: Change the type of solvent or the pH of the mobile phase, the type of stationary phase, or the temperature. Increasing the plate number does not change the separation factor, so look for conditions that change the selectivity itself.

分離度.desc: The degree of separation of two adjacent peaks, Rs = 2(tR2 − tR1)/(W1 + W2). Rs of about 1.5 gives nearly baseline separation. It is proportional to the square root of the plate number.

about.p: Resolution Rs is a number expressing how well two adjacent peaks are separated, found as Rs = 2(tR2 − tR1)/(W1 + W2). W is the baseline width of the peak (found by the tangent method). Using the width at half height W½, Rs = 1.18(tR2 − tR1)/(W½1 + W½2), and for Gaussian peaks the two give the same value. For example, a difference in retention time of 0.50 min with half-height widths of 0.15 min each gives Rs ≈ 2.0. Peak width, not just the difference in retention time, determines separation.

For Gaussian peaks of similar height, at Rs = 1.0 the peak centers are four standard deviations σ apart, and about 2% of each peak extends onto the other side. At Rs = 1.5 the spacing is 6σ and the overlap about 0.1%, nearly baseline separation. Pharmaceutical tests often set system-suitability requirements of Rs of at least 1.5 or at least 2.0. When peak heights differ greatly or there is tailing, quantifying the small peak is harder even at the same Rs.

Resolution is determined by three factors, the plate number N, the separation factor α and the retention factor k, as in Rs = (√N/4)·((α − 1)/α)·(k/(1 + k)). N acts through √N, so doubling the column length raises Rs only about 1.4-fold and doubles the time. Raising k to about 2–10 is enough. α has the largest effect: going from α = 1.05 to 1.10 nearly doubles Rs. The basic approach is therefore first to enlarge α by changing the mobile-phase composition or pH or the type of stationary phase.

The English word resolution refers to different things in different fields. In mass spectrometry it means mass resolution expressed as m/Δm, and in spectroscopy wavelength resolution, the ability to distinguish nearby wavelengths; these are quantities separate from chromatographic resolution. Chromatographic resolution is a value found for a particular pair of peaks, so when reporting it, state which pair. When transferring a method, check that the resolution of the hardest-to-separate pair meets the requirement. Changing conditions can also swap the order of peaks, so confirm peak assignments as well.

faq.q: What does a resolution of 1.5 mean?
faq.a: For Gaussian peaks of similar height, the peak centers are 6σ apart and the overlap is about 0.1%, nearly baseline separation. At 1.0, each overlaps by about 2%.

faq.q: How can resolution be increased?
faq.a: The most effective way is to enlarge the separation factor α by changing the mobile-phase composition or pH or the stationary phase. Increasing the plate number and raising the retention factor moderately also help.

faq.q: What is the formula for resolution from half-height widths?
faq.a: Rs = 1.18(tR2 − tR1)/(W½1 + W½2). The baseline width W is about 1.70 times the half-height width, so for Gaussian peaks both formulas give the same value.

逆相クロマトグラフィー.desc: Liquid chromatography using a nonpolar stationary phase such as ODS (C18) and a polar mobile phase such as water–methanol. The more hydrophobic a component, the later it elutes.

about.h: Why it is called reversed phase
about.p: Early liquid chromatography centered on methods using highly polar silica gel as the stationary phase and a nonpolar solvent such as hexane as the mobile phase (normal phase). Methods using a nonpolar stationary phase and a polar mobile phase reverse this polarity relationship and are therefore called reversed phase. The representative stationary phase is ODS (C18), silica with octadecyl groups bonded to its surface, and the mobile phase is a mixture of water with methanol or acetonitrile. It is the most widely used separation mode in HPLC today.

In reversed phase, the more hydrophobic a component, the more strongly it interacts with the alkyl chains of the stationary phase and the later it elutes. In a water-rich mobile phase, hydrophobic components are partitioned into the stationary phase as if pushed out of the water, so increasing the proportion of organic solvent decreases retention. Elution strength is said to increase in the order methanol, acetonitrile, tetrahydrofuran. As a rule of thumb, raising the organic solvent fraction by 10% lowers the retention factor by roughly a factor of 2 to 3, though this varies with the compound.

Acids and bases lose much of their retention when ionized, so a buffer with a pH about 2 units away from the pKa is used to keep them in either the neutral or the ionized form. Silanol groups remaining on the silica surface interact with basic compounds and cause peak tailing. To suppress this, end-capping is used to cap the remaining silanols with small silyl groups. Silica-based packings degrade readily in strongly acidic or basic mobile phases, so check the usable pH range before use.

about.h: Choosing the mobile phase in practice
about.p: Acetonitrile has a lower viscosity than methanol, giving lower back pressure, and absorbs less in the ultraviolet, making it suited to detection at short wavelengths. Methanol is inexpensive, and because changing the solvent type also changes selectivity, the two are used alternately to improve separations. In LC-MS, volatile additives such as formic acid or ammonium acetate are used. For samples containing components with very different retention, gradient elution, increasing the organic solvent fraction during the analysis, is used. Reversed-phase packings are also widely used in solid-phase extraction to concentrate samples.

faq.q: What is the difference between reversed phase and normal phase?
faq.a: Reversed phase uses a nonpolar stationary phase and a polar mobile phase, and normal phase uses a polar stationary phase and a nonpolar mobile phase. Highly polar components elute early in reversed phase and late in normal phase.

faq.q: How do I choose between methanol and acetonitrile?
faq.a: Acetonitrile has low viscosity, lowering back pressure, and suits UV detection at short wavelengths. Methanol is inexpensive and has different selectivity, so it is worth trying as a substitute when a separation is inadequate.

faq.q: Can a C18 column be used with a purely aqueous mobile phase?
faq.a: With ordinary C18 columns, a very high water fraction can drive the mobile phase out of the pores and cause retention to drop suddenly. For water-rich conditions, choose a column designed for that purpose.

水素炎イオン化検出器.desc: A GC detector, abbreviated FID, that measures as a current the ions produced when organic compounds burn in a hydrogen flame. It is highly sensitive to hydrocarbons and barely responds to water, CO2 or permanent gases.

about.h: Measuring ions formed in a flame
about.p: The flame ionization detector (FID) is a GC detector that burns the gas leaving the column in a hydrogen–air flame, collects the ions produced by combustion of organic compounds at an electrode, and measures them as a current. The current is thought to come from chemi-ionization, in which carbon-containing fragments react with oxygen in the flame to form ions such as CHO⁺ and electrons. A pure hydrogen flame produces almost no ions, so the baseline current is extremely small, giving high sensitivity to hydrocarbons and a wide linear range spanning many orders of magnitude.

about.h: Response depends on the number and bonding of carbons
about.p: For hydrocarbons, the FID response is roughly proportional to the number of carbon atoms, so equal masses of hydrocarbons give signals of nearly the same size. Carbons bonded to oxygen, halogens or nitrogen respond less, and carbonyl carbons barely respond. The effective carbon number puts this idea in numbers and is used to estimate relative response. Because the FID hardly responds to water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide or permanent gases, it is well suited to samples containing water and to organic compounds in air.

The thermal conductivity detector (TCD) responds to nearly every component but has low sensitivity, while the electron capture detector (ECD) is specialized and highly sensitive for halogenated compounds and the like. The FID lies in between, a general-purpose detector that measures a broad range of organic compounds with high sensitivity. However, because it burns the analytes, it is destructive, so analytes cannot be recovered after detection or passed on to another detector placed after it in series. To measure CO or CO2, a methanizer can convert them to methane over a nickel catalyst before they enter the FID.

Because sensitivity differs from compound to compound, quantitation by FID requires a calibration curve or relative response factor obtained with standards. For hydrocarbon mixtures, area percentages approximate mass percentages, but they deviate considerably when oxygenated compounds are present. In routine operation, keeping the hydrogen, air and makeup gas flows at the values recommended for the instrument is essential for stable sensitivity. Because hydrogen is used, the plumbing must be checked for leaks and the safety function that cuts the hydrogen supply when the flame goes out must be verified.

faq.q: Why does the FID not respond to water?
faq.a: Water is already fully oxidized, so it yields no carbon-containing fragments in the flame and produces almost no ions. This allows only the organic compounds to be measured even in samples whose solvent or main component is water.

faq.q: Is correction needed for quantitation with an FID?
faq.a: Yes. The response depends not only on the number of carbons but also on how they are bonded to oxygen or halogens. Accurate quantitation requires determining the sensitivity for each compound with standards.

faq.q: What carrier gas is used with an FID?
faq.a: Helium, nitrogen and hydrogen are common. The fuel hydrogen and air are supplied separately from the carrier gas, and a makeup gas may be added to stabilize sensitivity.

内部標準法.desc: A quantitation method in which a fixed amount of an internal standard is added to the samples and standards, and the analyte is quantified from its peak-area ratio to the internal standard. It cancels variations in injection volume and losses during sample preparation.

about.h: The idea of measuring by ratio
about.p: The internal standard method adds the same amount of an internal standard to both samples and standards and quantifies the analyte from the ratio of its signal to that of the internal standard. Variations in injection volume, concentration by solvent evaporation, and losses during sample preparation affect the analyte and internal standard in the same proportion, so they cancel in the ratio. Once a relative response factor is obtained from the relationship between concentration ratio and area ratio, the concentration can be calculated from the sample's area ratio. It is a basic idea not only in GC and LC but also in quantitation by NMR.

Choose an internal standard that is not originally present in the sample, is chemically similar to the analyte, behaves the same way during sample preparation, and does not overlap other peaks. In LC-MS, compounds labeled with stable isotopes of the analyte are widely used to cancel matrix effects, in which coexisting sample components suppress ionization. However, deuterium-labeled compounds can elute slightly earlier than the analyte in reversed-phase LC, and ¹³C- or ¹⁵N-labeled compounds, which co-elute completely, are considered better for correction.

about.h: How it differs from external standard and standard addition
about.p: The external standard method builds a calibration curve from standards alone and obtains concentration from the absolute sample signal, so variations in injection volume or instrument sensitivity translate directly into error. The standard addition method adds analyte to the sample itself to correct for changes in sensitivity caused by coexisting components. The internal standard method is strong at correcting variations during the procedure, but it cannot fully correct when coexisting components affect the analyte and internal standard differently. Depending on the sources of error, these methods are sometimes combined.

about.h: When it is added determines the result
about.p: To correct for losses during sample preparation, the internal standard must be added before extraction or concentration, as early as possible. If it is added just before injection, it corrects only for injection and measurement variation. As a guide, choose an amount that gives a sufficiently large internal standard peak and an area ratio near the middle of the calibration curve. In ¹H NMR quantitation, an internal standard of reliable purity and the sample are weighed accurately, and the purity or content of the sample is obtained directly from the ratio of signal integrals and numbers of hydrogens.

faq.q: What is the difference between internal and external standard methods?
faq.a: The external standard method quantifies from the absolute signal, and the internal standard method from the ratio to the internal standard's signal. The internal standard method cancels variations in injection volume and preparation losses but requires choosing a suitable internal standard.

faq.q: When should the internal standard be added?
faq.a: Before the operation you want to correct for. To correct for losses in extraction and concentration as well, the rule is to add it right after weighing the sample, before sample preparation begins.

faq.q: Why are isotope-labeled internal standards so widely used?
faq.a: They have nearly the same chemical properties as the analyte, so recovery in sample preparation and ionization behavior match, while mass spectrometry can distinguish them by their mass difference.

ネルンスト式.desc: The relation between electrode potential and activity, E = E° + (2.303RT/nF) log(oxidized/reduced). At 25 °C for a one-electron reaction, the potential changes by about 59.2 mV per tenfold change in activity.

about.h: Form and meaning of the equation
about.p: The Nernst equation describes how the electrode potential of a redox reaction Ox + ne⁻ ⇌ Red depends on the activities of the oxidized and reduced forms: E = E° − (RT/nF) ln(a(Red)/a(Ox)). E° is the standard electrode potential, when all activities are 1. In common logarithms the coefficient is 2.303RT/nF, which at 25 °C is 0.05916/n V. For a one-electron reaction the potential changes by about 59.2 mV for each tenfold change in the activity ratio, and for a two-electron reaction by about 29.6 mV. Nernst derived it from thermodynamics in 1889.

about.h: A worked example and equilibrium constants
about.p: For Fe³⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ Fe²⁺ (E° = +0.771 V) with an Fe³⁺:Fe²⁺ activity ratio of 10:1, E = 0.771 + 0.0592 × log 10 = +0.830 V at 25 °C. For a whole cell, the fact that the emf becomes zero at equilibrium gives the relationship between standard emf and equilibrium constant, log K = nE°/0.05916 (25 °C). For the Daniell cell (Zn and Cu, E° = 1.10 V, n = 2), log K is about 37, so the reaction goes essentially to completion. It is linked to the standard Gibbs energy by ΔG° = −nFE°.

What enters the Nernst equation is activity, not concentration. In solutions of high ionic strength, activity coefficients deviate considerably from 1, so plugging in concentrations directly can be off by several to several tens of millivolts. In practical analysis, the potential when the oxidized and reduced forms are at equal concentration in a defined medium (for example 1 mol/L sulfuric acid) is used as the formal potential E°′, and calculations are done with concentrations. For reactions involving hydrogen ions, the potential also depends on pH; when H⁺ and electrons are equal in number, it shifts about 59 mV negative per unit rise in pH (25 °C).
