pH glass electrodes and ion-selective electrodes rely on their potential changing with the activity of the target ion according to the Nernst equation. The coefficient is proportional to absolute temperature, reaching about 64.1 mV per electron at 50 °C, so calibration and measurement are done at the same temperature. Ion-selective electrodes also respond slightly to other coexisting ions, and this effect is estimated with selectivity coefficients in the Nikolsky–Eisenman equation. The equation applies to potentials at equilibrium, with essentially no current flowing. In electrolysis or voltammetry, where current flows during measurement, overpotential and other effects must be considered separately.

faq.q: Where does the value of 59 mV come from?
faq.a: Inserting the value for 25 °C (298.15 K) into 2.303RT/F gives about 0.0592 V. For a one-electron reaction, a tenfold change in activity changes the potential by about 59.2 mV. As temperature rises, this value increases proportionally.

faq.q: Can I put concentrations into the Nernst equation?
faq.a: In dilute solutions this works as an approximation, but strictly it is activity. At high ionic strength, correct with activity coefficients or calculate with concentrations using a formal potential determined in the same medium.

faq.q: What is the difference between standard potential and formal potential?
faq.a: The standard electrode potential is the value in the ideal state where all activities are 1; the formal potential is the potential actually shown in a specific medium when the oxidized and reduced forms are at equal concentration. The formal potential includes effects of complexation and activity coefficients.

ガラス電極.desc: A pH electrode that uses the membrane potential created by the difference in hydrogen-ion activity across a thin glass membrane. Ideally it changes by about 59.2 mV per pH unit at 25 °C, and it is calibrated with two or more standard buffers.

about.p: A glass electrode is a pH electrode using a thin glass membrane that responds to hydrogen ions. Inside the glass bulb are an inner solution of fixed pH and an inner electrode (such as silver–silver chloride), and a membrane potential arises according to the difference in hydrogen-ion activity inside and outside the membrane. The membrane surfaces carry hydrated gel layers, where ion exchange gives rise to the potential. In practice, it is often used as a combination electrode with a built-in reference electrode, so the potential difference is measured with a single probe. The speed of response depends on the condition of the membrane.

The electrode potential follows the straight line E = E₀ − S × pH, with the slope S ideally 2.303RT/F. At 25 °C it is about 59.16 mV/pH; it changes in proportion to absolute temperature, being about 54.2 mV at 0 °C and about 61.5 mV at 37 °C. pH meters therefore have temperature compensation. What is compensated, however, is only the change in the electrode's slope; changes in the pH of the sample itself with temperature are not corrected. Report the measurement temperature with the pH.

To fix the intercept and slope of the line, calibrate with two or more standards of different pH. JIS standards at 25 °C are 4.01 for phthalate, 6.86 for neutral phosphate and 9.18 for borate. The zero point is set with the neutral standard, and the slope with another standard bracketing the measurement range. A slope below about 90–95% of the theoretical value (the guide differs by manufacturer), slow response or unstable readings signal a dirty or aged membrane or a clogged liquid junction in the reference electrode. In that case, clean or replace the electrode.

In strongly basic solutions, above about pH 12, with much sodium present, the glass membrane also responds to sodium and the pH reads lower than the true value (alkaline error). Errors also arise in strongly acidic solutions below about pH 1. In samples with few ions, such as pure water or rain, the junction potential is unstable and readings take time to settle. Electrodes respond poorly if allowed to dry, so when not in use they are kept in the storage solution specified by the manufacturer (such as potassium chloride solution) and not left standing in pure water.

faq.q: How many mV does the potential change per pH unit?
faq.a: Ideally about 59.2 mV at 25 °C. The slope is proportional to absolute temperature and is about 61.5 mV at 37 °C. Real electrodes are usually slightly below the theoretical value.

faq.q: Why calibrate with two or more standards?
faq.a: Because both the intercept (zero point) and slope of the line relating potential to pH must be determined. A single standard can set only the intercept. After a two-point calibration, checking with another standard gives extra confidence.

faq.q: How should a glass electrode be stored?
faq.a: To keep the membrane from drying, store it in the storage solution specified by the manufacturer (such as potassium chloride solution). Long immersion in pure water can dilute the inner solution and worsen the response.

電位差滴定.desc: A titration in which the potential difference between an indicator electrode and a reference electrode is measured, and the equivalence point is found where the potential changes most steeply. End points can be found even in colored or turbid samples.

about.h: Detecting the end point by potential instead of color
about.p: Potentiometric titration measures the potential difference between an indicator electrode and a reference electrode immersed in the sample during the titration and determines the end point from the sharp change in potential near the equivalence point. The indicator electrode's potential changes with the logarithm of the target ion's activity according to the Nernst equation, and because the activity changes by orders of magnitude around the equivalence point, an S-shaped titration curve results. No indicator color needs to be observed, so it works for colored or turbid samples and avoids differences in color judgment between people. Most automatic titrators today use this approach.

about.h: Choosing the electrode for each reaction
about.p: A pH glass electrode is used as the indicator electrode for acid–base titrations, a silver electrode for precipitation titrations with silver ion, and a platinum electrode for redox titrations. Ion-selective electrodes are also used in chelatometric titrations and fluoride determinations. The usual reference electrode is the silver–silver chloride electrode, whose potential is stable. The basic principle is to choose an electrode that responds to an ion whose activity changes greatly in the reaction, and when leakage of chloride from the reference electrode into the sample is a problem, a reference electrode with a double junction is used.

about.h: Locating the end point and a worked example
about.p: The end point is found as the inflection point of the titration curve, determined from the maximum of the first derivative ΔE/ΔV or the point where the second derivative crosses zero. A Gran plot, which linearizes the data before the equivalence point, can estimate the equivalence point even when the change near the end point is small. For example, when Fe²⁺ is titrated with Ce⁴⁺ in 1 mol/L sulfuric acid, the formal potentials are 0.68 V and 1.44 V, so the potential at the equivalence point is their average, about 1.06 V, and the potential jumps sharply around it.

Potentiometric titration can follow titrations with several equivalence points in a single run. Polyprotic acids such as phosphoric acid show an equivalence point for each step, and when a mixture of iodide, bromide and chloride is titrated with silver nitrate, equivalence points appear in order of increasing solubility. It can also be used for titrations in nonaqueous solvents lacking suitable indicators; titration of weak bases with perchloric acid in acetic acid is widely used in pharmaceutical testing. Calibration and checks that the electrode response has not become sluggish are prerequisites for obtaining an accurate end point.

faq.q: What is the difference between potentiometric titration and titration with an indicator?
faq.a: An indicator shows the end point by a color change, whereas potentiometric titration finds the equivalence point from a sharp change in electrode potential. Potentiometric titration works for colored or turbid samples and samples with several equivalence points, and it is easy to automate.

faq.q: What reference electrode is used in potentiometric titration?
faq.a: The silver–silver chloride electrode is the most common. The activity of the internal chloride is held constant, so its potential is stable and only the change in the indicator electrode's potential is measured.

faq.q: Why is the end point found from the second derivative?
faq.a: The maximum of the first derivative corresponds to the inflection point, but finding by interpolation the point where the sign of the second derivative changes is more objective and reproducible than reading the position of a maximum by eye.

原子吸光分析.desc: A method in which the sample is atomized in a flame or graphite furnace, and the concentration is found from how much light of the wavelength characteristic of the target element is absorbed by ground-state atoms. A hollow cathode lamp is used as the light source.

about.p: Atomic absorption spectrometry (AAS) turns a sample into atomic vapor at high temperature, passes light of a wavelength characteristic of the target element through it, and determines concentration from the absorption by ground-state atoms. Walsh proposed it as an analytical method in 1955. As in the Beer–Lambert law, absorbance is proportional to the number of atoms in the light path. The light source is a hollow cathode lamp with a cathode made of the target element; by irradiating with an emission line even narrower than the atomic absorption line, it achieves high sensitivity and selectivity against other elements.

Even in a hot flame, only a tiny fraction of atoms are in the excited state. An estimate for the sodium line at 589 nm shows that at 2500 K only about 1.7×10⁻⁴ of the atoms are excited. In methods that measure emission, the number of these few excited atoms changes greatly with temperature, so fluctuations in flame temperature affect the signal. Atomic absorption counts the ground-state atoms, which make up the vast majority, so it is relatively insensitive to temperature. On the other hand, the lamp must be changed for each element, and simultaneous multielement analysis is not its strength.

Atomization methods include flame AAS, in which the sample solution is nebulized into a flame, and graphite furnace (electrothermal) AAS, in which a small amount of sample is placed in a graphite tube and heated electrically. Flame AAS is fast and reproducible; the air–acetylene flame is used for many elements, and the hotter nitrous oxide–acetylene flame for elements that are hard to atomize. In the graphite furnace, sample atoms remain in the light path longer, so concentrations orders of magnitude lower than with a flame can be measured, but each measurement takes longer and is more susceptible to matrix components.

In atomic absorption, chemical interference occurs, in which the analyte forms compounds that do not dissociate readily in the flame and atomization is hindered; so does ionization interference, in which atoms ionize in the flame and are lost; and background absorption, in which absorption and scattering of light by salt particles and molecules raise the apparent absorbance. Chemical interference is countered by adding releasing agents or using a hotter flame, ionization interference by adding an easily ionized element such as potassium, and background by correction with a deuterium lamp or the Zeeman effect. There are also methods that measure arsenic and selenium after conversion to hydrides and mercury as atomic vapor.

faq.q: What is the difference between atomic absorption and atomic emission analysis?
faq.a: Atomic absorption measures light absorbed by ground-state atoms, and atomic emission measures light emitted by excited atoms. Atomic absorption is less affected by temperature, while emission methods such as ICP optical emission spectrometry excel at measuring many elements simultaneously.

faq.q: How do I choose between flame and graphite furnace?
faq.a: When concentrations are high enough and there is plenty of sample, use the fast, reproducible flame method. When concentrations are low or the sample is small, use the more sensitive graphite furnace.

faq.q: Why can't atomic absorption measure many elements at once?
faq.a: Because the light source is a hollow cathode lamp that is different for each element. The lamp and wavelength must be switched to measure the elements one by one, and ICP optical emission spectrometry and similar methods are better for simultaneous multielement analysis.

ICP質量分析.desc: A method, abbreviated ICP-MS, that measures elements ionized in an inductively coupled plasma with a mass spectrometer. It can measure ultratrace elements and isotope ratios, but watch out for polyatomic interferences.

about.h: Ionizing in a plasma and separating by mass
about.p: In ICP mass spectrometry (ICP-MS), a sample solution is turned into a mist and carried into an argon inductively coupled plasma, where temperatures of about 6000–10000 K break it down into atoms and ionize them. Argon's ionization energy is high, 15.76 eV, so many metallic elements with lower ionization energies become singly charged cations efficiently. The ions pass through two cones with small holes into the vacuum, where they are usually sorted by mass with a quadrupole and counted. Many elements can be measured at the same time, quickly, down to ng/L (ppt) concentrations.

Isobaric interferences arise when isotopes of different elements share the same mass number, as with ⁵⁸Fe and ⁵⁸Ni or ¹¹⁴Cd and ¹¹⁴Sn. Some elements also form doubly charged ions in the plasma; ¹³⁶Ba²⁺ appears at m/z 68 and overlaps ⁶⁸Zn. With samples high in salts, salt deposits on the cones and the sensitivity drifts down over time, and matrix effects occur in which heavy ions change the sensitivity, as if pushing lighter ions aside. A common rule of thumb is to dilute samples to about 0.2% or less of total dissolved solids before measurement.

The first step is to choose an isotope with few interferences and to apply corrections that subtract the contribution of an overlapping element, calculated from another of its isotopes. With helium in a collision cell, larger polyatomic ions lose more energy in collisions and can be removed by their difference in kinetic energy. Reaction gases such as oxygen can shift the analyte to another mass; measuring arsenic as ⁷⁵As¹⁶O⁺ at m/z 91 avoids the interferences at m/z 75. Instruments with two quadrupoles select masses before and after the reaction, removing interferences more reliably.

about.h: Isotope ratios and a widening range of uses
about.p: Because ICP-MS measures each isotope of an element separately, isotope dilution, in which an enriched isotope is added to the sample and the amount is found from the change in ratio, gives extremely accurate results. Lead isotope ratios are used to trace the sources of pollution. Applications keep widening: laser ablation, which removes material from a solid surface with a laser and introduces it directly; single-particle methods, which count the signal from each particle; and coupling with HPLC to measure each chemical form of arsenic or mercury. The sample introduction method is chosen to fit the purpose.

faq.q: How do you choose between ICP-OES and ICP-MS?
faq.a: ICP-OES suits concentrations of about µg/L and above, tolerates salty samples, and covers everything from major to trace components. ICP-MS suits ultratrace levels around ng/L and isotope ratio measurements, but samples high in dissolved solids must be diluted.

faq.q: What is an isobaric interference?
faq.a: It is the overlap at the same m/z of isotopes of different elements that share a mass number, such as ⁵⁸Fe and ⁵⁸Ni. It is handled by choosing another, interference-free isotope or by subtracting the contribution calculated from the signal of another isotope of the overlapping element.

faq.q: Why is argon used for the plasma?
faq.a: It is chemically inert and hardly forms compounds with the sample, and its high ionization energy lets it ionize many elements efficiently. It is also obtained from air in large amounts and is relatively inexpensive.

検出限界.desc: The smallest amount or concentration at which a component can be judged to be present, distinguishable from the blank. Three times the standard deviation σ of the blank divided by the slope of the calibration curve (3σ/slope) is widely used.

about.h: What the limit of detection is
about.p: The limit of detection (LOD) is the smallest amount or concentration at which a component can be judged to be present, distinguishing it from a blank. It is distinguished from the limit of quantitation (LOQ), the smallest concentration at which a value can be reported accurately. A common way to find it is 3σ/slope, three times the standard deviation σ of repeated blank measurements divided by the slope of the calibration curve, with 10σ/slope used for the LOQ. For example, with σ = 0.0015 and a slope of 0.030 L/mg, the LOD is 0.15 mg/L and the LOQ 0.50 mg/L.

If the blank signal follows a normal distribution, the probability that a blank shows a signal 3σ above its mean by chance is about 0.13% one-sided. So exceeding 3σ means the error of judging a component "present" when it is absent (a false positive) is rare. On the other hand, when a sample at exactly the LOD concentration is measured, half its signals fall below the decision line, so the probability of a miss (a false negative) is not negligible. In the approach that sets both false-positive and false-negative probabilities at 5%, the LOD is about 3.3σ.

Besides repeated blank measurements, chromatography often takes the concentration at which the ratio of peak height to baseline noise (S/N) is 3 as the LOD and the concentration at which it is 10 as the LOQ. ICH Q2 also describes finding it as 3.3σ/slope from the standard deviation of the calibration residuals or of the intercept. Values differ with the method used, so when reporting, state how it was found and conditions such as the number of blank measurements. Values based on S/N also change with how the noise is measured.

A detection limit found by introducing standards directly into the instrument expresses the instrument's performance. With real samples, dilution or concentration in preparation, contamination from containers and reagents, and changes in sensitivity due to the matrix are added, so the method detection limit, found from blanks processed by the same procedure as the samples, is normally larger. When a result falls below the detection limit, report it not as "0" but as "below the detection limit (< 0.15 mg/L, for example)", giving the limit value. Especially in trace-element analysis, the method detection limit is strongly affected by control of contamination during preparation.

faq.q: What is the difference between the limit of detection and the limit of quantitation?
faq.a: The LOD is the smallest concentration that can be judged present; the LOQ is the smallest at which a value can be reported with sufficient precision. As guides, 3σ/slope and 10σ/slope are used respectively.

faq.q: How is the detection limit found from the S/N ratio?
faq.a: Measure a low-concentration standard and take the concentration at which the ratio of peak height (S) to baseline noise (N) is 3 as the LOD. The LOQ is the concentration at which S/N is 10.

faq.q: Does "not detected" mean it is absent?
faq.a: No. It means less than the detection limit of the method, not necessarily zero. In reports, give the limit value, as in "< detection limit value".

検量線.desc: A line, obtained by measuring standards of known concentration, that relates concentration to the measured value (absorbance, peak area and so on). It is used to find concentrations from sample readings. Avoid extrapolating beyond its range.

about.p: A calibration curve is a line showing the relationship between concentration and measured value (absorbance, peak area, emission intensity and so on), obtained by measuring standard solutions of known concentration. The basic approach is to prepare several standards of different concentrations, including a blank, that bracket the sample concentration, and to fit a straight line y = ax + b by least squares. For evaluating linearity, the guideline for pharmaceutical analytical methods (ICH Q2) also recommends a minimum of five concentrations. Standards are matched to the sample in solvent and acid concentration and measured under the same conditions.

From the sample's measured value y, the concentration is x = (y − b)/a. For example, if the calibration curve is y = 0.0250x + 0.0030 (x in mg/L) and the sample's absorbance is 0.428, then x = (0.428 − 0.0030)/0.0250 = 17.0 mg/L. If the sample was diluted for measurement, multiply by the dilution factor at the end to return to the original concentration. If the measured value exceeds that of the most concentrated standard, do not extend the line to read it (extrapolate); dilute the sample into the range and measure again.

about.h: Pitfalls of linearity and the correlation coefficient
about.p: Even with a correlation coefficient r of 0.999 or more, a calibration curve may be slightly curved, because over a wide concentration range r stays close to 1 despite curvature. Linearity is checked by plotting each point's residual against concentration and looking for systematic trends. On the high-concentration side, the slope tends to fall because absorbance levels off or the detector saturates. Whether to force the line through the origin should also be decided after checking the blank value and the size of the intercept; do not fix it at the origin without justification.

Variation in injection volume and losses in sample preparation can be corrected by the internal standard method, in which a fixed amount of an internal standard is added and the calibration is built on peak-area ratios. For samples whose sensitivity changes with coexisting components, the standard addition method, which adds standard to the sample itself, or matrix matching, which prepares standards with a composition close to the sample, is used. The slope (sensitivity) and the scatter of the blank are also used to estimate the limit of detection (3σ/slope) and limit of quantitation (10σ/slope). Sensitivity changes from day to day, so the calibration is checked at each analysis.

faq.q: How many points should a calibration curve have?
faq.a: Generally about five or more, including the blank, at concentrations bracketing the measurement range. Guidelines such as ICH Q2 recommend a minimum of five concentrations for evaluating linearity.

faq.q: Must a calibration curve pass through the origin?
faq.a: Not necessarily. A blank signal or reagent effects can produce an intercept. Fix the line at the origin only after confirming that the intercept can be regarded as zero.

faq.q: What do you do with a sample outside the calibration range?
faq.a: Dilute a concentrated sample into the range, measure again and multiply by the dilution factor. Concentrate a dilute sample or add standards at the low end of the range. Avoid extrapolation.

有効数字.desc: The reliable digits of a measured value plus the last, uncertain digit. In addition and subtraction, match the value with the fewest decimal places; in multiplication and division, the value with the fewest significant figures.

about.p: Significant figures are the digits of a measurement that carry meaning, consisting of the certain digits plus a final uncertain digit. If a buret is read as 12.35 mL, the second decimal place includes an estimate by eye, and there are four significant figures. Zeros that only mark place value are not counted, so 0.00120 g has three significant figures: 1, 2 and 0. When zeros trail, as in 1200, the number of significant figures is ambiguous, so writing it in exponential form as 1.20×10³ makes clear that there are three.

In addition and subtraction, round the decimal places of the result to match the coarsest value (the one with the fewest decimal places). In multiplication and division, give the result the same number of significant figures as the value with the fewest. Keeping one or two extra digits in intermediate steps and rounding only at the end prevents rounding errors from accumulating. Defined numbers and counted numbers have no uncertainty and are not included in judging the number of figures. With the 2019 revision of the SI, the Avogadro constant, 6.02214076×10²³ mol⁻¹, also became an exact defined value.

For logarithms such as pH, the number of digits after the decimal point corresponds to the number of significant figures in the original number. pH 4.56 has two decimal places, so [H⁺] = 10^−4.56 ≈ 2.8×10⁻⁵ mol/L, written with two figures. The integer part, 4, only indicates the position of the decimal point. Besides rounding half up, there is a method that, when the digit is exactly 5, rounds in the direction that makes the result even, and the Japanese standard JIS Z 8401 includes it as one of its rounding rules. It is a device to avoid a bias toward rounding up when many values are rounded.

The rules of significant figures are a convention for conveying uncertainty quickly. Writing 12.35 mL does not convey whether the last digit is ±1 or ±3. When precise discussion is needed, state the uncertainty explicitly, as in 12.35 ± 0.02 mL, or evaluate it using the concept of measurement uncertainty. Conversely, copying every digit from a calculator display does not make the measurement more precise. In reporting experiments, it is important to judge the meaningful digits from the instrument's graduations and how it was read.

faq.q: How many significant figures does 0.00120 have?
faq.a: Three. The leading zeros only indicate place value and are not counted; count the 1, the 2 and the trailing 0. The trailing zero shows that the measurement was made to that digit, so it is significant.

faq.q: How many significant figures does 100 have?
faq.a: It cannot be determined from that form alone. Writing it with an exponent, as 1×10² for one figure or 1.00×10² for three, conveys the intended number clearly.

faq.q: How are significant figures counted for pH?
faq.a: The number of digits after the decimal point corresponds to the number of significant figures in the hydrogen-ion concentration. pH 7.00 has two, so [H⁺] is written as 1.0×10⁻⁷ mol/L.

当量点.desc: The point in a titration at which the amount of standard solution added has reacted exactly with the analyte according to the reaction equation. Strictly, it is distinguished from the end point, where the indicator changes color.

about.p: The equivalence point is the theoretical point at which the substance in the sample and the added standard solution have reacted exactly, in the proportions of the reaction equation. The end point, by contrast, is the point taken as the equivalence point in an actual experiment, such as a change in indicator color or a sudden change in potential. If the indicator's transition range is offset from the equivalence point, the difference between end point and equivalence point becomes the titration error. Choosing the right indicator is nothing other than bringing the end point as close as possible to the equivalence point. In standardization, which fixes the concentration of the standard solution, titrating with the same indicator and conditions also helps errors cancel.

about.h: The equivalence-point pH depends on acid and base strength
about.p: At the equivalence point of an acid–base titration, the solution is an aqueous solution of the salt formed. For a strong acid with a strong base (HCl and NaOH), the salt does not hydrolyze, so the pH is about 7 at 25 °C. When a weak acid is titrated with a strong base, the conjugate base (such as acetate) hydrolyzes to produce OH⁻, so the pH is on the basic side, about 8.7 for 0.05 mol/L sodium acetate. When a weak base is titrated with a strong acid, the conjugate acid (NH4⁺) releases H⁺, giving the acidic side, about 5.3. The equivalence-point pH can be calculated from the salt concentration and Kb = Kw/Ka.

about.h: Titration curve shape and the pH jump
about.p: A titration curve plots pH against the volume added. Near the equivalence point a pH jump appears, in which a tiny volume changes the pH greatly, and it is larger the higher the concentration and the stronger the acid or base. In the titration of a weak acid, the region before the equivalence point is a buffer where the pH changes gradually, and at the half-neutralization point pH = pKa. If the acid is too weak or too dilute, the pH jump becomes indistinct and the end point is hard to find with an indicator, so the equivalence point is found by potentiometric titration from the maximum of the derivative curve.

faq.q: Are the end point and the equivalence point the same thing?
faq.a: No. The equivalence point is a theoretical point set by the reaction equation, and the end point is the point actually observed, such as an indicator color change. The difference between them is the titration error, so choose an indicator whose transition range falls near the equivalence point.

faq.q: Is the pH at the equivalence point always 7?
faq.a: It is 7 only for a strong acid with a strong base. Titrating a weak acid with a strong base gives the basic side, and titrating a weak base with a strong acid gives the acidic side.

faq.q: How many equivalence points does a polyprotic acid have?
faq.a: If the pKa values of the steps are far enough apart, an equivalence point appears for each step. Titrating sodium carbonate with hydrochloric acid shows two end points, at about pH 8.3 and about pH 4, which the Warder method makes use of.

pH指示薬.desc: A weak-acid or weak-base dye whose color changes with the pH of the solution. Choose one whose transition range falls within the steep pH change near the equivalence point. Phenolphthalein and methyl orange are typical examples.

about.p: A pH indicator is a weakly acidic (or weakly basic) dye whose acid form HIn and base form In⁻ have different colors. The equilibrium HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻ shifts with pH, and the eye sees one color or the other once that form is roughly 10 times or more as abundant as the other. The transition range is therefore about ±1 around the indicator's pKa. In phenolphthalein, the colorless lactone ring in acid opens in base to give a quinoid dianion with extended conjugation, which is red. In strongly basic solution it changes again to a colorless form.

about.h: Common indicators and their transition ranges
about.p: Typical transition ranges for common indicators are pH 3.1–4.4 for methyl orange (red → yellow), 3.8–5.4 for bromocresol green (yellow → blue), 4.2–6.2 for methyl red (red → yellow), 6.0–7.6 for bromothymol blue (yellow → blue), and 8.0–9.8 for phenolphthalein (colorless → red). Thymol blue has two transition ranges, 1.2–2.8 (red → yellow) and 8.0–9.6 (yellow → blue). The values differ slightly between references and standards, and they also change with temperature, solvent, and salt concentration.

An indicator is itself a weak acid, so adding a lot of it consumes titrant and blurs the color change. A few drops is the basic rule. At the phenolphthalein end point, carbon dioxide dissolving from the air makes the red color fade gradually, so a color that persists for about 30 seconds is taken as the end point. Using two indicators with nearby ranges, or a mixed indicator that combines an indicator with a dye, sharpens the color change and makes the end point easier to see. For turbid or colored samples, switch to potentiometric titration.

A universal indicator is a mixture of several indicators whose color changes continuously over a wide pH range, and paper soaked in it is pH test paper. Anthocyanins in red cabbage and grape skins are natural indicators whose color also changes with pH. Measuring the ratio of absorbances of an indicator's acid and base forms with a spectrophotometer gives a precise pH through the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, a method used to measure the pH of seawater. Phenol red is added to cell culture media so that pH changes can be seen at a glance.

faq.q: Why is the transition range pKa ± 1?
faq.a: Because the human eye sees one color once one of the two colored forms is roughly 10 times or more as abundant as the other. In the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, ratios of 10 and 1/10 correspond to a pH 1 above and 1 below the pKa.

faq.q: Why does the red color of phenolphthalein fade over time?
faq.a: Near the end point, carbon dioxide from the air dissolves to form carbonic acid and lowers the pH slightly. That is why the end point is taken when the red color lasts about 30 seconds. Left for a long time in strong base, it can also change to another colorless form.

faq.q: What happens if you add too much indicator?
faq.a: The indicator also reacts with the titrant as an acid or base, so the end point shifts. The color also becomes too intense and the change is harder to see. Add the specified small amount, and the same amount in both standardization and sample titrations.

一次標準物質.desc: A substance that is highly pure, stable without absorbing moisture or decomposing, and can be weighed accurately. It serves as the reference for fixing the concentration of standard solutions. Examples include potassium hydrogen phthalate, sodium carbonate and sodium oxalate.

about.p: In volumetric analysis, results cannot be determined unless the exact concentration of the standard solution is known. A primary standard is a substance whose amount in moles can be determined directly from its weighed mass, and it serves as the reference for determining (standardizing) the concentration of standard solutions. The requirements are high purity and well-defined composition, easy drying without absorbing moisture or decomposing, no reaction with carbon dioxide or oxygen in air, and fast, stoichiometric reaction. The larger the molar mass, the larger the mass weighed and the smaller the relative weighing error.

about.h: Choose a substance that reacts like the titration
about.p: A primary standard is chosen so that it undergoes the same kind of reaction with the standard solution as the actual titration does. If standardization and titration use the same reaction and the same indicator, any bias in judging the end point enters both in the same way and has less effect on the result. Besides potassium hydrogen phthalate, sulfamic acid, a solid strong acid that hardly absorbs moisture, is used to standardize bases. Sodium chloride is used for silver nitrate in precipitation titrations, and potassium dichromate for sodium thiosulfate in iodometric titrations. In Japan, reference materials for volumetric analysis are specified in JIS standards.

about.h: How it differs from a secondary standard
about.p: Sodium hydroxide is deliquescent and absorbs carbon dioxide, and hydrochloric acid is volatile, so neither can be made into a solution of exact concentration from its mass. Instead, solutions whose concentrations have been determined with a primary standard are used as secondary standards for routine titrations. Because a secondary standard's concentration can change over time, it is restandardized periodically. Also, a primary standard and a certified reference material (CRM), whose composition values and uncertainties are given on a certificate, overlap in part but are terms for different ideas and are used distinctly.

For example, to standardize roughly 0.1 mol/L sodium hydroxide, 0.4084 g (2.000 mmol) of potassium hydrogen phthalate is dissolved in water and titrated; if 20.00 mL is required, the concentration is 2.000 mmol ÷ 20.00 mL = 0.1000 mol/L. Weighing 0.4 g on a balance with 0.1 mg divisions gives a relative weighing error of about 0.025%, smaller than the reading error of the buret. If too little is weighed, this advantage is lost.

faq.q: Why can't sodium hydroxide be a primary standard?
faq.a: It absorbs moisture from the air and deliquesces, and it also absorbs carbon dioxide and turns into sodium carbonate, so the exact amount in moles cannot be determined from its weighed mass.

faq.q: What is used to standardize hydrochloric acid?
faq.a: Sodium carbonate is common. It is neutralized as a diprotic base all the way to carbon dioxide, and the end point is detected with an indicator that changes color on the acidic side, such as methyl orange.

faq.q: What is the difference between a primary standard and a secondary standard?
faq.a: A primary standard is a substance whose amount in moles is determined directly from its mass. A secondary standard is, for example, a solution whose concentration is determined with a primary standard, and it is restandardized periodically because its concentration can change.

標定.desc: The operation of determining the exact concentration of a standard solution by titration against a primary standard or similar. Sodium hydroxide and potassium permanganate solutions must always be standardized after preparation before use.

about.h: Fixing the concentration of a standard solution
about.p: Standardization is the operation of determining accurately the approximate concentration of a standard solution used in titration, by titration against a primary standard or similar. Substances such as sodium hydroxide, from which a solution of accurate concentration cannot be made from the weighed mass, are first prepared at an approximate concentration and then standardized. In Japan, the ratio of the actual concentration to the nominal concentration (for example 0.1 mol/L) is commonly expressed as a factor f, such as f = 1.012. In titration calculations, the nominal concentration multiplied by the factor is used.

about.h: Requirements and examples of primary standards
about.p: A primary standard must be of high purity, non-hygroscopic and stable in air, accurately weighable and of large molar mass. A large molar mass means a larger mass is weighed for the same amount in moles, reducing the relative weighing error. Typical examples are potassium hydrogen phthalate (204.22 g/mol) for sodium hydroxide solution, sodium carbonate for hydrochloric acid, sodium oxalate for potassium permanganate solution, potassium iodate for sodium thiosulfate solution, and zinc or calcium carbonate for EDTA solution. Primary standards are dried at a specified temperature before use and cooled in a desiccator before weighing.

Potassium hydrogen phthalate acts as a monoprotic acid and reacts 1 : 1 with NaOH. Suppose 0.5106 g is weighed, dissolved in water and titrated with about 0.1 mol/L NaOH solution using phenolphthalein as indicator, requiring 24.85 mL. The amount is 0.5106 ÷ 204.22 = 2.500×10⁻³ mol, so the NaOH concentration is 2.500×10⁻³ ÷ 0.02485 = 0.1006 mol/L and the factor is 1.006. Standardization is done three or more times, and the mean is adopted after checking the scatter.

Sodium hydroxide is deliquescent and absorbs carbon dioxide from the air, turning into sodium carbonate, so its concentration changes even after the solution is made. It is stored in a container fitted with a soda-lime tube and restandardized periodically. Potassium permanganate solution reacts with organic matter and the like in the solution to form manganese dioxide and change concentration, so after preparation it is left to stand, the precipitate filtered off, and then standardized. A standardized solution is sometimes used to determine the concentration of another solution, and the former is then treated as a secondary standard.

faq.q: What is the difference between standardization and titration?
faq.a: Titration is the general operation of determining the amount of analyte with a standard solution of known concentration. Standardization is determining the accurate concentration of that standard solution itself by titration against a primary standard or similar.

faq.q: What is the factor?
faq.a: The actual concentration of a standard solution divided by its nominal concentration. If a solution labeled 0.1 mol/L is actually 0.1012 mol/L, the factor is 1.012.

faq.q: Why does sodium hydroxide solution need standardization?
faq.a: Because solid NaOH absorbs water and carbon dioxide, so an accurate concentration cannot be made from the weighed mass. The solution also absorbs carbon dioxide during storage and changes concentration.

キレート滴定.desc: Titration based on complex formation between a chelating agent such as EDTA and metal ions. EDTA binds metals 1 : 1 regardless of their charge and is used to determine water hardness and metal ions.

about.p: Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) is a hexadentate ligand that coordinates to a metal ion at six sites: two nitrogens and the oxygens of four carboxy groups. A single molecule wraps around the metal ion and forms several five-membered chelate rings, giving complexes far more stable than those of monodentate ligands. As a result, it almost always forms 1 : 1 complexes even with metals of different charge, such as Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Zn²⁺ and Fe³⁺. A major advantage in titration calculations is that the moles of EDTA added can be taken directly as the moles of metal ion.

about.h: pH and the conditional formation constant
about.p: EDTA is an acid that dissociates in four steps, and the form that binds metals strongly is fully deprotonated Y⁴⁻. At low pH the fraction of Y⁴⁻ becomes small, and the conditional formation constant, the apparent stability including the effect of pH, decreases. Fe³⁺, whose complex is very stable, can be titrated even in acid at pH 1–2, but Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ do not give a clear end point unless the pH is around 10. On the other hand, raising the pH too far precipitates metal hydroxides, so it is important to hold the pH that suits the purpose with a buffer. These pH differences can also be used to determine coexisting metals separately.

The end point of a complexometric titration is detected with a metal indicator that changes color when it forms a complex with the metal. Eriochrome Black T (EBT) at pH 10 is red when complexed with Mg²⁺ and the like and blue when free. As EDTA is added, the metal transfers from the indicator to EDTA, and when it has all transferred the color turns blue. Water hardness is often expressed in mg/L as the total Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ converted to the mass of CaCO3, and Ca²⁺ alone can be found by precipitating Mg(OH)2 at pH 12–13 and titrating with NN indicator (calconcarboxylic acid).

faq.q: Do you need to consider the metal's charge in EDTA titrations?
faq.a: Not for the mole ratio. EDTA forms complexes almost 1 : 1 regardless of charge, so you can set moles of EDTA = moles of metal ion.

faq.q: Why is a buffer added?
faq.a: Because the strength of binding between EDTA and the metal changes greatly with pH, and complex formation also releases H⁺. Holding the pH constant with a buffer keeps the conditional formation constant large enough and makes the indicator color change sharp.

faq.q: What is used to standardize an EDTA standard solution?
faq.a: Solutions of high-purity zinc or calcium carbonate dissolved in acid are commonly used. Titrating with the same indicator and pH as the samples helps errors cancel.

溶解度積.desc: The constant Ksp obtained by multiplying the ion concentrations, each raised to the power of its coefficient, in a saturated solution of a sparingly soluble salt; for AgCl, [Ag⁺][Cl⁻]. Solubilities of salts with different formula types cannot be compared by the size of Ksp.

about.p: The solubility product Ksp is the product of the concentrations of the dissolved ions, each raised to the power of its coefficient, when a sparingly soluble salt is in equilibrium between solid and saturated solution; it is the equilibrium constant for dissolution. For AgCl ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻, Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻], and for Ag2CrO4, Ksp = [Ag⁺]²[CrO4²⁻]. The solid is treated as having constant concentration and is not included. It is constant at a given temperature; for AgCl at 25 °C a value such as 1.8×10⁻¹⁰ (mol/L)² is used. It is linked to the standard Gibbs energy by ΔG° = −RT ln Ksp.

Calculate the ion product Q, the product of ion concentrations in the same form as Ksp; if Q > Ksp a precipitate forms, and if Q < Ksp the solid dissolves. For example, if equal volumes of 2.0×10⁻⁴ mol/L silver nitrate and sodium chloride solutions are mixed, both ions are 1.0×10⁻⁴ mol/L immediately after mixing, and Q = 1.0×10⁻⁸ greatly exceeds Ksp = 1.8×10⁻¹⁰, so AgCl precipitates. Differences in solubility product can also be used to precipitate and separate ions one after another.

The solubility product and solubility are different quantities. The molar solubility s in pure water is s = √Ksp for an AgCl-type salt and s = (Ksp/4)^(1/3) for an Ag2CrO4-type salt; the calculation changes with the form of the expression. For this reason, salts of different formula types cannot be compared for solubility by the size of Ksp. Also, adding a common ion lowers solubility, but adding an unrelated salt raises the ionic strength, decreases activity coefficients and actually raises solubility slightly. Strictly, Ksp is defined in terms of activities.

When ions of the precipitate form complex ions, solubility is greater than predicted from Ksp alone. AgCl dissolves in aqueous ammonia as [Ag(NH3)2]⁺, and at very high chloride concentrations species such as AgCl2⁻ form and solubility rises. In gravimetric analysis, a slight excess of precipitant is added to reduce precipitate losses through the common-ion effect, but too much can backfire through complex formation. The indicator concentration in the Mohr method and the conditions for separating metal ions as sulfides or hydroxides are also designed from solubility products.

faq.q: What is the difference between solubility and the solubility product?
faq.a: Solubility is the amount of salt dissolved in a saturated solution, and the solubility product is the equilibrium constant given by the product of ion concentrations raised to their coefficients. For an AgCl-type salt, solubility is the square root of Ksp, and the conversion formula changes with the composition of the salt.

faq.q: What are the units of the solubility product?
faq.a: They depend on the form of the expression: (mol/L)² for AgCl and (mol/L)³ for Ag2CrO4. Thermodynamically it is treated as a dimensionless quantity defined with activities, and units are often omitted.

faq.q: Does adding an unrelated salt change solubility?
faq.a: It can raise it slightly. The ionic strength increases and activity coefficients decrease, so more ions can dissolve while satisfying the same Ksp. This is called the salt effect.

モール法.desc: A precipitation titration of chloride ion with silver nitrate using potassium chromate as the indicator. The end point is signaled by reddish-brown Ag2CrO4 forming after AgCl, and it is carried out in neutral to weakly basic solution.

about.h: A titration with two precipitation steps
about.p: The Mohr method is a precipitation titration in which chloride ions in a sample are titrated with standard silver nitrate, using potassium chromate as the indicator. It was devised by Mohr in the mid-19th century. White AgCl precipitates first; when Cl⁻ is nearly gone, excess Ag⁺ forms red-brown Ag2CrO4 with CrO4²⁻, and the color change of the yellow solution signals the end point. Ag2CrO4 precipitates after AgCl because of the different forms of their solubility products and because the indicator concentration is kept low.

about.h: The reasoning behind the indicator concentration
about.p: At the equivalence point, [Ag⁺] = √Ksp(AgCl) ≈ 1.3×10⁻⁵ mol/L. The chromate concentration at which Ag2CrO4 just begins to precipitate is Ksp(Ag2CrO4)/[Ag⁺]², which is about 6×10⁻³ mol/L taking Ksp as 1.1×10⁻¹². In practice, at this concentration the yellow of chromate is so intense that the red-brown is hard to see, so a lower concentration is used. The end point then lags slightly behind the equivalence point, so a blank with a chloride-free sample is run and the indicator correction is subtracted.

The Mohr method is carried out in neutral to weakly basic solution (pH about 6.5–10), because in acid chromate turns into dichromate and in strongly basic solution silver oxide precipitates. In samples containing ammonium salts, silver forms ammine complexes at high pH, so the pH is kept near neutral. Bromide can be titrated the same way, but iodide and thiocyanate are unsuitable because chromate adsorbs on the precipitate and the end point becomes unclear. Ba²⁺ and Pb²⁺ interfere by precipitating as chromates.

about.h: Where it is used and alternative methods
about.p: Because it is simple, the Mohr method has been widely used to determine chloride in tap water, wastewater, food salt content and so on. For acidic samples or samples containing interfering ions, the Volhard method (a back titration in which excess silver nitrate is added and the remainder titrated with thiocyanate) or the Fajans method, which uses an indicator that changes color by adsorbing on the precipitate surface, is chosen. Potentiometric titration following the potential with a silver electrode needs no color judgment, can determine mixed halides one after another, and is well suited to automatic titrators.

faq.q: How does the color change at the end point of the Mohr method?
faq.a: During the titration, white AgCl precipitates and the solution is the yellow of chromate; at the end point red-brown Ag2CrO4 forms and the precipitate and solution take on a slight reddish tint. The change is subtle, so judge it by comparison with the color of the blank.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Mohr and Volhard methods?
faq.a: The Mohr method titrates directly with silver nitrate in neutral to weakly basic solution with potassium chromate as indicator. The Volhard method is a back titration of excess silver with thiocyanate, carried out in nitric acid solution with Fe³⁺ as indicator.

faq.q: Can iodide be determined by the Mohr method?
faq.a: It is not suitable. Chromate and other ions adsorb strongly on the AgI precipitate, so the end-point color change is unclear. For iodide, methods using adsorption indicators or potentiometric titration are used.

ヨウ素滴定.desc: Titration based on the redox chemistry of iodine. I2 liberated by an oxidizing agent is titrated with sodium thiosulfate, and starch is added near the end point. Used to determine copper, dissolved oxygen and chlorine.

about.p: Titrations using iodine come in two types. In iodometry, an indirect method, excess potassium iodide is added to a sample containing an oxidizing agent and the I2 formed is titrated with a sodium thiosulfate standard solution; in iodimetry, a reducing agent (such as ascorbic acid or sulfite) is titrated directly with an iodine standard solution. Iodine dissolves in water at 25℃ only to the extent of about 0.3 g per liter, but in the presence of iodide ions it forms the triiodide ion I3⁻ and dissolves well, so potassium iodide is also added to the standard solution.

Thiosulfate ions and iodine react in the ratio 2S2O3²⁻ + I2 → S4O6²⁻ + 2I⁻. This relation holds properly only in the neutral to weakly acidic range. In strongly acidic solution thiosulfate decomposes and sulfur precipitates, and in basic solution iodine turns into hypoiodite, which oxidizes thiosulfate all the way to sulfate, so the ratio shifts. The reaction between the oxidizing agent and iodide is fast in acid, so once the iodine has been liberated, titrate without leaving the solution strongly acidic for long.

about.h: Sources of error and how to prevent them
about.p: In acidic solution, oxygen from the air oxidizes iodide to give I2 (4I⁻ + O2 + 4H⁺ → 2I2 + 2H2O), making results high. This reaction is accelerated by light and copper ions, so stopper the flask, keep it in the dark and titrate promptly. Iodine is volatile, so add potassium iodide in ample excess to keep it as I3⁻. Sodium thiosulfate solutions slowly decompose because of dissolved carbon dioxide and bacteria, so store them with a little sodium carbonate added and standardize them regularly against potassium iodate or a similar standard.

about.h: Determining dissolved oxygen, copper and chlorine
about.p: In the Winkler method for dissolved oxygen in water, the oxygen is absorbed and fixed by manganese(II) hydroxide, and on acidification it oxidizes iodide. One mole of O2 corresponds to 4 mol of thiosulfate, so if a 100 mL sample requires 10.00 mL of 0.0100 mol/L solution, the dissolved oxygen is 8.0 mg/L. Copper(II) is determined through 2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → 2CuI + I2, with thiocyanate added near the end point to release iodine adsorbed on CuI. The available chlorine of bleach and the peroxide value of fats and oils are measured on the same principle.

faq.q: Why is potassium iodide added in excess?
faq.a: To make the reaction with the oxidizing agent fast and complete, and to keep the iodine formed in solution as I3⁻, preventing losses by volatilization. The excess iodide does not affect the reaction with thiosulfate.

faq.q: Why does sodium thiosulfate solution need to be standardized?
faq.a: Because the pentahydrate crystals effloresce easily and the solution decomposes through carbon dioxide and bacteria, changing its concentration. Its concentration is fixed by titrating the iodine liberated from excess potassium iodide by a primary standard such as potassium iodate or potassium dichromate.

faq.q: Why is iodometric titration not done in basic solution?
faq.a: Because in basic solution iodine turns into hypoiodite and iodate ions, which oxidize thiosulfate all the way to sulfate, so the 2 : 1 stoichiometry no longer holds.

逆合成解析.desc: A way of planning syntheses that starts from the target molecule and hypothetically disconnects bonds that known reactions can form, working back to readily available precursors. It is written with the arrow "⇒".

about.p: Retrosynthetic analysis is a method of synthesis planning systematized by E. J. Corey. Instead of thinking forward from the starting materials, you start from the target molecule and ask which bond, if formed last, would split it into simpler precursors. One retrosynthetic step is written with the arrow "⇒", and this is repeated until readily available starting materials are reached. A single molecule can be disconnected in many ways, so several routes are drawn and compared, and the best one is chosen on the basis of the number of steps, yield, availability of starting materials, safety and so on.

Hypothetically cutting a bond is called a disconnection, and the idealized fragments it produces are called synthons. Synthons take forms such as C⁻ and C⁺ and often do not exist as such, so they are replaced by reagents actually used (synthetic equivalents). For example, disconnecting the C−C bond next to a carbonyl group, the nucleophilic carbon synthon corresponds to a Grignard reagent or an enolate, and the electrophilic carbon synthon to an aldehyde or ketone. The principle is to disconnect at positions that correspond to the reverse of reactions known to proceed reliably.

A C−C bond joining two aromatic rings is easiest to think of as disconnected in correspondence with the Suzuki–Miyaura coupling (aryl halide + boronic acid). Reversing a C=C double bond to a Wittig reaction (carbonyl compound + phosphorus ylide) fixes the position of the double bond reliably. A cyclohexene ring can be split by the Diels–Alder reaction into a diene and a dienophile, and esters and amides are split into carboxylic acid derivatives and alcohols or amines. Functional group interconversion (FGI), converting one functional group into another to make a disconnection easier, is also a common move.

The overall yield of a linear multistep synthesis is the product of the step yields, so even at 80% per step it falls to about 41% after four steps and about 11% after ten. Retrosynthesis therefore favors fewer steps and disconnections that split the molecule into large fragments near its middle. A convergent synthesis, in which two or more fragments are made separately and joined at the end, shortens the longest linear sequence and makes a higher overall yield easier to achieve. When there are functional groups that should not react, the protection and deprotection steps are also counted when comparing routes.

faq.q: How does retrosynthetic analysis differ from predicting reactions?
faq.a: Predicting reactions is forward thinking, from starting materials to products; retrosynthetic analysis is backward thinking, from the target molecule to starting materials. In synthesis planning, routes are devised by retrosynthesis and each step is then checked as a forward reaction.

faq.q: What is a synthon?
faq.a: An idealized fragment produced when a bond is disconnected in retrosynthesis. It often does not exist in that form, and in practice a reagent that plays the same role (a synthetic equivalent), such as a Grignard reagent or an aldehyde, is used.

faq.q: What makes a good synthetic route?
faq.a: Few steps and a high overall yield, starting materials that are available and safe, and little by-product and waste (atom economy). Routes with fewer protecting-group installations and removals are generally favored.

保護基.desc: A group that temporarily converts a functional group that should not react into another form to protect it. Examples are acetals for ketones, TBS ethers for alcohols and the Boc group for amines; it is removed after the reaction.

about.p: When you want only some functional groups of a polyfunctional molecule to react, a group that temporarily converts the functional groups you do not want to react into another form is called a protecting group. The basic sequence has three steps: attach the protecting group (protection), carry out the desired reaction, and finally remove it to restore the original functional group (deprotection). A good protecting group goes on and comes off in high yield, survives the intervening reaction conditions, and is removed under conditions that do not damage the rest of the molecule. Acetals for ketones, silyl ethers for alcohols and carbamates for amines are typical examples.

Protecting groups are chosen by what they are stable to and what removes them. Acetals are stable to bases and hydride reducing agents and are removed by aqueous acid. TBS ethers are stable to bases and Grignard reagents and are removed by fluoride ion or acid. Among amine protecting groups, Boc is removed by acid, Fmoc by base and Cbz by catalytic hydrogenation. Orthogonal protection, combining protecting groups whose removal conditions do not interfere with each other, lets several functional groups of the same type be distinguished and handled in sequence. Solid-phase peptide synthesis is a representative application.

Protecting groups are convenient, but protection and deprotection add two steps, require reagents, solvents and purification, and the removed protecting group becomes waste. Yield also drops; for example, if protection and deprotection each proceed in 90% yield, the overall yield is multiplied by 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81 from these steps alone. For this reason green chemistry recommends avoiding unnecessary derivatization, and one goal is synthesis without protecting groups, using chemoselective reagents or enzymes that react only with the target functional group.

In planning a synthesis, first identify which functional groups will interfere at which steps, then choose a protecting group that survives all those conditions and can be removed gently at the end. Some protecting groups also change the stereoselectivity of a reaction through neighboring-group participation, or improve crystallinity to make purification easier. Conversely, a bulky silyl group can change how a reaction proceeds. The stability and removal methods of protecting groups are compiled in tables in specialist reference books, which serve as the starting point for choosing one.

faq.q: What is orthogonal protection?
faq.a: Combining several protecting groups that can be removed under conditions that do not affect each other. For example, using one group removed by acid and another removed by base lets you remove only one of them and react that site first.

faq.q: What protecting groups are used for alcohols?
faq.a: Silyl ethers such as TBS, benzyl ethers, esters such as acetyl, and acetal-type groups such as THP. They are removed by fluoride ion, catalytic hydrogenation, basic hydrolysis and acid, respectively.

faq.q: Is synthesis without protecting groups better?
faq.a: It is considered desirable when possible because it reduces steps and waste. However, using protecting groups is often more reliable and gives a higher overall yield, so the decision depends on the goal.

鈴木・宮浦カップリング.desc: A reaction that forms C−C bonds from aryl halides and organoboron compounds in the presence of a palladium catalyst and a base. It is widely used to make biaryls, and the boron reagents are stable and of low toxicity.

about.p: The Suzuki–Miyaura coupling reacts an aryl halide or aryl triflate, Ar−X, with an organoboron compound such as a boronic acid, Ar'B(OH)2, or a boronic ester, in the presence of a palladium catalyst and a base, to make Ar−Ar'. Biaryl structures, with two aromatic rings joined directly, are common in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals and liquid-crystal materials, and this method has become indispensable for making them. Akira Suzuki shared the 2010 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Heck and Negishi for developing such reactions. It can also join two alkenyl groups or an aryl and an alkenyl group.

The reaction proceeds through three elementary steps. First, Pd(0) inserts into the C−X bond of Ar−X by oxidative addition, giving Ar−Pd(II)−X. Next comes transmetalation, in which Ar' moves to palladium from the organoboron compound, activated by the base as a borate. Finally, reductive elimination releases Ar−Ar' and regenerates Pd(0). Oxidative addition occurs most readily in the order C−I > C−Br > C−Cl, and using inexpensive aryl chlorides requires measures such as electron-rich, bulky phosphine ligands.

about.h: How it differs from other couplings
about.p: The organoboron compounds of the Suzuki–Miyaura coupling are relatively stable to air and water, easy to handle and of low toxicity, and the borate by-products can be washed out with water. It tolerates many functional groups, including carbonyls, esters and nitro groups, and proceeds even in water-containing solvents. The Migita–Kosugi–Stille coupling (usually just called the Stille coupling), using organotin compounds, suffers from toxicity, and the Kumada–Tamao–Corriu coupling (Kumada coupling), using Grignard reagents, from limited functional-group tolerance. The Heck reaction, which joins alkenes and aryl halides, uses no organometallic reagent and differs in leaving a C=C through β-hydride elimination.

faq.q: Why is a base needed?
faq.a: The boron of a boronic acid has low nucleophilicity, so a base is added to convert it into a negatively charged borate, which makes it easier to hand the organic group over to palladium in transmetalation.

faq.q: Which aryl halides react most readily?
faq.a: The ease of oxidative addition runs I > Br > Cl, and iodides and bromides react under mild conditions. Chlorides are inexpensive but often need catalysts with highly active ligands.

faq.q: How much catalyst is used?
faq.a: In the laboratory, a few mol% or less relative to the substrate is typical, and highly active catalysts work at less than 0.1 mol%. The higher the turnover number (TON), the less palladium is used and the less remains in the product.

ヘック反応.desc: A reaction that joins an aryl halide and an alkene in the presence of a palladium catalyst and a base. Through insertion and β-hydride elimination, a substituted alkene (usually the E isomer) is obtained.

about.h: Attaching an aryl group to an alkene
about.p: The Heck reaction couples an aryl halide or aryl triflate with an alkene in the presence of a palladium catalyst and a base, replacing one of the alkene's hydrogens with the aryl group. It was reported by Mizoroki around 1971 and by Heck in 1972, so it is also called the Mizoroki–Heck reaction. Heck shared the 2010 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Negishi and Suzuki. Electron-poor alkenes such as acrylate esters, as well as styrene, are commonly used. The substituted alkene product keeps a double bond that can be transformed further.

First, Pd(0) undergoes oxidative addition to the aryl halide to give Ar−Pd(II)−X. Next, the alkene coordinates, and migratory insertion (syn addition), in which the aryl group moves to an adjacent alkene carbon, gives an alkylpalladium. β-Hydride elimination then releases the substituted alkene, leaving H−Pd(II)−X. Finally, a base such as triethylamine or potassium carbonate removes HX and regenerates Pd(0). Unlike Suzuki–Miyaura coupling, there is no transmetalation step. The oxidation state of palladium thus changes 0 → II → 0.

With acrylate esters, the aryl group bonds to the less hindered terminal carbon, and β-hydride elimination also occurs on the same face (syn), so mainly the E cinnamate ester is obtained. The intramolecular Heck reaction can form rings and is also used to create quaternary carbon stereocenters. With chiral phosphine ligands, asymmetric synthesis is possible. Halide reactivity is I > Br ≫ Cl, and aryl chlorides need electron-rich, bulky ligands. Iodobenzene and styrene give mainly (E)-stilbene.

The Heck reaction is used to manufacture cinnamate-type UV absorbers and intermediates for pharmaceuticals. It proceeds with small amounts of catalyst, but recovering and reusing the expensive palladium and, for pharmaceuticals, removing residual palladium from the product to below regulatory limits are essential steps. Isomers in which the alkene's double bond has migrated can form as by-products, and these are suppressed by the choice of base and additives (silver salts, tetraalkylammonium halides and so on). The color of the solution after reaction and precipitated palladium black also indicate catalyst deactivation.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Heck reaction and Suzuki–Miyaura coupling?
faq.a: In the Heck reaction the partner is an alkene, and a substituted alkene forms via insertion and β-hydride elimination. In Suzuki–Miyaura coupling the partner is an organoboron compound, joined by a C−C single bond via transmetalation.

faq.q: What is the base for in the Heck reaction?
faq.a: To remove HX from the H−Pd−X formed by β-hydride elimination and regenerate Pd(0). Without a base, the catalytic cycle does not turn over.

faq.q: Why is it called the Mizoroki–Heck reaction?
faq.a: Because Tsutomu Mizoroki and Richard Heck reported the reaction independently in the early 1970s. Mizoroki, who reported first, is named first, and the name is also used in the English-language literature.

ウィッティヒ反応.desc: A reaction that makes alkenes from aldehydes or ketones and a phosphorus ylide, Ph3P=CR2. A C=C forms exactly where the C=O was, and formation of the strong P=O bond is the driving force.

about.p: The Wittig reaction converts an aldehyde or ketone with a phosphorus ylide Ph3P=CR2 into an alkene, forming the C=C exactly where the C=O was. Wittig reported it in 1954, and it was recognized by the 1979 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Unlike dehydration of an alcohol, the double bond does not migrate and isomers are not mixed in, so it is used when a double bond must be placed in a defined position. In retrosynthetic analysis it appears as disconnection of a C=C into a carbonyl compound and an ylide.

about.h: Making the ylide and the course of the reaction
about.p: The ylide is obtained by making a phosphonium salt from triphenylphosphine and an alkyl halide and removing a hydrogen from the carbon next to phosphorus with a strong base such as butyllithium or sodium hydride. The ylide carbon attacks the carbonyl carbon nucleophilically, and via a four-membered oxaphosphetane containing phosphorus and oxygen the system splits into the alkene and triphenylphosphine oxide Ph3P=O. Formation of the very strong P=O bond is the driving force of the whole reaction. The pathway through the oxaphosphetane has been examined by low-temperature NMR and other methods.

The E/Z geometry of the alkene formed is broadly set by the type of ylide. Non-stabilized ylides bearing only alkyl groups tend to give mainly the Z isomer at low temperature. Stabilized ylides, whose negative charge is stabilized by an ester or ketone carbonyl, give mainly the E isomer. Semi-stabilized ylides bearing groups such as phenyl often give mixtures of E and Z. When the E isomer is wanted, the Horner–Wadsworth–Emmons reaction, which uses carbanions derived from phosphonate esters, is commonly used.

The triphenylphosphine oxide by-product often has a polarity close to that of the product, and removing it by column chromatography or crystallization takes effort. The by-product of the Horner–Wadsworth–Emmons reaction is a phosphate salt, which has the advantage of being removed by washing with water. Also, only part of the large reagent ends up in the product in the Wittig reaction, so its atom economy is low. Reactivity also differs greatly with the combination: stabilized ylides, for example, react poorly with ketones.

faq.q: Does the Wittig reaction give the E or the Z isomer?
faq.a: Non-stabilized alkyl ylides tend to give mainly Z, ylides stabilized by an ester or similar group mainly E, and semi-stabilized ylides tend to give mixtures.

faq.q: How does it differ from the Horner–Wadsworth–Emmons reaction?
faq.a: That reaction uses carbanions of phosphonate esters instead of phosphorus ylides; it differs in readily giving the E isomer and in that the phosphate by-product can be removed by washing with water.

faq.q: How is triphenylphosphine oxide removed?
faq.a: Besides column chromatography, it can be precipitated from a solvent in which it dissolves poorly, such as hexane, and filtered off, or the product can be crystallized.

ディールス・アルダー反応.desc: A concerted [4+2] cycloaddition between a diene in the s-cis conformation and a dienophile, forming a cyclohexene ring. It is stereospecific: the configuration of the dienophile is retained in the product.

about.h: Making a six-membered ring in one step
about.p: The Diels–Alder reaction is a [4+2] cycloaddition in which a conjugated diene and a dienophile (an alkene or alkyne) combine in a single step through a cyclic transition state to form a cyclohexene ring. Diels and Alder reported it in 1928, and the two received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1950. It forms two σ bonds and up to four stereocenters at once, and since all the atoms enter the product its atom economy is 100%. It is a standard reaction for building the skeletons of ring-containing natural products and drugs.

The diene must adopt the s-cis conformation, in which both terminal carbons can reach the dienophile; cyclopentadiene, locked in s-cis, is so reactive that it dimerizes at room temperature (it is cracked back to the monomer by heating before use). In frontier-orbital terms, the diene HOMO and dienophile LUMO usually interact, so electron-withdrawing groups such as carbonyls on the dienophile and electron-donating groups on the diene speed the reaction. Lewis acids lower the dienophile LUMO further and accelerate the reaction.

Because it is a concerted reaction in which bonds form simultaneously, the cis/trans relationship of the dienophile is preserved in the product (stereospecificity). With cyclic dienes, the endo adduct, in which the dienophile's substituent points toward the diene, tends to predominate under kinetic control (the endo rule). For a substituted diene and dienophile, 1-substituted dienes tend to give mainly the "ortho" product and 2-substituted dienes the "para" product. These are explained by the relative sizes of orbital coefficients. A trans dienophile gives the product with trans substituents as a racemate.

At high temperature the retro-Diels–Alder reaction can return the starting materials; heating dicyclopentadiene to obtain cyclopentadiene uses this. Combinations such as furan and maleimide, which add and dissociate repeatedly at moderate temperatures, are used in thermally rearrangeable polymers and self-healing materials. Using a carbonyl group or imine as the dienophile makes six-membered rings containing oxygen or nitrogen (the hetero-Diels–Alder reaction). Run intramolecularly, the reaction can also form several rings at once. Enzymes that catalyze Diels–Alder reactions have also been found in living organisms.

faq.q: Why must the diene be in the s-cis conformation?
faq.a: Unless it is s-cis, the two terminal carbons of the diene cannot reach the two carbons of the dienophile at the same time. Dienes locked in s-trans do not react.

faq.q: What is the endo rule?
faq.a: The tendency, in reactions with cyclic dienes, for the endo adduct, in which a carbonyl or similar group of the dienophile points toward the diene, to form mainly. It is explained by secondary orbital interactions in the transition state and is a result of kinetic control.

faq.q: Is the Diels–Alder reaction driven by heat or by light?
faq.a: By heat. Under the Woodward–Hoffmann rules, [4+2] is thermally allowed. It is [2+2] cycloaddition that proceeds photochemically.

収率.desc: The amount in moles of product actually obtained as a fraction of the theoretical yield, the amount formed if all of the limiting reagent became product. The overall yield of a multistep synthesis is the product of the step yields.

about.p: The yield is the amount of product actually obtained as a fraction of the theoretical yield, the amount that would form if all of the limiting reagent became product. Compare amounts in moles rather than dividing masses directly. For example, if the limiting reagent is 0.0200 mol and the reaction forms a product (molar mass 150.0 g/mol) 1 : 1, the theoretical yield is 3.00 g; obtaining 2.40 g gives a yield of 80.0%. Using a reagent added in excess as the basis underestimates the yield, so first identify the limiting reagent from the coefficients of the equation.

about.h: Overall yield of a multistep synthesis
about.p: The overall yield of a linear multistep synthesis is the product of the yields of the individual steps. Even at 90% per step, ten steps give 0.9¹⁰ ≈ 0.35, about 35%, and at 80% per step the yield falls to about 11%. For this reason synthesis planning puts weight on reducing the number of steps. In a convergent synthesis, in which fragments are made separately and joined at the end, the longest route has fewer steps, which makes a higher overall yield easier to achieve. For example, at 90% per step, a longest route of five steps gives an overall yield of about 59%.

about.h: How it differs from conversion and selectivity
about.p: Conversion is the fraction of the starting material that reacted and was consumed, and selectivity is the fraction of the consumed starting material that became the target product; on the same starting material, yield = conversion × selectivity. A conversion of 90% and a selectivity of 80% give a yield of 72%. Also distinguish in writing between a yield measured directly in the reaction mixture by NMR or GC and an isolated yield after purification. A yield above 100% suggests a calculation error or solvent, inorganic salts or other material remaining in the product.

about.h: What the yield alone does not tell you
about.p: The yield is the basic measure of a reaction's efficiency, but it says nothing about how little waste is produced or how good the process is. Even at 100% yield, a reaction with many by-products has a low atom economy, and using large amounts of solvent or excess reagents gives a large E-factor. When a product is obtained as a mixture of isomers, report the combined yield and the ratio; when its purity is low, report the purity as well. In industrial processes, conditions are chosen by weighing the price of raw materials, ease of purification and safety alongside the yield. The yield of a step that uses an expensive raw material has an especially large effect on the overall cost.

faq.q: How is the yield calculated?
faq.a: Find the theoretical yield from the amount in moles of the limiting reagent and the coefficients of the equation, divide the amount of product actually obtained by it, and multiply by 100. It is important to compare amounts in moles rather than dividing masses directly.

faq.q: What is the difference between yield and conversion?
faq.a: Conversion is the fraction of starting material consumed; yield is the fraction that became the target product. With side reactions the conversion can be high while the yield is low; on the same starting material, yield = conversion × selectivity.

faq.q: Why can a yield exceed 100%?
faq.a: Solvent, water, inorganic salts or by-products may remain in the product, or the limiting reagent or coefficients may have been mixed up in the calculation. Dry the product again and check its purity.

原子効率.desc: The fraction of reactant atoms incorporated into the desired product, found by dividing the molar mass of the desired product by the total molar mass of the reactants. It is a guide to how much by-product is formed.

about.h: An efficiency set by the equation alone
about.p: Atom economy is the fraction of the reactants' atoms that end up in the target product: the molar mass of the target product divided by the sum of the molar masses of the reactants multiplied by their coefficients in the equation, times 100. It was proposed by Trost in 1991 and was adopted as one of the 12 principles of green chemistry. Because it can be calculated from the equation alone, it serves as a guide for comparing synthetic routes before doing any experiments. Catalysts and solvents do not appear in the equation and are not included. Reactants are counted in the stoichiometric amounts needed to make the target product.

Addition reactions, rearrangements, Diels–Alder reactions and catalytic hydrogenation, in which all the reactant atoms enter the product, have an atom economy of 100%. In substitution and elimination reactions, on the other hand, the departing groups become by-products and the value is lower. For example, the substitution of bromoethane with sodium hydroxide to make ethanol gives 46.07 ÷ (108.97 + 40.00) × 100 ≈ 31%, and the rest becomes sodium bromide. Reactions in which only part of a large reagent enters the product, such as the Wittig reaction, are also low.

Yield describes the amount of product actually obtained, while atom economy describes where the atoms go on paper; they are separate measures. Even a reaction with 100% yield releases many by-products if its atom economy is low. Conversely, even at 100% atom economy, unreacted starting material, excess reagents, solvents and substances used in purification become waste, so the actual amount of waste is assessed with the E-factor or PMI. Even when a by-product is recovered and used, it is generally not counted as target product under the definition of atom economy. A reaction with both high yield and high atom economy is one that produces little waste.

Atom economy motivates replacing reactions that use stoichiometric reagents with catalytic ones. In ibuprofen manufacture, a well-known example replaced an older six-step route (atom economy about 40%) with a three-step catalytic route of about 77%.
