In practical evaluation, reaction mass efficiency, which combines atom economy with yield and excess of reagents (the mass of product as a fraction of the actual mass of raw materials), is also used. Atom economy is just one measure and is judged together with safety and energy.

faq.q: How is atom economy calculated?
faq.a: Write the equation, divide the molar mass of the target product by the sum of the reactants' molar masses multiplied by their coefficients, and multiply by 100. Catalysts and solvents are not included.

faq.q: What is the difference between atom economy and yield?
faq.a: Atom economy is a theoretical value set by the equation and reflects the amount of by-products. Yield is the fraction actually obtained in an experiment. Only when both are high can a reaction be called low-waste.

faq.q: Which reactions have 100% atom economy?
faq.a: Reactions in which all the reactant atoms enter the product, such as addition reactions, rearrangements, Diels–Alder reactions and catalytic hydrogenation. Substitution and elimination reactions do not reach 100%.

付加重合.desc: Polymerization in which monomers link one after another by opening C=C double bonds and the like. No by-product is released, and the repeat unit has the same composition as the monomer. Examples are polyethylene and polystyrene.

about.h: Double bonds open and link up
about.p: Addition polymerization is polymerization in which C=C double bonds or similar groups of the monomer open and monomers add one after another to an active chain end. No atoms are lost, so there is no by-product, and the repeat unit has the same composition as the monomer. Many commodity plastics are made this way, such as polyethylene from ethylene, polystyrene from styrene and poly(vinyl chloride) from vinyl chloride. Because a double bond becomes two single bonds, the reaction is exothermic, and heat removal is important when polymerizing on a large scale.

By the type of growing chain end, it is divided into radical, cationic, anionic and coordination polymerization. Suitability depends on the monomer's substituents: monomers with electron-donating groups, such as isobutylene and vinyl ethers, suit cationic polymerization, while those with electron-withdrawing groups, such as acrylonitrile and cyanoacrylates, suit anionic polymerization. Coordination polymerization with Ziegler–Natta catalysts and the like gives highly stereoregular polymers, such as polypropylene with its side groups aligned in the same orientation.

Most addition polymerizations are chain polymerizations, in which a single initiated chain adds many monomers in a short time and grows long. High-molecular-weight polymer therefore forms from the very beginning of the reaction, and over time it is mainly the yield that increases. This contrasts with step-growth polymerization, in which reactions between functional groups proceed little by little and molecular weight does not rise until conversion is extremely high. In living polymerization, however, with neither termination nor chain transfer, molecular weight increases as monomer is consumed and polymers with narrow distributions are obtained.

about.h: Heat of polymerization and ceiling temperature
about.p: In addition polymerization a π bond becomes a σ bond, so the reaction is exothermic; the enthalpy of polymerization is about −70 kJ/mol for styrene and about −56 kJ/mol for methyl methacrylate. On the other hand, monomers lose freedom of motion when joined into a chain, so entropy decreases. Raising the temperature therefore brings ΔG = ΔH − TΔS toward zero, and above the ceiling temperature, where polymerization and depolymerization balance, polymer can no longer be obtained. Monomers with bulky substituents and small heats of polymerization, such as α-methylstyrene, have low ceiling temperatures.

faq.q: Can addition polymerization occur through double bonds other than C=C?
faq.a: Yes. Formaldehyde polymerizes by opening its C=O double bond to give polyoxymethylene (polyacetal resin). Addition polymerization is not limited to C=C; it occurs with monomers having multiple bonds that can open and link up.

faq.q: Are addition polymerization and polyaddition the same?
faq.a: No. Polyaddition, as in polyurethane synthesis, is polymerization in which additions between functional groups proceed stepwise; its course resembles condensation polymerization and is distinguished from addition polymerization, which proceeds by a chain mechanism.

faq.q: What familiar polymers are made by addition polymerization?
faq.a: Polyethylene, polypropylene, polystyrene, poly(vinyl chloride), acrylic resin (poly(methyl methacrylate)) and others, used widely in packaging, containers, building materials and more.

縮合重合.desc: Polymerization in which functional groups join while releasing a small molecule such as water. The molecular weight builds up stepwise; nylon 66 and polyesters are typical examples.

about.p: Condensation polymerization is polymerization in which each time two functional groups react to form a bond, a small molecule such as water, an alcohol or hydrogen chloride is released. Typical examples are nylon 66, made from hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid with loss of water, and poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET), made from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid. Because of the released molecules, the composition of the repeat unit is smaller than the sum of the monomers. In addition polymers, the repeat unit has the same composition as the monomer.

In condensation polymerization, monomers and oligomers can all react with each other, so molecular weight rises slowly, step by step. The extent of reaction of functional groups p and the number-average degree of polymerization Xn obey the Carothers equation Xn = 1/(1 − p). Even at p = 0.98, Xn is 50, and only at p = 0.999 does it reach 1000. The molecular-weight distribution also broadens: the dispersity approaches 1 + p, about 2 at high conversion. Very high extents of reaction are essential to obtain high-molecular-weight products.

Even a slight imbalance in the amounts of the two monomers stops growth once the functional group in deficit is used up. With a ratio of functional groups r (≤ 1), even at complete reaction Xn = (1 + r)/(1 − r), only about 199 for r = 0.99. For this reason, nylon 66 is made by first forming the 1 : 1 salt of diamine and dicarboxylic acid (nylon salt) and then polymerizing. Esterification is an equilibrium reaction, so the water or glycol released is removed at high temperature under reduced pressure to shift the equilibrium toward the products.

about.h: How it differs from chain polymerization and polyaddition
about.p: In chain polymerizations such as addition polymerization, monomers add one after another to an active species formed by an initiator, so high-molecular-weight chains form from early in the reaction. In condensation polymerization, even though monomers are consumed early, molecular weight rises only at the end of the reaction. Step-growth polymerization that releases no molecule, as for polyurethanes, is called polyaddition. Nylon 6, made by ring-opening polymerization of caprolactam, also releases no small molecule. Mixing in trifunctional monomers increases branching, and at a certain extent of reaction a network gel forms.

faq.q: What is the difference between condensation and addition polymerization?
faq.a: In condensation polymerization a small molecule such as water is released each time functional groups react, and growth is stepwise. In addition polymerization multiple bonds such as C=C open and join without by-products, and growth is by chain reaction.

faq.q: How can molecular weight be increased in condensation polymerization?
faq.a: A very high extent of reaction is needed. Make the monomer stoichiometry exactly 1 : 1 and remove released water or similar at high temperature under reduced pressure to shift the equilibrium toward the products.

faq.q: What polymers are made by condensation polymerization?
faq.a: Polyamides such as nylon 66, polyesters such as PET, polycarbonates and phenolic resins. Many are used as fibres, bottles and engineering plastics.

ラジカル重合.desc: Chain-growth polymerization in which radicals generated from an initiator add to monomers and proceed through three stages: initiation, propagation and termination. High-molecular-weight polymer forms from the start of the reaction.

about.p: In radical polymerization, an initiator such as AIBN or benzoyl peroxide first decomposes by heat or light to form radicals, which add to the C=C of a monomer in the initiation step. Propagation, in which the next monomer adds to the resulting carbon radical, is repeated hundreds or thousands of times, and the chain is completed by termination, in which two growing radicals meet and their unpaired electrons disappear. Termination occurs by combination, in which the ends of two chains bond, and by disproportionation, in which a hydrogen atom transfers to give two chains.

At steady state, the rates of radical formation and termination balance, and the radical concentration is proportional to the square root of the initiator concentration [I]. The polymerization rate Rp = kp[M][R·] is also proportional to [I]^(1/2), so quadrupling the initiator doubles the rate. On the other hand, the number of monomers a chain adds before terminating (the kinetic chain length) is proportional to [M]/[I]^(1/2), and adding more initiator lowers the molecular weight. That rate and molecular weight move in opposite directions in this way is the basis for setting the conditions of a radical polymerization.

When a growing radical abstracts a hydrogen atom from the solvent, a thiol or the like, that chain stops growing, and the new radical formed starts the next chain. This is called chain transfer; because the number of radicals does not change, the polymerization rate changes little and only the molecular weight falls. Industrially, small amounts of chain-transfer agents such as 1-dodecanethiol are added to control molecular weight. Inhibitors such as hydroquinone, by contrast, trap radicals and stop the polymerization itself, so they are used to prevent monomers from polymerizing during storage.

Radical polymerization proceeds even in the presence of water and many functional groups and works for a wide range of monomers, including styrene, acrylic esters, vinyl chloride and vinyl acetate, making it the most widely used polymerization method in industry. It can be run in bulk, solution, suspension or emulsion, chosen for the purpose. On the other hand, termination cannot be avoided, so the molecular-weight distribution is broad (dispersity of about 1.5–2 or more), and chain lengths and end structures are hard to control. To overcome this, living (controlled) radical polymerizations that suppress termination have been developed.

faq.q: Why is the molecular weight high from the start of a radical polymerization?
faq.a: Because a single initiated radical adds hundreds to thousands of monomers during the short time before it terminates. While conversion is low, the mixture is high-molecular-weight polymer plus unreacted monomer, and it is mainly the yield that increases with time.

faq.q: What happens to the molecular weight if more initiator is used?
faq.a: There are more radicals, which meet each other more readily, so each chain is shorter and the molecular weight falls. In the steady-state approximation, the molecular weight is inversely proportional to the square root of the initiator concentration, and the polymerization rate is proportional to it.

faq.q: Why does oxygen delay polymerization?
faq.a: Oxygen reacts rapidly with growing radicals to form unreactive peroxy radicals, which hinders polymerization. For this reason, dissolved oxygen is usually removed before polymerization, for example by bubbling nitrogen through the mixture.

数平均分子量.desc: The average molecular weight of a polymer obtained by dividing its total mass by the total number of molecules (moles), Mn = ΣNiMi/ΣNi. It is strongly influenced by the numerous low-molecular-weight components.

about.p: Synthetic polymers are collections of chains of different lengths, so molecular weight is expressed as an average. The number-average molecular weight Mn is the total mass divided by the total number of molecules (amount in moles), Mn = ΣNiMi/ΣNi. Because every molecule counts equally as one, it is pulled strongly by the numerous low-molecular-weight components. Dividing Mn by the formula weight of the repeat unit gives the number-average degree of polymerization, the average number of monomers per chain. The molecular weights given by the Carothers equation for step-growth polymerization or set by the amount of initiator in living polymerization correspond to Mn.

about.h: A little low-molecular-weight material lowers it greatly
about.p: A calculation shows how sensitive Mn is to low-molecular-weight components. If 1 g of oligomer with molecular weight 1000 is mixed into 99 g of a uniform polymer of molecular weight 1.0×10⁵, the amounts in moles are 9.9×10⁻⁴ mol and 1.0×10⁻³ mol, nearly equal, and Mn becomes 100 g ÷ 1.99×10⁻³ mol ≈ 5.0×10⁴, half the original. Meanwhile, the weight-average molecular weight, which is weighted by mass, is about 9.9×10⁴ and barely changes. Residual monomer and solvent also make Mn appear lower.

Mn is obtained by methods that count molecules. Colligative properties such as osmotic pressure and vapor pressure lowering depend on the number of dissolved particles, so they give Mn. End-group analysis, counting chain ends by NMR or titration, also gives Mn if the number of ends per chain is known, though precision drops as molecular weight increases and ends become scarce. The widely used size-exclusion chromatography (GPC) gives relative values calibrated with standards such as polystyrene, so for different types of polymer they can deviate from the true values.

Mechanical properties of polymers such as tensile strength rise sharply with Mn at low molecular weights and level off above a certain point. Chain ends act like defects, so these properties are thought to be closely related to Mn, which reflects the number of ends. Melt viscosity, on the other hand, is strongly affected by heavy chains and is related to the weight-average molecular weight. For this reason, materials are generally characterized not by Mn alone but by giving the molecular weight distribution together with the weight-average molecular weight and the dispersity, the ratio of the two.

faq.q: What is the difference between number-average and weight-average molecular weight?
faq.a: The number average counts each molecule equally, while the weight average weights each component by its mass. If there is any distribution, the weight average is always larger, and the ratio of the two is the dispersity, which expresses the breadth of the distribution.

faq.q: How is number-average molecular weight measured?
faq.a: From colligative properties such as osmotic pressure, or by end-group analysis using NMR and similar methods. GPC also gives it, but as a relative value calibrated with standards that can deviate depending on the type of polymer.

faq.q: How is the number-average degree of polymerization obtained?
faq.a: Divide the number-average molecular weight by the formula weight of the repeat unit. For example, polystyrene with Mn of 3.1×10⁴ divided by the formula weight 104 gives a number-average degree of polymerization of about 300. The mass of the end groups is usually ignored.

重量平均分子量.desc: The average molecular weight weighted by the mass of each component, Mw = ΣNiMi²/ΣNiMi. It is strongly influenced by high-molecular-weight components and is always larger than Mn when there is a distribution.

about.p: The weight-average molecular weight Mw averages the molecular weight of each component weighted by the fraction of the total mass it represents: Mw = ΣwiMi = ΣNiMi²/ΣNiMi. Heavier molecules have more mass per chain, so Mw is pulled strongly by high-molecular-weight components. If there is any distribution of molecular weight, it is always larger than the number-average molecular weight Mn, and the ratio Mw/Mn, the dispersity, expresses the breadth of the distribution. If all molecules have the same length, Mw = Mn and the dispersity is 1.

about.h: A little high-molecular-weight material raises it greatly
about.p: If 1 g of a component with molecular weight 1.0×10⁷ is mixed into 99 g of a uniform polymer of molecular weight 1.0×10⁵, Mw becomes 0.99 × 1.0×10⁵ + 0.01 × 1.0×10⁷ ≈ 2.0×10⁵, almost double. In terms of moles, however, the added component is tiny, so Mn is about 1.01×10⁵ and barely changes. This is the opposite of Mn, which drops greatly with a little low-molecular-weight material, and looking at both values lets you infer on which side the distribution has a long tail.

A representative method for obtaining Mw directly is static light scattering. The intensity of scattered light is proportional to the square of a particle's mass, so heavier molecules scatter more strongly, and Mw is obtained from the scattering of the solution as a whole. It is an absolute method that needs no calibration with standards. Coupling size-exclusion chromatography (GPC) with a multi-angle light scattering detector measures the molecular weight of each eluted slice and gives the distribution. The viscosity-average molecular weight obtained from viscosity usually lies between Mn and Mw, closer to Mw.

The melt viscosity of polymers is strongly affected by heavy chains; above the molecular weight at which chains entangle, the zero-shear viscosity is known to be roughly proportional to Mw raised to the 3.4 power. By this relationship, doubling Mw increases the viscosity about tenfold. Controlling Mw is therefore important for adjusting flow in injection molding and extrusion. On the other hand, a long high-molecular-weight tail increases elasticity in the melt, which can be advantageous in processes such as film forming.

faq.q: Why is the weight-average molecular weight larger than the number average?
faq.a: Weighting by mass increases the contribution of heavy molecules. If there is any distribution of molecular weight, Mw > Mn always holds, and the two are equal only when all molecules have the same molecular weight.

faq.q: How is weight-average molecular weight measured?
faq.a: Obtaining the absolute value by static light scattering is the representative method. GPC also gives it, but as a relative value calibrated with standards, so combining it with a light scattering detector makes it accurate.

faq.q: Why is it called a "weight" average?
faq.a: Because each component is weighted by its mass (weight) fraction in the average. It is also sometimes called the mass-average molecular weight.

分散度.desc: The ratio Mw/Mn of the weight-average to the number-average molecular weight (symbol Đ). It expresses the breadth of the molecular-weight distribution; it is 1 if all molecules have the same length and is never less than 1.

about.p: When there are Ni molecules of molecular weight Mi, the number-average molecular weight is Mn = ΣNiMi/ΣNi and the weight-average molecular weight is Mw = ΣNiMi²/ΣNiMi. Mn is the total mass divided by the total number of molecules and can be obtained from end-group analysis or osmotic pressure. Mw is the average weighted by the mass of each component and can be obtained from light scattering. For example, mixing 1.0 g each of components with molecular weights 1.0×10⁴ and 3.0×10⁴ gives Mn of 1.5×10⁴ and Mw of 2.0×10⁴, a dispersity of about 1.33.

Dispersity Đ = Mw/Mn is a measure of the breadth of the molecular-weight distribution. If all molecules have the same length, Mw = Mn and Đ = 1, and the broader the distribution, the larger it becomes. It used to be called the polydispersity index (PDI), but the name dispersity and the symbol Đ are now used following IUPAC recommendations. Even at the same Mn, a different dispersity means different melt viscosity, strength and processability, so it is reported together with Mn and Mw as a basic figure describing polymer quality.

The molecular-weight distribution of step-growth polymerization (polycondensation) follows Flory's most probable distribution, with Đ = 1 + p, which approaches 2 as the extent of reaction p approaches 1. In radical polymerization the theoretical values are about 1.5 if termination is only by combination and about 2 if by disproportionation, but in practice the conditions change as conversion rises, and the distribution is often even broader. In living anionic polymerization, with no termination or chain transfer, all chains start almost simultaneously and grow at the same rate, so Đ is close to 1, at 1.1 or below.

The molecular-weight distribution is generally measured by gel permeation chromatography (GPC). Molecules elute in order of their size in solution, largest first, and the molecular weight at each elution volume is found from a calibration curve of log M against elution volume made with standards such as polystyrene. Mn, Mw and Đ are calculated from the distribution obtained in this way. Because the values are equivalents obtained by comparing size with the standards, however, they deviate from the true values for polymers of different shape. Adding a light-scattering detector gives absolute molecular weights that do not rely on standards.

faq.q: Can the dispersity be less than 1?
faq.a: No. Mw is a mass-weighted average, so whenever there is a distribution it is larger than the number average Mn; only when all molecules have the same molecular weight is Mw = Mn and the dispersity 1.

faq.q: Are the polydispersity index (PDI) and dispersity the same thing?
faq.a: Both refer to Mw/Mn. IUPAC now recommends the term dispersity and the symbol Đ.

faq.q: What is the dispersity of a natural protein?
faq.a: A particular protein is synthesized with a defined sequence and length according to genetic information, so a sample of a single kind of molecule has a dispersity of 1. This is a major difference from synthetic polymers.

カロザースの式.desc: The relation between the number-average degree of polymerization of a step-growth polymerization and the extent of reaction p, Xn = 1/(1 − p). Even at p = 0.99, Xn is only 100, showing that high molecular weight requires an extremely high extent of reaction.

about.p: The Carothers equation, presented in 1936 by Carothers, who developed nylon 66, relates the number-average degree of polymerization Xn of step-growth polymerization to the extent of reaction p. Considering two bifunctional monomers in equal amounts, each reaction reduces the number of molecules by one. If the initial number of molecules is N0, the number at extent of reaction p is N = N0(1 − p), so Xn = N0/N = 1/(1 − p). Here Xn is the average number of monomer units, counting each diol and each dicarboxylic acid as one.

This equation shows how hard it is to obtain high molecular weight in step-growth polymerization. At p = 0.90, Xn = 10; at 0.99, 100; at 0.999, 1000. Raising the degree of polymerization tenfold requires reducing unreacted functional groups to one tenth. Nylons and polyesters with useful strength need degrees of polymerization of several hundred, so the extent of reaction must be well above 99%. For this reason, in esterification, which is an equilibrium reaction, the by-product water is removed under reduced pressure to drive the reaction, and high-purity monomers with few side reactions are used.

When the molar ratio r of the two types of functional groups departs from 1, the functional group in excess caps both chain ends, and Xn decreases to (1 + r)/(1 + r − 2rp). In systems containing monomers with three or more functional groups, networks form and the system gels. In Carothers's treatment, with f the average functionality, gelation occurs at p = 2/f. For 2 mol of glycerol and 3 mol of phthalic acid, f = 2.4 and p = 0.833, but Flory's statistical theory gives about 0.707, and gelation actually occurs earlier than Carothers predicted.

When the rate is proportional to the concentrations of both functional groups, as in polyesterification with an added catalyst, 1/(1 − p) increases in proportion to time, and Xn grows linearly with time. Without an added catalyst, when the carboxylic acid itself acts as the catalyst, the rate is proportional to the square of the carboxy concentration times the hydroxy concentration, and 1/(1 − p)² increases in proportion to time. Xn therefore grows more and more slowly late in the reaction, which shows the advantage of adding a catalyst. In chain polymerization, high-molecular-weight chains form from the beginning, so this equation does not apply.

faq.q: How do I get molecular weight from Xn in the Carothers equation?
faq.a: Multiply Xn by the average mass of the monomer residues that make up the repeat unit. For nylon 66, use the average of the diamine and dicarboxylic acid residues, noting that two residues make one repeat unit.

faq.q: Can the Carothers equation be used for addition polymerization?
faq.a: No. It is for step-growth polymerization, in which reactions between functional groups proceed little by little; in addition polymerization, where chains grow by a chain mechanism, high-molecular-weight chains form from the start.

faq.q: How is the extent of reaction p measured?
faq.a: By counting the remaining functional groups. In polyesterification, a small sample is taken and its carboxy groups are titrated with base and compared with the initial amount. It can also be found from the amount of water formed.

ゲル浸透クロマトグラフィー.desc: A method that separates polymers by their size in solution on a column packed with a porous gel. Larger molecules elute first, and the molecular-weight distribution is found by comparison with standards.

about.p: Gel permeation chromatography (GPC) is the name used when separating synthetic polymers in organic solvents; when proteins and the like are separated in aqueous systems it is called gel filtration, and the two together are called size-exclusion chromatography (SEC). Separation depends only on the fraction Kd of pore volume a molecule can enter, which ranges from 0, for molecules that cannot enter the pores at all, to 1, for those that can enter all of them. The elution volume is Ve = V0 + Kd·Vi (V0 is the interstitial volume between particles, Vi the pore volume), so every component elutes between V0 and V0 + Vi.

Because GPC separates by molecular size, polymers that are more expanded in solution elute earlier even at the same molecular weight. Benoit and coworkers showed that when elution volume is plotted against the product of intrinsic viscosity and molecular weight, [η]M, which corresponds to size in solution, polymers of different kinds fall on a single line (universal calibration). If the constants of the Mark–Houwink equation [η] = KMᵃ are known, molecular weights of other polymers can be converted from a calibration line made with polystyrene standards. A viscometer detector measures [η] on the spot.

The basic detector is the differential refractive index (RI) detector, which responds to almost all polymers, and UV absorption detectors are also used for polymers with aromatic rings. Adding a multi-angle light scattering (MALS) detector gives the absolute molecular weight at each elution position without calibration. Each column has a set range of molecular weights it can separate; molecules too large to enter the pores all elute together at V0 and cannot be separated further (the exclusion limit). Columns with pores suited to the molecular weight range of the sample are chosen and several are connected in series.

Polystyrene and acrylic polymers are measured in THF or chloroform, but polyethylene and polypropylene do not dissolve in any solvent at room temperature, so they are measured by high-temperature GPC at about 135–160℃ using 1,2,4-trichlorobenzene or a similar solvent. For highly polar polymers, a salt such as lithium bromide is added to DMF to suppress aggregation of the molecules and adsorption on the column. Samples are made up as dilute solutions of about 1 mg/mL and filtered to remove insoluble material. If too concentrated, viscosity effects distort the peaks.

faq.q: Are GPC and SEC the same thing?
faq.a: The principle is the same: both separate by molecular size. The name GPC is usually used when synthetic polymers are measured in organic solvents and gel filtration when biopolymers are measured in aqueous systems, while SEC is the name covering both.

faq.q: What is the exclusion limit?
faq.a: It is the size (molecular weight) at which molecules can no longer enter the column's pores at all. Larger molecules all elute at the same volume without being distinguished, so a column with a pore size suited to the sample must be chosen.

faq.q: How is the molecular weight of polyethylene measured?
faq.a: It does not dissolve at room temperature, so it is measured by high-temperature GPC using a solvent such as 1,2,4-trichlorobenzene, with the columns and detector held at about 135–160℃. The sample is also dissolved by heating at the same temperature.

熱重量測定.desc: Thermal analysis (TG) that continuously measures the change in a sample's mass while its temperature is varied. Mass losses from dehydration, decomposition and combustion and gains from oxidation reveal composition and thermal stability.

about.p: In thermogravimetry (TG), the mass of a sample suspended in or placed in a furnace is measured continuously with a precise balance while the temperature is raised at a constant rate. Many instruments can measure changes down to µg, and samples of a few mg to a few tens of mg are used. The atmosphere is switched to an inert gas such as nitrogen to observe thermal decomposition, or to air or oxygen to observe combustion and oxidation. Plotting the DTG curve, the derivative of the mass curve with respect to temperature, shows the temperature of the fastest mass loss as a peak and makes overlapping steps easier to distinguish.

The start of a mass loss is expressed as the intersection of the horizontal line before the loss and the tangent to the steepest part (the extrapolated onset temperature). When comparing the heat resistance of polymers and the like, the temperature at 5% mass loss, T5%, is also often used. Comparing the mass loss of each step with a reaction equation lets you estimate composition. For example, copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate loses water stepwise, two, two and then one molecule, with mass losses of 14.4%, 14.4% and 7.2%, totaling 36.1%. The mass remaining at the end gives the amount of ash or inorganic matter.

about.h: The temperature is not a property of the substance
about.p: The decomposition temperature seen in TG is not an intrinsic property like a melting point but an apparent value set by the balance between the rate of reaction and the heating rate. Raising the heating rate shifts decomposition to higher temperatures. Turning this around, the activation energy of a decomposition reaction can be found from curves measured at several heating rates by methods such as the Ozawa–Flynn–Wall method. In addition, at high temperature the gas density falls and the buoyancy changes, so the apparent mass increases; this is corrected using a curve measured with an empty container.

about.h: Analyzing the evolved gas at the same time
about.p: TG alone does not tell you what was lost. In TG-MS and TG-IR, the evolved gas is led into a mass spectrometer or an infrared spectrometer to identify water, carbon dioxide, solvents and so on at the same time. For pharmaceutical crystals, the mass lost and the temperature distinguish a hydrate from a solvate and from loss on drying. Instruments that measure simultaneously with DSC or DTA can distinguish decomposition, which changes mass, from melting and crystal transitions, which do not. The sample amount and particle size change heat transfer and gas escape, so they are kept consistent.

faq.q: Why can the mass increase even while the sample is being heated?
faq.a: When metals or compounds in low oxidation states are oxidized in air, they take up oxygen and gain mass. A change in gas buoyancy at high temperature can also increase the apparent mass, so a curve measured with an empty container is used for correction.

faq.q: Does changing the heating rate change the results?
faq.a: Yes. With fast heating the temperature rises before the reaction can keep up, so mass losses shift to higher temperatures and neighboring steps overlap more easily. Keep the heating rate the same for samples being compared.

faq.q: How are TG and DSC used differently?
faq.a: TG measures changes in mass and DSC measures heat flow. Changes in mass such as dehydration and decomposition are quantified by TG, while changes without mass change such as melting and the glass transition are examined by DSC.

示差走査熱量測定.desc: Thermal analysis (DSC) that measures the difference in heat flow into or out of a sample and a reference. It is used to quantify heats of fusion and reaction and to measure glass transition temperatures and heat capacities.

about.p: DSC heats and cools a sample and a reference (an empty pan, alumina or similar) on the same program and records the difference in heat flow into or out of them. There are power-compensation instruments, which measure the difference in power needed to keep the two at the same temperature, and heat-flux instruments, which convert the temperature difference between the two into heat flow by calibration. If temperature and heat are calibrated with a substance of known melting point and heat of fusion, such as indium, the enthalpy of transitions and reactions can be quantified in J/g from the peak area. Compared with DTA, which measures only the temperature difference, its strength is the quantification of heat.

The glass transition involves no latent heat and is a discontinuous increase in heat capacity, so on a DSC curve the baseline shifts in a step toward the endothermic side, and its midpoint or similar is taken as the glass transition temperature Tg. Melting is a first-order transition with latent heat, so it appears as an endothermic peak whose area is the heat of fusion. Crystallization is an exothermic peak, and heating a quenched polymer above Tg shows the exotherm of cold crystallization. In samples stored for a long time, a small endothermic peak (enthalpy relaxation) overlaps the step at Tg, so take care not to mistake it for melting.

For semicrystalline polymers, the crystallinity is estimated by dividing the heat of fusion by the heat of fusion of the 100% crystalline polymer, ΔH°. When cold crystallization occurs during heating, its exotherm is subtracted from the heat of fusion so that only the crystals present before the measurement are counted. For example, for PET with cold crystallization of 20.0 J/g, melting of 50.0 J/g and ΔH° = 140 J/g, the crystallinity is (50.0 − 20.0)/140 = 21.4%. The value of ΔH° differs slightly between sources, so use the same value when comparing.

The DSC curve of a polymer depends strongly on its temperature history during molding and storage (thermal history). To see the actual state of a product, use the first heating; to compare the materials themselves, use the second heating after melting once and cooling at a constant rate. A higher heating rate increases sensitivity, but peaks shift to higher temperature and broaden, so it is important to match the rate, sample mass, pan and purge gas between samples being compared. If the sample does not sit flat against the bottom of the pan, heat transfer is poor and peaks broaden or shift in temperature, so pay attention to how the sample is packed.

faq.q: How do DSC and DTA differ?
faq.a: DTA measures the temperature difference between the sample and a reference and is used mainly to find the temperatures of transitions and reactions. DSC measures the difference in heat flow, so enthalpies are easier to quantify from peak areas, and changes in heat capacity can also be measured.

faq.q: In DSC, is endothermic or exothermic plotted upward?
faq.a: Depending on the instrument and standard, endotherms are drawn either up or down. Always check the "endo" and "exo" directions marked on the graph's axis before reading it.

faq.q: Is the glass transition temperature a single fixed value?
faq.a: The glass transition is a change spread over a temperature range, and the value shifts by several degrees depending on whether the onset, midpoint or endpoint is taken and on the heating rate. When reporting it, state which point was taken and the measurement conditions.

ガラス転移温度.desc: The temperature Tg at which amorphous regions change from a glassy state to a rubbery state (supercooled liquid). It involves no latent heat and appears in DSC as a step in the baseline.

about.p: The glass transition temperature Tg is the temperature at which an amorphous polymer or glass changes from the glassy state, in which large-scale chain motion is frozen, to the rubbery state (supercooled liquid), in which chains can move cooperatively. Across Tg the modulus drops by several orders of magnitude, and the heat capacity and thermal expansion coefficient increase discontinuously. Because no latent heat is involved, it differs from melting and appears in DSC as a step change in the baseline. Representative values are about 100 °C for polystyrene and about −70 °C for natural rubber, and whether Tg is above or below room temperature largely determines how a material is used.

about.h: The value depends on how it is measured
about.p: The glass transition occurs when molecular motion can no longer keep up with the observation time; it is not a thermodynamic phase transition. Changing the heating or cooling rate therefore shifts Tg, and faster measurements give higher values. Values from DSC, dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) and thermomechanical analysis (TMA) also disagree, and the peak of the DMA loss tangent often comes out higher than the DSC value. When reporting Tg, always include the method, the heating rate, and how it was defined, such as the midpoint or onset of the step. JIS and ISO standards specify measurement procedures.

Tg rises with a stiffer main chain, bulkier side groups and stronger attraction between polar groups, and falls with a more flexible main chain. At low molecular weight, the freely moving chain ends increase and Tg drops, approaching a constant value as the number-average molecular weight increases. The Tg of random copolymers and miscible blends is estimated by the Fox equation, 1/Tg = w1/Tg1 + w2/Tg2 (absolute temperature, w the mass fraction). Equal amounts of components with Tg values of 373 K and 213 K give about 271 K (about −2 °C).

Mixing in small molecules such as plasticizers increases the space between chains, makes them move more easily, and lowers Tg. Adding plasticizer to rigid poly(vinyl chloride) to make sheets and hoses that are soft at room temperature is an example. Nylons and sugar glasses absorb water and their Tg drops, so their properties change with humidity. In amorphous pharmaceutical formulations, storage well below Tg is needed because otherwise molecules move and crystallize more readily, so Tg is one of the guides for setting storage conditions.

faq.q: What is the difference between glass transition temperature and melting point?
faq.a: The melting point is a first-order transition in which crystals melt with latent heat, while the glass transition is the onset of chain motion in amorphous regions without latent heat. Semicrystalline polymers show both Tg and a melting point.

faq.q: Why does the glass transition temperature differ between methods?
faq.a: Because the glass transition depends on the relationship between the rate of molecular motion and the observation time. Different heating rates or measurement frequencies give different values, so report them together with the measurement conditions.

faq.q: How can the glass transition temperature be lowered?
faq.a: By adding plasticizers, copolymerizing with flexible components, or making side chains longer and more flexible. Conversely, incorporating rigid ring structures into the main chain raises Tg.

ブラッグの式.desc: The relation 2d sin θ = nλ between a crystal's interplanar spacing d, the diffraction angle θ and the X-ray wavelength λ. The angle read on a diffractometer is 2θ, so it is halved to use θ in calculations.

about.h: Derived from the path difference between neighboring planes
about.p: When X-rays strike parallel planes of atoms in a crystal at an angle θ, the waves reflected from each plane overlap. The difference in path length between waves reflected from two neighboring planes is 2d sin θ, and when this is a whole-number multiple of the wavelength λ the waves reinforce and a diffracted beam appears. This is Bragg's law, 2d sin θ = nλ. It was derived in 1912–1913 by Lawrence Bragg, who shared the 1915 Nobel Prize in Physics with his father Henry, builder of the X-ray spectrometer; Lawrence was 25 when the prize was awarded. The law made it possible to measure the spacing of atomic planes from diffraction angles.

about.h: A worked example and the effect of wavelength
about.p: The lattice constant of rock salt, NaCl, is about 0.5640 nm, so the spacing of the (200) planes is d = 0.2820 nm. With Cu Kα radiation (λ = 0.15406 nm), sin θ = 0.15406/(2 × 0.2820) gives θ ≈ 15.85°, which appears at 2θ ≈ 31.7° on the diffractometer scale. Measured with Mo Kα radiation (λ = 0.07107 nm), the same planes appear at 2θ ≈ 14.5°. Thus the value of 2θ changes with the X-ray wavelength used, while the interplanar spacing d is fixed by the substance. For matching against databases and comparing with the literature, comparing d is the reliable way.

about.h: Range of measurable spacings and precision
about.p: Because sin θ cannot exceed 1, measurable spacings are limited to d ≥ λ/2, giving a lower limit of about 0.077 nm with Cu Kα. Conversely, large spacings appear at small angles; d = 5 nm gives 2θ ≈ 1.8°, so layered materials and regular nanostructures are measured with small-angle scattering instruments. Differentiating the law gives Δd/d = −cot θ·Δθ, so for the same angular error the error in d is smaller for high-angle peaks with θ near 90°. This is why high-angle peaks are emphasized when lattice constants are determined precisely.

Bragg's law applies in the same way to diffraction of electrons and neutrons as well as X-rays. In wavelength-dispersive X-ray fluorescence instruments, an analyzing crystal of known spacing is rotated to pick out X-rays of a particular wavelength at the angle given by Bragg's law. Laboratory Cu Kα radiation consists of two lines of slightly different wavelength, Kα1 and Kα2, so high-angle peaks appear split in two. Near 2θ = 100° the separation reaches about 0.34°, which needs care when reading peak positions.

faq.q: How should n in the equation be handled?
faq.a: nth-order diffraction can be treated the same as first-order diffraction from imaginary planes with spacing d/n. So n is usually set to 1, and the order is absorbed into the plane indices, writing the second order of (100) as the first order of (200).

faq.q: Why do peaks split in two because of Kα1 and Kα2?
faq.a: Cu Kα radiation contains Kα1 at 0.15406 nm and Kα2 at 0.15444 nm, so the same planes give slightly different diffraction angles. The difference widens with angle, so high-angle peaks appear as two.

faq.q: How do you find the lattice constant from diffraction angles?
faq.a: Find the spacing d of each peak with Bragg's law and put it into the relation with the plane indices; for a cubic crystal, a = d√(h² + k² + l²). Precision is improved by using several peaks and averaging or least-squares fitting.

粉末X線回折.desc: A method (XRD) that shines X-rays on a powder sample and identifies crystalline phases from the positions and intensities of the diffraction peaks. It distinguishes polymorphs of the same composition, and peak widths also give crystallite sizes.

about.p: Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) irradiates a collection of fine crystallites with X-rays and measures the angles and intensities of the diffracted beams reinforced by the crystal's lattice planes. The diffraction condition is given by Bragg's law 2d sin θ = nλ, and the peak positions give the interplanar spacings d. The angle read on the instrument is 2θ, the angle between the incident and diffracted beams; take care not to confuse it with θ. Laboratory instruments mostly use Cu Kα radiation (wavelength 0.15406 nm). In a powder the crystals are randomly oriented, so diffraction from all lattice planes is observed at once.

Each crystalline phase has a set of d spacings and intensity ratios as characteristic as a fingerprint, so phases are identified by matching against databases such as the ICDD PDF. A major strength is distinguishing polymorphs of the same composition but different crystal structure (for example the anatase and rutile forms of TiO2), which makes it indispensable for controlling pharmaceutical crystal forms and evaluating catalyst and battery materials. Amorphous material gives no sharp peaks but a broad hump (halo), so XRD is also used to judge whether a sample is crystalline.

Phase proportions are found from peak-intensity ratios or by the Rietveld method, which fits the whole pattern to one calculated from crystal structures. The Rietveld method also gives precise lattice constants and can be used to estimate the composition of solid solutions. Small crystallites broaden peaks, so the Scherrer equation D = Kλ/(β cos θ) can estimate crystallite sizes below about 100 nm. Lattice strain also broadens peaks, however, so separating the two accurately requires analyzing how the broadening depends on angle.

Plate- or needle-shaped crystals tend to align on the sample holder (preferred orientation), making particular peaks too strong so that intensity ratios no longer match the database. A sample surface at the wrong height shifts peak positions, so the instrument is checked with a reference material. Minor phases become hard to detect below roughly a few per cent, depending on conditions. Powder XRD examines crystal structure; the kinds and amounts of elements are examined separately by XRF or similar methods. Grinding the sample finely and uniformly before measurement is also important.

faq.q: What can powder X-ray diffraction tell you?
faq.a: The kinds of crystalline phases (identification), the proportion of each phase, lattice constants, crystallite size, and whether the sample is crystalline or amorphous. It does not directly give elemental composition.

faq.q: What is 2θ?
faq.a: The angle between the incident and diffracted X-rays, the value on the horizontal axis of a diffractometer. What goes into Bragg's law is half of it, θ, so divide by two before calculating.

faq.q: Are crystallite size and particle size the same?
faq.a: Not necessarily. A crystallite is a single-crystal domain that contributes to diffraction, and one particle often consists of several crystallites, so particle size is measured separately, for example by electron microscopy.

蛍光X線分析.desc: A method (XRF) that excites a sample with primary X-rays and determines the kinds and amounts of elements from their characteristic X-rays (fluorescent X-rays). It measures many elements nondestructively but struggles with light elements.

about.h: Measuring X-rays characteristic of each element
about.p: X-ray fluorescence analysis (XRF) irradiates a sample with primary X-rays to eject inner-shell electrons and measures the characteristic X-rays (fluorescent X-rays) emitted when outer electrons fall into the vacancies. The energies of characteristic X-rays are fixed for each element and, following Moseley's law, increase with atomic number. For example, the Kα line of iron is about 6.40 keV and that of copper about 8.05 keV. The peak energies reveal which elements are present and the intensities how much. The positions of strong peaks are the basis of element identification.

Wavelength-dispersive XRF (WDX) separates X-rays by wavelength using Bragg reflection from an analyzing crystal, giving high resolution suited to precise quantitation with little peak overlap. Energy-dispersive XRF (EDX) measures X-ray energies directly with a semiconductor detector, so it can measure many elements simultaneously in a short time, and small portable instruments exist. Many instruments can measure elements from around sodium up to uranium, but measuring light elements requires a vacuum or helium in the sample chamber to avoid absorption by air.

Fluorescent X-ray intensity depends not only on the amount of the target element but also on absorption and excitation by coexisting elements (matrix effects). Calibration is therefore made with standards of similar composition, or the fundamental parameter method, which corrects by physical theory, is used. The intensity from powder samples varies with particle size and packing, so samples are homogenized by pressing into pellets or fusing with borate into glass beads. What is measured is the average composition to a depth of roughly µm to mm below the surface.

about.h: Where it is used and how it differs from other methods
about.p: Because it measures many elements non-destructively without dissolving the sample, it is widely used for composition analysis of cement, steel and rocks, screening of electronic components for hazardous elements such as lead and cadmium, and investigation of cultural properties. ICP-OES and ICP-MS require the sample to be dissolved but can measure lower concentrations. XRF gives the amounts of elements but not crystalline phases (examined by powder X-ray diffraction) or chemical states within a few nm of the surface (examined by XPS). Methods are chosen to suit the purpose.

faq.q: Why are light elements hard to measure by XRF?
faq.a: The lower the atomic number, the more often inner-shell vacancies are filled by Auger electron emission rather than X-rays, and the X-rays emitted are lower in energy, so they are easily absorbed by the sample and the air.

faq.q: What is the difference between XRF and powder X-ray diffraction?
faq.a: XRF examines which elements are present and how much; powder X-ray diffraction examines crystal structure (crystalline phases). Polymorphs of the same composition cannot be distinguished by XRF.

faq.q: Is XRF non-destructive?
faq.a: Samples can be measured without dissolving them, so it is basically non-destructive. For accurate quantitation, however, samples are sometimes prepared by grinding or fusion, in which case the sample's form is lost.

X線光電子分光.desc: A method (XPS) that finds binding energies from the kinetic energies of photoelectrons emitted by X-rays, probing the elements and chemical states in the top few nm of a surface. Chemical shifts reveal which atoms an element is bonded to.

about.p: XPS irradiates a sample in ultrahigh vacuum with X-rays such as Al Kα (1486.6 eV) or Mg Kα (1253.6 eV) and measures the kinetic energy EK of the electrons ejected by the photoelectric effect. The binding energy is found as EB = hν − EK − φ (φ is the spectrometer work function). Binding energies are fixed for each element and orbital, so elements are identified from the positions of peaks such as C 1s, O 1s and Fe 2p, and the surface composition is estimated from peak areas corrected with sensitivity factors. Hydrogen and helium cannot be measured.

Even for the same element, the binding energy shifts by several eV depending on what it is bonded to. This is called the chemical shift: the more electrons are pulled away by bonding to highly electronegative atoms, the more tightly the core electrons are bound to the nucleus and the higher the binding energy. For C 1s, roughly, C−C and C−H are at 284.8 eV, C−O at 286.5 eV, O−C=O at 289 eV and CF2 at 292 eV. Metals and their oxides also give different values, so XPS is used to study the extent of surface oxidation and the proportions of functional groups introduced by surface treatment.

Photoelectrons generated inside a sample travel while undergoing inelastic scattering, so only those generated within roughly a few nm of the surface can escape without losing energy. The information depth of XPS is therefore a few nm, giving information entirely different from SEM-EDS, which includes depths of about a µm, or X-ray fluorescence, which measures even deeper regions. Changes in composition deeper down are examined by depth profiling, measuring while gradually sputtering away the surface with argon ions, although sputtering can change the chemical state.

In insulating samples, the surface charges positively by the amount of photoelectrons lost, shifting all peaks toward higher binding energy. The usual practice is to neutralize the charge with an electron flood gun and correct by setting the C 1s of adventitious hydrocarbon on the surface to a value such as 284.8 eV, but this reference value differs slightly between sources. Surfaces also become contaminated quickly, so hydrocarbons or oxygen picked up during sample handling and storage change the results. It is important to record how the measured surface was prepared.

faq.q: How deep does XPS see?
faq.a: Photoelectrons can escape without scattering from depths of roughly a few nm, so XPS gives information from the top few nm of the surface. Deeper regions are examined by depth profiling, measuring while sputtering with ions.

faq.q: Can XPS measure hydrogen?
faq.a: No. Hydrogen and helium have small photoionization cross sections and no core levels. The presence of hydrogen is inferred indirectly, for example from the chemical shifts of carbon and oxygen.

faq.q: How do you choose between XPS and EDS?
faq.a: XPS is suited to examining the elements and chemical states of the top few nm of a surface, averaged over a wide area; EDS is suited to examining the elements of tiny regions seen in the SEM, over a depth of about 1 µm depending on the accelerating voltage and sample.

エネルギー分散型X線分光.desc: A method (EDS) that analyzes elements by measuring, by energy, the characteristic X-rays generated by an electron beam. Attached to an SEM it analyzes tiny regions; the analysis depth depends on conditions but is about 1 µm.

about.p: In EDS, characteristic X-rays emitted from the sample under the electron beam are received by a semiconductor detector, which measures the energy of each photon as the size of an electrical signal. Silicon drift detectors (SDDs), which need no liquid-nitrogen cooling, are now standard, with an energy resolution of about 120–130 eV at Mn Kα (5.9 keV). This is coarse compared with about 10 eV for wavelength-dispersive spectroscopy (WDS), so peaks close in energy overlap. A well-known example is sulfur Kα, molybdenum Lα, and lead Mα, which all fall near 2.3 keV.

To excite characteristic X-rays efficiently, a rule of thumb is that the beam energy should be at least about twice the energy needed to eject an electron from that shell. Observing copper K lines (which need about 9 keV to excite) takes around 15–20 kV. The volume the beam spreads into grows with higher voltage and lower sample density; estimated with the Kanaya–Okayama formula, it is about 1 µm in iron and about 3 µm in silicon at 15 kV. Dropping to 5 kV shrinks it to about 0.16 µm even in iron, allowing smaller regions to be analyzed, but only the lower-energy L and M lines can then be used.

In EDS quantification, measured X-ray intensities are converted to composition with corrections for atomic number, absorption, and secondary fluorescence (ZAF correction). Standardless methods are convenient, but errors can reach several percent or more. For accurate work, the surface is polished flat and measured without tilt. Insulators are given a conductive coating, but carbon coating is usual because gold M lines overlap elements such as sulfur. The detection limit is roughly 0.1 mass%, and quantification of light elements such as boron, carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen is less accurate.

about.h: Mapping and peaks that are easy to misread
about.p: Collecting a spectrum at each point while scanning the beam gives element maps, images color-coded by the distribution of each element, which are used to locate phases, segregation, and foreign particles. If the count rate is too high, two photons arrive at once and a sum peak appears at their combined energy. Excitation of silicon in the detector can also produce an escape peak 1.74 keV below the true peak. X-rays from the stage and chamber parts can mix in as well, so care is needed not to “detect” elements that are not there.

faq.q: What is the difference between EDS and WDS?
faq.a: EDS measures X-rays of all energies at once with a semiconductor detector, so many elements can be surveyed quickly. WDS separates wavelengths with analyzing crystals, giving better resolution and detection limits, and suits resolving overlapped peaks and quantifying trace elements.

faq.q: Can EDS measure light elements?
faq.a: With a thin window or a windowless detector, elements from about boron upward can be detected, but their low-energy X-rays are easily absorbed by the sample itself and by surface contamination, so quantification is less accurate than for heavier elements.

faq.q: Is it all right to coat a sample with gold?
faq.a: It is fine for imaging only, but for elemental analysis gold M lines (about 2.1 keV) overlap peaks such as sulfur and phosphorus, so carbon coating is the usual choice. Elements from the coating are excluded when interpreting results.

ヒュッケル則.desc: The rule that a cyclic, planar, fully conjugated molecule is especially stable, that is, aromatic, when it has 4n + 2 π electrons (2, 6, 10 …). Benzene, pyridine and furan have six π electrons.

about.p: According to Hückel's rule, four conditions are needed for a molecule to be especially stabilized as aromatic: it must be cyclic, it must be planar, every ring atom must have a p orbital in unbroken conjugation, and the number of π electrons must be 4n + 2 (n = 0, 1, 2 …). Benzene, with six π electrons (n = 1), is the classic example. A planar conjugated ring with 4n π electrons is instead destabilized and is called antiaromatic. Cyclooctatetraene has eight π electrons, but it avoids antiaromaticity by not being planar and adopting a tub shape.

In heterocycles, what matters is whether a heteroatom's lone pair counts as π electrons. The nitrogen of pyridine contributes one electron to a p orbital as part of a double bond, and its lone pair, in an sp² orbital in the plane of the ring, is not counted. The nitrogen of pyrrole forms three σ bonds (to two carbons and a hydrogen) and puts its lone pair in a p orbital, contributing two electrons, for 4 + 2 = 6 π electrons. The oxygen of furan has two lone pairs; only the one in a p orbital is counted, and the other stays in the plane.

Hückel's rule applies to ions as well as neutral molecules. 1,3-Cyclopentadiene is not aromatic because of its sp³ CH2, but the cyclopentadienide ion C5H5⁻, formed by losing H⁺, has p orbitals on all five carbons and is aromatic with six π electrons. This is why cyclopentadiene has a pKa of about 16, very acidic for a hydrocarbon. Likewise, the cycloheptatrienyl cation (tropylium ion) C7H7⁺ is a 6π-electron aromatic species and is stable for a cation.

faq.q: Can a molecule be aromatic without exactly six π electrons?
faq.a: Yes. With n = 0 in 4n + 2 there are two, and with n = 2 there are ten. The cyclopropenyl cation C3H3⁺ is aromatic with two π electrons, and naphthalene with ten.

faq.q: Why does the lone pair on pyrrole's nitrogen join the π system?
faq.a: Once the nitrogen forms three σ bonds to two carbons and a hydrogen, putting the remaining pair in a p orbital makes the whole ring a 6π-electron aromatic system, which is a large stabilization. In exchange, nearly all of its basicity is lost.

faq.q: How can you check whether a compound is aromatic?
faq.a: Useful signs are that ring protons appear downfield in ¹H NMR (around δ 6.5–8.5) because of the ring current, that the compound tends to undergo substitution rather than addition, and that its heat of hydrogenation is smaller than expected.

複素環式化合物.desc: A cyclic compound with atoms other than carbon (nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur and so on) in the ring. Examples include pyridine, pyrrole, furan and imidazole, and the purines and pyrimidines of the nucleobases.

about.p: Heterocyclic compounds include aromatic ones such as pyridine and pyrrole and saturated ones such as tetrahydrofuran (THF) and piperidine. Many frameworks are fused to a benzene ring or another heterocycle, such as indole, quinoline, and purine. Systematic names follow the Hantzsch–Widman system, which uses the prefixes oxa for oxygen, aza for nitrogen, and thia for sulfur; the three-membered rings oxirane and aziridine are examples. However, trivial names such as pyridine and furan are retained as the official names.

Aromatic heterocycles differ in behavior depending on how electron-rich the ring is. Five-membered rings such as pyrrole, furan, and thiophene are electron-rich because the heteroatom's lone pair joins the π system, and they react rapidly with electrophiles. Six-membered rings such as pyridine and pyrimidine are electron-poor because the electronegative nitrogen withdraws electrons from the ring, and they react more readily with nucleophiles. Heating pyridine with sodium amide brings about the Chichibabin reaction, which puts an amino group at the 2-position. By resonance energy, aromaticity is usually ranked benzene > thiophene > pyrrole > furan, although the order can change with the criterion used.

Saturated heterocycles differ greatly in reactivity with ring size. Three-membered epoxides and aziridines are highly strained and open easily with nucleophiles, which makes them valuable synthetic intermediates. Five- and six-membered rings have little strain and are stable, and THF and 1,4-dioxane are used as solvents. The basicity of nitrogen also depends on the ring: the conjugate acid of piperidine has a pKa of about 11.1, while in morpholine, which contains oxygen, the inductive effect lowers it to about 8.4. In drug molecules, this difference is used to tune basicity and water solubility.

about.h: Heterocycles in living things and in drugs
about.p: Many basic molecules of life contain heterocycles: the bases of nucleic acids, the porphyrin rings of heme and chlorophyll, the thiazolium ring of vitamin B1, and the pyridine ring of vitamin B6. One survey found that about 60% of small-molecule drugs approved in the United States contain a nitrogen heterocycle. Heteroatoms act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors and change basicity, water solubility, and how readily a molecule is metabolized, so replacing a carbon of a benzene ring with nitrogen to adjust properties is common practice in drug design.

faq.q: Are all heterocyclic compounds aromatic?
faq.a: No. Saturated heterocycles such as THF, piperidine, and epoxides are not aromatic. Only rings that are planar, conjugated, and have 4n + 2 π electrons are aromatic.

faq.q: Why are heterocycles so common in drugs?
faq.a: Heteroatoms form hydrogen bonds and charge interactions with targets and let chemists adjust basicity, water solubility, lipophilicity, and susceptibility to metabolism. Well-established methods for synthesizing diverse frameworks are another reason.

faq.q: Why does pyridine undergo nucleophilic substitution readily?
faq.a: Nitrogen withdraws electrons from the ring, leaving the carbons at the 2- and 4-positions electron-poor, and when a nucleophile adds, the negative charge rests on the electronegative nitrogen and is stabilized.

等電点.desc: The pH (pI) at which the net charge of an amino acid or protein is zero. For an amino acid it is the average of the two pKa values on either side of the net-zero form; for glycine it is about 6.0.

about.p: An amino acid is a fully protonated cation in acidic solution and a deprotonated anion in basic solution, and in between the zwitterion, with zero net charge, predominates. The isoelectric point pI is the average of the pKa values of the two dissociation steps on either side of this net-zero form. For glycine (pKa 2.34 and 9.60), pI = (2.34 + 9.60)/2 = 5.97. For amino acids with acidic or basic side chains, decide which two pKa values bracket the net-zero form by following the changes in charge step by step.

For amino acids with a carboxy group in the side chain, such as aspartic acid and glutamic acid, the pI is the average of the pKa values of the α-carboxy and side-chain carboxy groups, which is low, about 2.8 for aspartic acid. For amino acids with basic side chains, such as lysine and arginine, the pI is the average of the pKa values of the two ammonium (or similar) groups, which is high, about 9.7 for lysine. Averaging all three pKa values is a common mistake; it is important to check which form has zero net charge.

When the solution pH is below the pI, amino acids and proteins are positively charged, and when it is above, negatively charged. In electrophoresis, positively charged species move toward the cathode and negatively charged ones toward the anode, and at a pH equal to the pI they hardly move. In a gel with a pH gradient, each protein stops and collects at the position of its own pI, which allows high-resolution separation as isoelectric focusing. Also, at the isoelectric point the electrostatic repulsion between protein molecules is small and solubility tends to fall, which is used in isoelectric precipitation.

faq.q: Does an amino acid carry no charge at its isoelectric point?
faq.a: Almost all of it is the zwitterion, with one positive and one negative charge in the same molecule, so the net charge is zero. The charges themselves do not disappear.

faq.q: Is the pI just the average of all three pKa values?
faq.a: No. Average only the pKa values of the two steps on either side of the form with zero net charge. For aspartic acid that is the average of 1.88 and 3.65, about 2.77.

faq.q: What determines the isoelectric point of a protein?
faq.a: It is set by the numbers of acidic and basic side chains on the surface and their individual pKa values, and a rough value can be estimated by calculation. Actual values are measured by isoelectric focusing and similar methods.

双性イオン.desc: An ion that carries one positive and one negative charge within the same molecule and is electrically neutral overall. Amino acids take the form H3N⁺−CHR−COO⁻ in water and in the solid.

about.h: Positive and negative charges in one molecule
about.p: A zwitterion is an ion with one positive and one negative charge within the same molecule, electrically neutral overall. Some chemists restrict the term to species whose charges are on non-adjacent atoms. Amino acids are the typical example: in water and in crystals, glycine exists not as uncharged H2NCH2COOH but as H3N⁺CH2COO⁻. Because the carboxy group (pKa about 2.3) is a much stronger acid than the conjugate acid of the amino group (pKa about 9.6), the form in which the proton has moved within the molecule is favored.

Amino acids have high melting points for their small molar masses, and many melt with decomposition above 200 °C. They dissolve readily in water and hardly at all in organic solvents such as diethyl ether. These are salt-like properties of ions attracting each other strongly in the crystal. In IR spectra, too, carboxylate absorption (around 1600 cm⁻¹) is seen instead of the C=O of COOH (around 1700 cm⁻¹). The dipole moment is also larger than expected for the neutral molecular form.

The form of an amino acid changes with the pH of the solution. The cation predominates in strong acid, the zwitterion near neutral, and the anion in strong base. The pH at which the net charge is zero is the isoelectric point, about 6 for glycine. Even at the isoelectric point the proportion of the molecular form (H2NCH2COOH) is tiny; almost all is zwitterion. Being neutral overall, the zwitterion does not move in electrophoresis. Solubility tends to be lowest at the isoelectric point, which is used to separate proteins by precipitation.

Good's buffers used in biochemistry, such as MES and HEPES, are zwitterions with a sulfo group and an ammonium group, designed to bind metal ions weakly and to cross membranes poorly. Phosphatidylcholine of cell membranes, trimethylglycine (betaine) and sulfamic acid are also zwitterions. They are also used in zwitterionic surfactants and HILIC stationary phases. Species with charges on adjacent atoms, such as phosphorus ylides, are usually called ylides to distinguish them. Zwitterionic polymers readily form hydration layers on surfaces and are studied as materials that resist protein adsorption.

faq.q: Why do amino acids form zwitterions?
faq.a: Because the carboxy group (pKa about 2) is a much stronger acid than the ammonium group (pKa about 9–10), the form in which a proton has moved from the carboxy group to the amino group within the molecule is more stable.

faq.q: How are zwitterions related to the isoelectric point?
faq.a: The isoelectric point is the pH at which the net charge is zero, and neutral amino acids exist there almost entirely as zwitterions, with small, equal amounts of cation and anion.

faq.q: Do zwitterions conduct electricity?
faq.a: With zero net charge they do not move in an electric field and contribute little to the electrical conductivity of the solution. Shifting the pH away from the isoelectric point makes them move as cations or anions.

ペプチド結合.desc: The amide bond −CO−NH− formed when water is lost from the carboxy group of one amino acid and the amino group of another. Resonance gives the C−N bond partial double-bond character and holds it planar.

about.h: The amide bond linking amino acids
about.p: A peptide bond is the amide bond −CO−NH− formed when one molecule of water is lost between the carboxy group of one amino acid and the amino group of another. A linear peptide of n amino acids has n − 1 peptide bonds, and n − 1 molecules of water are lost. A free amino group (the N-terminus) remains at one end of the chain and a carboxy group (the C-terminus) at the other, and by convention the sequence is written from the N-terminus. Proteins are tens to thousands of amino acids linked by peptide bonds.

about.h: Why it is fixed in a plane
about.p: Because the nitrogen's lone pair is in resonance with the carbonyl group, the C−N bond has partial double-bond character, with a length of about 0.133 nm, between a single bond (about 0.147 nm) and a double bond. The six atoms Cα−C(=O)−N(H)−Cα therefore lie almost in one plane, and there is no free rotation about C−N. The sterically favored trans form is usual, but in peptide bonds preceding proline the cis form also appears to some extent. The flexibility of the backbone comes from rotation about the single bonds on either side of Cα (φ and ψ).

Hydrolysis of the peptide bond is thermodynamically favorable, but at neutral pH and room temperature it is extremely slow, so proteins are stable in water for a long time. In the body, proteases select and cleave peptide bonds at specific positions. To break proteins down to amino acids in the laboratory, the standard method is heating in 6 mol/L hydrochloric acid at about 110 °C for about 24 hours. Under these conditions tryptophan is destroyed, and asparagine and glutamine become aspartic acid and glutamic acid, which must be taken into account in analysis.

about.h: Chemical synthesis and appearance in spectra
about.p: Simply mixing a carboxylic acid and an amine only forms a salt, so peptide synthesis activates the carboxy group with a coupling agent such as a carbodiimide and protects amino groups that should not react with Boc or Fmoc groups. Solid-phase synthesis, which joins amino acids one by one on a resin, was developed by Merrifield and recognized by the 1984 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. In IR, the position of the amide C=O stretch (amide I, about 1650 cm⁻¹) is a clue to the secondary structure of proteins.

faq.q: What is the difference between a peptide bond and an amide bond?
faq.a: The bond has the same form, −CO−NH−. An amide bond formed between amino acids is specifically called a peptide bond. It is the bond that makes up the protein backbone.

faq.q: Why does the peptide bond rotate with difficulty?
faq.a: Because resonance between the nitrogen's lone pair and the carbonyl group gives the C−N bond partial double-bond character. The six atoms are therefore held almost in one plane.

faq.q: How many peptide bonds does a peptide of n amino acids have?
faq.a: A linear peptide has n − 1. A tripeptide has two, and two molecules of water are lost as it forms. A cyclic peptide has n.

アノマー.desc: Either of two isomers that differ only in the configuration at the anomeric carbon (C1 of glucose), which becomes a new stereocenter when a sugar cyclizes. The α and β forms interconvert in water and show mutarotation.

about.p: In the open-chain form of a monosaccharide, a hydroxy group within the molecule adds to the carbonyl carbon to form a hemiacetal ring (a hemiketal ring for a ketose). The former carbonyl carbon becomes a new stereocenter, the anomeric carbon, and the orientation of the OH on it gives two anomers, α and β. The anomeric carbon is C1 in glucose, an aldose, and C2 in fructose, a ketose. Because anomers are diastereomers that differ only in the configuration of the anomeric carbon, they differ in properties such as specific rotation, melting point and solubility.

In water the ring opens slightly and passes through the open-chain form, so the α and β forms interconvert and the specific rotation drifts toward an equilibrium value (mutarotation). The equilibrium ratio differs from sugar to sugar: the β form predominates for glucose, whereas the α form is the major one for mannose. Ring opening is accelerated by acid or base. In a glycoside, by contrast, the anomeric OH is bonded to another group, so the ring cannot open, the anomer is fixed, no mutarotation occurs, and that carbon shows no reducing property.

about.h: Which anomer is more stable depends on the substituent
about.p: The β form predominates for glucose because only the β form can place every ring substituent equatorial in the chair conformation. However, when the anomeric carbon of a pyranose ring carries an electronegative substituent such as OCH3 or Cl, the sterically less favorable axial position is preferred more than expected; this is called the anomeric effect. It is explained by interactions such as that between a lone pair on the ring oxygen and the antibonding orbital of the C−X bond. So equatorial is not always more stable, and the equilibrium ratio varies with the sugar and the solvent.

about.h: Telling anomers apart in biology and analysis
about.p: The difference between anomers matters a great deal in living systems. Both are polysaccharides of glucose, but starch, with α-1,4 linkages, is broken down by human digestive enzymes, while cellulose, with β-1,4 linkages, is not. Enzymes distinguish substrate anomers strictly, so controlling whether a glycosidic bond forms as α or β is a central challenge in carbohydrate synthesis. In analysis, α and β forms are distinguished and their ratio measured by ¹H NMR, from differences in the chemical shift of the anomeric hydrogen and its spin coupling constant with the neighboring hydrogen.

faq.q: What is the difference between an anomer and an epimer?
faq.a: Epimers are diastereomers that differ in the configuration at only one of several stereocenters. Anomers are the particular epimers that differ at the anomeric carbon created by ring closure.

faq.q: How are α and β assigned?
faq.a: Compare the substituent on the anomeric carbon (usually OH) with the reference atom on the carbon that sets D/L. If they are on the same side in the Fischer projection, it is α; if on opposite sides, β. In the Haworth formula of D-glucose, α has the C1 OH pointing down and β pointing up.

faq.q: Does sucrose have anomers?
faq.a: In sucrose the anomeric carbons of glucose and fructose are bonded to each other, so the rings cannot open and it does not interconvert between α and β. The linkages are fixed as α-D-glucose and β-D-fructose.

相補的塩基対.desc: A fixed pair formed by nucleic acid bases through hydrogen bonding. In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds and guanine with cytosine through three; in RNA, uracil replaces thymine.

about.p: In 1953, Watson and Crick, drawing on X-ray diffraction data from Franklin and others, proposed a model in which DNA is a double helix with adenine pairing with thymine and guanine with cytosine. Each of these pairs consists of a purine and a pyrimidine, so the distance between the points where the sugars of the two strands attach is nearly the same, keeping the width of the helix constant. In B-form DNA there are about 10.5 base pairs per turn, spaced about 0.34 nm apart. It is also essential for correct pairing that the bases exist as their keto and amino tautomers.

Bases can also pair in ways other than the Watson–Crick pattern. In RNA, guanine and uracil often form a wobble base pair held by two hydrogen bonds, and in 1966 Crick used it to explain why a single tRNA can read more than one codon. Hoogsteen pairs, which use a different face of the purine, form triple-stranded DNA, and four guanines arranged in a ring form a G-quartet; stacked G-quartets make a G-quadruplex. G-quadruplexes are stabilized by potassium ions and are also found at the ends of telomeres.

about.h: Hydrogen bonds are not the whole story of stability
about.p: A G−C pair has one more hydrogen bond than an A−T pair, but the stability of the double helix is not determined by the number of hydrogen bonds alone. In water, the bases of an unwound single strand also hydrogen-bond to water, so the gain from pairing is small, and stacking between base pairs lying above and below one another contributes a large share. For this reason, the standard way to predict duplex stability is the nearest-neighbor model, which adds up energies assigned to each combination of two adjacent base pairs.

about.h: Applications in genetic engineering and nanotechnology
about.p: The selective binding of complementary sequences is used in PCR primers, probes that find specific sequences, antisense nucleic acids and siRNA that suppress gene activity, and guide RNAs for genome editing. The melting temperature of a short oligonucleotide can be roughly estimated with the Wallace rule, Tm ≈ 2 × (number of A + T) + 4 × (number of G + C) ℃; for 20 bases with 10 G + C, it is about 60 ℃. DNA origami, which folds a long single strand into shapes with many short strands, also relies on base-pairing rules in its design.

faq.q: Why do purines pair with pyrimidines?
faq.a: Pairing a large purine with a small pyrimidine makes every pair nearly the same width, keeping the double helix uniform. Among such pairs, A−T and G−C are the ones whose hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors line up.

faq.q: How is base pairing different in RNA?
faq.a: Uracil pairs with adenine in place of thymine. RNA also frequently forms guanine–uracil wobble pairs, and a single strand folds back on itself to make partial duplexes and complex three-dimensional structures.

faq.q: Are there artificial base pairs?
faq.a: Yes. Artificial base pairs held together by shape and hydrophobicity rather than hydrogen bonds have been developed, and in 2014 an E. coli strain able to replicate DNA containing an artificial base pair was reported. Research toward expanding the genetic alphabet is under way.
