けん化価.desc: The mass (mg) of potassium hydroxide needed to saponify 1 g of a fat or oil. It is larger the smaller the average molecular weight of the constituent fatty acids; for tripalmitin it is about 209.

about.p: The saponification value is the mass of potassium hydroxide (mg) needed to saponify 1 g of a fat or oil. A triglyceride molecule has three ester bonds and consumes three KOH, so the saponification value = 3 × 56.11 × 1000/M, where M is the molar mass of the fat. It is therefore inversely proportional to molecular weight and is larger for fats rich in short fatty acids. It is about 209 for tripalmitin (807.3 g/mol) and about 263 for trilaurin (639.0 g/mol), made of lauric acid with 12 carbons. Conversely, the average molar mass of a fat can be estimated from its saponification value.

To determine the saponification value, excess ethanolic potassium hydroxide is added to the sample, the mixture is heated under reflux to saponify it, and the remaining KOH is titrated with standard hydrochloric acid (a back titration with phenolphthalein as indicator). A blank without sample is run the same way, and the KOH consumed is calculated from the difference in titration volumes. For example, with 0.500 mol/L HCl, a blank of 25.00 mL and 11.50 mL for a 2.000 g sample, the saponification value is (25.00 − 11.50) × 0.500 × 56.11/2.000 ≈ 189.

about.h: How it differs from other indices
about.p: The saponification value counts KOH consumed by both esters and free fatty acids, so subtracting the acid value, the KOH that neutralizes only free fatty acids, gives the ester value. Unsaponifiable matter such as sterols and hydrocarbons does not react with KOH, so the more there is, the lower the saponification value. It is independent of the iodine value, which reflects the number of double bonds: the saponification value reflects chain length and the iodine value the degree of unsaturation. Combining the two narrows down the type of fat considerably.

about.h: Quality control of fats and soapmaking
about.p: Most vegetable oils have saponification values of about 190, but coconut oil, rich in short fatty acids such as lauric acid, is high at about 250–265, and this difference is used to identify oils and detect adulteration. In soapmaking, the saponification value is used to calculate the amount of base needed to saponify the fat completely. When sodium hydroxide is used, the value is converted by multiplying by the molar mass ratio 40.00/56.11 ≈ 0.713. In practice, slightly less base than calculated is often used so that no unreacted base remains.

faq.q: What is the unit of the saponification value?
faq.a: It is the mass of KOH (mg) per gram of fat, so the unit is mg KOH/g. By convention it is often written as a number without the unit.

faq.q: How do I convert when using sodium hydroxide?
faq.a: The amount in moles is the same, so the mass of NaOH is the mass of KOH multiplied by 40.00/56.11 ≈ 0.713. The saponification value itself is expressed as the mass of KOH by standard convention.

faq.q: Which fats have high saponification values?
faq.a: Fats whose constituent fatty acids have short average chains and low average molecular weight. Typical examples are coconut oil and palm kernel oil, which are rich in lauric acid with 12 carbons.

固相抽出.desc: Sample preparation in which a sample solution is passed through a stationary phase packed in a cartridge to retain the analytes, which are then washed and eluted with a small volume of solvent (SPE). It removes interferences and concentrates at the same time.

about.h: Retaining on a cartridge and recovering
about.p: Solid-phase extraction (SPE) is a sample preparation method in which a sample solution is passed through a cartridge packed with sorbent so that the analytes are retained, interferences are washed away, and the analytes are then eluted with a small volume of solvent. The basic procedure has four steps: conditioning to wet the sorbent, loading the sample, washing and elution. The principle is the same as chromatography, and the combination of sorbent and solvents determines what is retained and what passes through. Because a large sample is transferred into a small eluate, cleanup and concentration happen at the same time.

For hydrophobic organic compounds in water samples, reversed-phase sorbents such as C18 and polymeric sorbents incorporating water-compatible components are used. To extract polar components from organic-solvent samples, normal-phase sorbents such as silica or Florisil are used. For ionic components there are cation- and anion-exchange sorbents, and mixed-mode sorbents, with both hydrophobic and ion-exchange character, suit selective extraction of acidic or basic drugs from interferences. Highly selective sorbents using antibodies or molecularly imprinted polymers are also available.

When recovery is low, find out at which step the analyte was lost by analyzing the effluent from each step. If retention is too weak, the analyte flows out during sample loading or washing (breakthrough). This also happens if the sample amount exceeds the sorbent's capacity or the flow rate is too fast. Conversely, if retention is too strong, the elution solvent cannot release it completely. For ionizable analytes, the basic approach is to set the pH about 2 units away from the pKa and switch the charge state between retention and elution.

about.h: Advantages over liquid–liquid extraction and applications
about.p: Compared with liquid–liquid extraction, solid-phase extraction uses less organic solvent, avoids emulsions and is easy to automate. For example, passing 500 mL of a water sample and eluting into 1.0 mL with 90% recovery gives a concentration factor of 500 × 0.90 = 450. It is widely used to prepare samples for analysis of trace pesticides and pharmaceuticals in environmental water and drugs in blood and urine. For pesticide residues in food, the QuEChERS method, which includes dispersive solid-phase extraction in which sorbent is added directly to the extract and shaken, is often used.

faq.q: What is the difference between solid-phase and liquid–liquid extraction?
faq.a: Liquid–liquid extraction partitions analytes between two immiscible liquids, while solid-phase extraction separates them by retention on a solid sorbent. Solid-phase extraction needs less solvent and is easier to use for concentration and automation.

faq.q: Why is conditioning necessary?
faq.a: A dry sorbent does not wet with the sample and cannot retain analytes adequately. For reversed-phase sorbents, the alkyl chains are wetted with methanol or similar and then replaced with water before the sample is passed through.

faq.q: Are solid-phase extraction and solid-phase microextraction the same?
faq.a: No. Solid-phase microextraction (SPME) exposes a thin fiber coated with sorbent to the sample or the gas above it to adsorb components, then desorbs them directly in the GC injector, using almost no solvent.

分配比.desc: In liquid–liquid extraction, the ratio of the total concentrations of a substance in the two phases (organic/aqueous). It includes all neutral and ionized forms, so for acids and bases it changes with the pH of the aqueous phase.

about.h: How it differs from the distribution constant
about.p: The distribution ratio D is the ratio of the total concentrations (organic phase/aqueous phase) of a substance divided between two phases in liquid–liquid extraction. All forms of the substance, molecular, ionic, complexed and so on, are counted together. The distribution constant KD, by contrast, is the concentration ratio of a single species (for example the molecular form) and is a constant fixed by temperature and the solvent pair. For a weak acid HA whose ionic form does not enter the organic phase, D = KD/(1 + 10^(pH − pKa)), and for a weak base D = KD/(1 + 10^(pKa − pH)), so D varies with the pH of the aqueous phase.

When an aqueous phase of volume Vw is extracted once with an organic phase of volume Vo, the fraction remaining in the aqueous phase is 1/(1 + D·Vo/Vw). With D = 9.0 and one extraction with an equal volume of organic solvent, 90% is extracted. Splitting the same amount of solvent into two halves leaves (1/(1 + 9.0 × 0.5))² ≈ 0.033, so about 97% is extracted. The more the solvent is divided and the more extractions, the better the efficiency, but the effort and the chances for loss also increase, so the number is chosen from the recovery required.

At a pH two or more units below the pKa for a weak acid, or two or more above it for a weak base, about 99% is in the molecular form and D nearly equals KD. Benzoic acid (pKa about 4.2), for example, is well extracted at around pH 2, but at pH 7 and above it is almost all anion and stays in the aqueous phase. Using this, an acid moved into the organic phase can be returned to the aqueous phase by shaking with basic water (back-extraction), separating it from neutral impurities. This is the basis of separating acidic, basic and neutral components in turn.

about.h: Extraction and separation of metal ions
about.p: When metal ions are extracted into the organic phase as complexes with a chelating reagent, the distribution ratio depends strongly on the pH of the aqueous phase and the reagent concentration. When an n-valent metal ion forms a neutral complex with n ligands, log D is a straight line of slope n against pH. The larger the ratio of two components' distribution ratios (the separation factor), the better a single extraction separates them. Choosing the pH creates conditions under which D differs greatly, so metals can be separated from each other; this is used in sample preparation for analysis and in hydrometallurgy.

faq.q: What is the difference between the distribution ratio and the distribution constant?
faq.a: The distribution constant is the concentration ratio of a single species and is a constant fixed by conditions. The distribution ratio is the ratio of total concentrations including all forms of the substance and changes with pH and complex formation.

faq.q: Does the distribution ratio have units?
faq.a: No. It is a ratio of concentrations in the same units, so it is dimensionless. The organic-phase concentration is usually the numerator and the aqueous-phase concentration the denominator. The larger it is, the more readily the substance moves into the organic phase.

faq.q: Is it better to extract once or several times?
faq.a: With the same amount of solvent, splitting it into several portions extracts more. With D = 4.0 and 100 mL of aqueous phase, one 100 mL portion extracts 80%, but two 50 mL portions extract about 89%.

マイクロ波分解.desc: A method of digesting a sample with acid in a closed vessel heated by microwaves. Under pressure the acid can be heated above its boiling point, and losses of volatile elements and contamination are small.

about.h: Heating the solution from the inside
about.p: In microwave digestion, microwaves at a frequency of 2.45 GHz heat the acid solution itself. The motion of polar molecules such as water and acids trying to follow the microwave's electric field, and the migration of dissolved ions, are turned into heat. The vessels are made of fluoropolymers and other materials that absorb hardly any microwaves, so the temperature rises faster than with heating that conducts heat through the vessel wall. Power is adjusted while temperature and pressure are monitored, so digestion follows a set heating ramp and holding time, giving good reproducibility.

about.h: Oxidizing power that grows at high temperature
about.p: The oxidizing power of nitric acid increases sharply with temperature, so raising it above the normal boiling point in a closed vessel makes the decomposition of organic matter much faster and more complete. Digestion releases gases such as CO2 and nitrogen oxides, raising the pressure in the vessel, so the more organic matter a sample contains, the less of it can be used at once. Hydrogen peroxide is added for organic matter that is hard to decompose, hydrofluoric acid for silicates, and aqua regia or other mixtures containing hydrochloric acid for platinum-group elements and some metals. Choosing the combination and amounts of acid to suit the sample is important.

Even with closed vessels, not every sample dissolves completely. Silicates remain undissolved without hydrofluoric acid, and silicon carbide and some oxides are also hard to dissolve. With samples rich in fats or aromatic compounds, carbon can remain in the digest, and residual carbon alters the signals of some elements in ICP emission spectrometry and ICP-MS. Some elements can also be lost, such as mercury when the vessel is opened, or form volatile species such as osmium tetroxide, so recovery is checked element by element.

In closed-vessel digestion, always respect the upper limits for pressure and sample amount. Perchloric acid can react explosively with organic matter at high temperature, so it must never be used with organic matter in closed vessels. Reactive samples, or samples of unknown composition, are first digested on a small scale as a trial. After digestion, cool the vessels thoroughly before opening them, and clean them by running them empty with acid to remove residues of the previous sample. Standard methods for digesting soils and sludges include US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Method 3051A and Method 3052, which uses hydrofluoric acid.

faq.q: How should the acid for digestion be chosen?
faq.a: Nitric acid is the basis for decomposing organic matter, with hydrogen peroxide added when it is hard to decompose. Add hydrofluoric acid for samples containing silicates, and hydrochloric acid for gold and the platinum-group elements. It is also important to choose acids that do not precipitate the elements being measured.

faq.q: Can a household microwave oven be used instead?
faq.a: No. Analytical instruments control the power by measuring temperature and pressure, and are built to protect against vessel rupture and acid fumes. Heating acids in a household microwave oven leads to accidents and corrosion of the appliance.

faq.q: Why is perchloric acid not used in closed vessels?
faq.a: Hot perchloric acid is an extremely strong oxidizing agent that can react explosively with organic matter. Digestions with perchloric acid are done in open systems with dedicated exhaust equipment, after the organic matter has first been decomposed with nitric acid.

標準添加法.desc: A method that measures the sample itself with known amounts of analyte added stepwise and finds the concentration by extending the line of signal versus amount added to zero signal. It corrects for changes in sensitivity caused by the matrix.

about.p: In the standard addition method, the sample solution is divided into several equal portions, standard is added to them in steps such as 0, 1, 2 and 3, and each is measured. Plotting signal on the vertical axis against amount added on the horizontal axis gives a line raised by the signal from the analyte already in the sample. The magnitude of the horizontal-axis intercept, where this line is extended to zero signal, is the concentration in the sample solution. With a single addition, Cx = ΔC × S0/(S1 − S0), but linearity cannot then be checked, so multiple additions are the norm.

about.h: Errors it can and cannot correct
about.p: Because the standards are measured in the same matrix as the sample, the standard addition method corrects proportional effects, in which coexisting salts and acids, viscosity, suppression of ionization in the plasma and so on change the sensitivity (slope). Additive effects such as spectral overlap and background, which add a constant signal regardless of concentration, are not corrected and remain as a positive error. These must be removed separately by background correction, subtraction of a blank, or choice of a different measurement wavelength or isotope.

about.h: Points to watch when using it
about.p: Because the concentration is found by extrapolation, the method assumes that the signal is proportional to concentration over the range of the additions. The amounts added are about one to several times the amount in the sample and should not exceed the linear range of the calibration. If the additions change the volume, correct for the dilution or prepare the solutions to the same final volume. Several solutions are made for each sample, which takes effort, so routine analyses with many samples often use matrix-matched external standards or the internal standard method instead.

faq.q: How does it differ from the internal standard method?
faq.a: The internal standard method adds a different substance and takes the ratio of signals to cancel variations in injection volume and sensitivity. The standard addition method adds the analyte itself to the sample and directly finds the sensitivity in that sample.

faq.q: Is a single addition enough?
faq.a: The calculation can be done, but linearity and the effect of the blank cannot be checked. The basic approach is to draw a line through at least two or three levels of addition.

faq.q: What if the sample has a blank that gives a signal of its own?
faq.a: A blank from reagents and the like is an additive effect, so standard addition does not correct for it. Subtract the blank signal before calculating.

室内再現精度.desc: The precision when measurements are repeated within the same laboratory while changing the day, analyst, instrument and so on. Its scatter is usually larger than that of repeatability, measured under the same conditions within a short time.

about.p: The precision (smallness of scatter) of an analytical method is divided into three levels by how far measurement conditions are varied: repeatability, intermediate precision and reproducibility. Intermediate precision is the precision obtained when the same sample is analyzed repeatedly within one laboratory while varying the day, analyst, instrument, reagent lot and so on. Because there are more sources of variation than in short-term repeats under uniform conditions, the scatter is usually larger, and the value is close to the variation that actually occurs in routine analysis.

about.h: Obtained by separating components of variation
about.p: Intermediate precision is measured with a design that combines the factors to be varied, for example two analysts each measuring in duplicate on different days, and is separated into within-day and between-day variation by one-way analysis of variance. Because variances add, the standard deviation of intermediate precision is sI = √(sr² + s(between-day)²). If the relative standard deviation for repeatability is 0.50% and the between-day component 0.40%, then sI = √(0.25 + 0.16) ≈ 0.64%. Adding standard deviations directly overestimates it.

Robustness is easily confused with intermediate precision. Robustness examines how unaffected results are when method conditions such as mobile-phase pH or column temperature are deliberately varied slightly, and it is evaluated during method development. Intermediate precision looks at the scatter caused by factors that creep in routinely even when the method is followed as written. Both are items of analytical method validation, but they differ in the kind of conditions varied and in the purpose of the evaluation.

In the validation of analytical methods for pharmaceuticals, the ICH Q2 guideline defines precision at three levels, and repeatability and intermediate precision are evaluated for ordinary methods. Which factors to study for intermediate precision, and to what extent, depends on the circumstances in which the method will be used. The resulting standard deviation is used to judge the expected range of routine results, to compare results when transferring a method between laboratories, and to estimate measurement uncertainty. Tracking daily values of a control sample on a control chart also confirms that intermediate precision is being maintained.

faq.q: Is intermediate precision the same as within-laboratory reproducibility?
faq.a: Essentially, yes. Both refer to precision within one laboratory with conditions such as day, analyst and instrument varied; the ICH Q2 guideline uses the term intermediate precision, and other documents call it within-laboratory reproducibility.

faq.q: What is the difference between intermediate precision and repeatability?
faq.a: Repeatability is the precision when the same analyst repeats measurements on the same instrument within a short time. Intermediate precision is the precision when the day, analyst or instrument is varied, and because there are more sources of variation it is usually larger.

faq.q: Is intermediate precision expressed as a relative standard deviation?
faq.a: In most cases it is expressed as a standard deviation or relative standard deviation, sometimes with a confidence interval. When scatter changes with concentration, it is given for each concentration level.

回収率.desc: The fraction of a known added amount that is recovered when a spiked sample is analyzed. It is found as (result for spiked sample − result for unspiked sample)/amount added × 100 and reflects trueness including sample preparation.

about.p: Recovery is the fraction of a known amount of analyte added to a sample that is regained in measurement. It evaluates together the losses in sample preparation, such as extraction, cleanup and concentration, and bias in measurement, so it is the basic test of the trueness of an analytical method. For samples that already contain the analyte, an unspiked sample is measured by the same procedure and its value subtracted: (spiked sample value − unspiked sample value)/amount added × 100. Depending on the purpose of the evaluation, the recovery of the preparation step alone (extraction efficiency) is sometimes determined separately.

Suppose an unspiked sample measures 0.80 mg/kg, and after adding an amount equivalent to 2.00 mg/kg and analyzing by the same procedure it measures 2.62 mg/kg. The recovery is (2.62 − 0.80)/2.00 × 100 = 91%. Without subtracting the unspiked value, 2.62/2.00 gives an overestimate of 131%, and including the original amount, 2.62/2.80 gives 94%, a different value. The amount added is generally checked at several concentrations matched to the range of interest (near the limit of quantitation, near a regulatory limit and so on).

Recovery departs from 100% because of losses in preparation, decomposition, matrix bias in measurement and so on. How much is acceptable depends on the purpose and concentration, and wider ranges are allowed at lower concentrations. In pesticide residue analysis, 70–120% is a commonly used guide. When it exceeds 100%, suspect overlapping interferences, ionization enhancement in LC-MS, or forgetting to subtract in the calculation. Along with recovery, the scatter of repeated measurements (precision) is also evaluated. If the scatter is large, individual results cannot be trusted even when the mean recovery is good.

An analyte added afterwards may be extracted more easily than analyte originally in the sample (taken up into tissue or bound). So good spike recovery does not guarantee that the analyte in real samples is fully extracted. It is combined with analyzing certified reference materials with reliable values to check trueness, and with adding an isotopically labeled internal standard at the start to correct for losses. Whether results are corrected for recovery follows the rules of each field. Choose a certified reference material whose matrix is close to the samples and whose analyte content is certified.

faq.q: How is recovery calculated?
faq.a: As (spiked sample value − unspiked sample value)/amount added × 100. It is important to subtract the amount originally present.

faq.q: Why can recovery exceed 100%?
faq.a: Possible causes include overlapping interfering peaks, increased sensitivity due to the matrix, contamination, or forgetting to subtract the unspiked value. Investigate the cause before judging the result.

faq.q: How is recovery related to trueness?
faq.a: Recovery is one indicator for evaluating the trueness (smallness of bias) of an analytical method including preparation. Combining it with analysis of certified reference materials gives a more reliable evaluation.

測定の不確かさ.desc: A quantity expressing the spread of values around a measurement result within which the true value may lie. The standard uncertainties of the factors are combined, and results are often reported with the expanded uncertainty using a coverage factor k = 2.

about.p: Measurement uncertainty expresses, in the form of a standard deviation, how wide a range should be allowed around a measurement result. An error is the difference from the true value, which in practice cannot be found because the true value is unknown; uncertainty, by contrast, can be evaluated from the information at hand. It is evaluated in two ways: Type A, statistically from the scatter of repeated measurements, and Type B, from values in calibration certificates, tolerances of glassware, the stated purity of reference materials and so on. Both are expressed as standard uncertainties before they are combined.

When a result y is calculated from several quantities, the standard uncertainty of each factor is weighted by its sensitivity coefficient and they are combined as the square root of the sum of squares. For products and quotients of mutually uncorrelated quantities, the relative combined standard uncertainty is the square root of the sum of the squares of the relative standard uncertainties. For example, with four factors of 0.20%, 0.10%, 0.15% and 0.50%, it is √0.3225 = 0.57%. Because the terms are squared before adding, the largest factor tends to dominate, and improving small factors has little effect.

The combined standard uncertainty uc multiplied by a coverage factor k is called the expanded uncertainty, U = k·uc; assuming a normal distribution, k = 2 gives a level of confidence of about 95%. Results are reported together with the value of k, as in "12.3 ± 0.2 mg/L (k = 2)". In estimating uncertainty it is important to list every factor that affects the result, such as losses in sample preparation, the calibration curve, preparation of standards and repeatability; drawing up this list is the heart of the evaluation.

faq.q: Are error and uncertainty the same thing?
faq.a: No. Error is the difference between a measured value and the true value, which cannot be found because the true value is unknown. Uncertainty is the width of scatter that should be allowed for in the result, and it can be evaluated from the information available.

faq.q: Why use the square root of the sum of squares instead of simply adding?
faq.a: Because scatter from mutually independent factors can partly cancel by chance, it is the variances (squares of the standard deviations) that add. Simply adding overestimates the uncertainty.

faq.q: Must k = 2 always be used?
faq.a: It is widely used by convention, but when the degrees of freedom are small a larger k may be chosen from the t distribution. The value of k used is stated in the report.

グラブス検定.desc: A test that judges whether the largest or smallest value in a data set is an outlier by comparing G = |x − x̄|/s with a critical value. The mean and standard deviation are found from all the data, including the suspect value.

about.p: Grubbs' test determines whether the maximum or minimum of a data set thought to follow a normal distribution is an outlier. It was proposed in 1950 by the American statistician Grubbs. The statistic G = |x − x̄|/s is calculated, and if it exceeds the critical value for the number of data n and the significance level, the value is judged an outlier. The mean x̄ and sample standard deviation s are calculated from all the data, including the suspect value. Calculating them after removing the suspect value makes G too large and makes a false outlier judgment more likely.

about.h: Decide on two-sided or one-sided first
about.p: Use a two-sided test to check whether either the maximum or the minimum is an outlier, and a one-sided test when only one direction matters. The critical values differ even for the same n and significance level; for example, with n = 7 at the 5% level, the critical value is about 2.02 for the two-sided test and about 1.94 for the one-sided test. Choosing the type of test after seeing the data biases the judgment conveniently, so decide in advance. Critical values are calculated from the t distribution or read from tables. One test examines only one value.

After removing one outlier, Grubbs' test can be applied again to the remaining data, but if there are two outliers on the same side, they inflate the standard deviation for each other and neither may be detected (masking). For such cases there are forms of the test that examine two values simultaneously. With few data the test has little power, and with many data even slight departures from normality affect the judgment. Whether the assumption of a normal distribution is itself reasonable must also be checked.

about.h: When a value is judged an outlier
about.p: Being judged an outlier by the test does not by itself justify discarding the value. First investigate causes such as recording errors, sample mix-ups or instrument malfunctions. If a cause is found, remove the value; if not, report the result together with how the outlier was handled. Another option is to use robust statistics that are less affected by outliers, such as the median and the median absolute deviation. ISO 5725-2, which covers interlaboratory studies, also uses Grubbs' test to check for outliers.

faq.q: What is the difference between Grubbs' test and Dixon's Q test?
faq.a: Grubbs' test uses the deviation from the mean divided by the standard deviation, while the Q test uses the gap to the neighboring value divided by the range. The Q test is quick for small data sets, and Grubbs' test uses information from all the data.

faq.q: May a value judged an outlier be deleted?
faq.a: Do not delete it on the basis of the test alone; first investigate the cause. If the cause is confirmed, remove it; if not, report it with a clear statement of how the outlier was handled.

faq.q: Is Grubbs' test related to the Grubbs catalyst?
faq.a: No. The test is named after the statistician Frank Grubbs, and the olefin metathesis catalyst after the chemist Robert Grubbs; they are different people.

18電子則.desc: The rule of thumb that transition-metal complexes tend to be stable when the metal's d electrons plus the electrons donated by the ligands total 18. Square-planar d⁸ complexes and some others have 16 electrons.

about.p: The orbitals that hold a transition metal's valence electrons are the 5 (n−1)d orbitals, 1 ns orbital and 3 np orbitals, 9 in all. When all of them are filled with electron pairs, the count is 18, and the 18-electron rule regards this as a stable configuration, like that of a noble gas. Carbonyl complexes such as Cr(CO)6, Fe(CO)5 and Ni(CO)4, and ferrocene, have 18 electrons and are stable compounds that can be isolated and stored; ferrocene in particular is stable even in air. It is easiest to think of it as the octet rule (8 electrons) used for main-group elements in organic compounds, extended to include the d orbitals.

In the commonly used ionic model, you first treat the ligands as closed-shell species such as CH3⁻, Cl⁻, H⁻ and C5H5⁻ and determine the metal's oxidation state. The metal's d-electron count is the group number minus the oxidation state; for example, Rh(I) is 9 − 1 = 8, d⁸. Adding the electrons donated by each ligand (2 for CO, PR3, Cl⁻ and CH3⁻, and 6 for η⁵-C5H5⁻) gives the valence electron count. The covalent model, which treats the ligands as neutral, gives the same count when done correctly.

The 18-electron rule is only a rule of thumb, and there are many exceptions. d⁸ metals such as Rh(I), Ir(I), Pd(II) and Pt(II) readily form square-planar 16-electron complexes; Wilkinson's catalyst, RhCl(PPh3)3, and Vaska's complex are examples. In catalytic reactions, a coordinatively unsaturated 16- or 14-electron complex often takes up the substrate at a vacant site, reaches 18 electrons by oxidative addition and returns by reductive elimination, so the reaction proceeds while the electron count shuttles between 16 and 18.

The 18-electron rule works best for low-oxidation-state organometallic complexes with strongly π-accepting ligands such as CO and phosphines. On the other hand, classical complexes with water or ammonia coordinated, such as [Cu(H2O)6]²⁺, and complexes of metals on the left of the periodic table (such as Ti and Zr) include many stable compounds that do not have 18 electrons. When bulky ligands crowd the metal, complexes are also stable with fewer electrons. The electron count is best used as a starting point for predicting a complex's reactivity.

faq.q: How do I find the d-electron count?
faq.a: Subtract the oxidation state from the metal's group number. For example, Fe(II) of group 8 iron is d⁶, and Pd(0) of group 10 palladium is d¹⁰. There is no need to count the 4s electrons of the electron configuration separately.

faq.q: Are complexes without 18 electrons unstable?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Square-planar d⁸ complexes are stable with 16 electrons, and many classical complexes are stable without 18 electrons. The 18-electron rule is a guide for low-oxidation-state organometallic complexes.

faq.q: Why count electrons in catalytic reactions?
faq.a: Because it shows at which steps ligand dissociation or substrate coordination can occur. An 18-electron complex has no room for a substrate to approach, so it is thought to react only after a ligand leaves and it drops to 16 electrons or fewer.

酸化的付加.desc: An elementary step in which a metal inserts into an A−B bond to give M(A)(B). The metal's oxidation state and coordination number each rise by 2, and its d-electron count falls by 2. The first step of cross-coupling.

about.p: Oxidative addition is an elementary step in which a coordinatively unsaturated, low-oxidation-state metal complex M inserts into a bond A−B, such as H−H, C−X (X is a halogen) or C−H, giving M(A)(B). A and B are each counted as anionic ligands, so the metal's oxidation state rises by 2, its coordination number rises by 2 and its d-electron count falls by 2. The valence electron count rises by 2, so a 16-electron complex becomes 18 electrons and a 14-electron complex becomes 16. For example, Pd(0) reacts with Ar−Br to give Ar−Pd(II)−Br.

about.h: What controls how readily it occurs
about.p: Oxidative addition is a reaction in which electrons flow from the metal into the antibonding orbital of A−B, so it occurs more readily with electron-rich metals, and strongly electron-donating phosphine ligands speed it up. For aryl halides, the weaker the C−X bond, the more readily it occurs, in the order C−I > C−Br > C−Cl. Unreactive substrates such as aryl chlorides are handled with bulky, electron-rich ligands such as P(t-Bu)3, which form highly reactive complexes bearing only one ligand.

Nonpolar bonds such as H2 approach the metal side-on and add in a concerted way, and the 2 H atoms end up cis to each other. Highly polar alkyl halides such as CH3I often react by an SN2-type mechanism in which the metal attacks carbon as a nucleophile; the configuration at carbon is inverted, and the 2 ligands may end up trans. Addition of palladium to aryl halides is in many cases thought to involve concerted addition of a complex that has lost some of its ligands to the C−X bond of the arene.

faq.q: Why is it called "oxidative"?
faq.a: Because when the 2 added ligands are counted as anions, the metal's oxidation state rises by 2; that is, the metal is formally oxidized. In the reverse reaction the oxidation state falls by 2, so it is called reductive elimination.

faq.q: Which metals undergo oxidative addition readily?
faq.a: Electron-rich, low-oxidation-state metals that are also stable in the oxidation state 2 higher, such as Pd(0), Ni(0), Rh(I) and Ir(I). An 18-electron complex must first lose a ligand to become coordinatively unsaturated.

faq.q: Which step is rate-determining in cross-coupling?
faq.a: It depends on the substrate and ligand, but with unreactive substrates such as aryl chlorides, oxidative addition is often rate-determining. With bulky ligands, reductive elimination or transmetalation can be rate-determining.

還元的脱離.desc: An elementary step in which 2 ligands on a metal form a bond and leave; the reverse of oxidative addition. The oxidation state and coordination number each fall by 2, and it occurs between ligands cis to each other.

about.p: Reductive elimination is an elementary reaction in which two ligands on a metal (X and Y) form a new bond X−Y and leave the metal; it is the reverse of oxidative addition. The metal's oxidation state falls by two, and so does its coordination number. Counting valence electrons, an 18-electron complex becomes a 16-electron one. Many bonds, including C−C, C−H, C−N, C−O and C−halogen, are formed in this step. In cross-coupling, it is the last step of the catalytic cycle, releasing the product and regenerating the low-valent metal.

Because the two ligands form a bond directly, they must be cis to each other. A complex with them trans first isomerizes to cis before elimination. The reaction is often concerted, and the configuration of a departing carbon is retained. For square-planar palladium(II) complexes, the larger the coordination angle (bite angle) of a bidentate phosphine ligand, the more the two groups are pushed together and the faster reductive elimination tends to be, a guide in ligand design. Ligands with large bite angles such as Xantphos are an example.

about.h: What affects how easily it occurs
about.p: Reductive elimination is easier the stronger the bond formed and the higher and more electron-poor the metal's oxidation state. Bulky ligands speed elimination by relieving crowding. Forming C(sp²)−C(sp²) is faster than C(sp³)−C(sp³), and forming C−H is especially fast. On the other hand, reductive elimination to form C−N and C−O bonds is slow, and for reactions such as the Buchwald–Hartwig amination the key was developing dedicated electron-rich, bulky phosphine ligands. From nickel(II), reductive elimination, especially to form C−N and C−O bonds, is often harder than from palladium(II), and methods that promote it by oxidizing nickel to Ni(III) have been studied.

In Suzuki–Miyaura coupling, after oxidative addition and transmetalation, Ar−Ar' is reductively eliminated from Ar−Pd(II)−Ar' to return Pd(0). In the Monsanto process, acetyl iodide is reductively eliminated from a Rh(III) acetyl complex to return Rh(I). Oxidative addition and reductive elimination are reverses of each other, so which direction is favored depends on bond strengths and the metal's stable oxidation states. Reductive elimination forming C−C bonds from platinum(IV) has been widely studied as an example in mechanistic work. In these examples, oxidative addition follows reductive elimination again, so the catalyst works repeatedly.

faq.q: How does the oxidation state change in reductive elimination?
faq.a: The metal's oxidation state falls by two, and its coordination number also falls by two. Pd(II), for example, returns to Pd(0). This is because the two departing ligands share electrons to form a new covalent bond.

faq.q: Does it occur between ligands that are trans?
faq.a: Not directly. The two ligands must be cis to each other, so a trans complex first isomerizes to the cis complex and then undergoes reductive elimination.

faq.q: How does it differ from oxidative addition?
faq.a: In oxidative addition an X−Y bond inserts into the metal, raising the oxidation state and coordination number by two. Reductive elimination is the reverse: two ligands bond and leave, lowering each by two.

β-水素脱離.desc: An elementary step in which a hydrogen on the β carbon of a metal alkyl complex moves to the metal, giving a metal hydride and an alkene. It requires a vacant coordination site and a syn-coplanar arrangement.

about.p: β-Hydride elimination is an elementary reaction in which, in an alkyl group bonded to a metal, a hydrogen on the β carbon, next to the carbon bonded to the metal (the α carbon), moves to the metal, giving a metal hydride and an alkene. It can be written M−CH2CH2R → M−H + CH2=CHR. The metal's oxidation state does not change, but because the hydride and alkene are newly coordinated, one vacant coordination site is used up. It is the reverse of 1,2-insertion, in which an alkene inserts into a metal–hydride bond. It is commonly seen for alkyl complexes of late transition metals such as palladium.

It requires a hydrogen on the β carbon, a vacant coordination site on the metal, and the ability of the four atoms M−C−C−H to adopt a nearly coplanar syn arrangement. A saturated 18-electron complex must first lose a ligand to create a vacancy. Methyl, neopentyl, benzyl and aryl groups, which have no β hydrogens, do not undergo this reaction. Arrangements in which the resulting alkene would be unstable, such as bridgeheads, and hydrogens in rings that cannot become syn-coplanar also eliminate with difficulty.

In the Heck reaction, the alkylpalladium formed by alkene insertion undergoes β-hydride elimination to release the substituted alkene. Because the elimination is syn, the position and stereochemistry (usually E) of the product's double bond are set in this step. Repeated β-hydride elimination and reinsertion move the metal along an alkyl chain, causing isomerization that shifts the position of an alkene's double bond. In olefin polymerization, β-hydride elimination is the main chain-transfer pathway, giving polymer chains with a vinyl group at the end.

about.h: Suppressing it as a side reaction
about.p: When sp³-carbon halides are used in cross-coupling, the alkylmetal intermediate tends to undergo β-hydride elimination, giving alkenes as by-products instead of the desired product. For alkyl couplings, therefore, bulky ligands that speed reductive elimination are chosen, or nickel catalysts, which are less prone to β-hydride elimination, are used. In amine arylation too, β-hydride elimination from the amido complex can give the reduced arene as a by-product. If the metal hydride formed reinserts into the alkene, isomeric products with a different branching pattern can also form.

faq.q: What conditions does β-hydride elimination require?
faq.a: Three: a hydrogen on the β carbon, a vacant coordination site on the metal, and the ability of M−C−C−H to line up syn-coplanar. If any is missing, it becomes difficult.

faq.q: Which alkyl groups do not undergo β-hydride elimination?
faq.a: Groups without a hydrogen on the β carbon, such as methyl, neopentyl, benzyl and aryl groups. Groups lacking β hydrogens are easier to handle in alkyl couplings.

faq.q: What is the reverse of β-hydride elimination?
faq.a: 1,2-Insertion of an alkene into a metal–hydride bond (hydrometalation). The two are in equilibrium, and repeating them isomerizes the alkene.

移動挿入.desc: An elementary step in which an alkyl or similar group on a metal moves to an adjacent CO or alkene ligand to form a new bond. With CO a metal acyl complex forms and a vacant coordination site opens up.

about.p: Migratory insertion is an elementary reaction in which an alkyl, hydride or similar group bonded to a metal moves to an adjacent unsaturated ligand on the same metal (CO, an alkene, an alkyne and so on) and forms a new bond. The migrating group and the accepting ligand must be cis to each other. The metal's oxidation state does not change, but because two ligands become one, a vacant coordination site is created and the valence electron count falls by two. The vacancy is often filled by an incoming ligand. Once the vacancy is filled, the valence electron count returns to its original value.

In CO insertion, the alkyl group moves to the CO carbon, giving a metal acyl complex M−C(O)R. Because two bonds form to the single CO carbon, it is called 1,1-insertion. Labelling experiments with CH3Mn(CO)5 showed that the methyl group moves to a CO already coordinated rather than an incoming CO inserting. It is a key step in making acetic acid by methanol carbonylation and in hydroformylation, which adds CO and hydrogen to alkenes to make aldehydes. The acyl complex formed gives carbonyl compounds by reacting with alcohols or water or by reductive elimination.

Insertion of an alkene into a metal–carbon or metal–hydrogen bond is called 1,2-insertion because new bonds form to both alkene carbons. The metal and the migrating group add to the same face of the alkene (syn addition). In olefin polymerization with Ziegler–Natta or metallocene catalysts, the growing polymer chain stays on the metal, and repeated insertion lengthens the chain. In the Heck reaction, insertion of the alkene into an arylpalladium forms a new C−C bond. The orientation of insertion is usually such that the alkene's substituent ends up in the sterically favorable position.

The reverse of migratory insertion is elimination: the reverse of alkene insertion is β-hydride elimination, and the reverse of CO insertion is decarbonylation. CO insertion is often reversible, shifting toward the acyl complex at high CO pressure. Alkene insertion forms a strong C−C σ bond and is generally favorable. Migratory insertion can be rate-determining: in methanol carbonylation, it becomes rate-determining in the process using an iridium catalyst. Which direction is favored changes with conditions such as the type of ligands, CO pressure and temperature.

faq.q: Why is it called "migratory" insertion?
faq.a: Formally it looks as if the ligand inserts into the M−R bond, but in fact R migrates to the adjacent ligand to form the bond. This has been confirmed by labeling experiments.

faq.q: Does migratory insertion change the metal's oxidation state?
faq.a: No. The metal's valence electron count falls by two and one vacant coordination site is created. Unlike oxidative addition and reductive elimination, it is an elementary reaction without a change in oxidation state.

faq.q: What is the difference between 1,1- and 1,2-insertion?
faq.a: 1,1-Insertion forms two bonds to one atom, as with CO, giving an acyl complex. 1,2-Insertion forms bonds to two adjacent atoms, as with an alkene.

π逆供与.desc: Bonding in which electrons flow from filled metal d orbitals into empty π* orbitals of ligands such as CO and alkenes. The ligand's multiple bond is weakened and the CO stretching wavenumber falls.

about.h: Donation and back-donation reinforce each other
about.p: When CO binds to a metal, two things happen at once: σ donation from the lone pair on carbon into an empty metal orbital, and π back-donation from filled metal d orbitals into the empty π* orbitals of CO. σ donation increases the electron density on the metal and strengthens back-donation, while back-donation drains electron density from the metal and makes it more receptive to σ donation, so the two reinforce each other (synergism). Because CO's π* orbitals are concentrated on carbon, CO binds to metals through carbon rather than oxygen. This is why CO, a very weak base on its own, binds metals strongly.

Electrons placed in π* by back-donation weaken the C−O bond, so the C−O stretching wavenumber serves as a yardstick for the strength of back-donation. Terminal CO appears at roughly 2100–1850 cm⁻¹, but CO bridging two metals receives electrons from both and appears lower still, around 1850–1750 cm⁻¹, which helps assign structures. Among ligands, NO⁺, CO, and PF3 are the strongest π acceptors, followed in decreasing order by phosphites, triarylphosphines, and trialkylphosphines, while amines are σ donors only and accept almost no back-donation.

The stronger the back-donation, the shorter and stronger the metal–ligand bond, and the longer and weaker the bonds within the ligand. In Zeise's salt, where ethylene is bound to platinum, the C=C bond is slightly longer than in free ethylene. In σ complexes of dihydrogen, metal d electrons enter the H−H σ* orbital, and when back-donation becomes strong, the H−H bond breaks and oxidative addition follows. The activation of nitrogen and oxygen molecules bound to metals also comes from back-donation, which underlies how catalysts activate small molecules.

Back-donation is strong for electron-rich metals in low oxidation states, and it stabilizes carbonyl complexes of Ni(0) and Fe(0). The more electron-rich the metal, the stronger the metal–CO bond and the harder it is for CO to dissociate. Conversely, when back-donation is weak, as in cationic complexes, the CO carbon becomes positively polarized and more open to attack by nucleophiles. Fischer added organolithium reagents to the carbon of carbonyl complexes and then alkylated the products, making carbene complexes with metal–carbon double bonds.

faq.q: How is the strength of back-donation measured?
faq.a: The usual way is to look at the C−O stretching wavenumber in the infrared spectrum. The stronger the back-donation, the more electrons enter π*, and the further the wavenumber shifts below the 2143 cm⁻¹ of free CO. Bond lengths from X-ray crystal structures are also a clue.

faq.q: Why does CO bind to metals through carbon rather than oxygen?
faq.a: Both the lone-pair orbital used for σ donation and the π* orbitals that accept back-donation are concentrated on carbon. Binding through carbon makes both interactions stronger.

faq.q: Do phosphines also accept back-donation?
faq.a: Yes. The σ* orbitals of the bonds between phosphorus and its substituents act as acceptors, and phosphines with electronegative substituents, such as PF3 and phosphites, are stronger π acceptors. Trialkylphosphines accept little back-donation and act mainly as σ donors.

円錐角.desc: The apex angle of a cone, with the metal at its apex, that encloses a phosphine ligand; a measure of ligand bulk proposed by Tolman. About 145° for PPh3 and about 182° for P(t-Bu)3.

about.h: Expressing ligand bulk as an angle
about.p: The cone angle is the apex angle of a cone with the metal at its apex, drawn to just touch the outer edges of a phosphine ligand's substituents, and it expresses the steric bulk of the ligand. Tolman proposed it in the 1970s, determining it from molecular models with the metal–phosphorus distance set at 2.28 Å. Representative values are about 118° for PMe3, about 145° for PPh3, about 170° for PCy3 (Cy = cyclohexyl) and about 182° for P(t-Bu)3. The larger the angle, the more space the ligand occupies and the fewer ligands fit around the metal.

Bulky ligands dissociate from the metal readily and favor reactive complexes with few ligands. In palladium-catalyzed couplings, bulky, electron-rich phosphines readily give Pd(0) species bearing only one ligand, which promotes oxidative addition of unreactive aryl chlorides. Steric repulsion between ligands also promotes reductive elimination, which releases the product. In this way the cone angle explains catalyst activity and selectivity and is used as an index when choosing ligands. Too large a ligand, however, can block the substrate from approaching the metal, so the best size depends on the reaction.

about.h: An index separate from electronic properties
about.p: Ligand properties are considered in two parts, steric size and electronic character. As an index of electronic character, Tolman also proposed the wavenumber of the CO stretching vibration of Ni(CO)3L complexes (the Tolman electronic parameter). The more strongly electron-donating the phosphine, the more back-donation from the metal into the CO antibonding orbital and the lower the wavenumber. Arranging ligands on a map with cone angle and electronic parameter as the two axes helps find ligands with similar properties and separate steric from electronic effects.

The cone angle treats a ligand as an axially symmetric cone, but real substituents are asymmetric and can turn to interlock with one another, so the value may not match the bulk within an actual complex. Errors are especially large for flat aryl groups and flexible substituents. For ligands whose shape is far from a cone, such as N-heterocyclic carbenes, indices such as the fraction of a sphere around the metal occupied by the ligand (%Vbur, percent buried volume) are used. For bidentate ligands there is a separate index, the bite angle.

faq.q: How is the cone angle determined?
faq.a: With the metal–phosphorus distance fixed, a cone is drawn tangent to the van der Waals radii of the outermost atoms of the substituents and its apex angle is measured. Today it is also often obtained from crystal structures or computed structures.

faq.q: What are ligands with large cone angles good for?
faq.a: They favor reactive complexes with few ligands and can speed up oxidative addition and reductive elimination. Bulky, electron-rich phosphines are widely used in couplings of aryl chlorides.

faq.q: What is the difference between cone angle and bite angle?
faq.a: The cone angle expresses the steric bulk of a monodentate ligand, and the bite angle is the angle formed by the two donor atoms of a bidentate ligand and the metal. The bite angle affects the geometry of the complex and the rate of reductive elimination.

触媒回転頻度.desc: The number of times product is formed per catalyst molecule per unit time. It is found by dividing the turnover number TON by the reaction time and expressed in h⁻¹ or s⁻¹. Abbreviated TOF.

about.h: A yardstick for comparing catalyst speed
about.p: The turnover frequency (TOF) expresses how many times per unit time one catalyst molecule (or one active site) completes the reaction, in units of s⁻¹ or h⁻¹. Whereas the turnover number (TON) expresses how many times the catalyst turns over in its lifetime, TOF expresses how fast it turns over. The two are related in that integrating TOF over time gives TON, but because catalysts deactivate or change speed during a reaction, the value at low conversion early in the reaction is usually reported as the initial TOF.

The value of TOF depends heavily on what goes in the denominator. For homogeneous complex catalysts the total amount of metal added is often used, but if only part of it is the working active species, TOF is underestimated. For solid catalysts, the number of metal atoms exposed at the surface, found from the chemisorption of hydrogen or carbon monoxide, is used as the denominator. For enzymes, the maximum turnover number per enzyme molecule is called the catalytic constant kcat, which reaches extremely large values of the order of 10⁶ s⁻¹ for carbonic anhydrase.

TOF can be related to the largest energy barrier in the whole catalytic cycle. In the energetic span model of Kozuch and Shaik, the difference δE between the lowest intermediate and the highest transition state in the cycle gives TOF ≈ (kBT/h)exp(−δE/RT). At 25℃, kBT/h is about 6.2×10¹² s⁻¹, so δE = 80 kJ/mol gives a TOF of about 0.06 s⁻¹ and 100 kJ/mol about 2×10⁻⁵ s⁻¹. A barrier difference of only 20 kJ/mol changes the rate by more than 3000 times.

TOF varies with temperature, concentration, pressure and solvent, so comparing values from different papers without matching conditions is meaningless. A catalyst with a large TOF that deactivates quickly and has a small TON is not practical. In pharmaceutical manufacturing, the amount of catalyst metal left in the product is also an issue; the ICH Q3D guideline sets the permitted daily exposure for oral palladium at 100 µg. For a daily dose of 10 g this corresponds to 10 ppm in the product, so processes are designed to reduce the amount of catalyst and to remove residual metal.

faq.q: What is the difference between TON and TOF?
faq.a: TON is the number of times one catalyst molecule forms product before it deactivates or the reaction ends, a dimensionless number. TOF is the number per unit time and expresses speed. TOF is a measure of activity; TON is a measure of lifetime and efficiency.

faq.q: Is an enzyme's kcat the same as TOF?
faq.a: The idea is the same: kcat corresponds to the TOF per enzyme molecule when the substrate is saturating. Because kcat is a constant expressing the maximum rate, the actual turnover rate under low substrate concentrations is smaller.

faq.q: Should TOF be given in h⁻¹ or s⁻¹?
faq.a: Both are used. h⁻¹ is common for catalysts in synthetic reactions, and s⁻¹ for enzymes and fast catalysts. Since 3600 h⁻¹ = 1 s⁻¹, convert to the same unit before comparing.

速度式.desc: An equation expressing how a reaction rate depends on the concentration of each substance. The orders a and b in v = k[A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ are determined by experiment, not from the coefficients of the chemical equation.

about.p: A rate law expresses how the reaction rate depends on the concentration of each substance, in the form v = k[A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ. The exponents a and b are the reaction orders with respect to each substance, and their sum is the overall order. Orders are quantities determined by experiment, not the coefficients of the chemical equation, and they can be zero, fractional or negative. The units of the rate constant k depend on the overall order: s⁻¹ for first order, L/(mol·s) for second order and mol/(L·s) for zero order. k changes with temperature, a relationship described by the Arrhenius equation.

Integrating a rate law over time gives how concentration changes with time. For a first-order reaction, ln[A] = ln[A]₀ − kt, and the half-life t½ = ln2/k does not depend on the initial concentration. For example, k = 1.0×10⁻³ s⁻¹ gives t½ ≈ 693 s (about 11.6 min). For a second-order reaction (second order in A), 1/[A] = 1/[A]₀ + kt, and the half-life 1/(k[A]₀) is longer the smaller the initial concentration. Plotting ln[A] or 1/[A] against time and seeing whether a straight line results reveals the order.

In the initial-rate method, only one substance's concentration is changed and the change in initial rate is examined. If doubling the concentration quadruples the rate the order is two, if it doubles the rate one, and if the rate is unchanged zero. The isolation method, in which everything except one substance is in large excess so that the reaction is treated as pseudo-first-order in that substance, is also common. For example, the hydrolysis of an ester in water, with water in large excess, hides the order in water and is observed as first order in ester. The orders found this way are combined to give the rate law.

For an elementary reaction, the order equals the number of molecules involved (the molecularity). For a multistep reaction, the rate law is determined by the combination of the rate-determining step and the steps before it, so it is a clue for inferring the mechanism. The difference between v = k[RX][Nu⁻] for SN2 and v = k[RX] for SN1 is the classic example. However, a mechanism consistent with the rate law is not proven correct by that fact. Other mechanisms may give the same rate law, so the decision is made together with isotope effects, detection of intermediates and so on.

faq.q: Are reaction orders the same as the coefficients in the chemical equation?
faq.a: They match for elementary reactions but generally not for multistep reactions. As the early rate of H2 + Br2 → 2HBr is proportional to [Br2] to the power 1/2, orders are determined by experiment.

faq.q: What are the units of a rate constant?
faq.a: They depend on the overall order. With concentration in mol/L and time in s, first order is s⁻¹, second order L/(mol·s) and zero order mol/(L·s).

faq.q: What is a pseudo-first-order reaction?
faq.a: A reaction of second or higher order in which one substance is in large excess so that its concentration can be regarded as nearly constant, making the reaction behave as first order in the remaining substance.

律速段階.desc: In a multistep reaction, the slowest step, which sets the overall rate. The structure of its transition state shows up in the rate law, isotope effects and substituent effects.

about.h: The step that sets the overall rate
about.p: In a multistep reaction, the overall rate is determined almost entirely by the slowest step. This is called the rate-determining step, the same idea as a narrow passage controlling the flow of people. Fast steps after the rate-determining step have little effect on the overall rate, and the reaction as a whole cannot be speeded up unless the rate-determining step is. On an energy diagram, the rate-determining step is the one whose transition state lies highest relative to the starting materials. Note that this is judged by position relative to earlier steps, not just by the height of a single barrier. Catalysts speed up reactions mainly by lowering the barrier of this step.

about.h: Which molecules appear in the rate law
about.p: Only the molecules involved in the rate-determining step and the steps before it appear in the rate law. In an SN1 reaction, the step in which the leaving group departs to give a carbocation is rate-determining, so the rate is v = k[RX], independent of nucleophile concentration. When a fast equilibrium precedes the rate-determining step, its equilibrium constant also enters the rate law. Conversely, reagents that join after the rate-determining step do not appear. Determining the rate law experimentally therefore lets you infer what is involved in the rate-determining step. In the one-step SN2, both substrate and nucleophile appear: v = k[RX][Nu⁻].

about.h: Clues for identifying the rate-determining step
about.p: Besides the rate law, kinetic isotope effects are widely used. If a C−H bond breaks in the rate-determining step, kH/kD is about 2–7 at room temperature; if not, it is about 1. kH/kD ≈ 1 for the nitration of benzene shows that C−H cleavage is not rate-determining. Examining substituent effects with the Hammett equation, the sign and size of ρ reveal the charge that develops in the transition state of the rate-determining step. Combining these, the nature of that transition state is inferred.

The rate-determining step is not fixed for a given reaction but changes with the catalyst, substrate, concentrations and temperature. In methanol carbonylation, oxidative addition of methyl iodide is rate-determining with a rhodium catalyst, but migratory insertion becomes rate-determining with an iridium catalyst. Also, the step that determines the overall rate and the step that determines which product forms (the product-determining step) may be different. In SN1 and E1, formation of the common carbocation is rate-determining, and the ratio of substitution to elimination products is decided in the fast steps that follow.

faq.q: How is the rate-determining step identified?
faq.a: It is inferred by combining the orders in the rate law, kinetic isotope effects, substituent effects, detection of intermediates and so on. It cannot be settled by a single experiment.

faq.q: Is the rate-determining step the step with the largest activation energy?
faq.a: Roughly, but strictly it is the step whose transition state is highest relative to the starting materials. If there is a stable intermediate earlier, the height of a single barrier is not enough to decide.

faq.q: What is the difference between the rate-determining step and the product-determining step?
faq.a: The rate-determining step sets the overall rate; the product-determining step decides which product forms. As in competing SN1 and E1 reactions, they can be different steps.

擬一次反応.desc: A method of treating a second-order reaction as first order by adding one reactant in large excess so that its concentration stays nearly constant. The apparent rate constant is k' = k[excess substance].

about.h: How large an excess is needed
about.p: In a second-order reaction such as A + B → P, if the initial concentration of B is made larger than that of A, the concentration of B hardly changes during the reaction and the reaction can be treated as first order in A. With B in 10-fold excess, even when all of A has reacted B has fallen by only 10% of its initial value, and the apparent rate constant k' = k[B] changes by at most 10%. For good accuracy, a guideline is an excess of 10-fold or more, preferably several tens of times. Later in the reaction the degree of excess actually grows, so the error is set mainly by how B falls early on.

Vary the concentration of B in several runs, find k' in each from the decay of A, and plot k' against [B]. The slope of the line is the second-order rate constant k, and the line passing through the origin also confirms first order in B. If the intercept is not zero, another pathway independent of B, for example reaction with water as solvent, is assumed to run in parallel, and the data are analyzed as k' = k0 + k[B]. Determining k from several points in this way, including a check of the reaction order, is more reliable than determining it from a single point.

In 1850 Wilhelmy followed the rate of inversion, the hydrolysis of sucrose in the presence of acid, by optical rotation, in one of the first quantitative studies of reaction rates. Because water is in large excess and the concentration of the acid catalyst does not change, this reaction is pseudo-first order in sucrose. Enzyme reactions are also pseudo-first order in substrate when the substrate concentration is far below the Michaelis constant. The same idea is used in experiments measuring fluorescence quenching and the reaction of radicals in solution with a large excess of reagent.

about.h: Points that are easy to confuse
about.p: A pseudo-first-order reaction has not itself become first order. Because k' contains the concentration of the substance in excess, changing the conditions changes both its value and the half-life ln2/k'. The unit of k' is s⁻¹ and that of the second-order rate constant k is L/(mol·s), and the two should not be confused. When the substance in excess is regenerated like a catalyst, or when the solvent itself is a reactant, its concentration is often not written in the rate law, so distinguish the apparent order from the true order.

faq.q: How large an excess is needed to treat a reaction as pseudo-first order?
faq.a: A guideline is 10-fold or more. With a 10-fold excess the concentration of the substance in excess changes by at most 10%, and several tens of times reduces the error to a few percent or less. Decide according to the accuracy needed.

faq.q: How is the second-order rate constant found from the pseudo-first-order one?
faq.a: Since k' = k[B], divide by the concentration of the substance B in excess. More reliable is to measure k' at several concentrations of B and take k as the slope of the line of k' against [B].

faq.q: What is a pseudo-zero-order reaction?
faq.a: A reaction in which the concentration of a reactant stays almost constant during the reaction, so the rate appears constant. It is seen, for example, in suspensions in which a solid drug dissolves to maintain its saturation concentration, and when a catalyst surface is saturated with reactant.

アレニウスの式.desc: The equation k = A exp(−Ea/RT) expressing the temperature dependence of a rate constant. The activation energy Ea is obtained from the slope of the straight line in a plot of ln k against 1/T.

about.p: The Arrhenius equation, k = A exp(−Ea/RT), is an empirical equation for how the rate constant k of a reaction increases with temperature T, proposed by Arrhenius in 1889. Ea is the activation energy and A the pre-exponential (frequency) factor. exp(−Ea/RT) can be interpreted as a measure of the fraction of collisions with energy exceeding the activation energy. Taking logarithms gives ln k = ln A − Ea/RT, so a plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line with slope −Ea/R. Temperature must always be absolute temperature.

If rate constants are known at two temperatures, Ea can be found from ln(k2/k1) = (Ea/R)(1/T1 − 1/T2). Conversely, if Ea is known, the rate at another temperature can be predicted. For example, for a reaction with Ea = 100 kJ/mol, raising the temperature from 25 °C to 35 °C increases the rate constant about 3.7-fold. The rule of thumb that the rate doubles for every 10 °C rise applies only to reactions with Ea of about 50 kJ/mol near room temperature; the larger Ea is, the greater the change with temperature.

The Eyring equation of transition state theory, k = (kBT/h) exp(−ΔG‡/RT), has a form similar to the Arrhenius equation but is expressed in terms of the Gibbs energy of activation, and for reactions in solution Ea ≈ ΔH‡ + RT. The pre-exponential factor A reflects the entropy of activation; the more strongly molecular motion is restricted in the transition state, the smaller A becomes. A catalyst changes the reaction pathway and lowers the activation energy, but it does not change the heat of reaction or the equilibrium constant. It is important not to confuse these points.

The Arrhenius equation is used in accelerated tests that measure the rate of degradation at high temperatures to estimate lifetime at room temperature, and it underlies stability testing of pharmaceuticals and durability evaluation of materials. However, plots deviate from straight lines when the reaction pathway or rate-determining step changes with temperature, when enzymes are deactivated at high temperature, or for reactions involving a pre-equilibrium. There are even cases where the apparent activation energy is negative. When extrapolating, confirm that the reaction mechanism does not change over the measured temperature range.

faq.q: How is the activation energy determined?
faq.a: Measure rate constants at several temperatures and obtain Ea from the slope −Ea/R of the line in a plot of ln k against 1/T. With only two points, use ln(k2/k1) = (Ea/R)(1/T1 − 1/T2).

faq.q: What are the units of the pre-exponential factor A?
faq.a: The same as the rate constant k. They depend on the reaction order, for example s⁻¹ for a first-order reaction and L/(mol·s) for a second-order reaction.

faq.q: What part of the Arrhenius equation changes when a catalyst is added?
faq.a: Mainly the activation energy Ea decreases, so the rate constant at the same temperature increases. Because the pathway changes, the pre-exponential factor may also change, but the equilibrium constant does not.

速度論的同位体効果.desc: The ratio of rate constants when an atom is replaced by its isotope. When a C−H bond breaks in the rate-determining step, kH/kD is about 2–7 at room temperature, which is used to infer reaction mechanisms.

about.p: Replacing hydrogen with deuterium hardly changes the electronic state or the potential energy surface. What changes is the vibrational frequency: the heavier C−D bond vibrates at a lower frequency than the C−H bond and has a lower zero-point vibrational energy. Stretching wavenumbers are about 3000 cm⁻¹ for C−H and about 2200 cm⁻¹ for C−D. If this bond breaks in the transition state and its stretching vibration disappears, the molecule with C−D has a larger activation energy, by the amount its zero-point energy is lower, and reacts more slowly.

The effect when the bond containing the isotope itself breaks or forms in the rate-determining step is called a primary isotope effect. For C−H versus C−D, the upper limit at room temperature estimated from the zero-point energy difference is about kH/kD ≈ 7, and values of 2–7 are commonly observed in practice. In E2 reactions, for example, the β C−H breaks in the rate-determining step, giving large values, whereas in aromatic nitration the C−H breaks after the rate-determining step, so kH/kD is almost 1. In reactions with significant proton tunneling it can exceed 10.

The small effect of replacing a C−H near the reaction center, rather than the bond that breaks, with deuterium is called a secondary isotope effect, with kH/kD of about 0.8–1.2. It tends to be slightly greater than 1 in SN1 reactions, where the reacting carbon changes from sp³ to sp², and less than 1 (an inverse isotope effect) in additions, where it changes from sp² to sp³, giving a clue to the change in hybridization in the transition state. The solvent isotope effect, on changing the solvent from H2O to D2O, is used to find out whether proton transfer is involved in the rate-determining step.

faq.q: If kH/kD is 1, does that mean the C−H bond is not broken?
faq.a: It means it is not broken in the rate-determining step. If the C−H bond breaks in a fast step after the rate-determining step, kH/kD is almost 1 even though the C−H breaks in the overall reaction.

faq.q: How is it measured?
faq.a: Either the rate constants of the deuterated and ordinary substrates are measured separately, or the two are mixed and allowed to react competitively, and the isotope ratio of the products is examined by mass spectrometry or NMR. Competition experiments reduce errors from differences in conditions.

faq.q: Do isotopes other than deuterium have effects?
faq.a: Yes. They occur with ¹²C versus ¹³C, for example, but the mass ratio is small, so the effect is also small, a few percent. The effect for H versus D, where the mass doubles, is the largest and most widely used.

ハメット則.desc: The relationship log(kX/kH) = ρσ for rate constants or equilibrium constants of benzene derivatives with meta or para substituents. The sign and size of ρ reveal the charge in the transition state.

about.p: Hammett quantified the electronic effects of substituents using the acid dissociation constants of substituted benzoic acids in water at 25 °C as the reference. σ = log(KX/KH), where KH is the acid dissociation constant of benzoic acid and KX that of the substituted benzoic acid. Electron-withdrawing groups stabilize the conjugate base, the carboxylate, and strengthen the acid, so σ is positive; for electron-donating groups it is negative. Typical σp values are 0.78 for nitro, 0.23 for chlorine, −0.17 for methyl and −0.27 for methoxy. Even for the same substituent, resonance acts differently at the meta and para positions, so σm and σp differ.

When the logarithms of the rate constants or equilibrium constants of other reactions are plotted against σ, the result is often a straight line, and its slope is the reaction constant ρ. A positive ρ means electron-withdrawing groups speed up the reaction and that negative charge forms or increases at the reaction center in the transition state. A negative ρ means a reaction in which positive charge develops. The larger |ρ|, the larger the change in charge, or the closer to the aromatic ring the charge develops. The ρ for alkaline hydrolysis of ethyl benzoates is about +2.5, reflecting the negative charge of the tetrahedral intermediate.

about.h: σ⁺ and σ⁻, and deviations from linearity
about.p: In reactions where positive charge can resonate directly with a para substituent, such as those forming benzylic carbocations, ordinary σ does not give a good straight line, and σ⁺, determined from the solvolysis of cumyl chlorides, is used instead. Conversely, when negative charge resonates directly, as with phenoxides, σ⁻ is used. When a plot bends partway, the rate-determining step or the mechanism may be changing with the substituent. Ortho substituents add steric effects, so they are normally not treated with the Hammett equation.

faq.q: What does the sign of ρ tell me?
faq.a: It tells you the sign of the charge that develops at the reaction center in the transition state of the rate-determining step. If ρ is positive, negative charge develops and electron-withdrawing groups speed the reaction; if ρ is negative, positive charge develops and electron-donating groups speed it.

faq.q: What does a ρ greater than 1 mean?
faq.a: It means the reaction is more strongly affected by substituents than the reference ionization of benzoic acid. With ρ = 2.5, for example, a difference of 0.4 in σ changes the rate constant 10-fold.

faq.q: Why can't it be used for ortho-substituted compounds?
faq.a: Ortho substituents are close to the reaction center, and steric effects, hydrogen bonding and the like overlap with the electronic effect, so σ alone cannot describe them.

定常状態近似.desc: The approximation that the concentration of a reactive intermediate is small and nearly constant, so its rates of formation and consumption are set equal. Used to derive the rate laws of multistep reactions.

about.h: Treating the intermediate concentration as nearly constant
about.p: The steady-state approximation treats a reactive intermediate in a multistep reaction as being at low concentration that stays nearly constant for most of the reaction, setting d[I]/dt ≈ 0. By equating the rates of formation and consumption of the intermediate, its hard-to-measure concentration can be expressed in terms of reactant concentrations and rate constants. Substituting this into the rate of product formation gives the overall rate law. It is the standard way to derive a rate law from a mechanism without solving a system of coupled differential equations.

The approximation holds when the intermediate is consumed much faster than it is formed. For consecutive reactions A → I → P with the rate constant k2 for consumption of I 100 times the rate constant k1 for its formation, after a short initial period [I]/[A] is exactly k1/(k2 − k1) and approximately k1/k2, a difference of about 1%. If k2 is comparable to k1, the intermediate accumulates and the approximation fails. Also, just after the reaction starts, the intermediate concentration is still rising, so the approximation cannot be used during that period.

about.h: How it differs from the pre-equilibrium approximation
about.p: It is often compared with the pre-equilibrium approximation, which assumes that the forward and reverse reactions of the first step are fast and at equilibrium and that a later step is slow. The steady-state approximation is more general: for A ⇌ I → P it gives v = k1k2[A]/(k−1 + k2), which reduces to the pre-equilibrium result when k−1 ≫ k2 and to the result with the first step rate-determining when k2 ≫ k−1. It does not set the intermediate concentration to zero; it means that the rate at which that concentration changes is negligible compared with the rates of formation and consumption.

Bodenstein introduced the steady-state approximation in the early 20th century for analyzing chain reactions, and the complex rate law for the formation of hydrogen bromide from hydrogen and bromine was also explained by a chain mechanism using this approximation. The Lindemann mechanism for gas-phase unimolecular reactions, which treats collisionally activated molecules as intermediates, the derivation of the Michaelis–Menten equation with the enzyme–substrate complex as the intermediate (the Briggs–Haldane treatment), and the treatment of radical concentration in radical polymerization are also based on this approximation. It is a basic tool for checking whether a rate law agrees with a mechanism.

faq.q: What is the difference between the steady-state and pre-equilibrium approximations?
faq.a: The pre-equilibrium approximation assumes the first step is a fast equilibrium, and the steady-state approximation assumes the intermediate's concentration is nearly constant. Depending on the conditions, the steady-state result includes the pre-equilibrium result.

faq.q: Is the intermediate concentration zero in the steady-state approximation?
faq.a: No. The concentration is small and nearly constant, and d[I]/dt ≈ 0 means its rate of change is negligible compared with its rates of formation and consumption.

faq.q: When can the steady-state approximation not be used?
faq.a: When the intermediate is about as stable as the reactants and accumulates, or right after the reaction starts while the intermediate concentration is still rising. In such cases, the coupled rate equations are solved numerically.
