カーティン・ハメットの原理.desc: The principle that when rapidly interconverting isomers each give a different product, the product ratio is set not by the population ratio of the isomers but by the free-energy difference between the transition states.

about.h: Conditions under which the principle holds
about.p: The Curtin–Hammett principle holds for reactions in which two interconverting isomers A and B each give a different product, when the interconversion of A and B is much faster than product formation. Chair flipping in cyclohexane and conformational changes by rotation about single bonds occur tens of thousands of times per second at room temperature, so many reactions meet this condition. The product ratio is then set not by the population ratio of A and B but only by the free-energy difference between the transition states leading to the two products.

about.h: The meaning seen through the equation
about.p: The product ratio can be written P_B/P_A = K × (k_B/k_A), where K is the equilibrium ratio of B to A and k_A and k_B are the rate constants for reaction from each. Even with K = 0.1 (about 9% B), if B reacts 1000 times faster than A, P_B/P_A = 0.1 × 1000 = 100, and 99% of the product comes from the minor isomer. The product of K and k_B/k_A can be expressed solely by the free-energy difference between the two transition states, so however carefully you measure the conformer ratio of the starting material, that alone does not give the product ratio.

If interconversion is slower than product formation, A and B react independently and the product ratio reflects the initial populations. Examples are reactions in which conformations are frozen at low temperature, and isomers of amides or biaryls with large rotational barriers. Under conditions where the products equilibrate with each other, the product ratio is under thermodynamic control, set by product stability. Before applying the principle, it is important to check the relative rates of three processes: interconversion of the isomers, formation of the products and interconversion of the products.

about.h: Eliminations in chair conformations and asymmetric catalysis
about.p: The E2 reactions of menthyl chloride and neomenthyl chloride are a classic example of the link between conformation and reactivity. In neomenthyl chloride the chlorine is axial in the stable conformation and elimination is rapid. Menthyl chloride can eliminate only from an unstable conformation in which the chlorine is axial, so it reacts far more slowly. In rhodium-catalyzed asymmetric hydrogenation, Halpern and coworkers showed that the minor catalyst–substrate complex reacts much faster and gives the major product.

faq.q: Why can the major product come from the minor conformer?
faq.a: If the minor isomer reacts fast enough, what it loses by reacting is promptly replenished from the major isomer through the fast equilibrium. The product ratio is decided only by which pathway has the lower transition state.

faq.q: When can the Curtin–Hammett principle not be used?
faq.a: When interconversion of the isomers is as slow as or slower than product formation. In that case the product ratio is found by solving the rate equations, including the initial populations and the individual rate constants.

faq.q: If I measure the conformer ratio by NMR, do I know the product ratio?
faq.a: Not under conditions where this principle holds. The population ratio K is included in the product ratio, but it is multiplied by the ratio of rate constants, so you need to know the energy difference between the transition states as well.

フロンティア軌道.desc: A molecule's HOMO (highest occupied molecular orbital) and LUMO (lowest unoccupied molecular orbital). Reactivity and regioselectivity are explained by the interaction of one molecule's HOMO with the other's LUMO.

about.p: Of a molecule's orbitals, the highest-energy filled one is called the HOMO (highest occupied molecular orbital) and the lowest empty one the LUMO (lowest unoccupied molecular orbital); together they are called the frontier orbitals. Kenichi Fukui showed that how readily a reaction occurs, and where, is determined mainly by the properties of these two orbitals. A nucleophile donates electrons from its HOMO, and an electrophile accepts them into its LUMO. The higher the HOMO, the more readily electrons are donated, and the lower the LUMO, the more readily they are accepted.

about.h: What sets the size of the interaction
about.p: When one molecule's HOMO overlaps with the other's LUMO, two electrons enter the newly formed bonding orbital and the system is stabilized. This stabilization is greater the smaller the energy gap between the two orbitals, and the larger the orbital coefficients (sizes) on the reacting atoms and the better their phases match. Overlap between two filled HOMOs is a four-electron repulsion and forms no bond. Considering how substituents change orbital energies and coefficients lets you predict the rate and direction of reactions.

In an ordinary Diels–Alder reaction, the pair of diene HOMO and dienophile LUMO mainly operates (normal electron demand). An electron-withdrawing group on the dienophile lowers its LUMO and an electron-donating group on the diene raises its HOMO, and both make the reaction faster. Regioselectivity is explained by bonding between the termini with the largest coefficients: 1-substituted dienes mainly give the "ortho" product and 2-substituted dienes the "para" product. The endo rule is also explained by a secondary overlap between the orbitals of the carbonyl group and the diene.

faq.q: Why is it enough to consider only the HOMO and LUMO?
faq.a: When all orbital interactions are added up, the HOMO–LUMO pair, with its small energy gap, contributes the most. It is not an exact calculation, but it is often a good enough approximation for grasping trends in reactivity and selectivity.

faq.q: What happens when a HOMO overlaps with a HOMO?
faq.a: Both contain two electrons, so both the resulting bonding and antibonding orbitals are filled, and overall there is no stabilization but rather repulsion. It therefore does not work toward bond formation.

faq.q: Can frontier orbitals be used for reactions other than pericyclic ones?
faq.a: Yes. Thinking of a nucleophile's HOMO attacking a LUMO such as the π* of a carbonyl group or the σ* of a C−X bond explains the backside attack of the SN2 reaction and the site of nucleophilic addition.

ヒュッケル分子軌道法.desc: A simple molecular orbital method that treats only π electrons and represents the interaction between adjacent carbons by the resonance integral β. It gives π orbital energies in the form α + xβ.

about.p: In the method Hückel introduced in 1931, the σ-bonded framework of a planar conjugated molecule is separated from the π electrons, and only the π electrons are treated. Molecular orbitals are built from combinations of the carbon 2p orbitals. The energy of an electron in a carbon 2p orbital is taken as the Coulomb integral α, the interaction between orbitals on neighboring carbons as the resonance integral β, and interactions between nonneighboring atoms and orbital overlap integrals are set to zero. With just this, solving the secular equations gives orbital energies and coefficients by hand.

For ethylene, the secular determinant gives E = α ± β, and because β is negative, α + β is the bonding π orbital. For a linear chain of N carbons, the orbital energies are Eₖ = α + 2β cos(kπ/(N + 1)) (k = 1, 2, …, N). The HOMO–LUMO gap shrinks from 2|β| in ethylene to about 0.69|β| in octatetraene, with eight carbons, and approaches zero as the chain becomes infinitely long. This formula qualitatively explains why UV-visible absorption shifts to longer wavelengths as conjugation grows.

The orbital coefficients c give the π electron density on each atom and the π bond order between atoms. The π bond order is the sum over occupied orbitals of the number of electrons times the product of the two atoms' coefficients. In butadiene, it is 0.894 for the terminal C1−C2 bond and 0.447 for the central C2−C3 bond, showing that the central bond has some π character and the terminal bonds are somewhat weaker than pure double bonds. Measured bond lengths follow the same trend. Heteroatoms can be handled by multiplying α and β by correction factors.

about.h: Where it helps and where it fails
about.p: Simple Hückel theory is still useful for capturing trends: judging aromaticity, finding the positions most likely to react, seeing the shapes of the HOMO and LUMO, and following shifts of absorption to longer wavelengths. On the other hand, because it ignores σ electrons and electron–electron repulsion, it handles absolute energies, nonplanar molecules, and molecules with uneven charge poorly. The value of β also varies widely depending on which experiment it is fitted to. The extended Hückel method proposed by Hoffmann in 1963 includes σ electrons and overlap integrals and was widely used in discussing bonding in inorganic complexes as well.

faq.q: Why is the resonance integral β negative?
faq.a: When orbitals on neighboring carbons overlap in phase, an electron is attracted by both nuclei and its energy drops. That is why α + β is the energy of a bonding orbital lower than α.

faq.q: Why is it acceptable to set the overlap integral to zero?
faq.a: The actual overlap is about 0.2–0.3, so strictly it is an approximation. Including overlap hardly changes qualitative conclusions such as orbital ordering and the pattern of coefficients, so it is left out to simplify the calculation.

faq.q: What is the difference between simple and extended Hückel theory?
faq.a: Simple Hückel theory treats only the π electrons of planar conjugated systems and keeps α and β as symbols. Extended Hückel theory includes all valence orbitals and overlap integrals and calculates numerically with parameters for each atom.

非局在化エネルギー.desc: The size of the stabilization from π electrons spreading over the whole molecule. It is found by comparison with a set of isolated double bonds; in Hückel theory it is 0.472|β| for butadiene and 2|β| for benzene.

about.h: Stabilization from π electrons spreading out
about.p: Delocalization energy is the stabilization gained when the π electrons of a conjugated molecule spread over the whole molecule. In simple Hückel theory it is found by comparing the π-electron energy of the real molecule with that of the same number of isolated double bonds (the π bonds of ethylene). For 1,3-butadiene it is the difference between 4α + 4.472β and 4α + 4β, 0.472|β|; for benzene, between 6α + 8β and 6α + 6β, 2|β|. Because β, the resonance integral, is negative, the size of the stabilization is given as an absolute value.

about.h: Comparing chains and rings reveals aromaticity
about.p: Even with the same six π electrons, the delocalization energy of open-chain 1,3,5-hexatriene is only about 0.988|β|, roughly half of benzene's 2|β|. The difference of about 1.01|β| can be regarded as a measure of the special stabilization from forming a ring, that is, aromaticity. In square cyclobutadiene, by contrast, the delocalization energy is zero, and a ring with four π electrons is not stabilized. The allyl cation, radical and anion all gain about 0.828|β| of stabilization, because the extra electrons in these species go into a nonbonding orbital that does not change the π energy.

about.h: How it differs from resonance energy
about.p: Delocalization energy is a theoretical quantity calculated with the Hückel approximation and expressed in β. Resonance energy, by contrast, is an experimental quantity obtained as the difference between measured heats of hydrogenation or combustion and estimates for a hypothetical localized structure. For benzene it is estimated at about 150 kJ/mol from heats of hydrogenation, and setting this equal to 2|β| gives |β| of about 75 kJ/mol. However, β determined from ultraviolet absorption energies comes out quite different, so note that the value of β depends on how it is obtained.

Delocalization energy is useful for comparing the relative stability of conjugated and aromatic compounds and for understanding what Hückel's rule means. However, simple Hückel theory ignores σ-bond strain and electron–electron repulsion, so it does not give the absolute size of the stabilization. It has also been pointed out that much of the stabilization of butadiene can be explained by the strength of σ bonds between sp² carbons rather than by π-electron delocalization. Today, more precise aromatic stabilization energies are obtained by quantum chemical calculations.

faq.q: Are delocalization energy and resonance energy the same?
faq.a: They are often used interchangeably, but delocalization energy usually refers to a theoretical value calculated by the Hückel method, and resonance energy to an experimental value estimated from measurements such as heats of hydrogenation.

faq.q: Why is delocalization energy expressed in |β|?
faq.a: In the Hückel method orbital energies are combinations of α and β, and the α terms cancel between the two states being compared. Because β is negative, the size of the stabilization is given as an absolute value.

faq.q: Why is the delocalization energy of cyclobutadiene zero?
faq.a: Two of the four π electrons go into orbitals that are neither bonding nor antibonding, so the π-electron energy equals that of two isolated double bonds. It is an example of the instability of antiaromatic systems.

反芳香族性.desc: The property by which a cyclic, planar, conjugated system with 4n π electrons fails to form a closed shell and is destabilized. Cyclobutadiene is the typical example, and a paratropic ring current appears in ¹H NMR.

about.h: Not the same as merely “not aromatic”
about.p: The term antiaromaticity was proposed by Breslow around 1965. It describes the property of molecules that are cyclic, planar, and conjugated with 4n π electrons, and that are less stable than open-chain molecules with the same number of double bonds. Molecules with no special stabilization or destabilization, because the ring is not planar or conjugation is interrupted, are called nonaromatic and kept distinct. With 4n π electrons, Hückel theory tends to give an open shell with one electron in each of two degenerate orbitals, and molecules distort their shape to avoid it.

There are three kinds of criteria: energetic, structural, and magnetic. Energetically, molecules are compared with open-chain references; structurally, alternation of long and short bonds is a sign. The magnetic criterion uses NICS, the calculated chemical shift at a virtual point placed at the ring center, which is negative for aromatic and positive for antiaromatic rings. In ¹H NMR, an antiaromatic ring in an external magnetic field sustains a paratropic ring current that moves hydrogens outside the ring upfield and those inside downfield, the opposite of aromatic rings.

In 1972, Baird showed that in the lowest triplet excited state the rules of aromaticity are reversed: rings with 4n π electrons are aromatically stabilized, and rings with 4n + 2 become antiaromatic (Baird's rule). Cyclooctatetraene, which avoids antiaromaticity in the ground state by adopting a tub shape, tends to become planar in its excited triplet. This idea is used to design reactions in which light changes a molecule's shape dramatically and materials whose properties switch under light. The aromaticity of transition states in concerted reactions can be understood in the same way.

about.h: Antiaromatic compounds that have been isolated
about.p: Cyclobutadiene on its own can be observed only at very low temperatures, but in 1965 Pettit and coworkers isolated it as a stable iron tricarbonyl complex and showed that oxidation releases it to act as highly reactive cyclobutadiene. Antiaromatic molecules can also be isolated when surrounded by bulky substituents. In 2012, an antiaromatic porphyrin analog stable even in air, a nickel norcorrole, was reported. Taking advantage of their small HOMO–LUMO gaps, such compounds are being studied as electronic materials.

faq.q: What is the difference between antiaromatic and nonaromatic?
faq.a: Antiaromatic molecules are less stable than open-chain molecules because of 4n π electrons in a planar, cyclic, conjugated system. Nonaromatic molecules have no special stabilization or destabilization from ring conjugation because the ring is not planar or conjugation is interrupted.

faq.q: What is NICS?
faq.a: It is the calculated shielding at a virtual point placed at, or slightly above, the center of a ring, with its sign reversed. It is negative for aromatic rings and positive for antiaromatic rings, and it serves as a magnetic index for comparing aromaticity numerically.

faq.q: Can antiaromatic molecules actually be isolated?
faq.a: Yes. Cyclobutadiene can be observed when trapped in solid argon at low temperature, and it can be isolated as a metal complex or when surrounded by bulky substituents. Stable antiaromatic porphyrin analogs have also been synthesized.

エンド則.desc: The empirical rule that in the Diels–Alder reaction the endo adduct, formed through a transition state in which the dienophile's unsaturated substituent points toward the diene's π system, is kinetically favored. It is explained by secondary orbital interactions.

about.p: When a cyclic diene and a dienophile give a bridged bicyclic product, the product in which the dienophile's substituent points toward the newly formed double bond (the side of the longer bridge) is called endo, and the one in which it points toward the opposite, shorter bridge (the CH2 bridge for cyclopentadiene) is called exo. Acyclic dienes form no bridge, but the same distinction is made according to whether the substituent tucks under the diene's π system in the transition state. Because Alder and Stein summarized it in 1937, it is also called Alder's rule.

The endo rule is generally explained by the secondary orbital interactions proposed by Woodward and Hoffmann: in the endo transition state, the π orbital of the dienophile's carbonyl group also overlaps with the inner carbons of the diene, which form no bond, and this stabilizes it. Computational studies, however, point out that differences in electrostatic interactions, dispersion forces and strain in the transition state also contribute substantially, and debate continues over whether the selectivity can be explained by secondary orbital interactions alone.

The endo rule is empirical and does not always hold. When the dienophile carries a methyl group or the like at the α position, steric repulsion in the endo transition state grows and the proportion of exo product increases. In intramolecular Diels–Alder reactions the exo product often dominates, depending on the length and shape of the tether. Long reaction at high temperature, where the reverse reaction occurs, shifts the outcome toward the thermodynamically more stable exo product. Methods that use bulky catalysts to obtain exo products selectively have also been developed.

The endo rule is used as a tool for predicting the relative configuration of new stereocenters. The relationship between substituents at the ends of the diene and those of the dienophile is decided by whether the reaction goes endo or exo, so knowing which transition state is followed fixes the stereochemistry of the product in one step. Even for dienophiles with moderate endo selectivity, such as acrylic esters, adding a Lewis acid such as AlCl3 is known to raise the endo selectivity greatly in some cases. The substituent of an endo product is sometimes epimerized with base to convert it to the exo product.

faq.q: How do you tell an endo product from an exo product?
faq.a: In a bicyclic product, if the substituent points toward the longer bridge carrying the new double bond it is endo; if toward the shorter bridge (CH2, when made from cyclopentadiene) it is exo. Checking with a molecular model is the sure way.

faq.q: Does the endo rule always hold?
faq.a: No. Substituents at the α position of the dienophile, intramolecular reactions and conditions where the reverse reaction occurs at high temperature can make the exo product dominant. Regard it as an empirical rule describing a tendency under kinetic control.

faq.q: What happens to endo selectivity when a Lewis acid is added?
faq.a: In many cases it increases. When the Lewis acid coordinates to the carbonyl group, it lowers the dienophile's LUMO and speeds up the reaction, and it also widens the energy difference between the endo and exo transition states.

ウッドワード-ホフマン則.desc: Rules that determine from orbital symmetry whether a concerted pericyclic reaction is thermally or photochemically allowed or forbidden. Thermal electrocyclic reactions are conrotatory with 4n electrons and disrotatory with 4n + 2.

about.p: Woodward and Hoffmann showed that in a concerted pericyclic reaction, the phases (symmetry) of the orbitals must connect continuously from reactants to products. If the orbitals overlap in phase at both ends where bonds form, the reaction is allowed and proceeds with a low activation energy. If the phases do not match it is forbidden and proceeds poorly in a concerted way. The frontier-orbital method based on the shape of the HOMO, orbital correlation diagrams, and the method based on the aromaticity of the transition state all give the same conclusions.

A reaction in which the two ends of a conjugated polyene bond to form a ring (and the reverse ring opening) is called an electrocyclic reaction. Thermally, if the number of π electrons involved is 4n (butadiene and cyclobutene), the ends rotate in the same direction, conrotatory; if it is 4n + 2 (hexatriene and cyclohexadiene), they rotate in opposite directions, disrotatory. Photoexcitation changes the HOMO to the next orbital up, so the mode of rotation swaps. The configuration of the substituents determines whether the product is cis or trans, and the reaction is stereospecific.

By the generalized rule, a reaction is thermally allowed if the total number of suprafacial (4q + 2)-electron components and antarafacial 4r-electron components is odd. The Diels–Alder reaction [π4s + π2s] has one and is allowed, while [π2s + π2s] for two ethylenes has two and is thermally forbidden, proceeding photochemically. The same reasoning is used for sigmatropic rearrangements, in which a σ bond migrates: [3,3] rearrangements such as the Cope and Claisen rearrangements and suprafacial [1,5]-hydrogen shifts are thermally allowed.

faq.q: Do "forbidden" reactions never occur at all?
faq.a: It means the energy barrier of the concerted pathway is high; they can occur through stepwise pathways via radicals and the like, or at higher temperatures. Many thermally forbidden reactions are photochemically allowed.

faq.q: How do you tell conrotatory from disrotatory?
faq.a: If the bonds at the two ends that open or close the ring rotate in the same direction (both clockwise, for example), the motion is conrotatory; if they rotate in opposite directions, it is disrotatory. Thermally, it is conrotatory with 4n π electrons and disrotatory with 4n + 2.

faq.q: How are the Woodward–Hoffmann rules related to frontier orbitals?
faq.a: Kenichi Fukui's frontier orbital theory gives the same selection rules by looking at the phases at the two ends of the HOMO. Hoffmann and Fukui received the 1981 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this work.

電子環状反応.desc: A concerted reaction in which the two ends of a conjugated polyene join through a σ bond to form a ring, and the reverse ring opening. Conrotatory and disrotatory modes swap between heat and light, and the reaction is stereospecific.

about.p: An electrocyclic reaction is the formation of a ring by joining the two terminal carbons of a single conjugated π system with a σ bond, together with the reverse ring opening. Bond reorganization occurs all at once through a cyclic transition state, so it is a concerted reaction and a kind of pericyclic reaction. The basic examples are the interconversion of butadiene and cyclobutene (4π electrons) and of hexatriene and cyclohexadiene (6π electrons). Unlike a cycloaddition, which forms two σ bonds between two components, only one σ bond forms or breaks within a single molecule.

When the ring forms, the terminal p orbitals rotate about 90° to make the σ bond. Rotation of both termini in the same direction is conrotatory, and in opposite directions disrotatory. Which occurs is determined by the phases at the ends of the HOMO. Thermally, 4π systems react conrotatorily and 6π systems disrotatorily; photochemically, excitation changes the HOMO to the next orbital up, so each is reversed. In general, 4n π electrons give thermal conrotation and 4n + 2 give thermal disrotation. These selection rules are a representative example of the Woodward–Hoffmann rules.

about.h: Stereospecificity and the direction of equilibrium
about.p: Because the reaction is concerted, the stereochemistry of the product is uniquely determined by the configuration of the starting material (stereospecificity). Thermal ring opening of cis-3,4-dimethylcyclobutene gives only the (2E,4Z) isomer. The direction of reaction, however, is set by thermodynamics, not by the selection rules. Cyclobutene is highly strained, so ring opening is thermally favored. In hexatriene ring closure, one π bond becomes a σ bond and a low-strain six-membered ring forms, so closure is favored. "Allowed" means the reaction can proceed quickly; it says nothing about the position of equilibrium.

The formation of vitamin D3 in the body is a classic example of photochemical and thermal electrocyclic chemistry. 7-Dehydrocholesterol in the skin absorbs ultraviolet light and undergoes a photochemical conrotatory 6π ring opening to previtamin D3, which then converts to vitamin D3 by a thermal [1,7] hydrogen shift. In synthesis, the Nazarov cyclization, which cyclizes divinyl ketones with acid to give cyclopentenones (a conrotatory 4π closure of a cation), is widely used. In each case, a strength of these reactions is that the selection rules let you predict the product stereochemistry in advance.

faq.q: Conrotation can go two ways; which one occurs?
faq.a: In cyclobutene ring opening, a substituent at C3 can rotate outward or inward, and it usually rotates outward, which is sterically favored. Electron-donating groups prefer outward rotation more strongly, while electron-withdrawing groups such as a formyl group may rotate inward (torquoselectivity).

faq.q: Why is the sense of rotation reversed between heat and light?
faq.a: When light promotes an electron to the next orbital up, the HOMO involved becomes an orbital with the opposite phase relationship at the termini. For lobes of the same phase to overlap, the sense of rotation must also be reversed.

faq.q: How does it differ from a cycloaddition?
faq.a: An electrocyclic reaction forms one σ bond between the ends of a single conjugated system, while a cycloaddition forms two σ bonds between two components. The Diels–Alder reaction is an example of a cycloaddition.

シグマトロピー転位.desc: A concerted rearrangement in which a σ bond adjacent to a π system migrates across the π system and forms anew at another position. Examples are the [3,3] Cope and Claisen rearrangements and [1,5]-hydrogen shifts.

about.p: Sigmatropic rearrangements are written in the form [i,j]. The atoms at each end of the σ bond that breaks are each numbered 1, and the two fragments joined by that σ bond are numbered along the π system. When the new σ bond forms between atom i of one fragment and atom j of the other, it is an [i,j] rearrangement. A hydrogen moving from position 1 to position 5 of a π system is a [1,5] shift, and bonding between the 3-positions of both fragments is a [3,3] rearrangement. Formally, the 1,2-shift of a carbocation is also a [1,2] sigmatropic rearrangement.

The Cope rearrangement, a [3,3] rearrangement, proceeds through a chair-shaped transition state formed by six atoms. The stereochemistry of the starting material therefore determines the configuration of the double bonds in the product. In 1962 Doering and Roth showed that meso-3,4-dimethyl-1,5-hexadiene gives almost exclusively (E,Z)-2,6-octadiene, while the racemate gives mainly the (E,E) isomer. In bullvalene, degenerate Cope rearrangements occur constantly, and the structure scrambles so much that all ten hydrogens appear equivalent in high-temperature NMR.

The Claisen rearrangement is the [3,3] rearrangement of allyl vinyl ethers, which contain oxygen; formation of a C=O bond drives it, and it gives γ,δ-unsaturated carbonyl compounds. The Johnson–Claisen rearrangement, generated in situ from an allylic alcohol and an orthoester, and the Ireland–Claisen rearrangement, which uses silyl ketene acetals of esters, form new C−C bonds and stereocenters predictably and are widely used in natural product synthesis. The anionic oxy-Cope rearrangement, in which the hydroxy group is made negatively charged, proceeds orders of magnitude faster.

Migration of the group across the same face of the π system is called suprafacial, and migration to the opposite face antarafacial. For thermal hydrogen shifts, the [1,5] shift involving six electrons is allowed suprafacially, and the [1,7] shift involving eight electrons is allowed antarafacially. As π systems become longer and more flexible, antarafacial migration also becomes geometrically possible. When carbon migrates, whether the migrating carbon keeps or inverts its configuration also enters the selection rules, and the pathway of a rearrangement can be checked from the stereochemistry of the product.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Cope and Claisen rearrangements?
faq.a: Both are [3,3] rearrangements. The Cope rearrangement occurs in the all-carbon framework of 1,5-dienes, and the Claisen rearrangement in oxygen-containing frameworks such as allyl vinyl ethers and allyl aryl ethers. Because the Claisen rearrangement forms C=O, it usually does not reverse.

faq.q: Do sigmatropic rearrangements occur in living organisms?
faq.a: Yes. Partway through the biosynthesis of phenylalanine and tyrosine, chorismate is converted to prephenate by a [3,3] rearrangement (a Claisen rearrangement), and the enzyme chorismate mutase greatly accelerates this reaction.

faq.q: Are sigmatropic rearrangements caused by heat or by light?
faq.a: Most occur thermally. By the Woodward–Hoffmann rules, the thermally allowed mode (suprafacial or antarafacial) is set by the number of electrons, and photoexcitation swaps the allowed mode.

構造活性相関.desc: The relationship between a compound's chemical structure and its biological activity (SAR). By changing the structure step by step and comparing activities, the parts needed for activity are distinguished from those that can be improved.

about.p: The structure–activity relationship (SAR) is the relationship between a compound's chemical structure and its biological activity, a way of thinking that underlies drug design. Once an active lead compound is found, analogs are synthesized in which the type or position of substituents, ring size, configuration and so on are changed one at a time, and their activities are measured. From the results, the parts essential for activity (the pharmacophore), the parts that can be changed while keeping activity, and the parts whose change raises activity are distinguished, and the compound is optimized toward greater potency and selectivity.

In SAR it is important to compare the potencies of compounds with condition-independent quantities. The IC50 for enzyme inhibition depends on measurement conditions such as substrate concentration, so for competitive inhibition it is converted to Ki with the Cheng–Prusoff equation and compared as pKi (−log Ki). An increase of 1 in pKi means binding is 10 times stronger. Because making a molecule larger tends to raise potency, ligand efficiency, the binding energy per heavy atom, is also examined to judge whether an improvement is worth the added size.

Expressing activity as an equation in physical-property values is called a quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR). In Hansch analysis, log(1/C) is expressed as a linear combination of the hydrophobic substituent constant π, the Hammett constant σ for electronic effects, steric constants and so on, to find which properties govern activity. Today calculations based on the three-dimensional structures of molecules and target proteins are also widely used, but all of them start from experimental SAR data. These equations rest on the premise that substituent effects are roughly additive.

faq.q: What is the difference between SAR and QSAR?
faq.a: SAR captures the relationship between changes in structure and changes in activity qualitatively, while QSAR expresses it quantitatively as an equation using numerical values such as π and σ.

faq.q: Can activity change suddenly and greatly?
faq.a: Yes. A pair in which a slight structural difference changes activity greatly is called an activity cliff, and it is a clue to finding interactions important for binding. Cases in which a single methyl group raises activity greatly are also known.

faq.q: Is activity the only thing examined in SAR?
faq.a: No. The relationships of solubility, membrane permeability, metabolic stability, toxicity and so on with structure are also examined, and compounds are optimized while balancing these against activity. These are sometimes collectively called structure–property relationships.

ファーマコフォア.desc: The features needed to bind the target and show activity, such as hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, hydrophobic regions and charges, together with their three-dimensional arrangement. Compounds with different skeletons can share one.

about.h: An arrangement of features, not atoms
about.p: A pharmacophore is an abstract model summarizing the molecular features needed to bind a given target and produce an effect, together with their three-dimensional arrangement. The features include hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, hydrophobic regions, aromatic rings, and sites that can carry a positive or negative charge, expressed through their distances and angles. IUPAC defines it as the ensemble of steric and electronic features necessary for interaction with the target and states that it is not a real molecule or a set of functional groups. Importantly, the term does not refer to a particular scaffold.

Because a pharmacophore is an arrangement of features, compounds with completely different scaffolds can satisfy the same pharmacophore. For example, morphine, pethidine and fentanyl look quite different, but each has a basic nitrogen that is protonated at physiological pH and an aromatic ring at a certain distance from it, and all act on opioid receptors. This idea is used in scaffold hopping, the search for compounds with scaffolds different from known drugs, and in designing new compounds outside the scope of existing patents.

Pharmacophore models are built in two ways. In the ligand-based approach, conformations of several active compounds are superimposed to extract the arrangement of shared features; using inactive compounds as well helps check the model's selectivity. In the structure-based approach, the sites that actually interact in a target–ligand complex, obtained from an X-ray crystal structure or similar, are extracted as features, and regions that must not overlap target atoms are added as excluded volumes. In both, the predictive performance is validated with compounds of known activity.

about.h: Use in drug discovery and caveats
about.p: Pharmacophore models are used in virtual screening to pick out compounds that meet the criteria from large databases, narrowing the candidates for synthesis and testing. They also help organize structure–activity relationship results and judge which parts of a molecule can be changed. However, the models simplify target flexibility, the role of water molecules and solvation effects, so a compound that fits is not necessarily active. Predictions must be confirmed experimentally. Structural features linked to toxicity are separately called toxicophores.

faq.q: What is the difference between a pharmacophore and a scaffold?
faq.a: A scaffold is a concrete core arrangement of atoms in a molecule, while a pharmacophore is the three-dimensional arrangement of features needed for activity. Different scaffolds satisfy the same pharmacophore if their features are in the same arrangement.

faq.q: How is a pharmacophore determined?
faq.a: Either by superimposing several active compounds and extracting their common features, or by extracting the interacting sites from the structure of a target–ligand complex.

faq.q: How does it relate to bioisosteres?
faq.a: Replacement with a bioisostere can be seen as a way to change properties or metabolism while keeping the pharmacophore's features. If a replacement loses a necessary feature, activity falls.

リピンスキーの5の法則.desc: The empirical rule that exceeding two or more of molecular weight 500, logP 5, 5 hydrogen-bond donors and 10 acceptors makes poor oral absorption or membrane permeation likely.

about.h: What the rule of five says
about.p: Lipinski's rule of five is an empirical rule compiled in 1997 by examining the properties of drugs that had been used orally. If two or more of four criteria apply, molecular weight over 500, logP over 5, more than 5 hydrogen-bond donors (the number of OH and NH) and more than 10 hydrogen-bond acceptors (the number of N and O), absorption or membrane permeation is taken to be likely to be poor. It gets its name because the threshold numbers are all multiples of five. It later came to be used to screen many drug candidates.

An oral drug must dissolve in the water of the gastrointestinal tract and then pass through lipid cell membranes into the blood. If a molecule is too large or has too many hydrogen-bonding groups, a lot of energy is needed to break its hydrogen bonds with water as it enters the membrane, so it permeates poorly. On the other hand, if logP is too large, it dissolves poorly in water. The rule of five expresses, in easily counted numbers, a guide for balancing dissolving with passing through membranes. Empirically, too, membrane permeability tends to fall as the molecular weight and the number of hydrogen bonds increase.

about.h: How to use it and its limits
about.p: The rule of five is a simple guide for screening candidate compounds: following it does not guarantee absorption, and violating it does not mean a compound cannot become an oral drug. There are many exceptions among drugs carried by transporters and large molecules derived from natural products. It is used together with Veber's criteria, which add the number of rotatable bonds (10 or fewer) and polar surface area (140 Å² or less), and the "rule of three", a guide for choosing fragments. What matters is to think about the balance of solubility and permeability behind the thresholds.

faq.q: How is a compound judged if only one criterion is exceeded?
faq.a: With only one, the rule of five does not immediately flag a problem. Exceeding two or more makes poor absorption likely, so revising the structure or formulation measures are considered.

faq.q: How are hydrogen-bond acceptors counted?
faq.a: In Lipinski's original definition, the number of acceptors is the total number of nitrogen and oxygen atoms. Donors are the number of OH and NH; NH2 is counted as two in some conventions and as one in others.

faq.q: Is the rule of five used for injectable drugs too?
faq.a: The rule of five is a guide for estimating oral absorption, so it is not applied as such to drugs given by injection or applied locally.

オクタノール/水分配係数.desc: The ratio P of the concentrations of the neutral compound when it partitions between 1-octanol and water. Its common logarithm, logP, expresses lipophilicity and is used as a guide to membrane permeation, absorption and metabolism.

about.p: The octanol/water partition coefficient P is the ratio of concentrations (octanol phase/water phase) when the neutral form of a compound is distributed between 1-octanol and water and reaches equilibrium. Because values span a wide range, it is expressed as the common logarithm logP: a logP of 0 means equal concentrations in both phases, and 2 means 100 times more in the octanol phase. In environmental science it is also written Kow or Pow. 1-Octanol has a long hydrocarbon chain and an OH group and dissolves some water, so it has been chosen as a model for phases that, like membrane lipids, have both polar and nonpolar character.

LogP describes partitioning between neutral forms and is a value characteristic of the compound. Acids and bases, however, stay almost entirely in the water phase once ionized, so the apparent partitioning at an actual pH is expressed as logD. For a weak acid, logD = logP − log(1 + 10^(pH − pKa)). For example, benzoic acid (logP about 1.87, pKa about 4.2) has a logD of about −1.3 at pH 7.4, partitioning into water much more than its neutral form does. LogD is the appropriate quantity when considering membrane permeation at physiological pH or retention in reversed-phase HPLC.

The basic measurement is the shake-flask method, in which the two phases are shaken to equilibrium and the concentration in each is measured; it is suited to logP values of about −2 to 4. At higher values, errors grow because the water-phase concentration is too low or tiny droplets are entrained, so methods such as comparing reversed-phase HPLC retention times with those of known substances are used. Prediction from structure is also widely practiced, and methods that add up substituent contributions (Hansch π values) or fragment contributions are used for estimates before a compound is synthesized.

about.h: Use in pharmaceuticals and the environment
about.p: In medicinal chemistry, logP is a guide to absorption, membrane permeation, protein binding and susceptibility to metabolism. Lipinski's rule of five holds that oral absorption tends to be poor when logP exceeds 5, and excessive lipophilicity tends to lower solubility and increase binding to off-targets. In environmental science, chemicals with larger logKow tend to concentrate more in the fat of organisms, so logKow is used for preliminary judgments of bioaccumulation potential. In both fields it is only a guide, and actual behavior is evaluated together with other properties.

faq.q: What is the difference between logP and logD?
faq.a: LogP is the partition ratio between neutral forms and does not depend on pH. LogD is the overall partition ratio at a given pH including ionized forms, and for acids and bases it changes greatly with pH. For non-ionizable compounds the two are equal.

faq.q: Why is 1-octanol used?
faq.a: Because it has a hydrocarbon chain and an OH group and contains some water, it was thought to resemble environments such as biological membranes where polar and nonpolar regions mix. A large body of accumulated data, which makes comparison easy, is another reason.

faq.q: What kinds of compounds have negative logP values?
faq.a: Highly polar compounds that partition into water more than into octanol. Examples include sugars, amino acids, and small molecules with many hydroxy or amino groups.

分布係数.desc: The ratio D of the concentrations of the whole compound, including the ionized form, in the octanol and aqueous phases. Its common logarithm, logD, depends on pH; for a weak acid it becomes smaller as the pH rises.

about.h: Lipophilicity reported at a stated pH
about.p: The distribution coefficient D is the ratio (octanol phase/aqueous phase) of the total concentrations of a compound, neutral and ionized forms together, when it is partitioned between octanol and water; it is usually expressed as its common logarithm, logD. Whereas logP, the ratio for the neutral form alone, is a single value for each compound, logD changes with the pH of the aqueous phase, so the pH is given with it, as in “logD7.4”. In pharmaceutical work the value at pH 7.4, close to the pH of blood, is the usual standard. For a compound that carries no charge, logD equals logP at every pH.

If the ionized form is assumed not to enter octanol, a weak base gives logD = logP − log(1 + 10^(pKa − pH)), where pKa is that of the conjugate acid. For an amine with logP 3.0 and pKa 9.5 at pH 7.4, 10^2.1 ≈ 126, so logD ≈ 3.0 − 2.1 = 0.9. Once past the pKa, each unit the pH moves in the direction of greater ionization lowers logD by about 1. Plotted against pH, logD is flat on the low-pH side for a weak acid and on the high-pH side for a weak base, and on the opposite side it falls along a line of slope about 1.

about.h: When the calculation does not hold
about.p: In reality the ionized form also passes into octanol to a small extent, paired with a counterion (ion-pair partitioning). So at pH values where ionization is extensive, logD does not keep falling as calculated but levels off at some value. This is also why the result depends on the kind of buffer and the salt concentration. For zwitterion-type compounds with both a carboxy group and an amino group, logD is usually largest near the isoelectric point, where the net charge is close to 0, but the shape of the profile depends on the proportions of the neutral and zwitterionic forms.

about.h: Measurement and use in drug design
about.p: The basic measurement is the shake-flask method: octanol and buffer saturated with each other are shaken together and the concentration in each phase is analyzed. When many compounds are compared, estimates from retention in reversed-phase HPLC are also used. The pH of the digestive tract ranges from acidic in the stomach to near neutral in the small intestine, so for oral drugs logD is examined at several pH values. If logD is too high, the compound dissolves poorly in water and is readily metabolized; if too low, it crosses membranes poorly, so a range of about 1–3 is sometimes taken as a guideline for a good balance.

faq.q: Are the distribution ratio and the distribution coefficient the same thing?
faq.a: They share the same idea: both express the ratio of the total concentrations of all forms of a substance. In analytical solvent extraction it is called the distribution ratio D for any pair of solvents; in pharmaceutical science it is usually called the distribution coefficient for the octanol/water pair.

faq.q: Why is logD often given at pH 7.4?
faq.a: Because blood and many tissue fluids have a pH of about 7.4, and lipophilicity under that condition is what matters for distribution in the body and membrane permeation. For oral absorption, values near pH 6.5, close to that of the small intestine, are also used.

faq.q: Can logD be negative?
faq.a: Yes. It is negative when the total concentration in the aqueous phase is larger; logD = −1 means the aqueous phase holds 10 times the concentration in the octanol phase. This is common for ionized acids and bases and for compounds with many hydroxy groups.

プロドラッグ.desc: A compound designed to have little activity itself and to be converted into the active form in the body by enzymes or chemical reactions. It is used to improve absorption, water solubility or delivery to the site of action.

about.h: Designed to become the active form in the body
about.p: A prodrug is a compound with little activity of its own, designed to be converted to the active form in the body by enzymes or chemical reactions. Problems with the active form itself, such as poor absorption, low water solubility, failure to reach the target site, or strong bitterness or irritation, are solved by temporarily changing its structure. Many prodrugs convert a carboxy or hydroxy group of the active drug into an ester or phosphate ester cleaved by esterases and similar enzymes. How readily the bond is cleaved to restore the active form is the key to the design.

The ACE inhibitor enalapril and the influenza drug oseltamivir are ethyl esters of carboxylic acids that are absorbed better and are hydrolyzed, in the liver and elsewhere, to the active forms. Levodopa, used for Parkinson's disease, crosses the blood–brain barrier, which dopamine itself cannot cross, via an amino acid transporter and is decarboxylated to dopamine in the brain. Fosphenytoin, given by injection, is a phosphate ester of poorly water-soluble phenytoin with improved water solubility.

about.h: Individual variation in activation, and a related idea
about.p: For prodrugs that need a specific metabolic enzyme for activation, genetic differences in that enzyme affect efficacy. The antiplatelet drug clopidogrel is converted to its active form by CYP2C19, and it is known to be less effective in people with low activity of this enzyme, so the genotype is sometimes checked before treatment. A prodrug is designed so that the active form is generated in the body. By contrast, a drug that acts while active and is then degraded predictably to an inactive form is called a soft drug, and the two are distinguished.

When evaluating a prodrug, compare doses in terms of the amount in moles of active drug it can produce, not the amount of prodrug given. Because the molar masses differ, equal milligram doses do not give equal amounts of active drug. Even if the prodrug is absorbed, it has no effect unless it is converted to the active form, so blood concentrations of the active form are measured to confirm both absorption and conversion. Historically, the discovery in the 1930s that the antibacterial Prontosil is reduced in the body to sulfanilamide was a forerunner of the prodrug concept.

faq.q: What are the main purposes of making a prodrug?
faq.a: Improving oral absorption, increasing water solubility, selective delivery to the site of action, prolonging the duration of action, and reducing taste or irritation. In every case the aim is to change how the drug is carried without changing the active structure.

faq.q: What converts a prodrug to its active form?
faq.a: Most are converted by hydrolytic enzymes such as esterases and phosphatases or by oxidative enzymes such as cytochrome P450. Some are designed to break down chemically at the pH of the body without enzymes.

faq.q: Is every drug that becomes active after metabolism a prodrug?
faq.a: Strictly, the term refers to compounds deliberately designed that way. However, drugs whose metabolite turns out to do most of the work, such as codeine being converted to morphine, are sometimes called prodrugs in a broader sense.

生物学的等価体.desc: An atom or group similar in size, shape, charge distribution and so on, so that biological activity is kept after replacement. Examples are tetrazole for a carboxy group and fluorine for hydrogen.

about.h: Parts that keep activity when swapped
about.p: Bioisosteres are atoms or groups similar in size, shape, charge distribution, acidity and so on, which can be swapped while keeping the interaction with the target. The concept grew out of isosterism, the idea that molecules or ions with the same number and arrangement of electrons show similar properties, proposed in the early 20th century and later extended to biological activity. Bioisosteres are sometimes divided into classical ones, with the same valence or number of atoms, and nonclassical ones, which differ in form but play a similar role.

A well-known example is the 1H-tetrazol-5-yl group in place of a carboxy group. Its pKa of about 4.5–4.9 is close to that of carboxylic acids, it is an anion at physiological pH, and the negative charge is spread over the ring. Fluorine in place of hydrogen is similar in size while making the site resistant to metabolism through the C−F bond. Other replacements used to improve properties include swapping readily hydrolyzed esters or amides for heterocycles and replacing a benzene ring with a saturated framework such as bicyclo[1.1.1]pentane.

about.h: What changes and what is kept
about.p: Bioisosteric replacement is done to change other properties while keeping the features needed for binding to the target. The aims include metabolic stability, membrane permeability, water solubility, reduced toxicity, chemical stability, and even circumventing patent claims. Whether a replacement is equivalent, however, depends not only on the group swapped but also on the target and its position in the molecule. It is not unusual for a replacement that worked in one compound to greatly reduce activity in another. Bioisosteres are clues for generating candidates, and their effects must be confirmed experimentally.

One replacement that hardly changes shape is swapping hydrogen for deuterium. A C−D bond is harder to break than a C−H bond, so if abstraction of that hydrogen is the rate-determining step of metabolism, the kinetic isotope effect can slow metabolism and prolong action. Deuterated drugs have actually been approved. However, there are cases where the metabolic pathway simply shifts to another position and no benefit results, so it is necessary to find out experimentally which step is rate-determining before using this approach.

faq.q: What is the difference between classical and nonclassical bioisosteres?
faq.a: Classical bioisosteres are replacements between atoms or groups with the same valence or number of atoms. Nonclassical ones differ greatly in structure but resemble each other in function, such as acidity or charge distribution; tetrazole and the carboxy group are a representative example.

faq.q: Why is fluorine used so often?
faq.a: It is close to hydrogen in size and changes shape little, the strong C−F bond resists metabolism, and its high electronegativity can tune the pKa and electron density of nearby groups.

faq.q: Does replacing a group with a bioisostere always preserve activity?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Equivalence is determined by how the compound interacts with the target, so successes in other compounds are only clues for candidates, and activity must be confirmed by testing.

ユートマー.desc: Of the enantiomers of a chiral drug, the one with higher desired activity. The less active one is called the distomer, and the ratio of their activities the eudismic ratio.

about.h: The terms and the eudismic ratio
about.p: Eutomer and distomer are terms popularized by Ariëns in the 1980s for the enantiomers of a chiral drug with the higher and lower desired activity. The ratio of their activities (binding strength or potency) is called the eudismic ratio, and its common logarithm the eudismic index. In 1956 Pfeiffer pointed out that the more potent a drug, the greater the tendency for its enantiomers to differ in potency (Pfeiffer's rule). It is thought that the better a molecule fits its binding site, the more the difference from its mirror-image shape matters.

about.h: Potency differences and changes in the body
about.p: For the β-blocker propranolol, the (S) isomer is said to block β receptors about 100 times more strongly than the (R) isomer. On the other hand, for the analgesic ibuprofen the (S) isomer is the active one, but part of the (R) isomer is converted one-way to the (S) isomer in the body, so taking the racemate does not waste the (R) isomer. Conversely, for compounds that racemize easily in the body, giving only the eutomer still produces both. Whether a compound is the eutomer is judged not only from in vitro activity but also including what happens to it in the body.

about.h: The “better” one is defined per activity
about.p: The eutomer is the stronger one for a given activity, so if there are several actions, a different enantiomer can be the eutomer. Dextrorphan, the enantiomer of the opioid analgesic levorphanol (the (−) isomer), has almost no analgesic action but acts as the active metabolite of the cough suppressant dextromethorphan. The distomer may not simply be ineffective; it can cause side effects or compete in metabolism, and Ariëns called such unwanted isomers “isomeric ballast.”

In 1992 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued a policy on the development of stereoisomeric drugs, requiring the pharmacology and pharmacokinetics of each enantiomer to be examined even when a racemate is developed. Since then there have also been chiral switches, in which a single enantiomer is taken from a drug already used as a racemate and redeveloped. In development, enantiomeric purity is controlled by chiral HPLC, and it is also confirmed that no racemization occurs during manufacture or storage. Where needed, the toxicity of the distomer is also examined separately.

faq.q: How is the eudismic ratio determined?
faq.a: Measure the activity of the two enantiomers under the same conditions and divide the activity of the eutomer by that of the distomer. For binding strength, take the ratio so that the stronger one is in the numerator, for example dividing the distomer's Ki by the eutomer's Ki.

faq.q: Is the distomer harmless?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Besides being weaker in the desired action, it may act on other receptors and cause side effects, or interfere with the metabolism or binding of the eutomer. Both are therefore evaluated separately.

faq.q: Why are some drugs still used as racemates?
faq.a: In some cases there is little advantage in using a single enantiomer, for example because it racemizes quickly in the body, the eudismic ratio is small, or both enantiomers contribute to therapy. If safety and efficacy have been established, the racemate is used.

グリーンケミストリー.desc: The idea of designing chemical products and processes so that hazardous substances and waste are not generated in the first place, rather than treated afterwards. It is summarized in the 12 principles of Anastas and Warner.

about.p: Green chemistry is the idea of designing chemical products and their manufacturing processes so that as little hazardous material and waste as possible is generated. In 1998 Anastas and Warner summarized it in 12 principles, including waste prevention, syntheses with high atom economy, use of less hazardous substances and solvents, energy efficiency, renewable feedstocks, catalysts in preference to stoichiometric reagents, design of products that degrade readily, and accident prevention. All the principles share the idea of not causing problems in the first place rather than dealing with them later.

Comparing processes against the principles needs numerical metrics. Atom economy, calculated from the reaction equation, shows the fraction of atoms that end up in the desired product but does not include the yield or solvents. The E-factor, the mass of waste per kg of product, and the process mass intensity (PMI), the mass of all materials put in divided by the mass of product, are therefore used. In pharmaceutical processes solvents and water often make up most of the input, so reducing and recovering solvents is the most effective improvement.

The 12 principles also include choosing less hazardous substances and conditions to prevent accidents such as explosions, fires and releases of harmful materials. In process chemistry, the heat of reaction is measured to estimate the temperature rise if cooling fails, and if necessary heat release is controlled by adding a reagent gradually, or continuous flow synthesis, which keeps little hazardous material in the reactor, is chosen. Reducing solvent, for example, lowers both the waste and the risk of fire. Reducing waste and preventing accidents are not separate efforts; it is important to consider both at the same design stage.

faq.q: How does green chemistry differ from environmental chemistry?
faq.a: Environmental chemistry studies the distribution, reactions and effects of substances in the environment. Green chemistry is the idea of designing products and processes that do not generate hazardous substances or waste in the first place, and it is something chemists work on at the synthesis and manufacturing stage.

faq.q: Is a reaction green if its atom economy is high?
faq.a: Atom economy is found from the reaction equation alone and does not include the yield, solvents, excess reagents or waste from purification. It needs to be assessed together with the E-factor, PMI, safety and energy use.

faq.q: Why does using a catalyst reduce waste?
faq.a: A stoichiometric reagent produces the same amount of by-product every time the reaction runs, whereas a catalyst is regenerated and works repeatedly, so only a small amount is needed. Raising selectivity and suppressing side reactions is another advantage.

E-ファクター.desc: The mass of waste (kg) generated per kg of product. A metric proposed by Sheldon; the smaller the value, the less waste. It is often calculated excluding water.

about.p: The E-factor is a metric proposed by Sheldon in 1992, expressed as E = mass of waste ÷ mass of product. Waste includes raw materials and reagents that did not become product, by-products, solvent not recovered and materials used in workup; solvent recovered and reused is not counted. The original definition excludes water, because including it makes the values so large that they are hard to compare, but values including water are sometimes reported alongside, so it is necessary to check which basis is used before comparing. The ideal value is 0.

Sheldon gave typical values by industry sector: below 0.1 for oil refining, from below 1 to about 5 for bulk chemicals, 5 to over 50 for fine chemicals and 25 to over 100 for pharmaceuticals. Pharmaceuticals have complex structures that need multistep syntheses and must reach high purity, so the waste per unit of product is large. On the other hand, bulk chemicals are produced in quantities orders of magnitude larger, so the ranking changes when total waste is compared. The E-factor is strictly a ratio expressing efficiency per unit of product.

about.h: Relation to PMI and atom economy
about.p: The process mass intensity, PMI, is the mass of all materials put in divided by the mass of product; counted on the same basis, E = PMI − 1. Because PMI is counted from the input side, it is easy to find without having to decide what counts as waste, and it is widely used in the pharmaceutical industry. Atom economy is a theoretical value calculated from the reaction equation, while the E-factor is the result of an actual process. Even a reaction with 100% atom economy can have a large E-factor because of waste from solvents and purification.

faq.q: Is water counted as waste?
faq.a: Not in Sheldon's original definition. Wastewater treatment also carries a burden, however, so values including water are sometimes reported alongside. When comparing, use the same basis.

faq.q: Can the E-factor be smaller than 1?
faq.a: Yes. In processes such as oil refining, with almost no by-products or solvent losses, it can be below 0.1. The ideal value is 0, with no waste at all.

faq.q: Is the toxicity of the waste taken into account?
faq.a: The E-factor counts mass only, so differences in toxicity are not reflected. Because it counts 1 kg of a heavy-metal salt the same as 1 kg of common salt, metrics weighted by toxicity or environmental impact have also been proposed.

プロセス質量強度.desc: The total mass of reactants, reagents, solvents and water put into a process divided by the mass of product. Widely used in the pharmaceutical industry; it is related to the E-factor on the same basis by PMI = E + 1.

about.p: Process mass intensity (PMI) is the total mass (kg) of material put into a process to make 1 kg of product. Besides reactants, reagents, catalysts and solvents, it includes water for workup, washing solvents, silica gel for purification and so on. The ACS Green Chemistry Institute Pharmaceutical Roundtable adopted it in the late 2000s as the main metric for comparing the environmental burden of processes, and it came into wide use in the pharmaceutical industry. In the ideal case, where all inputs become product, PMI = 1.

For multistep processes, the inputs of each step are converted to a basis of 1 kg of final product and added up. Here, counting an intermediate made in an earlier step as an input of a later step would count it twice. For example, if the PMI of step 2 is 30, of which 1.2 kg is the intermediate from step 1, and the PMI of step 1 is 20, the overall value is (30 − 1.2) + 20 × 1.2 = 52.8. In convergent syntheses, the branches are weighted in the same way according to how much of each intermediate is used, and added.

about.h: What PMI alone does not show
about.p: Because PMI counts only mass, it does not reflect the toxicity or flammability of solvents, the energy used in reactions, or the burden of producing the raw materials. A process using a little of a highly toxic solvent can have a smaller PMI than one using a lot of a harmless solvent. When solvents are recovered and reused, the value depends on how the recovered amount is counted, so make the counting consistent when comparing. Judgment is therefore made in combination with solvent selection guides, safety assessments and life cycle assessment, and PMI is best used as a yardstick of progress in improvement.

Breaking PMI down by step or by type of input shows where there is room for improvement. In many pharmaceutical processes, solvents and water make up most of the input, and extraction, crystallization and washing often account for a larger share than the reaction itself. When choosing a synthetic route, the effect of changes such as cutting steps, making the route convergent or switching to catalytic reactions is compared using predicted PMI. Peptides made by solid-phase synthesis have also been reported to have PMI values orders of magnitude larger than small-molecule drugs.

faq.q: Should I use PMI or the E-factor?
faq.a: Counted on the same basis, E = PMI − 1, and they convey the same information. Inputs are easy to collect from records and need no judgment about what is waste, so PMI is often used for pharmaceutical processes. State the basis when reporting.

faq.q: How is the PMI of a multistep process calculated?
faq.a: Convert the inputs of each step to a basis of 1 kg of final product and add them up. An intermediate from an earlier step is not counted as an input of the later step; instead the inputs used to make that intermediate are counted.

faq.q: What is the ideal value of PMI?
faq.a: 1. It corresponds to the case in which all the material put in becomes product and no solvents or workup materials are used. Actual pharmaceutical processes have much larger values.

溶媒選択ガイド.desc: A list that assesses solvents by toxicity, flammability, environmental impact, ease of recovery and so on, and sorts them into classes such as recommended, problematic and to be avoided. Pharmaceutical companies and others produce them.

about.h: Why guidance on choosing solvents is needed
about.p: In manufacturing processes for pharmaceuticals and the like, the solvents used for reaction, extraction, crystallization and washing often account for most of the mass of material put in, so the choice of solvent strongly affects the amount of waste, the health of workers and the risk of fire. Pharmaceutical companies and industry groups have therefore produced lists that assess common solvents against shared criteria. The guides compiled by the ACS Green Chemistry Institute Pharmaceutical Roundtable (ACS GCI PR) and by the European collaborative project CHEM21 are widely consulted.

about.h: How solvents are assessed and classified
about.p: Most guides score solvents for safety (flash point, electrostatic charging, tendency to form peroxides and so on), health (GHS hazard categories, exposure limits) and environment (effects on water and air, boiling point and ease of recovery), and combine these to classify them. The CHEM21 guide uses four classes: recommended, problematic, hazardous and highly hazardous. The classification is pulled strongly toward the worst item, so a solvent with a problem on just one point does not reach the top class either. The score for each item is also shown, so you can check on which point a solvent was marked down.

Diethyl ether has a low flash point of about −45℃ and readily forms peroxides, so replacing it with tert-butyl methyl ether (MTBE) or 2-methyltetrahydrofuran is recommended. For dichloromethane, substitutes to consider are ethyl acetate or 2-methyltetrahydrofuran for extraction, and mixtures such as ethyl acetate and heptane for chromatography. Polar aprotic solvents such as DMF, NMP and DMAc raise concern over reproductive toxicity and are subject to regulation in Europe, and the search for alternatives continues.

“Recommended” does not mean harmless; it means fewer problems than the others compared. Some solvents are rated differently by different guides, and even the same solvent may or may not be suitable depending on what it is used for and whether it is recovered. A substitution can also change reaction rates, solubility, ease of separation from water and the crystal form obtained in crystallization, so it has to be checked by experiment. It is worth remembering that reducing the number of different solvents used across a whole process makes recovery and reuse easier and also cuts waste.

faq.q: Why do different guides rate the same solvent differently?
faq.a: Because they weight the criteria differently, score them differently, and reflect the regulations and toxicity information available when they were drawn up. It is important to look at the items behind a rating and check which points matter for your own use.

faq.q: Is water the greenest solvent?
faq.a: It is safe and cheap, but not always the best. Wastewater contaminated with organic matter needs treatment, and water's large heat of vaporization means removing it takes energy. Comparisons should include mixing with organic solvents and the workup.

faq.q: Is there any point in using a guide at small laboratory scale?
faq.a: Yes. Processes often inherit laboratory conditions, and choosing a less problematic solvent from the start reduces the effort of substitution and revalidation at scale-up. It also protects the health of the people doing the work.

超臨界二酸化炭素.desc: Carbon dioxide above its critical point (about 31℃, about 7.4 MPa). Its dissolving power can be tuned by changing its density and it is removed by depressurization, so it is used as a solvent for extraction and reactions.

about.p: Above the temperature and pressure of its critical point, a substance no longer shows a distinction between gas and liquid and becomes a supercritical fluid. The critical point of carbon dioxide is about 31℃ and about 7.4 MPa, and the density at the critical point is about 0.47 g/cm³. The triple point of carbon dioxide is about −56.6℃ and about 0.52 MPa, so at atmospheric pressure it does not become liquid, and dry ice sublimes directly at −78.5℃. In the supercritical state it combines a liquid-like density with a gas-like low viscosity and fast diffusion, so it quickly penetrates fine pores in a sample.

Near the critical point, a small change in pressure changes the density greatly. At 40℃ the density is about 0.28 g/cm³ at 8 MPa, about 0.63 g/cm³ at 10 MPa and about 0.84 g/cm³ at 20 MPa. Dissolving power generally rises with density, so components can be dissolved out one after another by raising the pressure in steps, and after extraction only the solute can be precipitated by depressurizing. That the properties of the solvent can be adjusted continuously in the same apparatus just by changing temperature and pressure is a feature ordinary liquid solvents lack.

Supercritical carbon dioxide behaves like a nonpolar solvent and dissolves hardly any highly polar substances such as salts and sugars. In contact with water it forms carbonic acid, and at high pressure the pH of the aqueous phase falls to around 3, so acid-sensitive substances and corrosion of equipment need attention. It also reacts with primary and secondary amines to form carbamic acids, so it is unsuitable as a reaction solvent for such substrates. It is nonflammable and of low toxicity, but it needs high-pressure equipment, and a leak into an enclosed space carries a risk of oxygen deficiency or carbon dioxide poisoning.

about.h: Use in extraction, chromatography and reactions
about.p: In food it is used to extract hop extracts, flavors and components of natural products, with the advantage that no solvent remains. In analysis and preparative work, supercritical fluid chromatography (SFC), whose mobile phase is supercritical carbon dioxide with a small amount of alcohol, is widely used to separate the enantiomers of chiral drugs and greatly reduces the use of organic solvents compared with HPLC. Because it mixes well with hydrogen and oxygen, it also serves as a solvent for reactions such as hydrogenation, and it is used for foaming polymers and for cleaning and drying precision parts.

faq.q: Is a supercritical fluid a gas or a liquid?
faq.a: Neither. Its density can be raised close to that of a liquid, but its viscosity is gas-like and it has no surface tension. When the pressure is changed, the density changes continuously without any gas–liquid boundary appearing.

faq.q: Why is carbon dioxide so often used as the solvent?
faq.a: Its critical temperature, about 31℃, is close to room temperature, making heat-sensitive substances easy to handle; it is nonflammable, of low toxicity and available cheaply at high purity. On depressurizing it returns to a gas, so no solvent remains in the product.

faq.q: What are the advantages of supercritical fluid chromatography?
faq.a: The low viscosity of the mobile phase keeps the pressure from rising much at high flow rates, so separations are fast. Because most of the mobile phase is carbon dioxide, solvent removal after preparative separation is quick and there is little organic solvent waste.

断熱温度上昇.desc: The temperature increase if all the heat of reaction goes into heating the reaction mixture. It is used to estimate MTSR, the maximum temperature that can be reached if cooling fails.

about.h: A worst-case estimate for loss of cooling
about.p: The adiabatic temperature rise ΔTad is the temperature increase if none of the heat of reaction escapes and all of it goes into heating the reaction mixture; it is found as ΔTad = Qr/cp, where Qr is the heat of reaction per kg of mixture and cp is the specific heat capacity. It is the starting point of process safety assessment, estimating the worst that can happen if the reactor cooling fails or stirring stops. Because a 10 K rise in temperature often makes a reaction about 2–3 times faster, there is a danger of a runaway reaction in which heat release drives further heat release.

ΔTad is determined not only by the size of the heat of reaction but also by the concentration of the reactants and the heat capacity of the mixture. For example, if the heat of reaction is 300 kJ per kg of mixture and the specific heat capacity is 2.0 kJ/(kg·K), ΔTad is 150 K. Diluting the same reaction twofold with solvent halves Qr and roughly halves ΔTad. Systems containing a lot of water, with its large heat capacity, heat up less. Dilution, however, lowers reactor efficiency and increases the amount of solvent, so the concentration is chosen by balancing safety against efficiency.

about.h: Separating the desired reaction from decomposition
about.p: In assessing severity, what matters is whether the temperature rise from the desired reaction sets off secondary reactions such as decomposition of the product or reaction mixture. The maximum temperature attainable if cooling fails, MTSR, is therefore compared with TD24, the temperature at which a runaway of the secondary reaction would occur within 24 hours, and with MTT, the technical limit of the equipment such as the boiling point of the solvent. Stoessel's criticality classes sort processes into levels by the order of these temperatures. The adiabatic temperature rise of a decomposition can be orders of magnitude larger than that of the desired reaction.

The heat of reaction, and how much unreacted reagent accumulates during the reaction, are found with a reaction calorimeter that measures heat flow while the reaction runs. The energy and onset temperature of decomposition are first screened by DSC on a few mg of sample and, if needed, examined in detail by adiabatic calorimetry. In small sample containers the container itself absorbs heat, so the measured temperature rise comes out lower than in reality. In the process, a semi-batch mode that adds the reagent gradually is used to reduce accumulation, and operation is set up so that dosing stops when cooling stops.

faq.q: What is the difference between the adiabatic temperature rise and MTSR?
faq.a: The adiabatic temperature rise is the temperature increase if the whole reaction proceeds adiabatically. MTSR is the maximum temperature obtained by adding to the operating temperature only the rise from reagent still unreacted when cooling stopped.

faq.q: How can the adiabatic temperature rise be made smaller?
faq.a: Reduce the heat of reaction per kg of mixture, for example by lowering the reactant concentration or using a solvent with a large heat capacity. To lower the temperature actually reached rather than the value itself, adding the reagent gradually to limit accumulation is effective.

faq.q: Why are measurements in small containers corrected?
faq.a: In an adiabatic calorimeter part of the heat released goes into warming the sample container, so the measured temperature rise is too small. A correction factor found from the ratio of the heat capacities of container and sample converts the result to a value closer to a real reactor.

連続フロー合成.desc: A method of running reactions while starting materials flow continuously through narrow tubes or channels. Heat is easy to remove and little hazardous material is in the reactor, so hazardous reactions are easier to run safely.

about.p: Continuous flow synthesis pumps solutions of starting materials into narrow tubes or channels, mixes and reacts them as they flow, and continuously collects product from the outlet. The reaction time is set by the residence time, the internal volume of the reactor divided by the flow rate, and can be adjusted through the flow rate or tube length. In batch operation, where starting materials are loaded together into a flask or vessel, time represents the progress of reaction; in flow, position along the tube plays that role, and the temperature or reagents can be changed at different points to link multistep reactions.

about.h: Easier control of heat and hazards
about.p: The smaller the tube's inner diameter, the larger the heat-transfer area per volume. For a circular tube, area/volume = 4/inner diameter, so a 1 mm tube has about 4000 m²/m³, orders of magnitude more than the few m²/m³ of a reactor of about 1 m³. This makes it easier to hold the temperature steady even for highly exothermic reactions such as nitrations, and because the amount of hazardous material in the reactor at any moment is small, the consequences of an accident are reduced. Unstable intermediates such as diazo compounds and azides can also be generated and used immediately in the next reaction.

In narrow channels diffusion distances are short, so mixing is fast. Even for extremely fast reactions, mixing and reaction times can be controlled precisely and kept short, and there are reports of handling unstable organolithium species without cooling to low temperatures. In photochemistry, by the Beer–Lambert law light is absorbed near the surface of the liquid, but in a thin channel light reaches the entire liquid. On the other hand, flow is unsuitable in some cases: reactions that produce solids tend to clog the tubes, and slow reactions require long residence times.
