In batch operation, enlarging the vessel makes the heat-transfer area small relative to volume, so scaling up without changing conditions is difficult. In flow, production can be increased by running longer under the same conditions or by adding identical channels in parallel. In pharmaceutical manufacturing, a guideline for continuous manufacturing (ICH Q13) has been established, and adoption is advancing as a way of manufacturing while monitoring quality continuously within the process. It is often combined with systems that follow composition by inline spectroscopy and adjust conditions automatically.

faq.q: How is residence time calculated?
faq.a: Divide the reactor's internal volume by the total flow rate after the streams merge. For example, flowing a total of 2.0 mL/min through a tube with an internal volume of 10 mL gives a residence time of 5 minutes, assuming the liquid volume does not change on mixing.

faq.q: Is flow synthesis always better than batch?
faq.a: No. It is strong for heat management, hazardous reactions, fast reactions and photochemistry, but batch is often better for reactions that produce solids, reactions that take a long time, and small-scale synthesis of many different products.

faq.q: How is production increased in flow synthesis?
faq.a: By running longer under the same conditions or by adding identical channels in parallel. Making the channels wider loses the advantages in heat transfer and mixing, so conditions must be re-examined.

超分子化学.desc: The chemistry of structures formed when molecules come together through noncovalent interactions such as hydrogen bonds and electrostatic interactions, and of their functions. Molecular recognition and self-assembly are its central themes.

about.p: Ordinary synthetic chemistry joins atoms with covalent bonds to make molecules, whereas supramolecular chemistry joins molecules through noncovalent interactions to make larger assemblies and their functions. Breaking a covalent bond usually takes several hundred kJ/mol, but interactions between molecules are weak and reversible, so assemblies come apart or reorganize depending on conditions. This reversibility underlies molecular recognition, in which molecules choose their partners, self-assembly, in which defined structures form spontaneously, and materials that respond to stimuli.

The interactions used in supramolecular chemistry vary greatly in strength. Textbook guideline values are 200–300 kJ/mol for ion–ion, 50–200 kJ/mol for ion–dipole, 5–50 kJ/mol for dipole–dipole, 0–50 kJ/mol for π-π interactions and less than 5 kJ/mol for van der Waals forces. Even if each is weak, binding becomes multiplicatively stronger when several interactions act at once (multivalent interactions). In water, the hydrophobic effect, which brings hydrophobic parts together, is also a major driving force.

about.h: Ways to achieve strong, selective binding
about.p: Binding strength is not set by the number of interactions alone. If a host is fixed in a shape suited to binding before it takes up the guest, little energy and freedom are lost in changing shape on binding, and association is strong. Cram called this preorganization. Whether host and guest match in size and shape (complementarity) also decides selectivity. The solvent competes as a partner too, so the same pair can bind with very different strength in different solvents.

about.h: Expansion to molecular machines and materials
about.p: Mechanically interlocked molecules, such as rotaxanes, in which an axle molecule is threaded through a ring molecule, and catenanes, in which rings are linked, have been developed into molecular shuttles, in which the ring moves along the axle, and molecular motors. The 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Sauvage, Stoddart and Feringa for research on molecular machines. Other subjects of research include self-healing polymers, linked by reversible bonds that rejoin after breaking, sensors that respond to particular ions or molecules, and capsules that carry drugs.

faq.q: What is the difference between a supramolecule and a polymer?
faq.a: A polymer is a single large molecule in which monomers are joined by covalent bonds. A supramolecule is a collection of several molecules held together by noncovalent interactions, and it comes apart or reorganizes reversibly when conditions change.

faq.q: What is host–guest chemistry?
faq.a: It is the chemistry of host molecules with a cavity or cleft that take up guest ions or molecules through noncovalent interactions, and it is a central field of supramolecular chemistry. Crown ethers, cyclodextrins, and calixarenes are examples of hosts.

faq.q: Who has received Nobel Prizes for supramolecular chemistry?
faq.a: Pedersen, Lehn and Cram received the prize in 1987 for work including crown ethers, and Sauvage, Stoddart and Feringa received it in 2016 for research on molecular machines.

水素結合.desc: An interaction in which a hydrogen bonded to a highly electronegative atom is attracted to a lone pair on another atom. Between neutral molecules it is a few to a few tens of kJ/mol, and it is directional.

about.p: A hydrogen bond is an attraction between a hydrogen bonded to a highly electronegative atom X, as in O−H, N−H or F−H, and a lone pair on another atom Y; it is written X−H···Y. Because X pulls electrons strongly, the hydrogen is polarized positive and binds to Y mainly through electrostatic attraction. Weakly polarized hydrogens such as C−H usually form only weak interactions. The accepting atom Y is likewise mostly O, N or F with a lone pair. Although a single hydrogen bond is weak, in large numbers, as in water or proteins, they greatly change the properties of the whole substance.

Hydrogen bonds between neutral molecules have energies of a few to a few tens of kJ/mol; for the gas-phase water dimer it is about 20 kJ/mol. That is more than an order of magnitude smaller than an O−H covalent bond (about 460 kJ/mol) and larger than dispersion forces, an intermediate strength. The closer X−H···Y is to a straight line, the stronger the bond, and bending weakens it, so hydrogen bonds are directional. In the O−H···O bonds of water and ice, the oxygen–oxygen distance is about 0.28 nm. Hydrogen bonds involving ions, such as F−H···F⁻, can exceed 150 kJ/mol.

about.h: Effects on boiling point and solubility
about.p: Water (boiling point 100 °C) boils far higher than hydrogen sulfide (about −60 °C), despite the latter's larger molar mass, because the molecules in liquid water are linked by hydrogen bonds. In ice each molecule forms four hydrogen bonds in an open network, so ice is less dense than water and floats on it. Carboxylic acids form dimers through two hydrogen bonds. Compounds that can form a hydrogen bond within the molecule (such as o-nitrophenol) form fewer intermolecular ones, so they boil lower than their isomers (p-nitrophenol) and distil more readily in steam distillation.

In the DNA double helix, adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds and guanine with cytosine through three. The α-helices and β-sheets of proteins are also held in shape by hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N−H groups. When a drug binds to its target, the arrangement of hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors matters too. In water, however, hydrogen bonds between solutes compete with hydrogen bonds to water, so they act less strongly than in organic solvents. In supramolecular chemistry, how many hydrogen bonds to use and in what arrangement are designed to create selective association.

faq.q: How strong is a hydrogen bond?
faq.a: Between neutral molecules it is a few to a few tens of kJ/mol, about 20 kJ/mol for the water dimer. It is much weaker than a covalent bond (hundreds of kJ/mol) and stronger than dispersion forces.

faq.q: Which atoms form hydrogen bonds?
faq.a: On the donor side, a hydrogen bonded to a highly electronegative atom such as O, N or F; on the acceptor side, an atom with a lone pair, such as O, N or F.

faq.q: What is an intramolecular hydrogen bond?
faq.a: A hydrogen bond between a donor and an acceptor site within the same molecule. It occurs in o-nitrophenol, for example, and because intermolecular hydrogen bonding decreases, the boiling point falls and solubility in water drops.

π-π相互作用.desc: The attraction between aromatic rings. It consists of dispersion forces and electrostatic interactions between quadrupoles, and the rings tend to adopt offset parallel-displaced or T-shaped arrangements.

about.p: The π-π interaction is the attraction that acts between aromatic rings, and it determines structure in many settings: the stacking of DNA bases, contacts between the aromatic side chains of proteins, the binding of drugs to their targets and the packing of molecules in organic crystals. Its strength depends on conditions, but for the benzene dimer in the gas phase it has been calculated at around 10 kJ/mol, so it is often weaker than a hydrogen bond. The distance between the planes of parallel stacked rings is about 0.34–0.38 nm, close to the 0.335 nm spacing between the layers of graphite.

about.h: What sets the orientation and strength
about.p: Most of the attraction comes from dispersion forces, but the orientation in which rings stack is decided mainly by electrostatic interactions. In 1990 Hunter and Sanders explained many arrangements with a model that treats an aromatic ring as negatively charged π electrons above and below the plane with a positively charged σ framework between them. Substituents on the ring change the charge distribution and so change the strength of the interaction and the preferred arrangement. The way rings stack can therefore be designed to some extent by choosing the electronic character of substituents.

The π-π interaction is not a bond formed by overlap of π orbitals; it is a combination of dispersion and electrostatic forces. The name “π-π stacking” also suggests rings piled directly on top of one another, but for rings like benzene a face-to-face arrangement is actually unfavorable, and offset or T-shaped arrangements are preferred. In water, the hydrophobic effect, in which aromatic rings gather away from water, also makes a large contribution. The cation–π interaction, in which a positive ion is attracted to the face of an aromatic ring, is treated as a different kind of interaction.

In organic semiconductors, how much neighboring molecules overlap in the crystal changes how easily charge flows. There are herringbone packings, as in pentacene, in which neighbors face each other at an angle, and stacked packings with faces parallel, and research aims to control the packing through molecular shape and substituents. In drugs, there are many examples in which binding is strengthened when an aromatic ring of the drug contacts the side chains of phenylalanine, tyrosine or tryptophan in the target protein, which gives a clue when considering the binding mode.

faq.q: How strong is the π-π interaction?
faq.a: It varies with ring size, substituents and solvent, but for the benzene dimer it is estimated at around 10 kJ/mol. It is weaker than a typical hydrogen bond, and larger aromatic rings bind more strongly because the contact area increases.

faq.q: How does it differ from the cation–π interaction?
faq.a: In the cation–π interaction a cation such as Na⁺ or an ammonium ion is electrostatically attracted to the electron-rich face of an aromatic ring. It is often stronger than the π-π interaction between neutral rings and is distinguished as a separate interaction.

faq.q: Are the layers of graphite held together by π-π interactions?
faq.a: Yes. Graphite consists of flat carbon layers stacked about 0.335 nm apart, held together mainly by dispersion forces. Because this binding is weak the layers slide easily, and peeling off a single sheet gives graphene.

クラウンエーテル.desc: A macrocyclic polyether with −CH2CH2O− as the repeating unit. The oxygens inside the ring selectively and strongly take up cations that fit the size of the cavity.

about.p: Crown ethers are macrocyclic polyethers with −CH2CH2O− as the repeating unit, discovered by Pedersen in 1967. They are named for their resemblance to a crown and are called by the total number of ring atoms and the number of oxygens, as in 18-crown-6. The lone pairs of the oxygens lining the inside of the ring coordinate to a cation, and because the outside is covered with ethylene groups, the complexes also dissolve readily in organic solvents. Compounds with fused benzene rings, such as dibenzo-18-crown-6, are also known.

A cation binds most strongly to the crown ether whose cavity matches its size. Typical cavity diameters are about 1.2–1.5 Å for 12-crown-4, about 1.7–2.2 Å for 15-crown-5 and about 2.6–3.2 Å for 18-crown-6, so 18-crown-6 fits K⁺, about 2.8 Å in diameter, well. The rings are flexible, however, and the strength of solvation also affects binding, so selectivity is not decided by size alone. With ions larger than the cavity, complexes in which two crown ether molecules sandwich the ion from above and below can also form.

Crown ethers take up the cations of salts and dissolve the salts in organic solvents in which they would not normally dissolve. Potassium permanganate, for example, dissolves in benzene in the presence of 18-crown-6 to give a purple solution. With the cation wrapped up, its association with the anion weakens, and since the anion is also poorly solvated, it behaves as a highly reactive "naked anion". Crown ethers are used in reactions that employ the fluoride ion of potassium fluoride as a nucleophile, and as phase-transfer catalysts.

faq.q: How do crown ethers differ from cryptands?
faq.a: A crown ether surrounds a cation with a flat single ring. A cryptand is cage-shaped, with two nitrogens joined by three chains, and wraps the cation in three dimensions, so it generally binds more strongly and selectively.

faq.q: How are crown ethers made?
faq.a: They are made by a Williamson-type ether synthesis in which an oligoethylene glycol and a compound with leaving groups at both ends are cyclized in the presence of a base. The template effect, in which the base's cation gathers the chain into a ring shape, raises the yield of cyclization.

faq.q: Are there precautions in handling them?
faq.a: Toxicity has been reported for some crown ethers, and they can be absorbed through the skin. Handle them with gloves and avoid inhaling them or getting them on the skin.

クリプタンド.desc: A cage-shaped ligand in which two nitrogens are joined by several polyether chains. It wraps a cation in three dimensions and binds it more strongly than a crown ether. The complex is called a cryptate.

about.h: A ligand with a three-dimensional cage
about.p: A cryptand is a bicyclic (cage-shaped) ligand in which two bridgehead nitrogens are linked by three polyether chains. Lehn and coworkers synthesized cryptands in 1969 and named the complexes in which a cation is enclosed in the cage cryptates. The name comes from the Greek for "hidden." In the representative [2.2.2]cryptand, two oxygens in each chain, six in all, and the two nitrogens point inward and surround K⁺ three-dimensionally. This work, along with that of Pedersen and Cram, was recognized by the 1987 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

The size of the cryptand cavity can be changed through the chain length. The numbers give the number of oxygens in each chain, and in order of increasing cavity size, among the alkali metal ions [2.1.1] binds Li⁺, [2.2.1] Na⁺ and [2.2.2] K⁺ most strongly. Ions too small for the cavity cannot get close enough to the donor atoms, and ions too large cannot enter. Because the cage shields the cation from the solvent and a shape suited to coordination exists before binding (preorganization), cryptands bind several orders of magnitude more strongly in the same solvent than crown ethers, which surround the cation with a flat ring.

about.h: How they differ from crown ethers
about.p: Crown ethers surround a cation with a nearly flat ring, leaving the cation open above and below, so complexes form and dissociate quickly. In a cryptand, entering or leaving the cage requires large motions of the chains, so complexation and dissociation are much slower. The strong binding arising from such bicyclic structures is sometimes called the macrobicyclic effect. On the other hand, cryptands take more steps to synthesize and are expensive, so for many purposes a crown ether is sufficient. Depending on whether the lone pairs of the bridgehead nitrogens point inward or outward, they adopt different conformations.

When a cryptand encloses the cation, the counteranion is freed from ion pairing with the cation and its reactivity rises greatly. This is used to promote nucleophilic reactions of anions such as fluoride and carbonate in organic solvents. Furthermore, when sodium is treated with [2.2.2]cryptand, Na⁺ fits into the cage and another sodium becomes the anion Na⁻, giving a salt called a sodide, reported by Dye and coworkers in 1974. This led to research on electrides, in which electrons themselves behave as anions.

faq.q: What do the numbers in [2.2.2] mean?
faq.a: They are the numbers of ether oxygens in each of the three chains linking the two nitrogens. In [2.2.2] all three chains have two oxygens; in [2.1.1] one chain has two and two have one. Smaller numbers mean a smaller cavity.

faq.q: Does [2.2.2]cryptand bind ions other than K⁺?
faq.a: Yes. Among monovalent ions K⁺, which fits the cavity, binds most strongly, but it also forms complexes with Na⁺ and Rb⁺. It binds doubly charged cations strongly as well; in water it binds Ba²⁺ more strongly than K⁺.

faq.q: What are cryptands used for?
faq.a: They are used to promote reactions by enclosing cations and raising anion reactivity, for selective uptake and separation of ions, and for synthesizing unusual salts such as sodides and electrides.

シクロデキストリン.desc: An oligosaccharide of glucose units linked in a ring by α-1,4 bonds. Those with 6, 7 and 8 units are called α, β and γ, and they include organic molecules in their hydrophobic cavities.

about.p: Cyclodextrins are oligosaccharides in which D-glucose units are joined in a ring by α-1,4 glycosidic bonds; they are made by the action of an enzyme (cyclodextrin glucanotransferase) on starch. Those with six glucose units are called α, seven β and eight γ. The molecule has the shape of a truncated cone (a bucket) open at both ends; primary OH groups line the narrow rim and secondary OH groups the wide rim, so the outside is hydrophilic. Inside the cavity, on the other hand, C−H groups and glycosidic oxygens point inward, creating a relatively hydrophobic environment.

The inner diameter of the cavity is about 0.47–0.53 nm for α, about 0.60–0.65 nm for β and about 0.75–0.83 nm for γ, with a depth of about 0.8 nm in each case. α can hold about one benzene ring, β naphthalene or adamantane, and γ larger molecules or two molecules. The solubility in water at 25 °C is about 14.5 g/100 mL for α and about 23.2 g/100 mL for γ, whereas β is low at about 1.85 g/100 mL. This is explained by a ring of hydrogen bonds between secondary OH groups that makes the β ring rigid.

about.h: Driving force and strength of inclusion
about.p: When a hydrophobic guest molecule enters the cavity in water, the water molecules that were inside are released and can form hydrogen bonds with the surrounding water, and van der Waals forces act between the guest and the cavity wall. These hydrophobic and dispersion effects are the main driving forces for inclusion. The association constants of 1 : 1 inclusion complexes are about 10²–10⁴ L/mol for many drugs and are larger the better the guest's size and shape fit the cavity. They are determined by the phase-solubility method, NMR titration or isothermal titration calorimetry.

Including a poorly water-soluble drug raises its apparent solubility and stability, so water-soluble derivatives such as hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin are used as formulation excipients. In food they are used to retain flavors and mask bitterness, and in household products for deodorizing. Sugammadex, a modified γ-cyclodextrin, is a drug that encapsulates the muscle relaxant rocuronium and reverses its effect. In analytical chemistry, the chiral cavity is used as a selector to separate enantiomers in capillary electrophoresis and GC. Inclusion can also keep volatile components stable as a powder.

faq.q: What is the difference between α-, β- and γ-cyclodextrin?
faq.a: The number of glucose units in the ring is six for α, seven for β and eight for γ. The more units, the larger the cavity, which changes the size of molecule it can hold. β has the lowest solubility in water.

faq.q: Why do cyclodextrins take up hydrophobic molecules?
faq.a: The inside of the cavity is relatively hydrophobic, so when a hydrophobic guest enters in water, the water in the cavity is released, which is stabilizing, and dispersion forces act between the guest and the wall.

faq.q: What are cyclodextrins used for in medicines?
faq.a: They are used as additives to raise the solubility and stability of poorly water-soluble drugs. Some, such as sugammadex, are drugs that act by encapsulating another drug themselves.

自己組織化.desc: The spontaneous gathering of molecules or metal ions into a defined structure through reversible interactions. The system settles into the thermodynamically stable structure while correcting errors.

about.h: Components gather into a shape by themselves
about.p: Self-assembly is the spontaneous gathering of molecules or metal ions into a defined structure through reversible interactions, without being put together piece by piece from outside. Hydrogen bonds, coordination bonds, π–π interactions and the hydrophobic effect are used. Living systems rely heavily on self-assembly, as in the DNA double helix, lipid bilayers and viral capsids. In supramolecular chemistry, building cages, grids and capsules by self-assembly, by designing the shapes of the components and the directions of their bonds, is one of the central themes.

When many components assemble, intermediates, oligomers and polymers with wrong connections also form. If the bonds can break and re-form to a suitable extent, these come apart and reassemble, settling into the thermodynamically most stable structure. If the bonds are too strong, the disordered aggregates formed first remain as they are. The product distribution also depends on concentration: dilute solutions favor closed cyclic structures and concentrated solutions favor chain polymers. The ratio of components, solvent and temperature also affect the outcome.

A square complex forms from 90° "corners" of palladium(II) and linear bridging ligands, and combining them with planar triangular ligands with three arms gives octahedral cages such as Pd6L4. The key point is that angle information determines the shape. Note that in English, self-assembly, in which a defined structure forms by settling to equilibrium, is sometimes distinguished from self-organization, in which patterns or rhythms are maintained while energy keeps flowing in and out. In Japanese both are frequently rendered by the same word, so it is necessary to check the meaning from context.

about.h: How it is confirmed and applied
about.p: Whether the system has converged to a single structure is checked by ¹H NMR showing one set of sharp signals consistent with the symmetry, DOSY, which gauges size from diffusion coefficients, composition by mass spectrometry, and single-crystal X-ray structure analysis. Applications include modifying surfaces with self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) of alkanethiols on gold, porous materials templated by surfactant micelles, and research using the cavities of cage complexes as reaction vessels. Efforts to use the microphase separation of block copolymers for fine patterning are also advancing.

faq.q: Does the solvent affect self-assembly?
faq.a: Strongly. In water the hydrophobic effect drives assembly, while assemblies held together by hydrogen bonds tend to fall apart in solvents that are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors. Solvent molecules can also enter the cavity and stabilize the structure.

faq.q: Why does a single structure form in high yield?
faq.a: Because the bonds are reversible, wrong aggregates are also reassembled and the system converges to the thermodynamically most stable structure. It is also important that the components are shaped so that only one structure closes without strain.

faq.q: Can self-assembly use covalent bonds?
faq.a: Yes, with dynamic covalent bonds that break and form depending on conditions, such as imines, disulfides and boronate esters. The resulting structures are often more robust than those built with coordination bonds.

会合定数.desc: The equilibrium constant K = [HG]/([H][G]) for the association H + G ⇌ HG of a host H and a guest G. A measure of binding strength, related by ΔG° = −RT ln K.

about.p: When a host H and a guest G associate 1:1, as in H + G ⇌ HG, the equilibrium constant K = [HG]/([H][G]) is called the association constant (also the binding constant or stability constant); with concentrations in mol/L its unit is L/mol. Its reciprocal 1/K is the dissociation constant Kd, which has the dimension of concentration. The larger K, the stronger the binding; at 25℃ every 10-fold increase in K makes the standard Gibbs energy ΔG° = −RT ln K about 5.7 kJ/mol more negative. Values vary greatly with solvent, temperature and salt concentration.

Association constants are determined by titration, adding the guest in small portions to a solution of the host and following a physical quantity that changes on association. Changes in ¹H NMR chemical shifts, UV-Vis absorbance, fluorescence intensity and so on are fitted to an equation derived from the association equilibrium to determine K. Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) measures the heat released or absorbed with each addition and gives K and the enthalpy of association ΔH° simultaneously. For an accurate determination, a common guideline is to choose concentrations so that the bound fraction covers roughly the range 20–80%.

Before the analysis, the stoichiometry of the complex, whether 1:1, 1:2 or otherwise, needs to be checked. Job plots, which vary the mole fractions at constant total concentration, have long been used, but it has been pointed out that they readily give wrong conclusions when several complexes coexist. Today it is recommended to fit titration data with several models and judge by comparing the size and pattern of the residuals. Also, using an approximate equation that assumes a large excess of guest at concentrations where that condition does not hold gives large errors.

faq.q: When is the association constant used, and when the dissociation constant?
faq.a: They express the same equilibrium in opposite directions: Kd = 1/K. Supramolecular chemistry usually uses the association constant K (L/mol), and biochemistry and pharmaceutical science the dissociation constant Kd (mol/L); when the free guest concentration equals Kd, half of the host is bound.

faq.q: Why can't very large association constants be measured?
faq.a: When K is large, almost all the added guest binds, and the titration curve becomes like two straight lines that hardly depend on K. In that case the concentrations are lowered, or a displacement titration that competes with another, more strongly binding guest is used.

faq.q: Why does the association constant change with the solvent?
faq.a: On association, the host and guest each lose their interactions with the solvent. In strongly solvating solvents such as water or solvents that are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, association competes with solvation, so even the same pair can have association constants that differ by orders of magnitude.
